Therefore almost all the schoolmen are idolaters. Fourth argument, taken from the actual practice of the Church of Rome. For although there are some who are ashamed of this doctrine, such as Gabriel Biel, Martinus Perusius, Ambrosius Catharinus, Bellarminus himself, and others, and so the Papists may seem free and clear of the crime of staurolatry, nevertheless, lest we seem to accuse them unjustly, I shall prove from the actual practice of the Church of Rome that it is manifestly guilty of staurolatry. I conclude the argument from fact thus. Those who invoke the cross, asking for those things which can be given by no creature but only by God alone, such as all that pertains to grace and glory, are bound by the crime of staurolatry; for prayer by which such things as pertain to grace and glory are asked is proper to latria and is owed to God alone, as Thomas acknowledges. But the Church of Rome invokes the cross, asking for things which can be given by God alone and which bear on either grace or glory; for they address and entreat the cross itself, as Thomas expressly admits. They ask for what pertains to grace when they cry out to the cross: O Cross, hail, our only hope, in this paschal season increase righteousness in the devout and pardon for the guilty. Also pertaining to grace are the things which Papistical preachers ask when they address the image of the crucified: You redeemed us, you reconciled us to the Father, as Bellarminus himself teaches, of whom more later. They ask for what pertains to glory in the antiphon: O Cross, more splendid than all the stars, renowned in the world, very lovable to men, holier than all things, who alone were worthy to bear the talent of the world, sweet wood bearing sweet burdens, save today the present throng gathered in your praises. Therefore the Church of Rome invokes the cross, asking that the things pertaining to grace and glory be given to it by the cross. Such invocation, however, is proper to latria and peculiar to God. Therefore the Papists commit staurolatry. To this should also be referred what I cited above from the second book of the Ceremonies, where it is said that everyone, from the supreme Pontiff down to the lowest acolyte, adores and kisses the cross. And although Gabriel Biel, Martinus Perefius, Ambrosius Catharinus, and others wish to appear more sensible, and reject and repudiate that doctrine as smacking of idolatry, it is nevertheless plain from what has been said that the Church of Rome embraces and maintains it; and this is enough for us, who strive to convict the Church of Rome of staurolatry

units.la: Tom. I. cont. 3. l. 2. c. 23. ac proinde & idololatriæ conuincere nitimur.
units.tr: Tom. I. cont. 3. l. 2. c. 23., and therefore of idolatry as well.

units.la: CAPVT IV.
units.tr: CAPUT IV.

units.la: In quo Bellarmini exceptionibus occurritur.
units.tr: In which Bellarmine's objections are met.

units.la: BELLARMINVS expresis verbis non audet negare latriam cruci deferendam esse, sed quod reipsa negat, animadvertere licebit illi, qui eius exceptiones rectè expenderit. Nam agnoscit quidem cruci latriam esse exhibendam, sed non proprie & per se, verùm improprie & per accidés, non vniuocè, sed analogicè, ita vt eos tantum idololatriæ reos esse existiment, qui propriam & vniuocam latriam cruci exhibent. Cum verò ab Ecclesia Romana non vniuoca & propria, sed analogica & impropria latria cruci præstetur, iniquè nos idololatriam Ecclesiæ Romanæ exprobrare contendit. Verum ordine disspiciamus & examinemus eius exceptiones.
units.tr: Bellarmine does not dare to deny in express words that latria is to be paid to the cross, but anyone who weighs his objections carefully will see that in fact he denies it. He grants that latria is to be shown to the cross, but not properly and per se; only improperly and per accidens, not univocally but analogically. So, in his view, only those who give the cross a proper and univocal latria are guilty of idolatry. Since the Roman Church pays the cross not a univocal and proper latria but an analogical and improper one, he argues that we unfairly charge the Roman Church with idolatry. But let us examine his objections in order.

units.la: Prima exceptio, veram quidem latriam exhiberi imaginibus & cruci Christi, sed impropriè & per accidens, id probat, quia imago aliquando accipitur pro ipso exemplari, & ea quæ fiunt circa ipsum exemplar si adesset præsens, fiunt circa imaginem, mente tamen defixa in exemplari. Sic concionatores alloquuntur imaginem crucifixi, eique dicunt, tu nos redemisti, tu nos Patri reconciliasti. Ista enim non dicuntur imagini, nec ut lignum est, nec ut imago est, sed ut accipitur loco exemplaris, id est dicuntur ipsi Christo, cuius tamen imago vicem gerit.
units.tr: His first objection is that true latria is indeed given to images and to the cross of Christ, but improperly and per accidens. He proves this because an image is sometimes taken for the prototype itself, and what is done to the prototype, if it were present, is done to the image, though the mind is fixed on the prototype. So preachers address the image of the crucified and say to it, "you redeemed us, you reconciled us to the Father." For these things are not said to the image, either as it is wood or as it is an image, but as it is taken in place of the prototype, that is, they are said to Christ himself, whose image stands in his place.

units.la: Respond. I. Negamus veram latriam debere impropriè & per accidens tribui imaginibus & cruci Christi. Nullo modo nec proprie & per se, nec improprie & per accidens tribuenda est. Deo soli in solidum debetur latria iuxta scripturam, Domino Deo tuo soli λατρεύσεις.
units.tr: Reply I. We deny that true latria should be given to images and to the cross of Christ improperly and per accidens. It is due to them in no way, neither properly and per se nor improperly and per accidens. According to Scripture, latria is owed wholly to God alone: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only [λατρεύσεις].

units.la: II. Si vera latria improprie & per accidens tribuitur cruci, & imaginibus, tum vera latria vere ac re ipsa non tribuitur; aut si vere & re ipsa tribuitur, sequitur cultum soli Deo debitum tribui imaginibus, ac proinde committi idololatriam; quia latria est cultus soli Deo debitus.
units.tr: II. If true latria is given improperly and per accidens to the cross and to images, then true latria is not truly and in fact given to them. Or if it is truly and in fact given, then it follows that the worship owed to God alone is given to images, and so idolatry is committed, because latria is the worship owed to God alone.

units.la: III. Ethnici etiam suam idololatri‒am tali distinctione excusarunt, dicentes, se simulacra Deorum suorum colere tantum per accidens & impropriè, numen ipsum proprie & per se; accusantur nihilominus idololatriæ. Sic Carpocratiani coluerunt imaginem Christi propter ipsum Christum, id est, improprie & per accidens: Christum vero proprie & per se, & tamen idololatriæ eam ob causam fuere damnati.
units.tr: III. The heathens also excused their idolatry by this same distinction, saying that they worshipped the statues of their gods only per accidens and improperly, and the deity itself properly and per se. Nevertheless they were accused of idolatry. So too the Carpocratians worshipped the image of Christ on account of Christ himself, that is, improperly and per accidens, but Christ properly and per se; and yet they were condemned as idolaters for this reason.

units.la: IV. Dicimus idololatriam commitci, si ea circa imaginem aut Christi crucem fiant, quæ fieri debent circa ipsum Christum. Exemplum concionatorum idololatricum est. Concionatores idololatræ sunt, qui sic alloquuntur imaginem crucifixi, tu nos redemisti, tu nos patri reconciliasti; sicut Israelitæ etiam idololatriæ accusantur, qui sic alloquebantur lignum, pater meus, & lapidem, tu peperisti me. Et qui tandem sunt illi vestri concionatores, qui imaginem crucifixi sic alloquuntur? Nū Augustinus, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, Basilius? Absit tam nefanda idololatria à tam piis pectoribus. Sunt vt intelligo, Franciscani & similes fraterculi. Atqui olim concionatores Israelis sacerdotes scilicet, & Prophetæ grauissimæ fuere reprehensi à Propheta Ieremia & seuerissimè à Deo puniti, quod lignum sic alloquerentur, pater meus es, & lapidem, tu peperisti me.
units.tr: IV. We say that idolatry is committed if things are done to an image or to the cross of Christ which ought to be done to Christ himself. The example of the preachers is idolatrous. Those preachers are idolaters who address the image of the crucified and say to it, "you redeemed us, you reconciled us to the Father." Likewise the Israelites were accused of idolatry who addressed wood with "you are my father," and stone with "you have begotten me." And who, then, are those preachers of yours who address the image of the crucified in this way? Is it Augustine, Jerome, Chrysostom, or Basil? Far be such unspeakable idolatry from such pious breasts. As I understand it, they are the Franciscans and similar little friars. Yet of old the preachers of Israel, namely priests and very serious prophets, were rebuked by the prophet Jeremiah and severely punished by God because they said to wood, "you are my father," and to stone, "you have begotten me."

units.la: Instat Bellarminus ab exemplo legati. Legatus Regis, ait, aliquando honoratur vt legatus, & tunc ipse proprie honoratur, licet propter alium honoretur: aliquando honoratur, loco Regis honore proprio Regibus, & tunc ipse improprie honoratur, proprie autem Rex tunc in ipso honoratur.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses the point by the example of an ambassador. A king's ambassador, he says, is sometimes honoured as an ambassador, and then he himself is properly honoured, although it is on account of another. Sometimes he is honoured in place of the king, with the honour proper to kings, and then he himself is improperly honoured, but the king is properly honoured in him.

units.la: Resp. I. Negatur eodem prorsus honore coli legatum Principis, quo ipse Princeps. Id euidenter videre licet in matrimoniis, quæ per legatos contrahuntur. Sponsæ alicuius Principis non licet idem obsequium præstare legato, quod Principi: aliud honoris & obsequii genus est, quod præstat legato, ab eo quod Principi suo exhibet. Idem agnoscit etiam ipse Bellarminus cap.24. cum ait, notum esse, qui honorat legatum seu famulum Regis ipsum Regem honorare, sed tamen longe aliter honorare. honorare ipsum Regem in propria persona, quam in famulo suo.
units.tr: Reply I. It is denied that a prince's ambassador is worshipped with exactly the same honour as the prince himself. This can clearly be seen in marriages arranged through ambassadors. A prince's bride may not render the same deference to the ambassador that she renders to the prince: the honour and deference paid to the ambassador is a different kind from that paid to her own prince. Bellarmine himself acknowledges this in chapter 24, when he says: It is known that whoever honours an ambassador or servant of a king honours the king himself, but honours him far differently: to honour the king in his own person is one thing, and to honour him in his servant is another.

units.la: Aperte hic docet, non eundem honorem exhiberi legatis & famulis regum ac Principum, qui ipsis regibus ac principibus defertur: sed aliter coli principem, aliter famulum.
units.tr: Here he plainly teaches that the same honour is not shown to the ambassadors and servants of kings and princes as is paid to the kings and princes themselves; the prince is worshipped in one way and the servant in another.

units.la: II. Etsi detur sic receptum esse inter reges & principes, ut honore eodem coli debeant legati eorum, quo principes; Deus tamen non vult legatis suis honorem sibi debitum deferri, & legati Dei etiam honorem divinum non admittunt. In legatis, qui a Christo missi, id est Apostolis ipse Christus representatus fuit, iuxta illud, qui vos recipit, me recipit, & tamen Apostoli noluerunt sibi eundem deferri honorem, qui Christo Principi debetur. Sic Paulus aversabatur eum, qui ipsi sacrificia volebat offerre. Sic Petrus cum ut legatus Dei adoraretur, id vetuit fieri. Angelus est legatus Dei, ut nomen ipsum declarat, & tamen eodem, quo Deus, honore coli noluit. Nam cum Iohannes procideret, ut adoraret, dixit ei; ne facito, sum tuus conservus, Deum adora.
units.tr: II. Even if it were granted that it is customary among kings and princes that their ambassadors should be honoured with the same honour as the princes, God does not want honour that is due to himself to be transferred to his ambassadors, and God's ambassadors do not accept divine honour. Among the ambassadors sent by Christ, that is, the Apostles, Christ himself was represented, according to the saying, He who receives you receives me; yet the Apostles did not want the same honour paid to themselves as is owed to Christ the Prince. So Paul shrank from the man who wanted to offer sacrifice to him. So Peter, when he was adored as God's ambassador, forbade it. An angel is God's ambassador, as the very name declares, and yet he did not want to be worshipped with the same honour as God. For when John fell down to worship him, he said to him: Do not do it; I am your fellow servant. Worship God.

units.la: Instat ab exemplo statuae, in qua Traianus triumphasse dicitur. Traianus mortuus nortuus, inquit, Romæ triumphauit, & sta-tua eius pro eo sedit in curru triumphali: nec nim potest dici statuam proprie triumphas-sed Traianum à statua repræsentatum.
units.tr: He presses with the example of the statue in which Trajan is said to have triumphed. "Trajan, when dead," he says, "triumphed at Rome, and his statue sat in the triumphal chariot in his place; for it cannot properly be said that the statue triumphed, but that Trajan was represented by the statue."

units.la: Respon. I. Ex hominum exemplis & moribus de Dei honore & cultu non est iudicandum. Videndum quid Deus lege sua præceperit, non quid hominum ferat consuetudo. Lege diuina præceptum est, non facies tibi sculptile, neque vllam similitudinem eorum, quæ sunt in cœlis. At Christus est in cœlis, Ergo imago Christi non est facienda.
units.tr: Reply I. Judgement about God's honour and worship is not to be made from the examples and customs of men. We must see what God has commanded in his law, not what human custom tolerates. The divine law commands: You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of those things which are in heaven. But Christ is in heaven. Therefore an image of Christ is not to be made.

units.la: II. Ipse Bellarminus cap. 4. diserte agnoscit, rationem esse dissimilem. Nam de cultu imaginum Christi agens, suam sententiam in hunc modum pronunciat. Quando, inquit, concipio & adoro imaginem ipsam vt Christi imaginem, ita vt Christus in obliquo ponatur non in recto, tunc adoratio fertur quidem in imaginem per se, & consequenter in Christum, sed non est adoratio vera latriæ, verum longè inferior. At Romani concipiebant & honorabant statuam illam vt Traiani in casu obliquo, sed honor qui in statuam per se ferebatur, idem Traiano consequeter debebatur, vt honor statuæ exhibitus non esset minor aut inferior. ferior eo, quo celebratur Traianus in statua repræsentatus. Nam quia in Traianum voluerunt honorem statuæ delatum ferri, non aliter statuam, aliter Traianum honorare voluerunt: sed & paulo post confirmat eandem sententiam Bellarminus, negans cultum illum, qui debetur Christo in imagine repræsentato, eundem esse, qui debetur Christo in se, cum ait, latriam convenire Christo, quando adoratur, ut est, in se, non autem, quando adoratur ut est in imagine per participationem.
units.tr: II. Bellarmine himself, in chapter 4, plainly acknowledges that the case is dissimilar. When he treats of the worship of images of Christ, he pronounces his opinion in this way: When I conceive of and adore the image itself as the image of Christ, so that Christ is placed in the oblique case and not the nominative, then the adoration is indeed directed to the image per se and consequently to Christ, but it is not the true adoration of latria; it is far inferior. But the Romans conceived of and honoured that statue as the statue of Trajan, in the oblique case; and the honour which was directed to the statue per se was consequently owed to Trajan, so that the honour paid to the statue was not less or inferior to that by which Trajan was honoured as represented in the statue. For since they wanted the honour paid to the statue to pass on to Trajan, they did not want to honour the statue in one way and Trajan in another. Shortly afterwards Bellarmine confirms the same opinion, denying that the worship owed to Christ as represented in an image is the same as that owed to Christ in himself, when he says: latria belongs to Christ when he is adored as he is in himself, but not when he is adored as he is in an image through participation.

units.la: II. Exceptio Imago non est per se & proprie adoranda eodem cultu, quo ipsum exemplar, ac proinde nulla imago adoranda est cultu latriæ proprie & per se. Resp. I. docuit supra proprie & per se colendas esse imagines Christi & sanctorum, nunc dicit nullam colendam cultu latriæ proprie & per se, sed improprie & per accidens. Itaque per accidens & improprie, & per se ac proprie erunt colendæ. At quomodo accidentalis & imprius latriæ cultus imaginibus debitus à vero & proprio erit distinguendus? aut si distinguatur, quando ille, quando hic erit exercendus? & qua scripturæ autoritate duplicem hunc
units.tr: II. The objection: An image is not to be adored per se and properly with the same worship as the prototype itself, and therefore no image is to be adored with the worship of latria properly and per se. Reply I. He taught above that the images of Christ and of the saints are to be worshipped properly and per se; now he says that none is to be worshipped with latria properly and per se, but improperly and per accidens. So they will be worshipped per accidens and improperly, and also per se and properly. But how will the accidental and improper latria owed to images be distinguished from the true and proper? Or if it is distinguished, when is the one and when the other to be exercised? And by what authority of Scripture will he prove this double worship of images?

units.la: iunc imaginum cultum probabit?, nos neque per se, & proprie, neq; per accidens & improprie latriam imaginibus deferendam assueramus; cum omne quicquid aliquo culturreligofo afficitur, non duplici, sed simplici & & vniformi cultu colatur. quit Bellarminus, quae exhibetur imagini propter aliud, est idem cultus cum eo, qui exhibetur Deo, aut alius minor si idem, ergo a-que colitur creatura, atq; ipse Deus; quae certe idololatria est: si est cultus minor, non ergo est latria: nam latria est summus cultus. Ex hac Bellarmini assertione, euinco, aut proprie latriadeberi imaginibus aut nullam. Latria, quae est minor cultus eo, qui exhibetur Deo, non est latria. At latria quae improprie & per accidens, tribuitur imaginibus, est minor cultus eo qui exhibetur Deo, Ergo cultus ille, qui improprie & per accidens tribuitur, non est latria. Vnde manifestū euadit, quod ante dixi, Bellarminum, licit verbo non ausit negare latriam cruci deferendam; reipsa tamen id facere.
units.tr: Now, how will he prove this twofold cult of images, since we hold that latria is to be given to images neither per se and properly, nor per accidens and improperly? For whatever is honoured with any religious worship is worshipped not with a double but with a single and uniform worship. Bellarmine says: What is offered to an image on account of something else is either the same worship as what is offered to God, or a lesser one. If it is the same, then the creature is worshipped equally with God himself, which is certainly idolatry. If it is a lesser worship, then it is not latria, for latria is the highest worship. From this assertion of Bellarmine I conclude that latria must be owed to images either properly or not at all. Latria, which is a lesser worship than what is offered to God, is not latria. But the latria that is ascribed to images improperly and per accidens is a lesser worship than what is offered to God. Therefore that worship which is ascribed improperly and per accidens is not latria. Hence it becomes plain what I said before: Bellarmine, though he does not dare to deny in words that latria is to be given to the cross, nevertheless does so in fact.

units.la: II. Latria, inquit, est summus cultus at cum per accidens & improprie defer-
units.tr: II. Latria, he says, is the highest worship; but when it is given per accidens and improperly...

units.la: 1. Latria, in Cap. 24 defertur cruci, non est amplius summus; quia latria propria est superior, Ergo non est latria, quæ cruci exhibetur.
units.tr: 1. Latria, which is given to the cross (Cap. 24), is no longer the highest kind of worship, because proper latria is the superior kind. Therefore what is offered to the cross is not latria.

units.la: III. De essentia veræ latriæ est exhiberi propter se, ait Bellarminus.
units.tr: III. The essence of true latria is to be offered for its own sake, says Bellarmine.

units.la: Latria non dicitur summus cultus, qui debetur vero Deo ut primo principio omnium rerum. Implicat autem contradictionem exhiberi summum cultum primo principio & propter aliud. Nam si primo principio, non ergo propter aliud; si propter aliud, non primo principio: Ergo veli-magini exhibetur cultus latriæ, per & propter se, & hæc est vera idololatria; vel non exhibetur per & propter se, & tunc ille non est cultus veræ latriæ. Rursum hic tenetur Bellarminus: nam si de essentia veræ latriæ est exhiberi per & propter se; Ergo non est vera latria, quando per accidens, & propter aliud ea cruci defertur. Aut igitur veram tribuunt cruci latriam, aut simpliciter nullam; cur igitur fingit accidentalem & impropriam latriam? Deinde cruci aut cultus latriæ exhibetur per & propter se, aut non; si per se & propter se, erit vera idololatria; si non, non est cultus veræ latriæ. Rursum ergo euincimus hic, Bellarmini distinctionem, omnem veræ laræ latriæ cultum adimere cruci, quia cultus latriæ per accidens & impro- prie cruci delatus non est vera la- tria, ac proinde nulla; siquidem latria nulla nisi vera est, eaque vna & sim- plex.
units.tr: Latria is not called the highest worship which is due to the true God as the first principle of all things. Moreover, it involves a contradiction to offer the highest worship both to the first principle and on account of something else. For if it is offered to the first principle, then not on account of something else; if on account of something else, then not to the first principle. Therefore either latria is offered to the image, through and on account of itself, and this is true idolatry; or it is not offered through and on account of itself, and then it is not the worship of true latria. Again, Bellarmine is held to this here: for if it is of the essence of true latria to be offered through and on account of itself, then when the cross is given that worship through accident and on account of something else, it is not true latria. Either they attribute true latria to the cross, or simply none; why then does he invent an accidental and improper latria? Next, the worship of latria is either offered to the cross through and on account of itself, or not; if through itself and on account of itself, it will be true idolatry; if not, it is not the worship of true latria. Therefore again we here prove that Bellarmine's distinction takes away from the cross every worship of true latria, since worship of latria given to the cross through accident and improperly is not true latria, and consequently is nothing; for latria is nothing unless it is true, and it is one and simple.

units.la: IV. Bellarminus eodem capite Car- pocratianos inter hereticos dicit suis- se numeratos, quod imaginem Christi colerent diuinis honoribus, id est, cultu latriæ. Atqui cum Christum colebant sine dubio imaginem eius colebant propter ipsum. Nonigitur, inquit, imagines licet colere cultu latriæ, etsi quis dicat se propter Deum vel Christum hoc facere, non propter imagines: nam hoc ipso quod eas colit diuinis honoribus concincitur eas colora propter ipsas, non propter Deum, quicquid ipse verbis dicat. Ex hac assertatione inferim° distinctione hac non eximi Bellarminum & Romanam Ecclesiam à reatu staurolatriæ & idololatriæ. Nam vt Carpocratiani illi hæretici censebantur, quod latria colerent imagines Christi, & tamen non per & propter se, sed propter Christum: ita etiam Bellarminum & Ecclesiam Romanam non excusat, & à reatu staurolatriæ idololatriæque liberat, quod negat se colere crucem Christi latriâ non
units.tr: IV. In the same chapter Bellarmine says that the Carpocratians were counted among the heretics because they worshipped the image of Christ with divine honours, that is, with the worship of latria. But when they worshipped Christ, they undoubtedly worshipped his image for his sake. Therefore, he says, images may not be worshipped with latria, even if someone says that he does this on account of God or Christ and not on account of the images: for by the very fact that he worships them with divine honours, it is concluded that he worships them for their own sake, not for God's, whatever he says in words. From this assertion I infer that by this distinction Bellarmine and the Roman Church are not freed from the guilt of staurolatry and idolatry. For just as those heretics the Carpocratians were thought guilty because they worshipped the images of Christ with latria, yet not per se and for their own sake but on account of Christ, so the Roman Church and Bellarmine are not excused, nor freed from the guilt of staurolatry and idolatry, by the fact that they deny that they worship the cross of Christ with latria not

units.la: ° Vide supra in margine. nō negat se colore crucéChristi latria non per se & proprie, sed tantum per accidens & improprie. Ipse satis evidenter testatum facit, non esse de essentia verae latriae, ut propter se exhibeatur, cum etiam illi reatu idololatriae constringantur, qui latria colunt imagines Christi licet non propter se, sed propter aliud. Quin etiam Ethnici simulacra & imagines suas coluerunt propter aliud, & tamen idololatriae crimine tenentur. Non igitur eximitur a staurolatria ac proinde idololatria is, qui cultum latriae defert cruci, licet per accidens & propter aliud. Satis enim hinc apparet non esse de essentia verae & propriae latriae ut exhibeatur per seu propter se.
units.tr: See above in the margin. ...deny that they worship the cross of Christ with latria per se and properly, but only per accidens and improperly. He makes it sufficiently clear that it is not of the essence of true latria that it be offered for its own sake, since even those who worship images of Christ with latria, though not for their own sake but for something else, are bound by the guilt of idolatry. Indeed, the heathen too worshipped their idols and images on account of something else, and yet they are held guilty of the crime of idolatry. Therefore he who gives latria to the cross, even though per accidens and on account of something else, is not excused from staurolatry and consequently not from idolatry. For it is clear enough from this that it is not of the essence of true and proper latria that it be offered per se or for its own sake.

units.la: V. Ipsi Pontifici veram & propriam latriam tribuunt cruci Christi; Adorant eam non improprie & peraccidens & propter aliud, sed proprie & per se. Bellarminus expresse id fatetur cap. 23. hoc fieri cum in die Parasceues crucifixus paulatim detegitur, ostenditur, & adorandus proponitur. Tunc enim omnia illa per imaginem ipsi Christo vere exhiberi debeatur. Proprie igitur & per se latriam exhibent cruci Christi.
units.tr: V. The Papists themselves attribute true and proper latria to the cross of Christ; they adore it not improperly, per accidens and on account of something else, but properly and per se. Bellarmine expressly admits this in chapter 23, saying that this is done when, on Good Friday, the crucifix is gradually uncovered, shown, and set forth to be adored. For then all those things are truly offered to Christ himself through the image. Therefore they offer latria to the cross of Christ properly and per se.

units.la: VI. Quæro denique num vxor si rogatu mariti fiat alterius, propterea excusetur, aut à crimine adulterii liberetur; si dixerit, se non propter se, sed propter maritum aut eius rogatu fecisse. Ita certè se res habet in cultu diuino; si quis cruci aut cuiuscunque creaturæ latriam deferat, siue propter se, siue propter aliud, nihilominus idololatriam committit.
units.tr: VI. Finally I ask: if a wife does something at the request of another man, is she excused on that account, or freed from the crime of adultery, if she says that she did it not for its own sake but for her husband, or at his request? Certainly that is how the matter stands in divine worship: if anyone gives latria to the cross or to any creature whatever, whether for its own sake or for something else, he nonetheless commits idolatry.

units.la: III. Exceptio. Cultus qui per se & proprie debetur, cruci vera & cæteris crucibus non est latria propriè, sed quidam cultus multo inferior, qui analogicè & reductiuè refertur ad speciem eius cultus, qui debetur exemplari.
units.tr: III. Exception. The worship which is due per se and properly is not latria properly speaking when it is given to the true cross and to other crosses, but a certain much inferior worship, which is referred analogically and reductively to the species of that worship which is due to the prototype.

units.la: Resp. Hæc non nisi verborum sunt ludibria.
units.tr: Reply. These are nothing but tricks of words.

units.la: I. Sequetur hinc præter tria cultus genera duliam, hyperduliam, & latriam, etiam quartum genus dari oportere; quia cultum, qui imaginibus Christi exhibetur, dicit sine comparatione esse inferiorem cultu, qui ipsi Christi competit.
units.tr: I. It would follow from this that, besides the three kinds of worship, dulia, hyperdulia and latria, a fourth kind must also be admitted; for the worship offered to the images of Christ is said to be inferior, without any comparison, to the worship that belongs to Christ himself.

units.la: II. Non elabitur hic inani distinctione. Cultus, quem tribuunt cruci Christi, non est inferior latria aut analogica, sed vniuoca latria, quod sic probo 1, à definitione vniuocorum.
units.tr: II. He does not escape by this empty distinction. The worship which they attribute to the cross of Christ is not an inferior or analogical latria, but a univocal latria, which I prove first from the definition of univocals.

units.la: Quæ alicui & secundum nomen, & secundum eiusdem nominis rationem tribuuntur, ea non analogicè, sed univocè illi tribuuntur. At latria quæ Christo ipsi exhibetur, & secundum nomen, & secundum nominis istius rationem Christi tribuitur. Ergo non analogicè, sed univocè latria cruci Christi tribuitur.
units.tr: Whatever is attributed to something both according to the name and according to the reason of that name is attributed to it not analogically but univocally. But latria, which is offered to Christ himself, is attributed to Christ both according to the name and according to the reason of that name. Therefore latria is attributed to the cross of Christ not analogically but univocally.

units.la: Minorem nominis ratio, seu definitio confirmat. Est enim λατρεία summus cultus qui soli Deo debetur. At ab Ecclesia Romana eiusmodi cultus tribuitur cruci Christi, cum preces soli Deo debitas offert cruci, petens ea, quæ à nulla creatura, sed à solo Deo conferri possunt, gratiam scilicet & gloriam, ut supra ostensum est. 2 à proprio effectu univocè latreias. Quod religiosa adoratione colitur ei univoca λατρεία tribuitur, quia religiosa adoratio, ait Thomas, est actus externus proprius λατρείας & religionis soli Deo debita. At crux & imagines crucis Christi religiosa adoratione coluntur ab Ecclesia Romana, ut ex Pontificali Romano videre licet, q; postquam præscripsit orationem ipsi Pontifici habendam in consecratione novæ crucis, tunc dicit ipsum Pontificem flexis genibus ante crucem ipsam deuotè, id est, religiosè adorare, eamque
units.tr: The minor premise is confirmed by the reason or definition of the name. For latria (λατρεία) [λατρεία] is the highest worship, which is due to God alone. But this kind of worship is attributed by the Roman Church to the cross of Christ, since it offers to the cross prayers due to God alone, asking for those things which can be conferred by no creature but by God alone, namely grace and glory, as has been shown above. Second, univocal latria is attributed to whatever is worshipped with that worship which is the proper effect of latria. For religious adoration, says Thomas, is the external act proper to latria and to religion, which is due to God alone. But the cross and the images of the cross of Christ are worshipped with religious adoration by the Roman Church, as may be seen from the Roman Pontifical. After prescribing the prayer which the Pontiff himself is to say at the consecration of a new cross, it then says that the Pontiff himself, on bended knees before the cross, devoutly, that is, religiously, adores it, and kisses it.

units.la: q.94. amque ex osculari: quin & ipse Bellarmin° agnoscit Pontificios colere crucem, & imagines crucis religiosa adoratione, dicens cum in die Parasceues crucifixus paulatim detegitur, & ostenditur, & adorandus proponitur, illa omnia per imaginem ipsi Christo vere exhiberi intelliguntur. Vide & Breuiarium Romanum parte hyemali ad 3. Martii in festo Inuentionis sanctæ crucis, vbi præscripsit orationes, quibus inuocari debet crux Christi: itidem in parte æstiuali, die exaltationis sanctæ crucis.
units.tr: q.94. and to kiss it. Indeed, Bellarmine himself acknowledges that the Papists worship the cross and images of the cross with religious adoration, saying: when on Good Friday the crucifix is gradually uncovered and shown and proposed for adoration, all those things are understood to be truly offered to Christ himself through the image. See also the Roman Breviary, winter part, at 3 March, on the feast of the Invention of the Holy Cross, where prayers are prescribed by which the cross of Christ is to be invoked; likewise in the summer part, on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross.

units.la: Quarta exceptio. Imaginibus atque adeo cruci Christi non debetur vera latria & simpliciter, sed cultus fine comparatione inferior, qui tamen reducitur ad latriam vt imperfectum ad perfectum.
units.tr: The fourth exception: True latria is not owed to images, and so not to the cross of Christ either, but a worship incomparably inferior, which is nevertheless referred to latria as the imperfect to the perfect.

units.la: Resp. Hæc exceptio cum à priori non differat, cum illa etiam corruit. Nam 1. ait, non esse veram latriam, quæ Christi cruci defertur in Ecclesia Romana. Atqui cui vniuoca latria defertur. Opponitur enim versus cultus analogico, tum in subiecta ratione Bellarmini, tum in exemplo, quod affert ex Ariftotele de pieto homine, qui analogicè tantum homo est & similitudinem hominis veri refert, sed non est homo verus. Vbi igitur cōstat vniuo-ce latriam imagini & cruci Christi ex-hiberi, verè etiā eā exhiberi cōstabit.
units.tr: Reply: This exception does not differ from the previous one, so it falls with it. For first, it says that the latria which the Roman Church pays to the cross of Christ is not true latria. But to whom univocal latria is paid, to him it is truly paid. For it is opposed to analogical worship, both in Bellarmine's own argument and in the example he brings from Aristotle about a painted man, who is a man only analogically and represents the likeness of a real man, but is not a real man. Therefore, where it is established that univocal latria is paid to the image and the cross of Christ, it will also be established that it is truly paid to them.

units.la: II. Qui veram latriam imagini & cruci Christi deferunt, ij simpliciter non secundum quid exhiberi dicit latriam, analogicè & æquiuocè, & secū-dum nomen tantum, non autē secundum nominis rationem exhiberi signi-ficat. At docuimus latriam vniuocè tribui, non analogicè, & secundum no-mē tantū, Ergo simpliciter deferatur.
units.tr: Second, those who pay true latria to the image and the cross of Christ say that latria is paid absolutely, not in a qualified sense; but analogical and equivocal worship, which is so only in name, does not signify that it is paid according to the meaning of the name. But we have shown that latria is attributed univocally, not analogically and only in name. Therefore it is paid absolutely.

units.la: III. Negamus cultum illum, qui imagini & cruci Christi defertur, esse imperfectum. Imperfectus cultus, teste Bellarmino est cultus inferior longe vera latria, qui tamen ad veram latriam reducitur, vt imperfectum ad perfectum. At si est inferior, ergo non est idem cultus qui Christo defertur. Eundem verò cultum deferri ab ipsis cruci, qui Christo defertur probaui-mus. Inuocans enim crucem agnoscunt, se illi incensum & suffitum offerre. Inuocatio crucis & sacrificium ipsi factum, certe perfectus est cultus, non imperfectus. Et cum Bellarminus fatetur in die Parasceues eos omnia facere per imaginem ipso Christo, quid aliud significat, quam eos eodem modo, adorare crucem ac si Christus praesens esset. Quod eodem modo, quo Christus praesens adoratur, ei perfecta tribuitur latria. At imago Christi eodem modo adoratur quo Christus praesens, Ergo imagini Christi perfecta tribuitur latria.
units.tr: Third, we deny that the worship which is paid to the image and the cross of Christ is imperfect. An imperfect worship, according to Bellarmine's own testimony, is a worship far inferior to true latria, which nevertheless is referred to true latria as the imperfect to the perfect. But if it is inferior, then it is not the same worship that is paid to Christ. We have, however, proved that the same worship is paid to the cross by them as to Christ. For in invoking the cross they acknowledge that they offer incense and fumigation to it. An invocation of the cross and a sacrifice offered to it is surely a perfect worship, not an imperfect one. And when Bellarmine admits that on Good Friday they do everything through the image to Christ himself, what else does this signify than that they adore the cross in the same way as if Christ were present? Since perfect latria is given to the one whom Christ present is adored in the same way, and the image of Christ is adored in the same way as Christ present, therefore perfect latria is given to the image of Christ.

units.la: Exceptio quinta, est Gregorij de Valent: cultum latriae imaginibus Christi & cruci deferimus, sed non sicut Christo.
units.tr: The fifth exception is that of Gregory of Valencia: We give the worship of latria to the images of Christ and to the cross, but not as to Christ.

units.la: Resp. I. monstrosa est distinctio, vt quae seipsam euertit. Nam latriam fatetur deferri cruci, sed non sicut Christo Deo. At latria est cultus summus soli Deo debitus. Talis certe cultus, nemini nisi vt Deo exhiberi potest. Sic igitur argumentor. Cultus soli Deo debitus nemini potest exhiberi nisi vt Deo. At latria est cultus soli Deo debitus. Ergo nulli exhiberi potest, nisi vt Deo. Cum igitur Gregorius de Valentia cruci eam competere fateatur, non aliter ei nisi vt ipsi Christo convenire poterit. II. Cultus divinus, qui soli Christo debetur, nullo modo competit creaturae; alias idololatria committitur: qa idololatria est, cum honor soli Deo debitus impenditur creaturae. Sane affectus conjugalis, quem uxor soli debet marito, no debet alteri deferri. Quod si alteri sese consociet, neq; vel it adulterii propterea condemnari, quia non eodem animo & affectu, quo marito, suo semet consociauit, num ab adulterij crimine immunem esse pronunciabis? Vt igitur illa manifeste adulterij rea est, quæ corporis sui copiam facit alteri, licet non faciat eo animo affectu quo marito: ita idololatriam committit is, qui imaginibus & cruci Christi idololatriam defert, licet dicat, se non ita deferre sicut Christo. Non licebat Israelitis sacrificia immolare & suffitum offerre cuiquam, nisi soli Deo; At si Diis alienis aut cuiquam creaturæ obtulissent num huiusmodi distinctione semet ab idololatriæ crimine liberare potuissent, quod obtulerint Diis alienis, sed non sicut Deo; certè in scriptura passim idololatriæ damnantur, quod sacrificia & suffitus obtulerunt creaturis.
units.tr: Reply: First, the distinction is monstrous, since it overturns itself. For he admits that latria is paid to the cross, but not as to Christ God. Yet latria is the highest worship, owed to God alone. Such worship can certainly be given to no one except as to God. So I argue thus: Worship owed to God alone can be given to no one except as to God. But latria is worship owed to God alone. Therefore it can be given to no one except as to God. Since Gregory of Valencia therefore admits that it belongs to the cross, it can belong to it only as it belongs to Christ himself. Second, divine worship, which is owed to Christ alone, in no way belongs to a creature; otherwise idolatry is committed, for it is idolatry when the honour owed to God alone is bestowed on a creature. Surely the conjugal affection which a wife owes to her husband alone must not be given to another. If she joins herself to another, and is not condemned for adultery on the ground that she does not join herself with the same mind and affection as she does to her husband, will you pronounce her free from the crime of adultery? Just as she is manifestly guilty of adultery who gives the use of her body to another, even though she does not do so with the same mind and affection as to her husband, so he commits idolatry who pays idolatrous worship to images and to the cross of Christ, even though he says that he does not pay it as to Christ. The Israelites were not permitted to offer sacrifices and incense to anyone except to God alone. But if they had offered them to strange gods or to any creature, could they have freed themselves from the crime of idolatry by such a distinction, saying that they offered to strange gods but not as to God? Certainly Scripture everywhere condemns as idolatry the offering of sacrifices and incense to creatures.

units.la: Affirmamus etiam ab Ecclesia Romana latriam cruci Christi exhiberi, sicut ipsi Christo Deo ac Domino nostro. Res ipsa certè id abundè testatur, quoniam ab illa salutem sperant. In quo spem salutis homo ponit, illi latriæ cultum exhibet sicut Deo, eoque Idololatria {a}olatra dicitur. Hinc Auarus idololatra vocatur, nō quod nummū ipsum, Deum esse credat, sed quod spem & fiduciam, quam in solo Deo ponere oportebat, in nummo collocat. At Ecclesia Romana spem salutis ponit in cruce, cantat enim ô crux ave, spes unica &c. Ergo latriæ cultum exhibet sicut Deo.
units.tr: We affirm also that latria is paid by the Roman Church to the cross of Christ, just as to Christ, our God and Lord. The very fact surely testifies to this abundantly, since they hope for salvation from it. He who places the hope of salvation in something pays to it the worship of latria as to God, and so is called an idolater. Hence the covetous man is called an idolater, not because he believes money itself to be God, but because he places in money the hope and trust which ought to be placed in God alone. But the Roman Church places its hope of salvation in the cross; for it sings, "O cross, hail, our only hope," etc. Therefore it pays the worship of latria as to God.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: In quo conclusio colligitur & defenditur, Pontificios esse idololatras.
units.tr: In which the conclusion is drawn and defended, that the Papists are idolaters.

units.la: HAACTENVS præmissæ principalis syllogismi fuerunt confirmatæ, ac primò quidem maior præmissa: Omnis stauro latra est idololatra. deinde & minor, At Pontificii sunt stauro latræ: sequitur nunc conclusio Ergo Pontificii sunt Idololatræ. Grauissimum certe & atrocissimum crimen est Idololatria, vt scriptura docet, cuius si Pontificij cōuincantur, merito à se tot hominum & regnorum secessionem factam esse fateri cogentur, mandate Euangelistâ Iohanne Fugite Idola. §. Verum huic malo medicinam aliquam conatur afferre Gregorius de Valentia: qui cum videret Bellarmini distinctiones mera esse ludibria & monstra, ipsea- liud doctrinæ aut distinctionis monstrum confinxit portentosos, nempe idololatriam quandam esse licitam, quia Apostolus Petrus 1. Epist. c. 4. v. 3 postquam graviora peccata commemorasset, à quibus abstinendum sit Christianis, postremo eos dehortatur ab illicitis Idolorum cultibus. Hinc concludit, Petrum insinuare voluisse idololatriam esse licitam. Distinctio hæc Gregoriana extat in Apologetico de Idololatria l. 2. c. 7. hisce verbis. Neque abunde profecto putaris B. Petrum insinuasse cultum aliquem simulachrorum [nempe sacrarum imaginum] rectum esse, cum fideles nominatim ab illicitis idolorum cultibus deterrere voluit. Quid enim attinebat ita determinatè cultus simulachrorum illicitos notare, si omnino nullos simulachrorum cultus licitos esse censuisset. Hæc Gregorius.
units.tr: Hitherto the premises of the principal syllogism have been confirmed: first the major premise, "Every stauro-latrist is an idolater," and then the minor, "But the Papists are stauro-latrists." There follows now the conclusion, "Therefore the Papists are idolaters." Idolatry is certainly a most grave and atrocious crime, as Scripture teaches; and if the Papists are convicted of it, they will be obliged to confess that with good reason so many men and kingdoms have seceded from them, in obedience to the Evangelist John's command: "Flee from idols" (1 John 5.21 is not the source; cf. §. Verum). But Gregory de Valentia tries to offer some remedy for this evil. Seeing that Bellarmine's distinctions were mere trifles and monsters, he devised a further monstrous distinction of his own, namely that a certain idolatry is lawful. For the Apostle Peter, in 1 Epist. c. 4 v. 3, after recounting the graver sins from which Christians must abstain, finally warns them "against the unlawful cults of idols." Hence he concludes that Peter meant to insinuate that idolatry is lawful. This Gregorian distinction stands in his Apologetic on Idolatry, book 2, chapter 7, in these words: "Surely you will not think that Blessed Peter insinuated that some worship of images [namely, of sacred images] is right, when he wished to deter the faithful by name from the unlawful cults of idols. For what would it have mattered to mark so specifically the unlawful worship of images, if he had judged that no worship of images was lawful at all?" Thus Gregory.

units.la: Resp. 1. nimis inepta est subtilitas Gregorij, qui ex Epitheto adjecto concludit idololatriam quandam esse licitam. Sic cum Cicero pro Milone de Clodio verba facit, & nefaria stupra Clodij vocat, liceret inde colligere, si vestigiis Gregorij insisteremus, quandam stupra esse licita. Quor sum enim attinebat ita determinate stuprū nefarium notare, si nullum omnino stuprum committere fas est? Sic cum Catullus Elegia in Comam Berenices, imprecatur ei quæ impuro sese polluerunt adulterio, inde inferre liceret vi rationis Gregorianæ, adulterium aliquod esse purum. Quorsum enim attinebat ita determinate adulterium impurum notare, nisi aliquod adulterium purum esse cèsuisset. II. Nego q; Petrus epitheto illo voluerit innuere licita quādā idololatriā, sed eā esse maximū & grauissimū crimē & maximè fugiendū. Nō enim epitheto illud distinguēdi, sed augēdi causa adhibuit, volens scilicet ostēdere omniū scelera tissimū esse.Epitheta teste Quintil. & ad adornandam & ad augendā oratione debent adhiberi.Hic vero habet vsū amplificandi.Cū enim Petrus dehortatus esset eosà lasciuijs; cupiditatibus vinolētijs commessationibus, comperationibus, vt postremū crimē idololatriæ augeret,& ab eo cauēdum esse doceret,amplificat illud Eptheto Sic cū oratores dicūt,omne scel°abominandū, omnē libidinē deformem, epithetaamplificādi causa adijciūtur.
units.tr: Reply 1: Gregory's subtlety is far too silly, for he infers from an added epithet that some idolatry is lawful. So when Cicero, in his speech for Milo, speaks about Clodius and calls Clodius's crimes "nefarious debauchery," one could infer, if we followed Gregory's footsteps, that some debauchery is lawful. For why would he have labelled the debauchery so specifically as nefarious, if it were not right to commit any debauchery at all? So too when Catullus, in the Elegy on Berenice's Hair, curses those who defiled themselves with "impure" adultery, one could infer by Gregory's reasoning that some adultery is pure. For why would he have labelled the adultery so specifically as impure, unless he had judged that some adultery is pure? 2. I deny also that Peter, by that epithet, meant to hint at some lawful idolatry; rather he meant it to be the greatest and gravest crime and to be most avoided. For he used the epithet not for distinguishing but for amplifying, wishing clearly to show that it is the most wicked of all wrongs. Epithets, as Quintilian witnesses, ought to be used both for adorning and for amplifying speech. Here it has the function of amplifying. For when Peter had warned them against wantonness, lusts, drunkenness, revelries and drinking parties, in order to magnify idolatry, the last of the crimes, and to teach that they must guard against it, he amplified it with an epithet. So when orators say "every crime is to be abominated" or "every lust is ugly," epithets are added for the sake of amplification.

units.la: Impa-
units.tr: Impa-

units.la: Imperitiam suam proderet, qui cum Gregorio hunc interret, quoddam scelus non esse abominandum, & libidinem quandam esse speciosam seu formosam, qualis illa fortasse, quae Romae in lupanaribus exercetur.Notare igitur licet hinc, in quas formas sese vertant Pontificii Doctores, vt dololatriam pudendam, quam in colendis imaginibus & crucae Christi committunt, defendant ac tegant. Cum negando & distinguendo obtinere non possunt quod volunt, tandem concedunt, sed ita vt fuco licet inepto suam pallient idololatriam. Quam nihil vero proficiant, ex iis quae hactenus disputata sunt, euidenter liquet: sequitur, vt ad Bellarminianae disputationis examen accedamus.
units.tr: He would betray his own lack of skill who, with Gregory, interpreted this to mean that some crime is not to be abominated, and that some lust is becoming or fair, such as perhaps that which is practised in the brothels of Rome. It may therefore be observed from this into what shapes the Papist teachers transform themselves, in order to defend and cover the shameful idolatry which they commit in the worship of images and of the Cross of Christ. Since they cannot obtain what they want by denying and distinguishing, at last they concede, but in such a way that they cloak their idolatry with a clumsy paint. How little they profit, is plainly clear from what has been argued so far; it follows that we should come to the examination of Bellarmine's disputation.

units.tr: So far we have shown that the Papists are cross-worshippers, and from their cross-worship we have concluded that they are idolaters. Since Bellarmine sets up a special disputation to excuse the idolatry that is committed above all over the cross of Christ, I have judged it worth the effort to test it by Scripture, as by a touchstone, so that the idolatry of the Roman Church may be more properly exposed and the truth of our doctrine more forcefully asserted. I shall examine this disputation in five chapters, of which the first...

units.la: D equiequitur Bellarminus, nempe à c. 26. libri secundi de Imaginibus Sanctorum, usque ad finem libri secundi, quæ singula iusta disquisitione excutiem.
units.tr: Then Bellarmine follows, namely from chapter 26 of the second book on the Images of the Saints to the end of the second book, and I shall examine each of these points with careful inquiry.

units.la: Capite 26. 1. errores. 2. Argumenta peculiaria quæ de Cruce inveniuntur proponit. 3. partitionem disputationis instituit. Antequam vero partes hasce examinem, prius considerandus est Titulus, quem huic capiti præfigit. Titulus est de ADORATIONE CRVCIS. Mirum. Cum in ipsa disputatione non adorandam, sed tantum sacram & venerabilem esse contedat thesis & conclusio disputationis, titulo convenire debent; quia argumentum disputationis seu rei disputandæ completi debet. At Bellarmini thesis dissidet ab ipso titulo. Nam non apponit adorandam esse crucem, nec pro adoratione crucis contendit, sed sacram tantum & venerandam dicit, & pro eius veneratione disputat. Aliud esse venerari, aliud adorare. Hieronymus in Epistola ad Marcellum ut migret Bethlehem, Tabernaculum dicit fuisse veneratum aludeis, & merito; quia erat typus rerum spiritualium; sed non dicit fuisse adoratum. [illegible, ~3 letters]cam etiam dicimus fuisse venera-m, quia erat signum præsentiæ diui-e, sed non fuit adorata. Adoratio igi-r à veneratione est distinguenda. Multa sût q; veneramur & magnifi-us, sed nō licet ea adorare. Signa Di-nitus instituta Augustinus veneran-i & honorificè tractanda esse docet, d non vult ea esse adoranda. Anti-uitas venerabilis dicitur, & homo-enerabilis, nec tamen antiquitas aut omo est adorandus. Quod si verò ve-erationem intelligit diuinam id est dorationem religiosam idololatriæ conuincitur, idq; hoc mo-lo. Qui diuinum honorem seu cultum im-endit creaturæ, est manifestus Idololatra. At qui adorationem religiosam ligno crucis exhibet, is diuinum honorem seu cultum cre-atura impendit. Ergo qui adorationem reli-giosam ligno crucis exhibet, manifestus est i-dololatra. units.tr: In chapter 26 he (1) lists the errors, as they are called, peculiar to the cross; (2) proposes the particular arguments that are found concerning the cross; and (3) sets up a division of the disputation. Before I examine these parts, I must first consider the title he prefixes to this chapter. The title is "On the Adoration of the Cross." Strange! Since the thesis and conclusion of the disputation itself maintain that the cross is not to be adored but only to be held sacred and venerable, the title ought to agree with it, because the subject of a disputation, or the matter to be disputed, must be complete. But Bellarmine's thesis differs from the title itself. For he does not assert that the cross is to be adored, nor does he argue for the adoration of the cross; he calls it only sacred and venerable, and disputes for its veneration. To venerate is one thing, to adore another. Jerome, in his letter to Marcellus, that he should move to Bethlehem, says that the Tabernacle was venerated by the Jews, and rightly, because it was a type of spiritual things; but he does not say that it was adored. [...] the ark too we say was venerated, because it was a sign of the divine presence, but it was not adored. Adoration, therefore, must be distinguished from veneration. Many things we venerate and magnify, yet it is not lawful to adore them. Augustine teaches that signs divinely instituted are to be venerated and honourably treated, but he does not want them to be adored. Antiquity is called venerable, and a venerable man, yet neither antiquity nor a man is to be adored. But if he understands veneration as divine, that is, as religious adoration, he is convicted of idolatry, and in this way: Whoever gives divine honour or worship to a creature is a manifest idolater. But whoever offers religious adoration to the wood of the cross gives divine honour or worship to a creature. Therefore whoever offers religious adoration to the wood of the cross is a manifest idolater. That Bellarmine, with his followers, contends must be done: who will doubt any longer that Bellarmine, with his followers, is held guilty of the crime of idolatry? He cannot deny the major premise. For it is of Thomas Aquinas himself, whose writings were confirmed by a divine miracle, witness Pius V. This Thomas, I say, defines idolatry thus...

units.la: Cap. 7. Quæst. 3. latriam in explanatione epistolę ad Ephes. definit. Idololatria est quando hõnor soli Deo debitus creaturæ impenditur: secunda secundæ, Idololatria inquit, est superstitio, quâ creaturæ diuinus cultus exhibetur. Neque appendixilla Gregoriana Sicvt Deo, eam Thomæ definitionem labefactare potest, vt & supra docui, siquidem Synodus Nicena, cuius sententia infallibilis censetur geminam rationem idololatriæ esse docet, creaturæ diuinum honorem tribuere absque illa appendice Sicvt Deo. Damnat enim Nestorium Idololatriæ, quod Christum filium Virginis Mariæ doceret esse merum hominem, & tamen diuinum cultum ei exhiberet, vnde & ἀνθρωπολατρίας à Cyrillo arguitur, & ἀνθρωπολάτρης à Iustiniano pronuntiatur. Minorem rursum ex Thoma probamus. Is vt supra ostendi adorationem religiosam dicit esse actum externum proprium latriæ, & religionis soli Deo debitæ. Adoratio autem seu veneratio illa, quam Bellarminus cruci deberi contendit, non potest de humana aut ciuili, quæ reuerentia & subiectio est inferiorum erga superiores, accipi, sed
units.tr: Question 3, chapter 7: ...defines idolatry in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians. Idolatry is when the honour due to God alone is given to a creature; idolatry, he says in the Second Part of the Second Part, is superstition by which divine worship is offered to a creature. Nor can that Gregorian appendix, "as to God," weaken this definition of Thomas, as I have shown above, since the Nicene Synod, whose judgment is deemed infallible, teaches that there are two kinds of idolatry: giving divine honour to a creature, without that appendix "as to God." For it condemns Nestorius for idolatry, because he taught that Christ, the son of the Virgin Mary, was a mere man, and yet offered him divine worship; hence Cyril charges him with anthropolatry [ἀνθρωπολατρίας], and Justinian pronounces him an anthropolatres [ἀνθρωπολάτρης]. Again, we prove the minor premise from Thomas. He, as I showed above, says that religious adoration is the external act proper to latria, and to the religion due to God alone. But that adoration or veneration which Bellarmine contends is owed to the cross cannot be understood of human or civil reverence, which is the reverence and subjection of inferiors toward superiors, but

units.tr: Cyrill. ad reginas de recta fide Constit. 6. cap. de summa trinit. & fide catho. ...must necessarily be understood of religious worship due to God alone [for there is no middle ground]. The thing itself shows this, if you attend to the mind and feeling with which they offer adoration to the cross: plainly the same with which they adore God himself, namely when they adore the cross and call upon it, asking for things that no creature can confer. Moreover, wooden and stone crosses are not capable of civil adoration, since they cannot acknowledge and receive the honour due, and it belongs only to those who live in this civil society, to which crosses do not belong. So much for the title.

units.la: VIDEAMVS NVNC IPSAS PARTES CAPITIS, AC PRIMO QVIDEM ERRORES VT VOCANT PECVLIARES DE CRVCE.
units.tr: Let us now look at the parts of the chapter itself, and first at the so-called peculiar errors concerning the cross.

units.la: I. Error seu Hæresis fuit Claudij Taurinensis, inquit Bellarminus, qui præter cateras imagines, crucem Domini execrabatur, teste Iona l. 1. Vixit autem Claudius Anno Domini 800. Idem eodem tempore docebant Pauliciani, a quoquodam Paulo sic appellati, teste Euthymio in panoplia parte 2. tit. 21.
units.tr: I. The error or heresy was that of Claudius of Turin, says Bellarmine, who, among other images, execrated the cross of the Lord, as Jonas witnesses in book 1. Claudius lived in the year of the Lord 800. At the same time the Paulicians, so called from a certain Paul, taught the same, as Euthymius witnesses in the Panoplia, part 2, title 21.

units.la: Resp. Quæ Claudij hæresis, quis error ejus fuerit, nullus melius quam Ionas Aurelianensis Episcopus nobis declarabit: Age ergo audiamus ipsum. Is licet hostis Claudij acerrimus in præfatione lib. de cultu Imaginum p. 691. sic de Claudio disserit. Cum super gregem sibi creditum pro viribus superintenderet, eumque prædicationis suæ instantia ad amorem cælestis patriæ, quantum videbatur accendere satageret; vidit eum inter cetera, quæ emendatione digna gerebat, superstitiosæ, imo pernitiosæ imaginum adorationi, quâ plurimi illarum partium laborant, ex inolita consuetudine deditam esse. Unde immoderato & indiscreto zelo succensus, non solum picturas sanctarum rerum gestarum, quæ non ad adorandum, sed solummodo ad instruendas nescientium mentes in Ecclesiis antiquitus fieri permissa, verum etiam cruces materiales, quibus ob honorem & recordationem redemptionis suæ, sancta consuevit, uti Ecclesia à cunctis parœciæ suæ Basilicis, dicitur deleuisse, evertisse, & penitus abdicasse. En quid execrat fuerit Claudius, Superstitiosam scilicet & perniciosam imaginum & crucium materialiū adorationem, qualis execraexecratio hæresis est dicenda, etiam ipse Ionas hærefin docuit, vt qui hanc Claudij sententiam probauit, saltem immoderatum zelum reprehendit, quo aboleuit, exturbauit, atque euertit imagines, picturas & cruces, quæ ad ornatum & historicam institutio- nem tolerari potuissent. Audiamus amplius quid execratus fuerit Claudius. Recitat & assumit Ionas argumen- tum Claudij, contra cultum imagi- num estque tale. Si opera manuum Dei non sunt adoranda & colenda, quanto magis opera manuum hominum adoranda & colenda non sunt. Quid Ionas ad illud? In huius sententia sensu nobiscum sobrie sapis, &c. Quid ergo imaginibus largitur? Hoc vnum, vt ob pulchritudinem & recordationem in Ecclesiis in gratiam indoctorum depingantur. Qua quidem ratione, inquit, nos figmenta & imagines non colimus, imagines tamen & habemus, & habentibus non præiudicamus. Audin' cultum imaginum Claudius damnauit, ac propterea eas tollendas judicauit, quas Ionas tolerari maluisset. Quem ergo nunc errorem, quam hæresin Claudij notas? Num hæresis est damnare cultum imaginum? Etiam Ionas accensendus sendus fuerit Claudio, cum eius sen-tentiæ sensum vt sobrium approbet. Num abolitio & exturbatio imagi-num hæresin sapit? Repugnat ius ca-nonicum quod hic pronunciat. Si non-nulli ex prædecessoribus aut maioribus no-stris fecerunt aliqua, quæ illo tempore potu-erunt esse sine culpa, & postea vertantur in errorem & superstitionem, docemur exem-plo Ezechiæ frangentis serpentem æneum, il-la sine tarditate aliqua & cum magna autho-ritate à posteris posse destrui. Recte igitur Claudius imagines & cruces execra-tus est, & passim exturbauit è templis, cum plebem Tauronensem ad superstitiosum & perniciosum cultum ijs abuti videret: si hæresis fuit, utique etiam Rex Ezechias hæreseos insimu-landus, qui cum videret populum circa serpentem æneum insanire, & in-censum ei adolere, quanquam Dei iussu & in signum Christi venturi ere-ctum, detestatus est & in frustra con-scidit. Cuius pio exemplo freti & hodie Christiani execrantur cruces & exturbant è templis, quia vident in-censum illis Papistas adolere. Ex mis-sali enim notum est. In missis solennibus sacerdotem facta crucireuerentia eam ter in-censare.
units.tr: Reply. What Claudius's heresy was, and what his error consisted in, no one will declare to us better than Jonas, bishop of Orléans. Let us hear him. Although he was the most bitter enemy of Claudius, in the preface to his book on the cult of images (p. 691) he speaks thus of Claudius: While he was watching over the flock entrusted to him as far as his strength allowed, and was striving by the urgency of his preaching to kindle in them a love of the heavenly homeland, he saw that among the other things in need of correction, they were given over to a superstitious, indeed pernicious, adoration of images, to which very many of that region were addicted through an ingrained custom. Kindled therefore by an immoderate and indiscreet zeal, he is said to have not only destroyed, overthrown and utterly rejected the paintings of holy events, which were allowed of old in the churches not for adoration but only for instructing the minds of the ignorant, but also the material crosses, which the Church had customarily kept in all the basilicas of his parish, as a sign of honour and remembrance of our redemption. Here is what Claudius execrated: namely the superstitious and pernicious adoration of images and material crosses. Such adoration is rightly to be called an execrable thing, and Jonas himself has taught this, since he approves Claudius's opinion and at least finds fault with his immoderate zeal, by which he abolished, drove out and overthrew images, paintings and crosses that could have been tolerated for decoration and historical instruction. Let us hear further what Claudius execrated. Jonas recites and adopts Claudius's argument against the cult of images, and it runs thus: If the works of God's hands are not to be adored and worshipped, much less are the works of men's hands to be adored and worshipped. What does Jonas say to this? In the sense of this opinion you are wise with us, soberly, etc. What then does he concede to images? This one thing: that they be painted in the churches for the sake of beauty and remembrance, for the benefit of the unlearned. For this reason, he says, we do not worship figments and images, yet we also have images, and we do not prejudice those who have them. Do you hear? Claudius condemned the cult of images and therefore judged that those images should be removed which Jonas would rather have tolerated. What error, then, or what heresy of Claudius do you now note? Is it heresy to condemn the cult of images? Jonas himself would be counted a Claudian, since he approves the sense of Claudius's opinion as sober. Does abolishing and driving out images savour of heresy? The canon law, which pronounces here, contradicts you: If some of our predecessors or ancestors have done certain things which at that time may have been without fault, but afterwards turn into error and superstition, we are taught by the example of Hezekiah, who broke the bronze serpent, that those things may be destroyed by posterity without any delay and with great authority. Claudius therefore rightly execrated images and crosses, and drove them out of the temples here and there, since he saw the people of Turin abusing them for superstitious and pernicious worship. If it was heresy, then surely King Hezekiah too must be charged with heresy, who, seeing the people going mad about the bronze serpent and burning incense to it, although it had been set up by God's command as a sign of the coming Christ, detested it and broke it into pieces. Trusting in this pious example, Christians today also execrate crosses and drive them out of the temples, because they see Papists burning incense before them. For it is known from the Missal: In solemn Masses the priest, after making reverence to the cross, incenses it three times.

Qui vero sunt cultores imaginum? Tu Bellarmine & tota antichriftiana cohors. Parum igitur hujus testis authoritas ad causam Iesuitarum promouendam confert. Et quid promoueret eam, cum ipsi Bellarmino fides & authoritas ejus fit suspecta. Est enim, inquit, hic author cautè legendus quoniam laborat eodem errore quo Abogardus & reliqui eius ætatis Galli, qui negabant sacris imaginibus vllum deberi cultum religiosum. D s
units.tr: Title: on the rite of celebrating Mass. incense it. Further, the Jesuit cites Jonas against Claudius. Why should we not cite the same man, with equal right, against the Jesuit? He condemns the adoration of images and calls it superstitious and pernicious. He declares that the churches of Gaul and Germany are free of it, as Baronius also rightly observed, who, after citing many passages from the books of Jonas, concludes thus: Jonas, although he fights very vigorously against Claudius, the breaker of images, equally attacks and lashes their worshippers, asserting that images are to be kept in the churches both for the adornment of the churches themselves and for the historical instruction of the people, and this, as he says, in accordance with the opinion of Blessed Gregory the Pope, writing to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles. But who are the worshippers of images? You, Bellarmine, and the whole Antichristian crew. So the authority of this witness contributes little to promoting the Jesuits' cause. And what would it promote, when Bellarmine's own trustworthiness and authority are themselves suspect? For this author, says he, is to be read with caution, since he labours under the same error as Abogardus and the other Gallic writers of his age, who denied that any religious worship was due to sacred images. D s

units.la: En caute legendum monet Ionam, & tamen nobis authoritatem eius contra Claudium obijcit. Cultum imaginum religiosum ab ipso negari fatetur, & tamen pro crucis adoratione eum citat. Atqui haec ipsa fuit causa cur Claudius exturbaret imagines; quia cultum diuinum eis exhiberi videbat.
units.tr: Behold, he warns that Jonas must be read with caution, and yet he throws Jonas's authority against Claudius at us. He confesses that Jonas denies religious worship to images, and yet he cites him in support of the adoration of the cross. And yet this very thing was the reason Claudius drove out the images: he saw that divine worship was being offered to them.

units.la: II. Error seu Haeresis. Circa annum Domini 1130. extiterunt Petrus Bruis & Henricus, qui similiter crucem Domini eiusque cultum oppugnabant, teste Petro Cluniacensi, qui contra eas epistolam prolixam & erudita illo ipso tempore scripsit ad omnes Episcopos. Circa idem tempus, vel paulo post extiterunt in Oriente Bogomiles qui idem iisdem argumentis docebant, teste Euthymio panopl. part. 2. tit. 23.
units.tr: II. The error or heresy. Around the year of the Lord 1130 there arose Peter Bruys and Henry, who likewise assailed the cross of the Lord and its cult, as Peter of Cluny witnesses; he wrote against them a long and learned letter at that very time, addressed to all bishops. About the same time, or a little later, there arose in the East the Bogomils, who taught the same things with the same arguments, as Euthymius witnesses in the Panoplia, part 2, title 23.

units.la: Respon. Fateor oppugnarunt crucem Domini, non veram scilicet passionem & mortem Christi, sed fictitiam, ut sunt materiales lignę & lapideę cruces superstitioni & idololatriae inseruientes. Oppugnatio haec non est error aut haeresis, sed arguit eorum pietatem & sapientiam. Nemo enim sapiens ait Honorius Augustodanus, adorat crucem sed Christum crucifixum. Ex Epistola Petri Cluniacensis satis apparet, eos venerationem crucium damnasse, easque propterea exterminatas & amotas voluisse. Quod vero Cluniacensis contra illos scripsit, non est mirum, fuit enim Abbas & Monachus superstitiosus, miraculorum sui temporis temerarius buccinator, idololatricæ venerationis crucis & sacrificij Missæ assertor.
units.tr: Reply. I grant that they assailed the cross of the Lord, not indeed the true passion and death of Christ, but the fictitious cross, that is, material wooden and stone crosses serving superstition and idolatry. This assault is not an error or heresy, but shows their piety and wisdom. For no wise man, says Honorius Augustodunensis, adores the cross, but Christ crucified. From the letter of Peter of Cluny it is quite clear that they condemned the veneration of crosses and wished them destroyed and removed on that account. That Cluny wrote against them is no wonder, for he was an abbot and a superstitious monk, a rash trumpeter of the miracles of his time, and a champion of idolatrous veneration of the cross and of the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: III. Error Wiclevistarum. Non minus crucis honorem detestati sunt Wiclevitæ apud Thomam Waldensem Tomo 3. tit. 2. Calvin. l. 1. Instit. c. 11. & 7. Magdeburg. cent. 4. c. 4. col. 3 o 2. cap. 6. col. 4 18. & 459. ubi etiam impudenter mentiuntur usum signi crucis Seculo IV. novum fuisse. Nam Tertullianus lib. de corona militis meminit signi crucis, cum tamen floruerit seculo II. sicut etiam cent. 7. c. 6. col. 191. mentiuntur Sergium Papam fuisse autorem primum, ut crux adoretur & oscularetur. Nam Sergius Papa sedit Anno Domini 688. at meminit adorationis & exosculationis crucis Euagrius. l. 4 c. 26. qui est centum annis antiquior Sergio. Meminit Hieronymus in Epistola ad Marcellum ut migret Bethlehem.
units.tr: III. The error of the Wycliffites. The Wycliffites detested no less the honour of the cross, as Thomas Waldensis reports in volume 3, title 2. Calvin, book 1 of the Institutes, chapters 11 and 7. Magdeburg Centuries, century 4, chapter 4, col. 302; chapter 6, col. 418 and 459, where they also shamelessly lie that the use of the sign of the cross was new in the fourth century. For Tertullian, in the book De corona militis, mentions the sign of the cross, although he flourished in the second century. Likewise century 7, chapter 6, col. 191, they falsely claim that Pope Sergius was the first author of the adoration and kissing of the cross. For Pope Sergius sat in the year of the Lord 688, but Evagrius, book 4, chapter 26, who is a hundred years older than Sergius, mentions the adoration and kissing of the cross. Jerome mentions it in his letter to Marcellus, to go to Bethlehem.

units.la: Resp. I. Wiclevitæ honorem crucis superstitiosum detestati sunt; Cum enim olim instituta esset crux, vt es- tis esset fidei in Christum crucifixum superstitiosi illi abutebatur ad cultum religiosę venerationis. Merito igitur hunc abusum Wicleviftæ viri pij fuere detestati. Atq; de hoc abusu etiā conquestus fuit, Ferus, & Andreas Mafius. Ferus, quam multa inquit, instituerunt san- cti bona intentione, quæ tamen nunc videm partim in abusu partim in superstitione ver- ti. Exempla sunt Festa, ceremonia, Imagines, Missæ, & cætera. Andreas Mafius ex di- ctis Lactatij, Tertulliani, Nazian. Basi- lij, pbat, monumetū crucis apud vetu- stissimos Christianos in vsu fuisse, non vt adoretur, sed vt testis esset Christi crucifixi. Hi igitur viri Pōtificij, qui hactenus in summo pctio habiti, hæreseos deinceps, teste Bellarmino erunt insimulandi.
units.tr: Reply. First, the Wycliffites detested the superstitious honour of the cross. For although the cross was once instituted as a sign of faith in Christ crucified, those superstitious men abused it for religious veneration. Rightly therefore did those godly men detest this abuse. And Ferus and Andreas Masius also complained of this abuse. Ferus says: How many things holy men instituted with good intention, which we now see have partly turned into abuse and partly into superstition! Examples are feasts, ceremonies, images, Masses, and others. Andreas Masius, drawing on the sayings of Lactantius, Tertullian, and Basil of Nazianzus, proves that a monument of the cross was in use among the most ancient Christians, not that it should be adored, but that it might be a witness of Christ crucified. Therefore these Papists, who until now have been held in the highest esteem, shall henceforth, as Bellarmine witnesses, be charged with heresy.

units.la: II. Centuriatores iniquissime men- dacij à mendace accusantur. Nō enim loquuntur absolutè & in genere de signo crucis sed in specie de signo crucis ab Alexandrinis posito. Hi Christiani facti, thoraces Serapidis abrasere, & loco eorum, vestibula domuum parietes, fenestras, notauere signo crucis Christi. Hoc ergo signum crucis à nouis Christianis loco insign. ū. Serapidis pidisInstitutu nouu fuisse dicunt centuriatos, & recte quidé; Haeten' enim domos suas signo thoracis, nunc ad Euangelij cognitione adductì, serapidis insignia aliaque ejusmodi idololatriae monumeta detrahút, & eorum loco crucem Christi tanquam tropeum statuerunt, idq; sine superstitione, quia non eo animo & fine vt adoretur, sed vt symbolum esset publicum profeßionis fidei suæ. Atque in eo initiati sunt Constantini piissimi Imperatoris exemplum, qui in nummis suis, in vexillis, scutis, armis militum inscribendam & insculpendam curauit crucem, vt partim signum esset profeßionis fidei; partim vt milites alienos à Christo, sensim hac ratione ad religionem crucifixi Christi traduceret.
units.tr: II. The Centuriators are most unjustly accused of lying by a liar. For they do not speak absolutely and in general about the sign of the cross, but specifically about the sign of the cross set up by the Alexandrians. These men, having become Christians, scraped the breastplates of Serapis off their houses, and in their place marked the vestibules, walls and windows of their homes with the sign of the cross of Christ. So the Centuriators say that this sign of the cross was a new institution of the new Christians in place of the insignia of Serapis, and they are right to say so. For having been brought to the knowledge of the gospel, they removed from their houses the emblems of Serapis and other such monuments of idolatry, and in their place set up the cross of Christ as a trophy. They did this without superstition, because they did it not with the intention and purpose that it should be adored, but to be a public token of their profession of faith. In this they followed the example of the most pious Emperor Constantine, who had the cross inscribed and engraved on his coins, banners, shields and soldiers' arms, partly as a sign of his profession of faith, and partly so that, by this means, he might gradually bring soldiers who were strangers to Christ over to the religion of the crucified Christ.

units.la: III. Tertullianus meminit quidem crucis, sed quæ non fuit permanens, aut subsistens in quadam materia, verum transiens à primis Christianis in aere digitis formari solita, in testimonium profeßionis fidei, vt scilicet testarentur se esse Christianos, quos crucis Christi minimè puderet. Centuriatores vero loquuntur de cruce permanète è ligno vel metallo compositâ, vel etiâ in Ecclesijs aut oratorijs picta, & ad adorationem posita.
units.tr: III. Tertullian indeed mentions the cross, but a cross that was not lasting or fixed in any material; rather, it was a transient one, which the first Christians were accustomed to form with their fingers in the air, as a testimony of their profession of faith, so that they might show that they were Christians, and were not at all ashamed of the cross of Christ. The Centuriators, however, speak of a cross that is permanent, made of wood or metal, or even painted in churches or oratories, and set up for adoration.

units.la: IV. Nec Sergium Centuriatores affecere injuriâ, cum primum authorem faciunt adorationis crucis. Loquuntur autem de publicâ adorationis institutione in Ecclesiâ Romanâ, quâ rectè Sergio vt primo authori tribuunt; quia is primum publico decreto crucem populo adorandam proposuit, teste Rheginone l. 1. Chron. in an. num. 622. Sergius Papa, inquit, sacrario B. Petri Apostoli magnam portionem ligni Dominica crucis reperit, quam & tempore illo ab omni populo in Basilica Constantiniana die exaltationis eius osculatur & adoratur. Quod vero Euagrius meminit osculationis & adorationis ab Apamaensibus cruci praestita, id fuit exemplum singulare non vero publicæ institutionis. Coeperunt quidem iam tum superstitiosi non nulli crucem adorare & exosculari; sed publico decreto adorationis & exosculationis crucis visus non dum erat stabilitus.
