units.tr: IV. Nor have the Centuriators wronged Sergius when they make him the first author of the adoration of the cross. They speak of the public institution of adoration in the Roman Church, and rightly ascribe it to Sergius as its first author, because he was the first to propose by public decree that the cross be adored by the people; so Rhegino testifies in book 1 of his Chronicle, under the year 622: Pope Sergius, he says, found in the sacristy of the blessed Apostle Peter a great portion of the wood of the Lord's cross, which at that time was kissed and adored by all the people in the Basilica of Constantine on the day of its exaltation. As for Evagrius' mention of the kissing and adoration of the cross by the people of Apamea, that was a singular example and not a public institution. Some superstitious people had indeed already begun at that time to adore and kiss the cross; but the public decree establishing the adoration and kissing of the cross had not yet been made firm.

units.la: V. Quod etiam Hieronymus meminit crucis adoratæ, id nihil aliud probat, quam iam tum Hieronymi temporibus à quibusdam inprimis à superst[?] titiofis mulierculis crucem adorari [?] coepisse: At nondum publice inualue-rat adoratio crucis. Hinc idem etiam redarguit mulierculas, quae crucis li-gno suo tempore jam abutebantur. Nondum igitur communiter tunc ab omnibus recepta erat adoratio crucis. Centuriatores vero de ejusmodi publica crucis adoratione loquuntur, cujus Sergium authorem statuunt.
units.tr: V. Likewise, when Jerome mentions the adoration of the cross, this proves nothing more than that already in Jerome's time the adoration of the cross had begun among some people, especially superstitious little women; but the adoration of the cross had not yet become widespread in public. Hence Jerome also rebukes those little women who were already abusing the wood of the cross in his time. Therefore the adoration of the cross was not yet received in common by all at that time. The Centuriators, however, speak of such public adoration of the cross, the author of which they hold to be Sergius.

units.la: Haec de Erroribus sequuntur argumenta peculiaria ut vocat, quae circa crucem inueniuntur. Argumenta vero ea tantum proponit, quae putat facile eludi posse. Firmissima autem & elusionem non ferentia, subdole reticet, in quo lesuitarum prodit vafritiem. Quia vero refutationem argumentorum propositorum in vltimum nempe 3o. caput reijcit, nos examen & castigationem refutationis, ordinem eius secuti, ibidem exequemur, atque alia praeterea argumeuta crucis cultum euertentia producemus.
units.tr: These are the arguments regarding the errors, which he calls peculiar, that are found concerning the cross. He sets out only those arguments which he thinks can easily be evaded. The most solid ones, which do not admit of evasion, he slyly passes over in silence, and in this he reveals the cunning of the Jesuits. Because he postpones the refutation of the arguments he has set out until the last, namely the thirtieth chapter, we shall follow his order and examine and censure his refutation there, and in addition we shall bring forward other arguments that overthrow the worship of the cross.

units.la: III. Partitionem disputationis instituit secundum crucis diuisionem. Crux juxta Pontificios in tres species diuiditur; in veram crucem, cui Christus ipse affixus fuit; in imaginem crucis: & in signum crucis transiens. De vera Christi cruce disserit cap. 26. de imagine crucis cap. 27. de signo crucis transeunte cap. 38. Nos vt singula accuratè examinare, & p merito castigare possimus, ordinem ab ipso institutum seruabimus.
units.tr: III. He lays out the division of the discussion according to the division of the cross. According to the Papists, the cross is divided into three kinds: the true cross, to which Christ himself was fastened; the image of the cross; and the sign of the cross made in passing. He discusses the true cross of Christ in chapter 26, the image of the cross in chapter 27, and the transient sign of the cross in chapter 38. So that we may examine each part accurately and censure it rightly, we shall keep the order that he himself has set.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: In quo caput 26. Bellarmini de vera cruc Domini examinatur & castigatur.
units.tr: In which chapter 26 of Bellarmine, on the true cross of the Lord, is examined and censured.

units.la: INhoc capite Bellarminus 1. agit de figura crucis. 11. de forma vexillorum crucis, & de Labaro seu vexillo Imperatoris. 111. de modo crucifixionis Christi. 1 v. Venerationem & cultum crucis veræ confirmat. Tres priores partes nihil faciunt ad controuersiam, sed lesuiticam produnt ostentationem: singula tamen examinabimus.
units.tr: In this chapter Bellarmine, first, treats of the shape of the cross; second, of the form of the standards of the cross and of the labarum or standard of the Emperor; third, of the manner of Christ's crucifixion; fourth, he affirms the veneration and worship of the true cross. The first three parts have nothing to do with the controversy and display only Jesuitical ostentation. Still, we shall examine each of them.

units.la: DE FORMA CRVCIS.
units.tr: ON THE FORM OF THE CROSS.

units.la: QVod ad figuram crucis Christi attinet, 1. proponit suam sententiam. 11. falsam refutat. Suam sententiam sicam sic describit. Sciendum inquit, tri- lignis factam esse, quorum vnum erat lo- cum, cui corpus adhærebat, alterum transfuer-sum superpositum longo, quibus affigebantur manus, tertium lignum erat infixum inligno pngo, vt in eo pedes crucifixi starent, & clauis figi possent. Id testatur Irenæus l. 2. c. 24. Iustinus, inquit, id est figura crucis fines & summitates habet quinque, duas in longitudinem, duas in altitudinem, vnam in medio in qua quiescit, qui clauis affigitur. Idem habet Iustinus in dialogo cum Tryphone vltra medium.
units.tr: As to the figure of Christ's cross, Bellarmine (1) sets out his own opinion and (2) refutes a false one. He describes his own opinion thus: "It should be known," he says, "that the cross was made of three pieces of wood. One was the upright beam, to which the body was attached; another was the transverse beam laid across the upright, to which the hands were fastened; the third piece of wood was fixed into the upright, so that the feet of the crucified man might stand on it and be nailed." Irenaeus testifies to this in book 2, chapter 24: "Justin," he says, "the figure of the cross has five ends and summits, two in length, two in height, and one in the middle, on which he rests who is fastened with nails." Justin says the same in his Dialogue with Trypho, beyond the middle.

units.la: Respond. I.
units.tr: Answer I.

units.la: Agnoscimus crucis figuram constare tribus lignis, idque sequenti declaratione testabor. Constabat igitur crux. I. erecto stipite. II. ligno transverso, cui manus brachijs expansis affixæ erant. III. ligno suppedaneo, cui insistebant pedes & simul clauis affixi erant; quod lignum vocant alij asserculum siue tabellam, innixi & fixi simul fuêre pedes, ne corporis tota moles à manibus solis penderet, vt quæ totum corpus sustinere non valuissent. Iustinus primus nobis tertium hoc lignum stipiti impactum aperuit, licet quod cornu instar fuisse docet, non probemus. Postquam enim E duo priora ligna defcripfiffet, ftipite arrectarium, & lignū tranfuerfarium, tertium fubiungit his verbis, καὶ τὸ τῶ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ὡς κέρας καὶ αὐτὸ ἴ- σχον ἐξὶν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐπιχείνται οἱ ζωγραφίμενοι & quod in medio impactum eft inftar cornu, ipfu eminet, cui innitutur ii, qui crucis fupplicium fubeunt. Ex Iuftino Tertullianus accepit idem, & fic nobis tradidit, cap. 10. aduerf. Iudæos. Vnicornis autem medio ftipitus palus. Rectè quidem in medio ftipitis palus cōftituitur, fed nōvnicor nis. Verba Irenæi à Bellarmino citata etiā huc erūt, vt mediū illud lignū cōfirmet. Medius enim ille finis eft tabel la illa in qua corp̄ requiefcit. Gregorius Nazianzen adftipulatur his verbis ἡλωσαν χεῖρας, τῶ δὲ ἀσφῆ λωσαν ὁ τῶ ὑπερτῶ ξύλῳ. Lignum illud impactum cui pedes affixi, quid aliud fuit quam aller ex crucis ligno arrectario prominens? Atque hunc afferem etiam in Chrifti cruce agnouit Gregorius Turonensis. In ftipite erecto ait foramen factum eft, Res quoq; parua tabula in hoc foramen infertus, fuper hanc vero, fuper hanc vero tabulam tanquam ftantis hominis facræ affixæ funt plantæ. Verum hæc neque ad præfentem controuerfiam, neque ad pietā[illegible, ~3 letters]ietatem quicquam faciunt. Quid huic materiali & exteriori adeo inhę- ret cruci?ad spiritualem & interiorem Christi crucem, passionem & mortem Christi dico, fides attollenda erat, pa- rum exemplo, q in cruce nō lignum, sed in ligno affixum Dominum conci- piebant & contéplabantur, teste Hie- ronymo in psalm 5. crux Christi columna est generis humani. In ipsa columna ædifi- cata est domus eius scilicet Christi: Ego crucem dico non lignum sed passionem.
units.tr: We acknowledge that the figure of the cross consisted of three pieces of wood, and I shall prove this by the following account. The cross therefore consisted of: (I) an upright stake; (II) a transverse beam, to which the hands were fastened with the arms outstretched; (III) a footrest, on which the feet rested and were nailed at the same time. Others call this piece a small plank or board. The feet were both propped up and fixed, so that the whole weight of the body would not hang from the hands alone, since the hands could not have borne the whole body. Justin was the first to reveal to us this third piece fixed into the upright, although we do not approve his claim that it was like a horn. For after describing the two earlier pieces, the upright stake and the transverse beam, he adds the third in these words: "And what is fixed in the middle like a horn is itself a projection, on which those who undergo the punishment of the cross rest" [καὶ τὸ τῷ μέσῳ πηγνύμενον ὡς κέρας καὶ αὐτὸ ἰσχὺν ἔχον ἐστίν, ἐφ' ᾧ ἐπικάθηνται οἱ σταυρούμενοι]. Tertullian took the same from Justin and so handed it down to us in chapter 10 of his work against the Jews: "Moreover, in the middle of the upright stake is a single peg." Rightly, indeed, a peg is placed in the middle of the stake, but not a single horn. The words of Irenaeus cited by Bellarmine will also serve here, to confirm that middle piece. For that middle projection is the little board on which the body rested. Gregory Nazianzen agrees with these words: "They nailed the hands; the feet they fastened to the wood..." [ἥλωσαν χεῖρας, τοῖς δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ... ξύλου]. That piece of wood fixed in, to which the feet were nailed, what else was it than a board projecting from the upright wood of the cross? Gregory of Tours also recognized this board in Christ's cross. He says that a hole was made in the upright stake, and a small board inserted into this hole; and on this board, as on that of a standing man, the sacred feet were fixed. But these things contribute nothing to the present controversy or to piety. Why should faith cling so closely to this material and external cross? Faith ought to be raised to Christ's spiritual and inward cross, I mean his passion and death. Those who looked on and contemplated the cross, not the wood but the Lord fastened to the wood, did so to good effect, as Jerome bears witness on Psalm 5: "The cross of Christ is the pillar of the human race. In that very pillar his house was built," that is, Christ's: "I call the cross not wood but the passion."

units.la: Solutio dubij subijcitur à Bellarmi- no.
units.tr: The solution of a doubt put forward by Bellarmine.

units.la: Vtrum autem lignum transuersum est supra positum ligno longo, ita vt non eminet ret lignum longum sursum versus, nō est cer- tum. Beda in quæstion. in Genesin, vbi de vi- ctoria Abrahæ loquitur, dicit crucem si- milem fuisse litera Græca T, qualem etiam fuisse olim Hebraicum T an docet Hieronymus in cap 9. Ezech. At beatus Augustinus Epistola 120 cap. 26. dicit lignum longum e- minuisse supra transuersum Et hoc est probabilius. Nam est conformius verbis Irenæi & verbis Apostoli ad Ephes. c. 3 vbi alludens ad figuram crucis nominat sublimitatem, profundum, longitudinem & latitudinem.
units.tr: Whether the transverse beam was placed above the long beam, so that the long beam did not project upward, is not certain. Bede, in his questions on Genesis, where he speaks of Abraham's victory, says the cross was like the Greek letter T, which Jerome also teaches the Hebrew T was once, in chapter 9 of Ezekiel. But blessed Augustine, in Epistle 120, chapter 26, says the long beam projected above the transverse one, and this is more probable. For it agrees better with the words of Irenaeus and with the words of the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter 3, where, alluding to the figure of the cross, he names the height, depth, length and breadth.

units.la: Porro qui dicunt crucem fuisse similem litera Thau, qui dicunt verum, quia parum differebat. E 2 Resp. I.
units.tr: But those who say the cross was like the letter Thau, they speak truly, because it differed little. Answer I.

units.la: Respond.I.Probo eorum sententi- am qui dicunt in cruce Christi, ligno erecto alterum transuersum fuisse im- missum,ita vt vertex arrectarij stipitis, veluti capitullum quoddam emineret, in quo deinde titulus,& αιτία criminis fuit fixa. Confirmat hanc sententiam descriptio crucis à Iustino institu. ξύλον γὰρ ἑστὼς ἐν ξύλῳ ait [arrectarius sc. stipes] ἀπ' ἧς ἐπὶ τὰ ἀνωτάτω μὲν & ἐκχεόμενον ὑπερεχόμενον, id est, vertex cui impingitur titulus, seu ἡ αἰτία. Quin & Augustinus cum Epistola 120. à Bellarmino citata, tum & in Psalmum 183. idem attestatur. Erat latitudo inquit, in qua portectae sunt manus, longitudo à terra surgens in qua erat corpus infixum, altitudo ab illo innexo ligno sursum quod eminet, profundum erat crux. Neque repugnat Cyprianus in libro de montibus Sina & Sion; verba eius haec sunt. Pontius Pilatus mente impulsa à Deo accepit tabulam & titulum scripsit tribus linguis, & in capite ligni clauis tabulam cum nomine Regis Iudaeorum transfixit. manifeste eminentiam seu capitellum indicat. Tabula vero illa cuius meminit, non super lignum, vt pictu- ræ vulgo repræsentant, sed in ipso capitello clauis fixa fuit. Bellarminus huc iuc tradit Irenæi & Apostoli Pauli verba, sed quâ probabilitate non vi-leo. Irenæi descriptio eminentiæ non neminit. Paulus loco citato de cruce Christi non loquitur, nec alludit ad crucem sed excellentiam & perfectionem charitatis Dei erga nos celebrat. Augustinus quidem & alij veteres de cruce Christi locum interpretantur, sed longe alium habet sensum. Extollit Apostolus charitatem Dei metaphora ducta à Geometricis dimensionibus, qua vult significare, eam omnibus partib. & numeris perfectissimam esse. Quod Beda & alij crucem cum littera Græca T componunt, id non de cruce illa in qua Christus mortuus est, intelligūt, sed de alia forma quæ æque fuit visitata, & in qua alij puniti fuêre. Neque enim una fuit crucis forma, put nunc non una est patibulorum forma, sed plures diuersæ; quædam crux fuit sine vlla eminentia seu vertice, formam Thau ad amussim referens, de qua Tertullianus. Ipsa enim litera Græcorum, Tau, nostra autem T, species crucis; &Isidorus, Tau litera speciem crucis demonstrat; Quædam vero vertice habebat, formam Tau non amussim representans;
units.tr: I approve the opinion of those who say that in Christ's cross an upright beam had a second, transverse beam set into it, so that the top of the upright post stood out like a little head, and the title and the charge of the crime were then fixed to it. Justin's description of the cross supports this opinion: "for a wood standing in wood [ξύλον γὰρ ἑστὼς ἐν ξύλῳ], projecting upward and raised above, that is, the top on which the title is struck, or the charge [ἡ αἰτία]." Augustine also attests the same thing, both in his Epistle 120, cited by Bellarmine, and in his commentary on Psalm 183: "There was breadth, he says, in which the hands were stretched out; length rising from the earth, in which the body was fixed; height, from that joined wood which projects upward; depth was the cross." Cyprian does not contradict this in his book on Mount Sinai and Sion. His words are these: "Pontius Pilate, moved in mind by God, took a tablet and wrote a title in three languages, and fixed the tablet with the name of the King of the Jews with a nail at the head of the wood." Here he clearly indicates the projection or little head. The tablet he mentions was not placed over the wood, as painters commonly depict it, but was nailed to the little head itself. Bellarmine here cites the words of Irenaeus and of the Apostle Paul, but I do not see with what plausibility. Irenaeus's description makes no mention of a projection. Paul, in the passage cited, does not speak of Christ's cross, nor does he allude to the cross; he praises the excellence and perfection of God's love toward us. Augustine and other ancient writers do indeed interpret the passage with reference to Christ's cross, but it has a quite different sense. The Apostle extols God's love by a metaphor taken from geometrical dimensions, meaning to signify that it is most perfect in all its parts and measures. As for Bede and others who compare the cross with the Greek letter T, they do not understand this of the cross on which Christ died, but of another form, which was equally in use and on which others were punished. For there was not one form of cross, just as there is not one form of gibbet today, but several different ones. One cross had no projection or head at all, and corresponded exactly to the form of the Tau, as Tertullian says: "For the letter of the Greeks, Tau, and our T, is the shape of a cross"; and Isidore: "the letter Tau shows the shape of a cross." Another cross did have a head, but did not represent the form of the Tau exactly.

units.la: E tans; siquidem Tau Græcum & Latinum vertice carent; in qua Christus fuit crucifixus. Quædam denique fuit decussata, cujus forma literam X referebat, quam Andreanam fuisse existimant, de quib. si placet Lipsium consule. Quod si vero censuerunt Tau Latinorum & Græcorum gessisse formam crucis Christi, id de exquisita similitudine, quæ examussim exprimit figuram T, non est intelligendum, sedque quadamtenus eam refert. Nam praeter capitellum, quo litera T caret, repræsentat figuram crucis: parua autem, illa differentia, quam facit capitellum non tollit similitudinem crucis cum littera Tau, ita ut hic Bellarmini æquitatem probem, qua statuit, eos qui dicunt crucem fuisse similem litera Tau, verum dicere, quia parum differebat. Si vero de absoluta loquuntur similitudinem falsum dicunt. Neque enim Tau Græcorum, & Latinorum crucis Christi speciem exquisitè referunt, cum hæc verticem habeat extantem quo caret Tau Græcum & Latinum. Quod Hieronymus dicit in cap. 9. Ezec. olim Hebraicum Tau habuisse similitudinem crucis, in eo fallitur, sequetur enim Hebraicas literas iteras fuisse mutatas. At non videtur probabile, Iudæos literas à Deo ipso acceptas abjecisse, & cum humanis inno gentilibus literis commutasse. Pij sacerdotes, Prophetæ, alijq; hanc mutationem non tulissent. Deceptus vero est Hieronymus errore originis, cuius fidem secutus est. Origenes scribit Tau Samaritanorum simile esse cruci aut Tau Latino vel Græco, sed recitat illud Origenes ex aliena fide, ἐδραίων ἀδετις ἰλεγε, inquit: Ipse igitur non vidit Alphabetum Samaritanorum, sed aliena fide id scripsit atque ita deceptus ipse, decepit Hieronymum, qui in illum locum expositionem Originis fere ad verbum transtulit: sed cum hæc omnia controversiam non attingant, pergamus.
units.tr: Still, the Greek and Latin Tau lack a head, and it was on a cross of this kind that Christ was crucified. Finally, there was a cross of crossed beams, whose shape resembled the letter X, which they think was the Andrean cross; on these kinds, if you wish, consult Lipsius. But if they thought that the Tau of the Latins and Greeks had the form of Christ's cross, this must not be understood as an exact resemblance, which expresses the figure T precisely, but as representing it only to a certain extent. For apart from the little head, which the letter T lacks, it represents the figure of a cross; that small difference which the head makes does not remove the resemblance of the cross to the letter Tau. So I approve Bellarmine's fairness here, when he holds that those who say the cross was like the letter Tau speak truly, because it differed little. But if they speak of complete similarity, they speak falsely. For the Greek and Latin Tau do not exactly represent the form of Christ's cross, since the cross has a projecting head, which the Greek and Latin Tau lack. As for Jerome's statement on chapter 9 of Ezekiel, that the Hebrew Tau once had the likeness of a cross, he is mistaken in this, for it would follow that the Hebrew letters had been changed. But it does not seem probable that the Jews rejected letters received from God himself and exchanged them for the letters of the heathen. Pious priests, prophets and others would not have endured such a change. Jerome was deceived by an error of origin, whose authority he followed. Origen writes that the Tau of the Samaritans is like a cross, or the Latin or Greek Tau, but Origen relates this on another's authority, "he said, the letter ἐδραίων ..." He himself therefore did not see the alphabet of the Samaritans, but wrote this on another's word, and so, being deceived himself, he deceived Jerome, who translated Origen's exposition on that passage almost word for word. But since all these matters do not touch the controversy, let us proceed.

units.la: Sequitur ut de falsa forma, quam Beda finxit, quædam dicamus. Quod Beda inquit Bellarminus scribit in suis collectaneis & floribus, crucem factam ex quatuor generibus lignorum, ex Cedro, Pino, Cypresso, & Buxo, & quod scribitur in historia Ecclesiastica de ligno erecto ex probatica piscina, &c. non habent veterum testimonia, nec videntur probabilia.
units.tr: Next, I should say something about the false form that Bede invented. Bellarmine writes, in his collections and flowers, that Bede says the cross was made from four kinds of wood: cedar, pine, cypress and box. What the Ecclesiastical History says about the wood raised up from the Probatic pool, and so on, has no support from the testimony of the ancients, nor does it seem probable.

units.la: Resp. Non minus hæc quam superiora riora à Controuersiâ sunt aliena: interim probamus candorem Bellarmini, qui hanc Bedæ fabulam agnoscit & reijcit. Impulit venerabilem Bedam affectus erga crucis lignū, vt hoc fingeret somnium. Cum enim superstitiose crederet, crucis lignū adhuc extare, vt verisimilitudinem aliquam superstitiosæ opinioni conciliaret, finxit ejusmodi lignis crucem constare, quæ maximæ erant durationis. Tales præposteri & superstitiosi affectus per multis Ecclesiarum contaminarùt fabulis, qualis & illa est, vt rem vnico saltem illustrem exemplo, quam de Gregorio Pontifice, & Traiano Imperatore commentus est Damascenus, Gregoriū scilicet, dum per forum Traiani iter faceret, preces habuisse ad Dominū pro Traiani anima, & ecce vocem diuinitus allatâ, preces tuas audiui & Traiano veniam do: tu vero non amplius me pro impiis orato. Nimis præposterus certe affectus erga preces pro defunctis Damascenum impulit ad hoc scribendū. Nam scholasticorum dogmati repugnat valere preces ad extrahendas animas è purgatorio extrahendas valere.
units.tr: Reply: these points are no less foreign to the controversy than the earlier ones. Meanwhile we commend Bellarmine's candour, since he acknowledges and rejects this fable of Bede. Affection for the wood of the cross moved the venerable Bede to invent this dream. Since he superstitiously believed that the wood of the cross still survived, he devised, to lend some plausibility to his superstitious opinion, that the cross was made of such woods as are most durable. Such perverse and superstitious affections have contaminated many fables in the Churches. Take, to illustrate the point with one notable example, the story that Damascene invented about Pope Gregory and the Emperor Trajan: that Gregory, while passing through the Forum of Trajan, made prayers to the Lord for Trajan's soul, and behold, a voice was brought from heaven: "I have heard your prayers and grant pardon to Trajan; but you must no longer pray for the impious." Certainly an excessively perverse affection for prayers for the dead moved Damascene to write this. For it contradicts the doctrine of the schoolmen that prayers avail to draw souls out of purgatory.

units.la: II. Opponimus hanc rationem Bellarmini
units.tr: II. We oppose this argument of Bellarmine.

units.la: Serm. de defunctis insid. larmini oppinioni Lipsij. Censemus inquit Lypsius, e quercu esse lignum crucis, quia frusta ligni huius, quae hodie extant, speciem hanc referunt, tum quia frequens & in Iudaea olim, & nunc quoq; arbor illa. At veterum testimonia non habet haec opinio, nec videtur probabilis. Cur non potius ex obeio aut pmto quodam ligno. Nysenus partem esse dicit arboris vilis contemptionisq;, quam aliae multae sunt.
units.tr: From Bellarmine's sermon on the dead, against the opinion of Lipsius. "We judge," says Lipsius, "that the wood of the cross is of oak, because the fragments of this wood that survive today show this appearance, and because that tree was common in Judaea both formerly and now." But this opinion has no support from the testimony of the ancients, nor does it seem probable. Why not rather from ebony, or from some other wood? Nyssen says it was part of a tree of base and contemptible kind, of which there are many others.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: De forma vexillorum crucis, & Labaro Imperatoris.
units.tr: On the form of the standards of the cross, and the Emperor's Labarum.

units.la: VEXILLA crucis ita describit: ut 1. formam eorum, 11. significationem declaret. De forma sic disserit. Illud non ignorandum est, veteres aliquid addidisse mysterij gratia, quod etiam nunc ex parte seruatur. Nam lignum longum producebant sursum versus, & flectebant ad modum baculi pastoralis, ut referret literam Graecam P. paulo inferius apponebant duo ligna transuersa ad similitudinem crucis Andreae, quae referrent literam Graecam X ita ut duae illae literae per abbreuiationem significarent Christum: infra illum ponebant lignum transuersum, quod vere perficit crucem & inde pendebat velum expansum: infra lignum transuersum uersum erat lignum in similitudinem hastæ, ad infimam partem addebat capulum ad commoditatem gestandi.
units.tr: He describes the standards of the cross in two parts: first their form, then their meaning. On the form he argues thus: "We must not be ignorant that the ancients added something for the sake of mystery, and that part of it is still kept even now. For they made a long piece of wood rising upwards and bent it at the top like a shepherd's staff, to represent the Greek letter P. A little further down they attached two crosspieces, like St Andrew's cross, which represented the Greek letter X, so that those two letters, by abbreviation, signified Christ. Below that they placed a crossbar, which truly completes the cross, and from it hung an outspread veil. Below the crossbar was a piece of wood in the likeness of a spear, and at the lowest end they added a handle for ease of carrying."

units.la: Respond. I. Negamus eiusmodi vexilla, qualia hic depinxit Bellarminus, Constantini temporibus ab Ecclesia vsurpata fuisse. In ipsis vexillis vero, vt & in vestibus, fenestris, parietibus, columnis, nummis & scutis crucem sculptam fuisse nouimus, sed eiusmodi vexilla, quæ & crucem & Christi nomen exprimerent Constantini ætate fuisse ab Ecclesia vsurpari, & haberi cepta negamus.
units.tr: Response I. We deny that standards of the kind Bellarmine depicts here were taken up by the Church in the times of Constantine. We know that a cross was carved on the standards themselves, as also on garments, windows, walls, columns, coins and shields. But we deny that standards of such a kind, which expressed both the cross and the name of Christ, were taken up and begun to be held by the Church in Constantine's age.

units.la: II. Si alicubi vexilla in formā quandā crucis mutauere, quid hoc ad rem? Vexilla illa non fuere processionalia, sed castrensia, vtpote quibus nonnisi in castris fuere vsi; neq; in templis, sed extra tépla in aliis locis fuere asseruata, tàtum abest, vt fuerint adorata aut adoranda populo proposita. Doceat Bellarm. à veteribus Christianis crucem circumferri solitam in hasta tanquam in processione, sicut hodie fit in Papatu: probet cultum diuinum à veteribus Christianis vexillis eiusmodi exhiberi solitum, vt nunc fit à Papicolis. Vsurparūt ea veteres Christiani in
units.tr: II. If somewhere they changed standards into some form of cross, what does that have to do with the matter? Those standards were not processional but military, since they were used only in camps. They were not kept in churches but were stored outside churches in other places, so far were they from being adored or set before the people for adoration. Let Bellarmine show that the cross was customarily carried about by the ancient Christians on a pole in procession, as is done today among the Papists. Let him prove that divine worship was customarily offered to standards of this kind by the ancient Christians, as now is done by the Papist worshippers. The ancient Christians used them

units.la: castris ad testificandam fidem suam in Christum crucifixum, qui vsus per fe non erat malus; sed progressu temporis & corrupta est doctrinæ veritas & vexilla illa in superstitionem & Idololatriam versa, ideoq; ab Ecclesiis nostris recte sublata.
units.tr: in camps to bear witness to their faith in Christ crucified, a practice which in itself was not evil. But as time went on, the truth of doctrine was corrupted, and those standards were turned into superstition and idolatry, and were therefore rightly removed by our churches.

units.la: Sequitur significatio.Hæc omnia inquit Bellarminus significabant crucem esse vexillum Imperatoris Christi; nam crucem testabatur ipsa figura: Christi nomen indicabat duæ literæ χρ; vexillum ex velo, hasta, & capulo dignoscebatur.
units.tr: Next comes the meaning. "All these things," says Bellarmine, "signified that the cross is the standard of Christ the Emperor; for the figure itself bore witness to the cross; the name of Christ was indicated by the two letters chi and rho; the standard was recognised from the veil, the spear and the handle."

units.la: Resp. I. ad significationem ergo non vero ad cultum & adorationem vexilla fuere proposita, ut patrum voces testantur, cruces nec colimus nec adoramus.
units.tr: Response I. The standards were therefore put forward to signify, not for worship and adoration, as the words of the Fathers bear witness: "we neither worship nor adore crosses."

units.la: II. Significationem illam imperfectè exprimit Bellarminus. Nam significabant ista omnia Christianis, crucem esse vexillum Christi Imperatoris, sed hoc fine, ut se sub Christi tanquam Imperatoris vexillo militare iudicarent, quem finem emittit Bellarminus, ut crucis adorationem tacite stabiliret. Viuebat enim Christiani tunc interEthnicos, & ab iis tanquam fatui videbantur, quod Christũ crucifixum adorarént, adorarent, ita vt illos per ludibrium, teste Tertulliano, religiosos crucis vo citarent; Christiani igitur id ostende- rent, se crucem Christi non erubescere, imo ea potissimum gloriari, signi ac vexilli loco eam sibi delegerunt, ipsorumq; ludibrijs crucem tanquam victoriae tropaeum & triumphi insigni opposuerunt.
units.tr: II. Bellarmine expresses that meaning imperfectly. For all these things signified to Christians that the cross is the standard of Christ the Emperor, but with this purpose: that they might judge themselves to be soldiers under the standard of Christ as their Emperor. Bellarmine puts forward this purpose so that he may quietly establish the adoration of the cross. For Christians at that time lived among the heathen, and were regarded by them as fools because they adored Christ crucified. So, as Tertullian testifies, the heathen mockingly called them worshippers of the cross. Christians therefore showed by their conduct that they were not ashamed of the cross of Christ, and indeed that they gloried in it above all. They chose it for themselves as their sign and standard, and set the cross against their mockery as the trophy of victory and the emblem of triumph.

units.la: De Labaro ita disserit, vt 1. mutationem ejus. 11. Formam describat. De mutatione sic disserit. Tale fere fuit in Labarum Constantini. Nam vt Eusebius refert l.9.hist.c.9. Labarum quod ante Imperatores gestari solebat & a militib. adorari, Constantinus in formam crucis redegit, hic tamen vt etiam vexilli formam non amitteret.
units.tr: On the Labarum he argues thus: first on its change, then he describes its form. On the change he says: "Something similar was the case with the Labarum of Constantine. For, as Eusebius reports in book 9 of his History, chapter 9, Constantine reduced to the form of the cross the Labarum which used to be carried before the emperors and adored by the soldiers; yet he did this so that it would not lose the form of a standard."

units.la: Respond.I. Quod a militibus dicit adoratum Labarum, id de ciuili adoratione intelligendum. Adorabant omnia signa seu vexilla Romani milites in primis praetorium signum, q; Labarum vocabatur, sed ciuili adoratione; quam ciuilem adorationem Constantinus deinde ptorio signo Christi nomine insignito deferri voluit, vt nõen Christi ludaeis & Paganis probrosum, omnibus honorificum redderet, atq; ita milites pedetetim ad Christū qué
units.tr: Response I. What he says about the Labarum being adored by the soldiers must be understood of civil adoration. The Roman soldiers adored all their standards, especially the praetorian standard, which was called the Labarum, but with civil adoration. Constantine afterwards wished this civil adoration to be transferred to the praetorian standard marked with the name of Christ, so that he might make the name of Christ, which was shameful to Jews and Pagans, honourable to all, and so gradually bring the soldiers to worship Christ, whom the Emperor himself worshipped.

units.la: Imperator colebat, colendum adduceret. Legati quidem & Tribuni Romanorū eandem adorationem in religiosam delabi, non illibenter interdū sinebant, quo militū animos quasi religione tum ad obeunda munia, tum ad ipsam pugnam eo magis abstringeret;
units.tr: The Roman legates and tribunes did not unwillingly allow this same adoration sometimes to slide into religious observance, so that it would bind the soldiers' minds, as it were by religion, both to the performance of their duties and to the battle itself.

units.la: Vnde Tertullianus Religio Romanorum tota Castrensis, signo veneratur, signa iurat, signa omnibus Diis praeponit; sed communiter moris erat, ciuiliter signa adorare, ita vt Constantin° ciuilem tantum adorationem, ab illo gentilitio vexillo, ad hoc Christianum transtulerint. Neq; enim adorationis gen° mutauit, ciuilem sc. in religiosam, sed tantū obiectū. Helena enim Constantini mater non adorauit lignum, ne quidem veram crucem, quia hic gentilius est error, & vanitas impiorum. mutauit obiectum, quia formam Aquilae deleuit, & nominis Christi signum, quod duabus Graecis literis exprimebatur χ, & ρ. intexuit.
units.tr: Hence Tertullian: "The whole religion of the Romans is military: it venerates the standard, swears by standards, and puts standards before all the gods." But it was customary in general to adore standards civilly, so Constantine transferred only the civil adoration from that gentile standard to this Christian one. For he did not change the kind of adoration, civil into religious, but only the object. For Helena, Constantine's mother, did not adore wood, not even the true cross, because that is a gentile error and the vanity of the impious. He changed the object, because he removed the form of the eagle and wove in the sign of the name of Christ, which was expressed by two Greek letters, chi and rho.

units.la: II. Nego quod Labarum in formam crucis rederit; in formam quae ipsi in aere apparuit, illud mutauit; ea autem fuit signum nominis Christi, quod constabat duabus Graecis literis χ & ρ coniunctis, ita vt ρ medio literae χ esset inserta.
units.tr: II. I deny that he turned the Labarum into the form of a cross. He changed it into the form that had appeared to him in the air. That was the sign of the name of Christ, which consisted of the two Greek letters chi and rho joined together, so that rho was inserted in the middle of chi.

units.la: ferta. Quod vero illud in formā crucis effictum dicitur σταυρὸς χρίσματι τὸ τροπαιοῦ, inde factum quod crucis similitudinem nonnihil referret. Atq; hoc ex ipsa origine causa mutationis huius conspicuum est. Nam cum Constantinus Maxentium esset aggressurus, & ambigenti & anxio apparuit in aëre signum non crucis sed Christi, ex duabus primis literis nominis Christi coflatum, τῆς σωτηρίας ἐπηγορίας τὸ σύμβολον, ut ait Eusebius ad huius figurae similitudinem post victoriam de Maxentio reportatā curauit formari Labarum, itaut hastile illam figuram retulerit, & ipsi velo etiam loco Aquilae eam intexuerit. Forma hastilis ex Eusebii descriptione talis fuit, ut hastile medium obliquè interfectum habuerit cornu transuersum, quod duas Græcas literas exprimebat, scilicet Græcanicam ρ decussatam & scissam per medium χ prout verba Eusebii sonant κατὰ τὴν μέσην διαίρεσιν. Formam veli Prudentius decantat.
units.tr: Carried. But that it is said to have been fashioned in the form of a cross, [σταυρὸς χρίσματι τὸ τροπαιοῦ], arises from the fact that it somewhat resembled the likeness of a cross. And this is evident from the very origin of the change. For when Constantine was about to attack Maxentius, and was uncertain and anxious, there appeared to him in the air a sign not of the cross but of Christ, compounded of the first two letters of the name of Christ, [τῆς σωτηρίας ἐπηγορίας τὸ σύμβολον], as Eusebius says. After the victory over Maxentius, he had the Labarum formed on the likeness of this figure, so that the shaft bore that figure, and he wove it into the veil itself in place of the eagle. The form of the shaft, according to Eusebius's description, was such that the shaft, cut obliquely through the middle, had a crosspiece which expressed two Greek letters, namely the Greek rho crossed and split through the middle by chi, as Eusebius's words sound: [κατὰ τὴν μέσην διαίρεσιν]. Prudentius sings of the form of the veil.

units.la: Christus purpureum gemanti textus in auro signabat labarum.
units.tr: Christ marked the purple standard with gold thread, [a verse from Prudentius]

units.la: Quomodo Christi nomen Christi in ipso velo fuerat expressum seu intexum deleta Aquilae forma.
units.tr: How the name of Christ was expressed or woven into the veil itself, with the eagle's figure removed.

units.la: Euseb. l. 1. de vita Constant. cap. 25.
units.tr: Euseb. l. 1. de vita Constant. cap. 25.

units.la: Sequitur Forma Labari, quam ex Eusebio describit Bellarminus.Fuit inquit, labarum hasta tota auro circumdata in cuius summitate posita erat corona pretiosa, infra eam cornu transuersum ad formam crucis, ex quo pendebat velum purpureum auro & gemmis ornatum, ad cuius partem intimam visebantur imagines Constantini & filiorum eius. In ipsa vero hasta sub corona erant litera nominis Christi.
units.tr: Next comes the form of the standard, as Bellarmine describes it from Eusebius. "The standard," he says, "was a long shaft wholly covered with gold, and at its top was set a precious crown. Beneath the crown was a crossbar in the form of a cross, from which hung a purple veil adorned with gold and gems. On the inner part of the veil were seen images of Constantine and his sons. On the shaft itself, under the crown, were the letters of the name of Christ."

units.la: Respond. I. non conuenit haec descriptio cum forma Eusebii, qui vult medium hastilis obliq; a cornu transuerso inter sectu fuisse, ita ut duas Graecas literas, quae primae erant literae nominis Christi expresserit, quae forma cum specie crucis nonnihil referret, dicitur Labarum ςαυρῶς σχῆμα ποικιλον. Ergo non simpliciter in ipsa hasta erat illae literae nominis Christi: sed hasta cum intersectione illius cornu transuersi referebat illas duas literas nominis Christi. Atque hanc formam Episcopi de signo crucis sunt interpretati propter similitudinem, ut Constantinum inde mysterium Christi crucifixi docerint.
units.tr: Reply I. This description does not agree with Eusebius's form. He says that the middle of the shaft was cut obliquely by the crossbar, so that it expressed two Greek letters, which were the first letters of the name of Christ. This shape, somewhat resembling the cross, is called the standard "a cross-like figure of varied form" [σταυροειδὲς σχῆμα ποικίλον]. So the letters of the name of Christ were not simply on the shaft itself. Rather, the shaft, where the crossbar intersected it, formed those two letters of the name of Christ. The bishops interpreted this form as a sign of the cross because of its resemblance, and so taught that Constantine learned from it the mystery of the crucified Christ.

units.la: II. Eam
units.tr: II. It (the cross)

units.la: II. Etiam, si vera sit forma Labarii Bellarmino posita, & crucis formam repræsentarit; nihil tamen huic causæ Pontificiæ accedit: Neque enim in templo fuit collocatum, & ad cultum propositum, sed p militari signo vsurpatum, & in Palatio Imperatoris repositum atque asseruatum fuit. Nunquam certè legimus, vel cruci, vel Labaro huic militari, extra templa Constantinū cultum aliquem diuinum exhibuisse, aut alios etiam id facere jussisse.
units.tr: II. Even if the form of the standard given by Bellarmine is true, and it represented the figure of the cross, nothing in it helps the Papist cause. For it was not placed in a temple and set up for worship, but was used as a military sign and kept and preserved in the emperor's palace. We never read that Constantine offered any divine worship to the cross, or to this military standard, outside the temples, or that he ordered others to do so.

units.la: III. De modo crucifigendi.
units.tr: III. On the manner of crucifixion.

units.la: DE modo crucifigendi sic disserit Bellarminus. Modus crucifigendi communis nonnerat, vt multi putant, funibus alligando, sed clauis figendo. Pictores vero solent solum Christum depingere clauis affixum, latrones autem & sanctum Petrum & Andream funibus, sed non ita est, omnes enim clauis figebantur, imo & omnes crucem suam ferebant, omnesque antea flagellis cadebantur. Vide Plutarchum de tardanum vindicta; Marcum Tullium act 7. in Verrem, Nonium Marcellum verbo patibulum, qui sic ait. De ligati ad patibulum circumferuntur, deinde crucifiguntur. Macrobium lib. 1. Saturn. cap. II. cap. 11. Iosephum lib. 6. de bello Iudaico cap. 13. & in vita sua. Adde quod ideo dubitatur quæ nam ex tribus repertis crucibus esset crux Dominica, quia omnes tres habebant foramina similia & clavos, &c.
units.tr: Bellarmine discourses thus on the manner of crucifixion: "The usual manner of crucifixion was not, as many think, by tying with cords, but by fixing with nails. Painters usually depict only Christ fixed with nails, but thieves, and St Peter and St Andrew, with cords. This is not so, for all were fixed with nails, and indeed all carried their own cross, and all were beforehand scourged with whips." See Plutarch, on the delay of divine vengeance; Marcus Tullius, Action 7 against Verres; Nonius Marcellus, under the word patibulum, who says: "Those bound to the patibulum are paraded about, then crucified." Macrobius, Saturnalia book 1, chapter 11; Josephus, Jewish War book 6, chapter 13, and in his Life. Add that people doubt which of the three crosses found was the Lord's cross, because all three had similar holes and nails, etc.

units.la: Resp. Neque hæc ad controversiam, sed ad ostentationem eruditionis facient; non tamen ut sibi videtur crucifixionis modum recte descripsit. Nam & funibus alligati & clavis fixi fuere; Clavis figebantur, sed funes fuere adminiculum, quibus circa humeros aut pectus medium fuere adstricti. Modus ergo hic videtur fuisse circumfixionis prout Scaliger eum in notis super Eusteb. Chron. describit. Primum fontes, pede in suppedaneum, seu lignum ex medio crucis stipite prominens, posito, crucem adscendebant, unde ascendere in crucem, insilire & excurrere in crucem apud Plautum, Ego dabo ei argentum primus qui in crucem excurrerit. Deinde pedibus asserti illi insistentes, funibus cruci fuere adstricti ad stipitem, quod ex Tertulliano colligitur. Tunc, inquit, Petrus ab altero cingitur cum cruci adstringitur. Tertio funibus constricti ad stipitem, binis clavis pedes in suppedaneo sunt confixi, & quidem singuli pedes
units.tr: Reply. These points do not bear on the controversy but serve only to display learning. Yet, as it seems to him, he has not correctly described the manner of crucifixion. For the victims were both tied with cords and fixed with nails. They were nailed, but the cords were an aid by which they were bound about the shoulders or the middle of the chest. So the manner here seems to have been that of fastening to the cross as Scaliger describes it in his notes on Eusebius's Chronicle. First the victims mounted the cross, a foot placed on a support, or a piece of wood projecting from the middle of the upright post; hence "to ascend the cross," "to leap up and run onto the cross" in Plautus: "I will give silver to the first who runs up onto the cross." Then, standing with their feet on that support, they were bound to the post with cords, as is gathered from Tertullian: "Then," he says, "Peter was girded by another when he was bound to the cross." Third, bound with cords to the post, their feet were fixed on the support with two nails, each foot with its own nail. Finally both hands were pierced with as many nails in the crossbeam, so that four nails were fixed in the victims, which Gregory of Tours also recognised as observed in Christ's cross: "The reason that there were four of the Lord's nails is this: two are fixed in the palms and two in the feet." The executioner then thrust a lance strongly through the middle of the diaphragm of the bound victim. What he adds about the finding of the three crosses is a fable and has nothing to do with the present matter.

units.la: Ex Tertulliano et Iosepho: notes of the margin as printed. pedes singuli clauis fixi. Deniq; ambæ manus totidem clauis in ligno transuersario transfixæ, ita vt quator clauis fixi fuerint sontes, quod etiam Gregorius Turonensis in Christi cruce obseruatum agnouit. Clauorum, inquit, Dominicorũ, quod quatuor fuerint hæc est ratio, duo sunt affixi palmis & duo plantis. Ita vero cõ strictos carnifex lacea per medium diaphragma strenuè trasfodit. Quod de inuentioe trium crucium addit, fabula est, & nihil ad rem præsentem facit.
units.tr: From Tertullian and Josephus: margin notes as printed. Each foot was fixed with its own nail. Finally both hands were pierced with as many nails in the crossbeam, so that four nails were fixed in the victims, which Gregory of Tours also recognised as observed in Christ's cross: "The reason that there were four of the Lord's nails is this: two are fixed in the palms and two in the feet." The executioner then thrust a lance strongly through the middle of the diaphragm of the bound victim. What he adds about the finding of the three crosses is a fable and has nothing to do with the present matter.

units.la: IV. Primum argumentum.
units.tr: IV. The first argument.

units.la: NVnc argumeta Bellarmini videamus. Primum est ex scripturis desumptum. Nam scripturæ testantur, ait, Christum non crucifixum casu aut inuitum, vel propter sua peccata, sed ipsum sponte elegisse vt altare summi sacrificij, quo placaretur Deus, vt scalam sibi ipsi ad regnum instrumentum liberationis generis humani, ac demum instrumentu, quo Diabolu vinceret, ac de eo triumpharet, ex quo sequitur crucem illam veram à Deo mirifice fuisse honoratam, & nobis omnibus amabilem & venerabilem esse debere. Syllogismus principalis est hic. Quod ab ipso Deo fuit mirifice honoratu, id à nobis amari & veneratione affici debeat. Crux illa vera ab ipso Deo fuit mirifice honorata. Ergo & à nobis amari & veneratione affici debet. Minor probatur, quia spōte elegit cru-ce, vt altare sūmi sacrificii, quo placa-retur Deus, vt scalam. &c. Resp. ad Maiorem à nobis amari & veneratioe affici debet, si constet illud in rerum natura extare. At negamus crucem vspiam in rerum natura extare. Neque enim dubium est, quin vel cæli in-iuriis aut saltem carie computruerit, aut vetustate sit erofa, idq; eo magis, si sub terram fuit defossa. Quod si arte aut studio seruatam dicas, certe vel in publico passionis loco, vel in priuato & occulto aliquo loco erit. Atqui in publico passionis loco seruari non po-tuit; quomodo enim in tot incen-diis & subuersionibus superstes ma-nere potuisset? Cum Vespasianus vrbem Hierosolymam obsideret. Ti-tus euerteret ac vastaret, num lig-num crucis Christi saluum manife-ste dixeris? Cum Andrianus Impe-rator terram sanctam Idolis Ethni-corum profanaret, atque in vrbe Templũ Ioui Olympio ædificaret, in loco crucis idolum Veneris poneret, nũ crucem seruari potuisse putaueris? Neq; in priuato aut occulto quodam loco fuit coseruata aut sub terram defossa. Tunc enim necessum fuisset crucem deponi. At non soliti fuere deponi cruces, neque Iudæi vel gentiles etiam id permisissent, audita præsertim fama de Christi resurrectione, quæ fama aspectu crucis tanquam visibili documento confutabatur. Deinde etiam huius depositionis & asseruationis nullus meminit Apostolus seu Historicus fide dignus. Quod vero mater Constantini Helena dicitur eam inquisiuisse, & miraculosè inuenisse, id fabulosum est, vt paulo post dicetur. II. Etiamsi constet eam in rerum natura extare, non tamen religiose colenda & adoranda esset. Non quidem contaminaremus eam, aut contumelia afficeremus, sed magnifaceremus, & ad rei gestæ memoriam conseruaremus; nequaquam vero adorandam, & latriæ cultu prosequendam statueremus. Quin si præsepe Christi adesset, non illud contemneremus, aut violaremus, sed honorifice tractaremus, religiose tamen neutiquam adoraremus, aut adorandam esse doceremus. Rursus ergo maior distinguitur: Quod Deus honorauit, nos etiam amare & venerari decet; scilicet amore & venerati[?]one ratione conuenienti ac debita, non in debita & illicita. Debitus autem & conueniens honor ex Dei institutione & voluntate æstimandus est. At nullibi instituit aut præcepit Deus, vt crucem illam in qua pependit Christus religiófo amore & veneratione prosequere-mur. Debitum interim amorem & veneratiońnem ei præstare non recusare-mus si extaret & in nostra esset potestate; non enim abijceremus eam, sed magnifaceremus, ad historicum vsum conseruaremus, at religiose non colere-mus. III. Quod Deus honore affecit scilicet tali qui permanet & perpetuo rei adoraret, id nobis amabile & venerabile erit. At tali honore non affecit lignum crucis, honor permanes est, qui rei ex natura vel institutione siue diuina siue humana competit. At ligno crucis non competit honor aliquis ex sua natura, neq; eo institutione aliqua legitima: sed si quis ei acceßit honor, ex sola pre-sentia obiecti honorabilis, Christi vi-delicet in eo suffixi, æstimatur; quo no amplius præsente, honor definit. Est i-gitur fallacia a non causa. Nam hono-re dicitur Deus affecisse crucem, non quod natura vel institutione iusta, efset honorabilis, sed quod Christum fi-lium suum, qui à natura Sanctus, & su-per omnia diligendus & honorandus, in se pendentem gestauit. Hic vero honor cum dependeat ex sola relatio-ne ad obiectum honorabile, relatione cessante etiam ipse cessat. Quare & li-gnum crucis, Christo ab eo remoto, omnem amisit honorem, & in pristi-nam conditionem est reuersum. Sic locus Exod 3. dicitur sanctitate & ho-nore quodam affectus, ob Dei præsen-tiam; Deo vero discedente, omnem il-lam suam sanctitatem & honore ami-sit, & ad pristinam naturam rediit. IV. Quod à Deo mirifice est honoratum, id nobis amabile & venerabile esse de-bet, scilicet quamdiu in abusum idolo-latricum non rapitur. Nam cum æne-us serpens hoc fuisset affectus honore à Deo, ut figura esset. Christi crucifixi, & ad eius adspectum morsi, ab ignitis serpentibus sanarentur; Israelitæ vero eo abuterentur ad Idololatriam, non amplius amore & veneratione dig-nus est habitus, sed comminutus fuit ab Ezechia, licet iussu diuino à Mose esset erectus. At lignea crux Christia-pud Pontificios in fœdissimam super-stitio titionem & idololatriam transiit,vt q folennibus missis illi incensum adolens, & vt singulare aduersus Satha˒nam propugnaculum colunt & adorant. Quare non debet amplius eflea-nabilis & venerabilis, sed comminui & tolli, sicut Ezechiæ æneus ille fer-pens,non erat amplius amabilis & venerabilis, postquam eo ad Idololatriam Ifraelito fuere abusi. Atque id-ipsum ius Pontificium præscribit his verbis. Si non nulli ex prædecessoribus & maioribus nostris fecerunt aliqua, quæ illo tempore potuerunt esse sine culpa, & postea ver-tuntur in errorem & superstitionem, doce-mur nos exemplo Ezechiæ frangentis ser-pentem æneum, illa sine tarditate aliqua & cum magna authoritate à posteris posse de-strui. V. Est fallacia ignorationis Elenchi, concludit enim argumentum crucem debere esse amabilem. At de amore & veneratione non est quæstio, sed de cursu latrias, an cultus latrias seu religiosus amor & veneratio deferenda sit cruci, quod nos negamus, Nomen amoris & venerationis à cultu latrias, id est, à religiosa veneratione seu adoratione diligenter distingui debet.
units.tr: Now let us look at Bellarmine's arguments. The first is taken from Scripture. "The Scriptures testify," he says, "that Christ was not crucified by chance or against his will, or because of his own sins, but that he himself freely chose it as the altar of the supreme sacrifice by which God was appeased, as a ladder to heaven for himself, as the instrument of the deliverance of the human race, and finally as the instrument by which he would conquer the devil and triumph over him. From this it follows that that true cross was marvellously honoured by God, and ought to be loved and venerated by all of us." The main syllogism is this: "What was marvellously honoured by God himself ought to be loved by us and affected with veneration. That true cross was marvellously honoured by God himself. Therefore it ought also to be loved and affected with veneration by us." The minor is proved because he freely chose the cross as the altar of the supreme sacrifice by which God was appeased, as a ladder, etc. Reply to the major: it ought to be loved and venerated by us, if it is certain that it exists in nature. But we deny that the cross exists anywhere in nature. For there is no doubt that it has either rotted from the injuries of the sky, or at least from decay, or has been eaten away by age, and all the more if it was buried under the ground. But if you say it has been preserved by skill or care, then surely it would be either in the public place of the Passion, or in some private and hidden place. Yet it could not have been preserved in the public place of the Passion; for how could it have survived so many fires and overthrows? When Vespasian besieged the city of Jerusalem, and Titus overthrew and laid it waste, would you say the wood of Christ's cross was plainly safe? When the Emperor Hadrian profaned the holy land with the idols of the Gentiles, and built in the city a temple to Jupiter Olympius, and placed an image of Venus in the place of the cross, would you think the cross could have been preserved? Nor was it kept in some private or hidden place, or buried under the ground. For then it would have been necessary to take the cross down. But crosses were not usually taken down, nor would the Jews or the Gentiles have permitted it, especially since the report of Christ's resurrection had been heard, a report that was refuted by the sight of the cross as a visible proof. Moreover, no apostle or trustworthy historian mentions any such taking down or preservation. As for the story that Constantine's mother Helena sought it out and miraculously found it, that is fabulous, as will be said a little later. II. Even if it were certain that it exists in nature, it would not be to be worshipped and adored with religious honour. We would not indeed defile it or treat it with contempt, but we would hold it in honour, and keep it in memory of the event; yet we would by no means set it up to be adored and pursued with the worship of latria. Indeed, if the manger of Christ were present, we would not despise or violate it, but would treat it with honour; yet we would by no means religiously adore it, or teach that it is to be adored. Again, then, the major is distinguished: what God has honoured, we too ought to love and venerate, namely with a love and veneration that is fitting and due, not with what is undue and unlawful. But the due and fitting honour is to be measured by God's institution and will. Yet nowhere has God instituted or commanded that we should pursue that cross on which Christ hung with religious love and veneration. Meanwhile we would not refuse to show it the due love and veneration if it existed and were in our power; for we would not cast it away, but would hold it in honour, and keep it for historical use, but we would not worship it religiously. III. What God has honoured with such honour as remains and is perpetual, that will be lovable and venerable to us. But the wood of the cross has not been endowed with such honour. Lasting honour is that which belongs to a thing by its nature or by institution, whether divine or human. But no honour belongs to the wood of the cross by its nature, nor by any lawful institution. If any honour has come to it, it is judged to arise solely from the presence of an honourable object, namely Christ fixed upon it; when he is no longer present, the honour ceases. There is therefore the fallacy of a false cause. For God is said to have honoured the cross, not because it was by nature or by just institution honourable, but because it bore in itself his Son Christ, who by nature is holy and to be loved and honoured above all things. This honour, since it depends solely on the relation to an honourable object, ceases when that relation ceases. Hence the wood of the cross, once Christ was removed from it, lost all its honour and returned to its former condition. So too the place in Exodus 3 is said to have been endowed with a certain holiness and honour because of God's presence; when God departed, it lost all that holiness and honour and returned to its former nature. IV. What has been marvellously honoured by God ought to be lovable and venerable to us, namely as long as it is not seized for the abuse of idolatry. For when the bronze serpent had been endowed by God with the honour of being a figure of the crucified Christ, so that those bitten by fiery serpents were healed by looking at it, yet the Israelites abused it for idolatry, it was no longer regarded as worthy of love and veneration, but was broken in pieces by Hezekiah, although it had been raised by Moses at God's command. But the wooden cross of Christ among the Papists has passed into the most foul superstition and idolatry, since they burn incense to it at solemn masses, and worship and adore it as a unique bulwark against Satan. Therefore it ought no longer to be lovable and venerable, but to be broken up and destroyed, just as Hezekiah's bronze serpent was no longer lovable and venerable once the Israelites had abused it for idolatry. And the Papal law itself prescribes this very thing in these words: "If some of our predecessors and forebears did things which at that time could be without fault, but afterwards turned into error and superstition, we are taught by the example of Hezekiah, who broke the bronze serpent, that those things can be destroyed by posterity without any delay and with great authority." V. This is the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi: the argument concludes that the cross ought to be lovable. But the question is not about love and veneration, but about the worship of latria: whether the worship of latria, that is, religious love and veneration, is to be paid to the cross. This we deny. The name of love and veneration must be carefully distinguished from the worship of latria, that is, from religious veneration or adoration.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus. At elegit crucem. Respond. quid hæc electio ad cultum latriæ? non probat hæc crucis electio latriam seu religiosam crucis adorationem. Quod Deus ad latrias veneratione elegit, id cultu latrias a nobis affici debet. At non elegit Deus crucem in hunc vsum, vt latria ipsi deferretur siue ppria siue impropria. Elegit Deus eam, vt Christus mortem in ea sustineret, non vt religiosa adoratio ei, etiam quæcunq; tribueretur. Si in hunc finem elegisset eam, mandato Dei & promissione exauditionis hæc electio stabilita & munita esset. At destituta est mandato & permissione exauditionis. Ergo non elegit eam ad cultum latrias.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses on: "But he chose the cross." I reply: what does this choice have to do with latria? This choice of the cross does not prove latria, that is, religious adoration of the cross. What God chose for latria, we must honour with latria. But God did not choose the cross for this use, that latria should be paid to it, whether proper or improper. He chose it so that Christ might endure death on it, not so that religious adoration should be paid to it, whatever is attributed to it. If he had chosen it for that end, the choice would have been confirmed and fortified by a command of God and a promise that prayers would be heard. But it is without command and without promise that prayers will be heard. Therefore he did not choose it for latria.

units.la: Instat. At elegit eam, vt esset altare sacrificij, in quo placaretur Deus.
units.tr: But he chose it to be the altar of sacrifice, on which God was propitiated.

units.la: Resp. Nihil ad rem. Non enim sequitur, Elegit crucem, vt esset altare sacrificii Christi; Ergo religiose estadoranda. Si eum ad cultum adorationis elegisset, omnino adoramus eam. At huius electionis ad cultum adorationis factæ, nullum extat testimonium in scripturis.
units.tr: Reply: this is beside the point. It does not follow that, because he chose the cross to be the altar of Christ's sacrifice, it is therefore to be adored religiously. If he had chosen it for the purpose of adoration, we would certainly adore it. But there is no testimony in Scripture to any choice made for the purpose of adoration.

units.la: Instat. Altare summi sacrificij quo Deus placetur, laeatur, merito est amabile & venerabile, ut crux Christi est altare summi sacrificii quo Deus placetur. Ergo crux amabilis & venerabilis esse debet.
units.tr: Objection: The altar of the supreme sacrifice, by which God is placated and delighted, is rightly lovable and venerable; the cross of Christ is the altar of the supreme sacrifice by which God is placated. Therefore the cross must be lovable and venerable.

units.la: ad Maiorem debet esse amabile & venerabile, nempe veneratione & amore debito atque congruenti, non vero indebito, qualis est latria, sive directa, sive indirecta, propria sive impropria.
units.tr: To the major premise: it must be lovable and venerable, namely with the love and veneration that are due and fitting, but not with undue worship, such as latria is, whether direct or indirect, proper or improper.

units.la: Mutatur genus praedicationis. Maior proprie intelligitur. Minor figurate; aut si proprie, falsa est. Est enim crux altare summi sacrificii Christi, locutione metaphorica, qua veteris Testamenti figurae ad mortem Christi trans feruntur. Cuius sensus est, crux est instar aeris, in qua sanguinem suum profudit, & semel obstulit ad Deum placendum. Hinc vero nequit concludi eam esse adorandam.
units.tr: The kind of predication changes. The major is understood properly, the minor figuratively; or, if the minor is taken properly, it is false. The cross is the altar of Christ's supreme sacrifice by a metaphorical manner of speaking, by which the figures of the Old Testament are transferred to the death of Christ. The sense is this: the cross is like the bronze altar, on which he poured out his blood and once offered it to placate God. From this, however, it cannot be concluded that it is to be adored.

units.la: Rursum ad maiorem respondeo, debet esse amabile & venerabile, scilicet quamdiu in abusum Deo erosum non transfertur, quod sit cum in idololatriam rapitur & ut Deus adoratur. Tunc enim, licet a Deo instituum & electum sit, abrogandum est, & tolledum, exemplo regis Ezechiae.
units.tr: Again, to the major I reply: it must be lovable and venerable, that is, so long as it is not turned to abuse. This happens when it is drawn into idolatry and worshipped as God. For then, although it was instituted and chosen by God, it must be abrogated and removed, after the example of King Hezekiah.

units.la: At crux Christi versa est in horredam idololatriam; quia ut Deus adoratur.
units.tr: But the cross of Christ has been turned into a horrible idolatry, because it is worshipped as God.

units.la: Etsi enim non dicat aut sentiant crucem esse ipsum Deum: tamen cum honorem Dei ipsi tribuat, fidem & spem in ea reponant, omnino ut Deum adorant. Nam ut auari dicuntur idololatræ & pecuniam ut Deum adorare, non quod pecuniam reputent, aut sentiant esse Deum; sed quod spem vitæ salutemque in ea colerent, quam in solo Deo vero collocare oportebat: ita & Papistæ sunt staurolatræ, & crucem ut Deum adorant, non quod ipsam statuant esse Deum, sed quod in & ex ea salutem sperent.
units.tr: For although they do not say or think that the cross is God itself, yet, since they attribute to it the honour of God and place their faith and hope in it, they worship it altogether as God. As the avaricious are called idolaters and worship money as God, not because they reckon or think money to be God, but because they cherish in it the hope of life and safety, which ought to be placed in the true God alone: so also the Papists are staurolaters, and worship the cross as God, not because they hold it to be God, but because they hope for salvation in and from it.

units.la: Instat. At elegit eam, ut sibi esset scala ad regnum cælorum.
units.tr: Objection: But he chose it to be a ladder for himself to the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Respond. I. Quæstio est de religioso amore, & cultu latrias, quem negamus deferendum cruci. Amabilem & venerabilem esse, si adesset, affirmamus, sed religiosè colendum negamus; amabilis & venerabilis est antiquitas, non tamen religiosè colenda. Tabernaculum teste Hieronymo fuit amatum & veneratum, sed non religiose cultum & adoratum, ut supra dictum. II. Hæc ratio electionis non euincit religiosum cultum & amorem crucis, utpote qui non exc-
units.tr: Reply I. The question concerns religious love and the worship of latria, which we deny is to be paid to the cross. We affirm that it is lovable and venerable, if it is present, but we deny that it is to be worshipped religiously. Antiquity is lovable and venerable, yet not to be worshipped religiously. The tabernacle, as Jerome testifies, was loved and venerated, but not religiously worshipped and adored, as said above. II. This reason of choice does not establish religious worship and love of the cross, since it is to be judged not from such a choice

units.la: ex electione tali, sed ex institutione & voluntate Dei æstimandus est. Nam licet elegerit sibi eam in scalam ad regnum cœlorum ; non tamen instituit eam in cultum & adorationem. III. Antecedens est falsum de cruce materiali seu lignea. Non enim lignum, sed passio & mors Christi fuit in ipsa scala, hoc est via, per quam pervenit ad gloriam, vt docetur ex Luc. 24. Nonne oportuit Christum pati ista, atque introire in gloriam Dei: A cruce spirituali ad materialem non valet consequentia. IV. De sepulchro Christi & monte oliveti etiam dici potest, quod fuerint ipsi scala, perueniendi ad regnum cœlorum, quis hinc volet se euincere, sepulchrum Christi & montem oliueti adorandum esse. V. Si cum scala volent crucem Christi conferre, non est dicenda scala, qua ad regnum cœlorum contendit, sed qua in victimam pro genere humano sese obtulit, & peccata nostra expiauit. Quid vero hæc scala adorationem crucis?
units.tr: but from the institution and will of God. For although he chose it for himself as a ladder to the kingdom of heaven, he did not institute it for worship and adoration. III. The antecedent is false with regard to the material or wooden cross. For it was not the wood but the passion and death of Christ that were the ladder, that is, the way by which he came to glory, as is taught from Luke 24: "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and so entered into the glory of God?" From the spiritual cross to the material cross the consequence does not hold. IV. Of Christ's sepulchre and the Mount of Olives it can also be said that they were a ladder for him to reach the kingdom of heaven. Who would wish to prove from this that the sepulchre of Christ and the Mount of Olives are to be adored? V. If they wish to compare the cross of Christ to a ladder, it should not be called the ladder by which he strove toward the kingdom of heaven, but the one by which he offered himself as a victim for the human race and expiated our sins. But what does this ladder have to do with adoration of the cross?

units.la: Instat. At fuit instrumentum liberationis generis humani, vt docent plurima plurima figura, quas collegit Iohannes Damascenus l.4. de Fide c.1 2. Idenim significavit lignu vitae in paradiso. Gen.c.2 Arca Noë lignea domu eius saluans. Gen.7 Virga Moysi aperiès mare. Exod.14. lignum aquas dulces reddes. Exod.15.sed praecipue serpes æneus exaltus in deserto. Numer.18.de quo Dominus Ioh 3. Sicut exaltauit Moses serpentem in deserto; ita exaltari oportet filium hominis, ut omnis qui credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Hinc videlicet, Ecclesiastes cuta Paulum ad Galat. c.6. dicit, Nos autem gloriari oportet in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi, in quo est vita, salus & resurrectio nostra.
units.tr: Objection: But it was the instrument of the liberation of the human race, as very many figures teach, which John Damascene gathered in book 4 On the Faith, chapter 1 2. For it signified the tree of life in paradise (Gen. 2); Noah's wooden ark saving his household (Gen. 7); the rod of Moses opening the sea (Exod. 14); the wood making the bitter waters sweet (Exod. 15); but especially the bronze serpent lifted up in the desert (Numb. 18), of which the Lord says in John 3: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." Hence the Church, following Paul in Galatians 6, says: "But we ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom is our life, salvation and resurrection."

units.la: Resp.I. Negatur ligneam crucem fuisse instrumentum liberationis nostrae. Si enim liberationis nostrae, etiam reconciliationis & salutis nostrae fuerit instrumentum. At hoc falsum est, quia instrumentum cooperatur causae principali. At nulla fuit in lignea cruce cooperatio. Quid enim lignum crucis ad salutem vel ad victoriam obtinendam contra Diabolum contulit? Instrumentum ergo fuit supplicii & mortis Christi, non vero reconciliationis & salutis nostrae.
units.tr: Reply I. It is denied that the wooden cross was the instrument of our liberation. For if it were the instrument of our liberation, it would also be the instrument of our reconciliation and salvation. But this is false, because an instrument cooperates with the principal cause, and there was no cooperation in the wooden cross. For what did the wood of the cross contribute to our salvation, or to obtaining victory over the Devil? It was therefore the instrument of Christ's punishment and death, but not of our reconciliation and salvation.

units.la: II. Esto fit instrumentum liberationis nostrae, num propterea adoranda? [illegible, ~6 letters]randa? Iudas proditor, carnifices, vir[illegible, ~3 letters]ae, quibus cæsus, claui quibus fixus, [illegible, ~3 letters]columna, cui alligatus, spineæ, quibus [illegible, ~3 letters]coronatus & similia non minori iure [illegible, ~3 letters]nstrumenta liberationis & salutis no[illegible, ~3 letters]træ possunt appellari, q; lignum cru[illegible, ~3 letters]cis; quia aliquo modo nobis salutem [illegible, ~3 letters]procurarunt. Quis hæc omnia dixerit [illegible, ~3 letters]eligiosè colenda. III. Distinguo maio[illegible, ~3 letters]rem; sed vt distinctio intelligatur, ar[illegible, ~3 letters]gumentū ad formam syllogismi reuo[illegible, ~3 letters]cabo. Syllogismus talis est. Quod Deus voluit esse instrumentum liberationis, id à no[illegible, ~3 letters]bis est adorandum. At voluit crucem esse instrumentum liberationis. Ergo à nobis ado[illegible, ~3 letters]randa est. Distinctio hæc est. Quod Deus voluit esse instrumentum liberatio[illegible, ~3 letters]nis, & simul obiectum adorationis, id adorādum est. At noluit Deus crucem esse obiectū adorationis: quia nullam creaturam vult esse obiectū adoratio[illegible, ~3 letters]nis; Et solus liberator noster est obiectum adorationis; nō verò instrumen[illegible, ~3 letters]tū liberatoris, seu liberationis nostræ, obiectū adorationis esse potest. IV. Ne[illegible, ~3 letters]atur etiam maior, id est, quia quod a[illegible, ~3 letters]orandū est, non debet esse pura crea[illegible, ~3 letters]tura. At lignum crucis est pura creatu[illegible, ~3 letters]ra. Quæ deinceps declarationis ergo in medium deducit Bellarminus peʒ se corruunt.
units.tr: II. Granted that it is the instrument of our liberation, is it therefore to be adored? Judas the traitor, the executioners, the rods with which he was struck, the nails with which he was fixed, the column to which he was bound, the thorns with which he was crowned, and the like, can with no less right be called instruments of our liberation and salvation than the wood of the cross, since in some way they procured salvation for us. Who would say that all these are to be worshipped religiously? III. I distinguish the major premise; but so that the distinction may be understood, I reduce the argument to the form of a syllogism. The syllogism is this: What God willed to be an instrument of liberation, that is to be adored by us. But he willed the cross to be an instrument of liberation. Therefore it is to be adored by us. The distinction is this: what God willed to be an instrument of liberation and at the same time an object of adoration, that is to be adored. But God did not will the cross to be an object of adoration, because he wills no creature to be an object of adoration; only our Liberator is the object of adoration. The instrument of the Liberator, or of our liberation, cannot be an object of adoration. IV. The major may also be denied, namely because what is to be adored ought not to be a mere creature. But the wood of the cross is a mere creature. Therefore whatever Bellarmine brings forward in the way of proof collapses of its own accord.

units.la: Damascéni interpretationes, I. sunt allegoricæ, ac proinde ad fidei dogma confirmandam inualidæ. II. Sunt coactę, & exiguam verisimilitudinem habent. III. Licet cõuenientes essent, apteque significarent hunc vsum crucis, eam scilicet esse instrumentum liberationis: tamen adorationem crucis euincere nequeunt. Nullius rei adoratio & cultus ex vsu eius, sed ex eius natura & Dei mandato atque institutione est æstimandus. Quod ad naturam crucis attinet, est lignum; ligno non debetur honor adorationis. Quod ad mãdatum Dei attinet, tale nullum de eius adoratione extat in sacris scripturis. IV. Nec ipse Damascenus fuit ita superstitiosus, vt ex figuris illis adorationem crucis voluerit euincere. V. Agnoscimus etiam serpentis æneï exaltationem, significasse exaltationem Christi in cruce, sed quid hoc ad adorationem crucis? Æneus serpens fuit Christi typus & imago, fuit etiam instrumentum sanationis & liberationis populi, neq; tamë religiosè cultus fuit & adoratus, sed postq; coli cœpit & adorari. dorari, rex Ezechias illū cōfregit. Eo- de plane modo crux Christi lignea, adorari nō debet, licet sit instrumetum liberationis, aut si adoretur tolli & cōminui debet. Deniq; Ecclesię auto- ritas, q. adducit, crucis adoratione ne- quaquam confirmat. Dictum eius ex Paulo sumptum, nō proprie de lignea cruce, sed metonymicè de Christo crucifixo intelligendū est. In hoc solo iubet nos gloriari nō in ligno. Quiglo- riatur, ait, Paulus, in Domino glorietur. Gloriabantur Iudæi in circumcisione & Lege. Aduersus hoc Paulus ait, se non gloriari, nisi in cruce Domini nostri Iesu Christi, i.e. in Iesu crucifixo, quem dicit se pdicare & cuius sanguine etiam vocat sanguinem crucis eadem metonymia, id est, Christi crucifixi. Vt igitur Paulus non intelligit crucem materiā lē seu lignum crucis, sed ligno affixum Dominum: Ita etiam Ecclesia, quæ Paulum secuta est, idem dicit.
units.tr: The interpretations of Damascene are, first, allegorical, and so invalid for confirming a dogma of faith. Second, they are forced and have little plausibility. Third, even if they were appropriate and aptly signified this use of the cross, namely that it is the instrument of our liberation, they still cannot prove the adoration of the cross. The adoration and worship of anything must be judged not from its use but from its nature and from God's command and institution. As to the nature of the cross, it is wood, and honour of adoration is not owed to wood. As to God's command, there is no such thing in the sacred Scriptures concerning its adoration. Fourth, Damascene himself was not so superstitious as to wish to prove the adoration of the cross from those figures. Fifth, we acknowledge that the lifting up of the brazen serpent signified the lifting up of Christ on the cross, but what has this to do with the adoration of the cross? The brazen serpent was a type and image of Christ, and it was also the instrument of healing and deliverance for the people; yet it was not worshipped and adored as a religious object, but only after it began to be venerated and adored, and King Hezekiah broke it in pieces. In exactly the same way, the wooden cross of Christ ought not to be adored, although it is the instrument of our liberation; and if it is adored, it ought to be removed and broken up. Finally, the authority of the Church, which they cite, by no means confirms the adoration of the cross. Its saying, taken from Paul, is not to be understood properly of the wooden cross, but metonymically of the crucified Christ. Paul bids us to glory in this alone and not in wood: "Let him who glories, he says, glory in the Lord." The Jews gloried in circumcision and the Law. Against this Paul says that he does not glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, in Jesus crucified, whom he says he preaches, and whose blood, by the same metonymy, he calls the blood of the cross, that is, of the crucified Christ. Therefore, just as Paul does not understand the cross as material, or the wood of the cross, but the Lord fastened to the wood, so also the Church, which followed Paul, says the same thing.
