units.la: Instat. At cruce Diabolum vicit & de eo triumphauit, vt patet ex epistola Colosf. 2. Chirographum decreti, quod erat contrarium nobis, tulit de medio tollens, affigens illud cruci, exspolians principatus & potestates, traduxit palam, confidenter
units.tr: Objection. But by the cross he conquered the Devil and triumphed over him, as is clear from the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2: "Having blotted out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."

units.la: 1. Cor. 1, 33. Coloss. 1, 16. confidenter triumphans illos in semetipso. Origenes Homil. 8. in Iosuæ dicit in Græcis habet, triumphans illos in ligno crucis, & licet nunc non habeamus in ligno, sed eum αὐτῷ in ipso; tamen optime referri potest ad crucem, de qua supra dixerat ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ, ut refert Theophrastus. Dicit ergo Origenes in cruce duos fuisse affixos Christum visibiliter passum sua & ad tempus: Diabolum invisibiliter, inultum & in sempiternum eius opprobrium: & hoc probat ex isto loco, ubi Apostolus utitur metaphora triumphi, indicare volens currum esse currum triumphalem, in cuius summa parte sedet Christus triumphans, & in summa parte trahitur Diabolus alligatus, & ostentatur quasi in pompa. Id enim significat verbum. ἐδειγμάτισεν & θριαμβεύσας.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 1.33; Col. 1.16. Triumphing over them confidently in himself. Origen, Homily 8 on Joshua, says: the Greek has "triumphing over them in the wood of the cross" [ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ]; and although we now do not have "in the wood" but "in it" [αὐτῷ], nevertheless it can very well be referred to the cross, of which he had spoken above as "in the wood" [ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ], as Theophrastus reports. Origen therefore says that two were fastened to the cross: Christ, who suffered visibly and for a time, and the Devil, invisibly, unavenged and to his everlasting shame. He proves this from that passage, where the Apostle uses the metaphor of a triumph, wishing to show that the cross is a triumphal chariot, on the highest part of which Christ sits triumphant, and on the lowest part of which the Devil is dragged bound and displayed as if in a procession. For the word signifies this: "having made a show of" [ἐδειγμάτισεν] and "triumphing" [θριαμβεύσας].

units.la: Resp. Ventosa est instantia, arguens vanissimam ingenii ostentationem, sed ad causam nihil confert. I. Negatur maior. Nō enim id, quo vel in quo Diabolum Deus vicit, continuo est adorandū, sed ipse Diaboli victor adoradus est. Is vero est solus Christus mediator noster, de quo id prædictum est Gen. 3. Semen mulieris, conteret caput serpentis, Cuius prædictionis complementum indicatur. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 8. Ad hoc patefactus est, ut destrueret opera Diaboli. II. Negatur gatur minor. Non enim cruce, id est ligno crucis, sed morte crucis, vicit Diabolum. Quod morti crucis competit, id perperam ad lignum crucis transferunt. Sed hoc solenne est Pontificiis Doctoribus, ut ab hac cruce, id est, passione & morte Christi, ad lignū crucis, in quo extensus fuit Christus, devoluantur. III. Locus Pauli ex 2. cap. Colos. non tribuit victoriam crucimateriali, sed Christo crucifixo; significatur isto loco Christum, cum in crucem ageretur, eo ipso tempore Diabolos in cruce egisse, ita ut hoc loco Paulus virtutem, non crucis ligneæ, sed passionis & mortis Christi prædicet. Agnosco illud ἐν σταυρῷ respondere præcedenti substantiuo τῷ σταυρῷ, prout Græcus scholastices & Origenes interpretantur; non tamen hæc lectio, ut Bellarminus opinatur, ligneæ cruci victoriam, & triumphum defert, sed morti seu crucifixioni Christi. Significatur enim morte Christi in cruce deiicisse Dæmones, seu Christum victorem & triumphatorem extitisse in cruce, id est, virtute crucifixionis suæ. Agnosco & illud, quod Origenes dicit in cruce duos fuisse affixos, Christum visibiliter, Diabolum invisibiliter, sub Diaboli
units.tr: Reply. The instance is empty, showing only a very vain display of wit, and contributes nothing to the case. First, the major premise is denied. For that by which, or in which, God conquered the Devil is not therefore to be adored; rather, the victor over the Devil himself is to be adored. And that victor is Christ alone, our mediator, of whom this was foretold in Genesis 3: "The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent," whose fulfilment is shown in 1 John 3.8: "For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the Devil." Second, the minor premise is denied. For it was not by the cross, that is, the wood of the cross, but by the death of the cross, that he conquered the Devil. What belongs to the death of the cross they wrongly transfer to the wood of the cross. But it is customary for the Papist teachers to slide from this cross, that is, the passion and death of Christ, to the wood of the cross on which Christ was stretched out. Third, the passage of Paul in Colossians chapter 2 does not ascribe the victory to the material cross but to Christ crucified. This passage signifies that Christ, when he was being led to the cross, at that very time subdued the devils on the cross, so that in this place Paul proclaims the power not of the wooden cross but of the passion and death of Christ. I acknowledge that the phrase "in the cross" [ἐν σταυρῷ] corresponds to the preceding noun "the cross" [τῷ σταυρῷ], as the Greek scholiasts and Origen interpret it; yet this reading, as Bellarmine supposes, does not attribute the victory and triumph to the wooden cross, but to the death or crucifixion of Christ. For it signifies that by the death of Christ on the cross he cast down the demons, or that Christ became victor and triumpher on the cross, that is, by the power of his crucifixion. I acknowledge also what Origen says, that two were fastened to the cross, Christ visibly and the Devil invisibly, under the figure of the Devil.

units.la: G Diaboli vero crucifixioe intelligit multa, quae vna cum Christo cruci sunt affixa. Chirographum nostrum vna cum eo crucifixum est, peccatum nostrum crucifium, mors & maledictio crucifixa An vero Origenes vult, haec omnia virtute crucis ligneę esse crucifixa? Nequaquam. Virtute crucifixionis Christi, haec omnia crucifixa esse intelligit. Cum enim Christum visibiliter spote sua & ad tempus dicit cruci affixum non crucem ligneam & externa, sed internam, exprimit, videlicet mortem Christi, & Christum inter patiendum egisse ista profitetur. Quare dum crucem docet esse veluti currum triumphalem, non hoc tantum indicare vult, Christum in cruce tanquam in curru triumphali insidentem triumphasse, sed ἐν αὐτῷ id est, per eam; virtute scilicet crucis, id est, mortis ignominiosae, ita ut Diabolo quo dammodo in cruce illa, quam ipsi fixerunt, suspenderit & ignominia, qua ipsi Christum affecerunt, ipsum affecerit.
units.tr: Of the crucifixion of the Devil, however, he understands many things which are fastened to the cross together with Christ. Our handwriting is crucified together with him; our sin is crucified; death and the curse are crucified. But does Origen mean that all these things are crucified by the power of the wooden cross? By no means. He understands that all these things are crucified by the power of Christ's crucifixion. For when he says that Christ was fastened to the cross visibly, of his own accord and for a time, he is not speaking of the wooden cross and the external thing, but expresses the internal, namely the death of Christ, and declares that Christ accomplished these things in suffering. Therefore, when he teaches that the cross is like a triumphal chariot, he does not mean only that Christ triumphed in the cross as one riding on a triumphal chariot, but in it, that is, through it: by the power, namely, of the cross, that is, of the ignominious death; so that he in some way humiliated the Devil in that cross which they had set up for him, and by the shame with which they had treated Christ, he treated the Devil in the same way.

units.la: Argumentum secundum.
units.tr: Second argument.

units.la: ARGUMENTUM secundum sumitur a mysteriis in ipsa cruce significatis. Nam, vt ait Augustinus Epist. 120. cap. 26. Qui mortuus est, quia noluit, etiam mortuus est, quando voluit, nec sine causa crucem potius, quam aliud instrumentum mortis elegit.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from the mysteries signified in the cross itself. For, as Augustine says, Epist. 120, chap. 26: "He who died because he was unwilling has also died when he was willing, and it was not without cause that he chose the cross rather than another instrument of death."

units.la: Respond.I. Maior huius argumenti, in hoc modo formetur, Quod significat mysteria, id est adorandum; negatur. Nam serpens æneus mysteria significavit, non tamen adorari debuit: aquaBaptismi, panis & vinum sacræ cœnæ sunt signa mystica, non tamen adoranda? Et quid? oleum & reliquæ ceremoniæ Papales sunt mysticæ, num propterea adorandæ.II. Si maior sic formetur. Quod significat mysteria id debet esse amabile & venerabile, respondeo per distinctionem amoris & venerationis ut supra; debet amabile esse & venerabile, hoc est, ut res sacra & religiosa, amari magnifieri, honorifice tractari; non vero diuino amore & veneratione, id est, cultu latrias affici. Sic æneus serpens mysteria significabat, non propterea cultus & adoratus fuit; ut res sacra & religiosa fuit habitus & honoratus, quia sacramētum erat diuinitus institutum, non vero religiosa adoratio ei debuit exhiberi. III. Negatur minor. Mysterium quidem redemtionis in ea est peractum & impletum, sed num propterea signisignificatio mysteriorum tribuenda est cruci? Si quam obtinet significationem illa vel est à Deo vel ab hominib. A Deo nullam habet; cum institutio significationis nullibi in sacris literis tradatur: & licet aliquam haberet à Deo & Dei institutione; vera quidem erit, nontamen propterea sequitur religiose adorandam esse crucem. Significatio ænei serpentis fuit à Dei institutione; non tamen propterea religiose adorari debuit. Si ab hominibus accepit significationem vana erit & falsa illa significatio, vt pote nudo hominum superstitiosorum instituto & imaginatione fundata, eoque ex tali significatione nulla ei debetur veneratio. Testimonium Augustini nihil aliud significat, quam singulari de causa crucis supplicium potius elegisse Christum, quam aliud mortis genus, quia scilicet cruci Deus imposuerat maledictionem, sicut docetur Deuter. 21. & Galat. 3. vt sic ipse pro nobis maledictio fieret, significationes mysticas hoc in loco nullas attribuit crucì.
units.tr: Response I. The major premise, if formulated thus, "What signifies mysteries is to be adored," is denied. For the bronze serpent signified mysteries, yet it ought not to have been adored. Do the water of Baptism and the bread and wine of the holy Supper not signify mysteries, yet are not to be adored? And what of it? Oil and the other Papal ceremonies are mystical; are they therefore to be adored? II. If the major is formulated thus, "What signifies mysteries must be lovable and venerable," I answer by distinguishing love from veneration, as above. It must be lovable and venerable, that is, as a holy and religious thing it must be loved, honoured and treated with respect; but it is not to be met with divine love and veneration, that is, with the worship of latria. So the bronze serpent signified mysteries, yet it was not worshipped and adored. It was regarded as a holy and religious thing and was honoured, because it was a sacrament divinely instituted; but religious adoration was not owed to it. III. The minor is denied. Indeed the mystery of redemption was accomplished and fulfilled on the cross; but is the signification of mysteries therefore to be ascribed to the cross itself? If it has whatever signification it holds, it holds it either from God or from men. From God it has none, since the institution of such a signification is nowhere handed down in the Holy Scriptures. And even if it had one from God and by God's institution, it would indeed be true, yet it would not follow that the cross is to be religiously adored. The signification of the bronze serpent came from God's institution; yet it was not for that reason to be religiously adored. If the cross received its signification from men, that signification is vain and false, being founded on the mere invention and imagination of superstitious men, and from such a signification no veneration is owed to it. Augustine's testimony means nothing more than that Christ chose the punishment of the cross rather than another kind of death for a particular reason: namely, that God had laid a curse upon the cross, as is taught in Deut. 21 and Gal. 3, so that he himself might become a curse for us. It attributes no mystical significations to the cross in this place.

units.la: Bellarminus vero minorem probat. I.In genere. II.In specie. In genere probat sic. Quid, inquit, crux mystica, significet docet Irenæus l. 3. Gregorius Nyssenus oratione de resurrectione. Augustinus in Epistola 119. & 120. Hieronymus & Theophylactus in cap. 3. ad Ephes. ubi de cruce exponunt verba Pauli, ut possitis comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit latitudo & longitudo, sublimitas & profundum. Nam latitudo vocatur lignum transversum. Sublimitas pars ligni ubi est titulus supra transversum; longitudo ligni pars a transverso usque ad terram, profundum pars eiusdem quæ latet sub terram.
units.tr: Bellarmine proves the minor premise. I. In general. II. In particular. He proves it in general as follows: What the mystical cross signifies is taught by Irenaeus, book 3; Gregory of Nyssa, in his oration on the resurrection; Augustine, in Epistles 119 and 120; and Jerome and Theophylact, on Ephesians chapter 3, where they expound the words of Paul, that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length, height and depth. For the breadth is called the transverse beam; the height is the part of the beam where the title is, above the cross-beam; the length is the part of the beam from the cross-beam down to the ground; the depth is the part of it that lies hidden beneath the ground.

units.la: Respond. I. Patres sic loquuti sunt de Christi cruce, ut non crucem materialem, sed spiritualem, passionem scilicet & mortem Christi, non exteriorem, sed interiorem, totum scilicet redemptionis nostræ mysterium in cruce materiali & externa impletum intelexerint. Audi Hieronymum in psalm. 95. Crux Christi columna est generis humani. In ipsa columna est ædificata domus eius, ego crucem dico, inquit, non lignum sed passionem. Quæcunque igitur Patres de vera illa cruce, id est, passione & morte Christi pronunciarunt, per veram Pontificii manituo ligno attribuunt. II.
units.tr: Reply. I. The Fathers spoke of Christ's cross in such a way that they understood not the material cross but the spiritual one, namely the passion and death of Christ; not the external but the internal, that is, the whole mystery of our redemption accomplished in the material and external cross. Hear Jerome on Psalm 95: The cross of Christ is the pillar of the human race. In that pillar his house was built. I say the cross, he says, not the wood but the passion. Whatever, therefore, the Fathers pronounced concerning that true cross, that is, the passion and death of Christ, the Papists attribute to the wood. II.

units.la: Quid tum si mysticum efficiant crucis lignum & mysterium in eo quærant & statuant, num adorationis aut latrias culcultum ei tribuunt? Certe ab adoratione eius longissime absunt, virtutem salutarem ei nullatenus tribuunt. III. Locum illum Ephes. 3. de cruce exponunt, fateror, sed allegorice. Allegoricae vero interpretationes non probant fidei dogmata. Verus & literalis census est de excellentia & perfectione charitatis Dei erga nos. Significat enim Paulus charitatem Dei in Christo exhibitam perfectissimam & immensam esse, atque adeo omni cognitione superiorem. IV. Etsi de cruce exponant: nullam tamen mysteriorum in ea significationem constituunt. Expresse dicit Theophylactus, cum GregorioNysseno illa ad crucem referre, quia scilicet per crucem Christi precipue manifestata sit Dei dilectio: mysteriorum ea significatorum aut adorationis illi debitae ne minima quidem fit mentio.
units.tr: What then if they make the wood of the cross mystical, and seek and assert a mystery in it? Do they therefore attribute to it adoration or the worship of latria? Certainly they are very far from adoring it, and by no means attribute saving power to it. III. I admit that they expound that passage in Ephesians 3 of the cross, but allegorically. Allegorical interpretations, however, do not prove the dogmas of faith. The true and literal sense concerns the excellence and perfection of God's love toward us. For Paul signifies that the love of God shown in Christ is most perfect and immense, and so surpasses all knowledge. IV. Even if they do expound it of the cross, they nevertheless set up no mystical significance in it. Theophylact, together with Gregory of Nyssa, expressly says that these things are to be referred to the cross, because God's love was chiefly made manifest through the cross of Christ; there is not even the slightest mention of mysteries signified by it, or of the adoration due to it.

units.la: II. Probat in specie sic. Primo, inquit, significabat ista figura totam perfectionem Christianam, ut Augustinus docet: profundum fidem, sublimitas spem, latitudo charitatem, longitudo perseverantiam. Secundo Christi passionis effectum: nam signum supremum significat, scilicet crucem Christi passione apertum & Deum placatum; litum; lignum sub terram infixum, infernum e-uacuatum & Diabolum deuictum: lignū transf-uersum respiciens ortum & occasum totum or-bem terrarum redemtum. Itaque proptereaChristum crucifixum adorent cælestia, terre-stria & inferna, vt Nyssenus deducit. Tertio duo brachia crucis sub uno titulo saluatoris, si-gnificant duo populos [inquit Irenæus] subuno capite Christo inter se connexos, iuxta illudIoh. 12. Ego si exaltatus fuero à terra omnia tra-ham ad meipsum.
units.tr: II. He proves it in particular as follows. First, this figure, he says, signified the whole Christian perfection, as Augustine teaches: the depth signifies faith, the height hope, the breadth charity, the length perseverance. Second, the effect of Christ's passion: for the highest sign, namely the cross, signifies Christ's passion, by which God was propitiated and opened; the cross set in the earth, the lower part fixed beneath the ground, signifies hell emptied and the devil conquered; the transverse beam, looking toward east and west, signifies the whole world redeemed. Therefore, as Nyssen deduces, the heavenly, earthly and infernal beings adore the crucified Christ for this reason. Third, the two arms of the cross under one title of the Saviour signify two peoples [says Irenaeus] joined to one another under one head, Christ, in accordance with that saying of John 12: If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.

units.la: Resp. I. Hæ significationes ex allego-rica loci Paulini interpretatione in sa-cris literis non fundata petuntur, ideo-que humanæ sunt & ad probādum fidei dogma ineptæ. Veræ significationes mysteriorum, à quibus res mysticæ sa-cræ amabiles & venerabiles æstiman-tur, peti debent ex diuina institutione. At nullibi in sacris literis harum significationum traditur institutio. II. Etsi fi-gura crucis significet perfectionē Christi-anam, Christi passionis effectum, du-os pedes sub uno capite Christo, inter se connexos, num propterea fuerit religiosè adoranda? Æneus serpens ipsum Christum significabat, non tamen religiosè fuit cultus & adoratus. Significa-tio mystica non est causa religiosè ado-ratio-
units.tr: Response I. These significations are sought from an allegorical interpretation of the Pauline passage, which is not founded in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore they are human and unfit to prove a dogma of faith. True significations of mysteries, by which sacred mystical things are judged lovable and venerable, ought to be sought from divine institution. But nowhere in the Holy Scriptures is the institution of these significations handed down. II. Even if the figure of the cross signifies Christian perfection, the effect of Christ's passion, and the two arms joined to one another under one head, Christ, is it therefore to be religiously adored? The bronze serpent signified Christ himself, yet it was not religiously worshipped and adored. A mystical signification is not the cause of religious adoration or latria.

units.la: { } Marginal notes are too damaged to read reliably. rationis seu latriæ. III. Significationes hasce, figuræ crucis tribuit & ex figura deducit. Quare hinc sequetur figuram crucis esse adorandam non lignum crucis. Verum de figura nō est quæstio, sed de ipso ligno crucis. Huius ergo significationes depromere debuisset, q; cum nō faciat, nec facere possit, lignea crucis adoratio vana est & idololatrica.
units.tr: ...of religious worship or latria. III. These significations the Papists attribute to the figure of the cross and deduce from the figure. Hence it would follow that the figure of the cross is to be adored, not the wood of the cross. But the question is not about the figure; it is about the wood of the cross itself. Therefore they ought to have drawn its significations from the wood, and since they do not do this, and cannot do it, the adoration of the wooden cross is vain and idolatrous.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus ex Minutio Felice in Octauio & ex Ambrosio, qui Serm. 56. crucis figuram dicit esse etiam naturaliter salutarem. Nam aues nunquam volarent, nisi expansis alis, crucis formam innitarentur, & quibus non moueretur, nisi ex malo & anthena crux fieret: & arrator terram non scinderet nisi exaratro & stiua crucem faceret & rursum alias extugo & Temone: Cælum ipsum crucem facit, si lineæ ducantur ab ortu ad occasum, ab Aquilone ad Austrum.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses further with Minucius Felix in his Octavius, and with Ambrose, who in Sermon 56 says that the figure of the cross is even naturally salutary. "For birds would never fly unless they spread their wings, leaning on the form of the cross; and the things that would not move unless the cross were made from the mast and yard; and the ploughman would not cut the earth unless with the plough and share he made a cross, and again with the yoke and pole. Heaven itself makes a cross if lines are drawn from east to west and from north to south."

units.la: Resp. 1. Non est quæstio de figura crucis, sed de ligno crucis, in quo Christus pependit. Huius enim virtute extollitur, hoc adorandum esse contendunt. Eius igitur mysteria cum deberent exponere, ad figuram deuoluuntur, quasi de figuræ virtute & adoratione certetur. II. Negatur virtutem esse salutarem naturaliter, si enim naturaliter salutaris est, non erit {a}erit talis ex Dei institutione, & mystica significatione carebit. Quod à natura salutare est & salutem confert, idà Dei institutione virtutem hac nō impetra-uit, sicut ç neus serpens Dei institutione cō ferebat salutem, & mysteriorum significationem obtinebant. Ergo non à natura. III. Crimé falsi committit. Non dicit Minutius Felix naturaliter esse salu-tarem. Verba eius hęc sunt Signum crucis naturaliter vijimus in naui, cum velis tremen-tibus vehitur, cum expansis palmulis labitur, & cum erigitur iugum, crucis signum est. Ratio-nem figurae exponit, nō naturalem eius vsum declarat. Ambrosius etiā nihil de naturali vsu crucis, habet, sed verę illius crucis, id est passionis & mortis Christi vsum indicat, ita vt I. proponat eam. II. exponat. III. illustret. Proponit cum eam dicit esse redemtionem & vitam no-stram. Exponit cum dicit Christum au-feredo per crucem humani generis in-iurias, omnes eas in sua passione con-sumsisse, vt vlterius non esset quod ho-mini noceret. Illustrat deinde hunc vsum à similitudine velorum expansorum, quæ foi mam crucis repræsentant. Vt naturæ vela nauium distendunt, in-star crucis dominicæ fluctus aquarum per-
units.tr: Response I. The question is not about the figure of the cross but about the wood of the cross on which Christ hung. For they contend that this wood is to be adored because of its power. Therefore, when they ought to expound its mysteries, they roll back to the figure, as though the dispute were about the power and adoration of the figure. II. I deny that it is salutary by nature. For if it is salutary naturally, it will not be such by God's institution, and it will lack mystical signification. What is salutary by nature and confers salvation does not obtain this power from God's institution, just as the bronze serpent conferred salvation and held the signification of mysteries by God's institution. Therefore it is not from nature. III. Bellarmine commits a falsehood. Minucius Felix does not say that the sign of the cross is naturally salutary. His words are these: "We see the sign of the cross naturally in a ship, when it is carried with trembling sails, when it glides with its little palms spread, and when the yoke is raised, there is the sign of the cross." He sets out the reason of the figure; he does not declare its natural use. Ambrose too says nothing about the natural use of the cross, but indicates the use of that true cross, that is, of Christ's passion and death, in such a way that he I. proposes it, II. expounds it, III. illustrates it. He proposes it when he says it is "our redemption and our life." He expounds it when he says that Christ, by the cross, took away the injuries of the human race, having consumed them all in his passion, so that nothing further could harm man. He then illustrates this use by the likeness of spread sails, which represent the form of the cross: as sails stretch the ships of nature, so in the manner of the Lord's cross the waves of the waters are broken through

units.la: {a} 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. perrumpunt ad portum perueniunt.Ita etiam Christiani hoc dominico crucis signo securi portum salutis petiût & periculum mortis euadût. Per hoc crucis signum, vt præcedentia luculenter declarât,intelligit Christi passionem crucis signo metonymicè signatam: quandoquidem bonis quibusq; autorib. familiare est,vt quod significati est,tribuant signo;hinc postmodum digreditur, & figuram crucis cum velo in arbore ex panfo comparat,de naturaliter salutari visu metionem nullam facies. IV.Quid tum si naturaliter salutarem figurâ crucis statuisset,attamē ab adoratione crucis fuere alienissimi. Cruces, inquit Minuti in Octauio,nec colimus, nec optamus. Ambrosius de Helena Constantini matre,nō inquit,adorauit lignū,quia hic gentilis est error & vanitas impiorum, sed adorauit illum qui pependit in ligno, scriptus in titulo. Quod de vitæ figurę significatione subiicit, id vt futuræ commentum per se corruit.
units.tr: {a} 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. They break through and reach harbour. So also Christians, secure in this sign of the Lord's cross, seek the harbour of salvation and escape the danger of death. By this sign of the cross, as the preceding words clearly show, he means Christ's passion, signified by metonymy through the sign of the cross, since it is customary for good authors to attribute to the sign what is signified. Afterwards he goes on to compare the figure of the cross with a sail on a yard spread out, and he makes no mention of a naturally saving sight. IV. Suppose he had said that the figure of the cross naturally saves: still, they were most alien to the worship of the cross. We neither worship crosses, says Minucius in the Octavius, nor desire them. Ambrose, speaking of Helena, mother of Constantine, says: She did not worship the wood, because that is a heathen error and the vanity of the impious; but she worshipped him who hung on the wood, whose title was written. What he adds about the significance of the figure of life collapses of itself as a fiction of the future.

units.la: Argumentum tertium.
units.tr: Third argument.

units.la: AB inuentione crucis ex qua multiplex testimonium sumitur, quod veneratio ligni crucis Deo placeat.
units.tr: From the finding of the cross, from which a manifold testimony is drawn that the veneration of the wood of the cross is pleasing to God.

units.la: Resp.I. Nulla commixtio est inuentæ crucis cum eius religiose cultu & adoratione. Nō sequitur propterea eam religiosè esse adorandam, etiamsi ea, quæ de inuentione crucis legūtur vera esse credantur. Si enim inuenta est crux Christi, non ideo inuenta est, vt religiosè coleretur, sed vt Euangelii doctrina eo magis apud Ethnicos recens conuersos confirmaretur, & tanto latius propagaretur. Est igitur fallacia à non causa.
units.tr: Reply I. There is no connection between the finding of the cross and its religious cult and adoration. It does not follow that it is to be religiously adored, even if what is read about the finding of the cross is believed to be true. For if the cross of Christ was found, it was not found so that it should be religiously worshipped, but so that the doctrine of the Gospel might be the more confirmed among the recently converted heathen and spread the more widely. This is therefore a fallacy of non-cause.

units.la: Deus voluit inueniri crucem, non vt religiosè coleretur, sed vt veritas doctrinæ de Christo crucifixo, quæ passim tunc in toto orbe spargebatur, confirmeretur. Cum enim Ethnici tùm de hac doctrina dubitarent, multi etiam eam negarent, voluit Deus ex ipso crucis aspectu, rei fidem facere eamq; confirmare. Ab inuentione igitur crucis ad eius adorationem non valeat consequentia. Non enim sequitur inuentio crucis Deo placuit, ergo etiam eius adoratio placet.
units.tr: God willed that the cross be found, not that it be religiously worshipped, but that the truth of the doctrine concerning the crucified Christ, which was then being spread everywhere through the whole world, might be confirmed. For since the heathen then doubted this doctrine, and many even denied it, God willed by the very sight of the cross to make and confirm faith in the thing. Therefore the inference from the finding of the cross to its adoration does not hold. For it does not follow: the finding of the cross pleased God, therefore its adoration also pleases him.

units.la: II. Negamus crucis inuentionem.
units.tr: II. We deny the finding of the cross.

units.la: Fabulam esse dicimus, & quidem mendacium Monachorum. Recte monuit Gelasius & Romana Synodus, quæ fuit 7o. Episcoporum; scripta de inuentione
units.tr: We say that it is a fable, and indeed a lie of the monks. Gelasius and the Roman Synod of seventy bishops rightly warned, in the writing concerning the finding

units.la: one crucis Dominicæ nouellæ sunt reuelationes, Et nonnulli eas Catholici legunt; sed cum hæc ad Catholicorum manus perueniunt, Beati Pauli Apostoli præcedat sententia. omnia probate, & quod bonum est tenete. Sed rationibus etiam vanitas fabulæ facile euincitur.
units.tr: of the one cross of the Lord, that new revelations are ... and some Catholics read them; but when these come into the hands of Catholics, the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul should go before: Prove all things, and hold fast that which is good. But the vanity of the fable is also easily refuted by reasons.

units.la: I. Accusaretur Apostoli & primitiua Ecclesia extremæ vecordiæ & ingratitudinis erga Deum, quod stante cruce tàm turpiter neglexissent, vel assulas quasdam ex ea de corpore aut abscindere, quæ ipsis in posterum sanctissimum & preciosissimum esset futuræ κεφαλίον καὶ ἀλεξικακον.
units.tr: I. The Apostles and the primitive Church would be accused of the utmost folly and ingratitude towards God, if, while the cross stood, they had so shamefully neglected it that they did not cut off from its body some splinters, which would be most holy and precious to them in the future as a κεφαλίον καὶ ἀλεξικακον [a charm and protection against evil].

units.la: II. post Apostolus Iacobus, & qui ab eo episcopi Hierosolymitam secuti sunt, officii sui plane fuissent immemores, atq; impietatis crimine notâdi esset quod lignum cuius veneratio & amor Deo placere, non studerint conseruare, aut amissam requirere. Persecutionibus dices pinm ipsorum conatum fuisse impeditum, sed multis etiam isto tempore inducijs, gaudia est Ecclesia. Nonne pace fruebatur sub Philippo Arabs, sub Alexandro Mammæa? cur de tanto thesauro inquirendo tanti episcopi & doctores non fuissent soliciti? commemorat memorat Eusebius, ligneam sedem ad hoc vsq; temporis seruatam, quam fratres isti, qui successioe ordinaria subsecuti sunt, omnib.manifestè monstrāt. Si illam seruare & monstrare potuerūt hostium odiis & persecutionibus nō ob statib.quidni & cruce Christi? III. post primitiua Ecclesia Christiana,q primis illis circiter trecentis annis floruit,gra- uissimam securitatis & profanitatis reprehensio merebitur,quod adeo negligeter religionem & salutem suam curauerit,vt crucem Christi instrumentū redeptionis nostræ neglexerit.Parū salutis suę cupidos fuisse primos illos Christianos necesse est,qui crucem illam tot mysteriis plenam,tantis dotibus & viribus ornatam nihil curarūt. Canunt Papistæ.O crux aue spes vnica,&c. Quæ tunc Ecclesiæ spes, cruce deperdita? In die in uetionis sanctę crucis, sic vocant eā, Ara crucis, lampas lucis, vera salus hominum: Nobis pronum fac Patronum, quem tulisti Dominum. Nū adeo profani fuerāt primi illi Christiani, vt salutis suæ rationem nō habuerint? Quomodo vero Christum propitium habere potuerunt, amissa cruce, q pronum nobis reddit patronum? Num adeo irreligiosi fuere vt lignum vitæ, quod pijs auget iustitiam, reisque donat veniam, si nô-luerint inquirere? Absit vt de prima illa & sanctaEcclefia tam finistre judicemus?
units.tr: II. Afterwards the Apostle James, and the bishops of Jerusalem who followed him, would have been utterly forgetful of their office, and would be branded with the crime of impiety, if they did not take care to preserve the wood whose veneration and love were pleasing to God, or to seek it when lost. It will be said that their attempt was hindered by persecutions; but the Church also rejoiced in many breathing-spaces at that time. Did she not enjoy peace under Philip the Arab, under Alexander Mammaea? Why were so many bishops and teachers not anxious to search out so great a treasure? Eusebius records that the wooden seat was preserved until that time, and that those brethren who followed in the ordinary succession showed it to all. If they could preserve and show that seat in spite of the hatred and persecutions of enemies, why not also the cross of Christ? III. Afterwards the primitive Christian Church, which flourished in those first roughly three hundred years, will deserve the gravest reproach of carelessness and irreligion, because it cared so negligently for religion and its salvation that it neglected the cross of Christ, the instrument of our redemption. It must be that those first Christians were little eager for their salvation, since they cared nothing for that cross, so full of mysteries and adorned with such gifts and powers. The Papists sing: O cross, hail, our only hope, etc. What then was the Church's hope, once the cross was lost? On the feast of the finding of the holy cross, they call it: Altar of the cross, lamp of light, true salvation of men: make the Lord whom you bore a kindly patron to us. Were those first Christians so profane that they took no account of their salvation? And how could they have Christ propitious to them, once the cross, which makes him a kindly patron to us, was lost? Were they so irreligious that they did not wish to seek the tree of life, which increases righteousness for the godly and grants pardon to the guilty? Far be it from us to judge so sinisterly of that first and holy Church!

units.la: IV. Primus omnium, qui de hac inuen-tione scribere potuit, & qui res Impera-toris Constantini optimè nouit, fuit Eu-sebius, qui vixit tempore Costantini. At nullam is facit mentionem huius histo-riæ, neq; in libris historię Ecclefiast. ne-que in libris de vita Constantini. Lib. 3. de vita Constantini capit, 39. 40. 41. 42. 43. Helenæ pietatem, quam declarauit in repurgatione montis Caluariæ, benefi-centiam eius in pauperes, munificen-tiam in Ecclesias; venerandam ætatem, sepulturam deniq; honorificâ prolixè describit Eusebius, sed inuentæ crucis, nullam facit mentionem. In Chronico quidem suo eius meminit, sed liber ille corruptissim9 est, & variis hallucinatio-nibus atq; nugis referrtfssimus, quas ex Scaligero, si libet prędiscito. V. Histori-ci, qui hæc fabulosam inuentione com-memorat, adeo inter se dissident, vt ma-gis eam destruant, quam confirmet. Fa-teor, vbi de re & substantia historiæ ex consentientibus grauissimorum & inte-gerrimorum testimoniis constat; circu-stantiarum quarundam varietatem Discordiam, Historiae fidem non dubiam & suspectam reddere: Sed ubi rei ipsius veritas & substantia, ex probatae incorruptaeque fidei testibus non habetur, tam eius falsitas ex varietate & discordia narrationis recte demonstratur. Varia autem dissensio historicorum de inventa cruce potissimum in loco, tempore & modo reperitur. Nam alii, ut Ambrosius in oratione de obitu Theodosii in Golgotha seu loco crucifixionis Christi defossam & refossam esse opinantur; alii in loco sepulchri, seu praedio Iosephi Arimathaeensis, quod & Baronio magis probatur; Alii, ut Eusebius in Chronico suo. Anno decimoquinto. Imperii Constantini; Alii ut Zonaras, cum baptizato Constantino, mater Helena, adscito Syluestro Papa, Hierosolymam esset profecta: alii denique anno primo post Concilium Nicenum: alii sic inuentam crucem esse scribunt, ut ex Titulo fuerit agnita, quia latrones crucis titulum non habuere; Cuius sententiae Authores fuere Chrysostomus & Ambrosius; alii vero auulsum narrant titulum
units.tr: IV. The first of all who could write about this finding, and who knew the affairs of the emperor Constantine best, was Eusebius, who lived in Constantine's time. Yet he makes no mention of this story, neither in his Ecclesiastical History nor in his books on the life of Constantine. In Book 3 of the Life of Constantine, chapters 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, Eusebius describes at length Helena's piety, which she showed in clearing Mount Calvary, her beneficence to the poor, her generosity to the churches, her venerable age and finally her honourable burial; but of the finding of the cross he makes no mention at all. He does mention her in his Chronicle, but that book is very corrupt, and full of various hallucinations and trifles, which, if you wish, you may learn beforehand from Scaliger. V. The historians who record this finding as a fable disagree so much among themselves that they overthrow it rather than confirm it. I grant that where the matter and substance of the history are agreed upon by the testimonies of the most weighty and upright men, a variety and discord in certain circumstances does not make the faith of the history doubtful or suspect. But where the truth and substance of the thing itself is not attested by witnesses of approved and uncorrupted faith, its falsity is rightly demonstrated by the variety and discord of the narrations. Now the historians' disagreement about the found cross is especially found in the place, the time and the manner. For some, like Ambrose in his oration on the death of Theodosius, believe that it was buried and dug up again in Golgotha, or the place of Christ's crucifixion; others in the place of the sepulchre, or the estate of Joseph of Arimathea, which Baronius also prefers; others, like Eusebius in his Chronicle, in the fifteenth year of Constantine's reign; others, like Zonaras, say that when Constantine was baptised, his mother Helena, with Pope Sylvester added, set out for Jerusalem; others finally say it was in the first year after the Council of Nicaea. Others write that the cross was found by means of the title, because the thieves did not have a title on their crosses; the authors of this opinion were Chrysostom and Ambrose. Others, however, relate that the title was torn off,

units.la: ex miraculo agnitam commemorát. In Breuiario enim recitatur ex Ruffinoe am ex languenti sanata agnitam fuisse. Cum enim Macarius Episcopus singulas cruces cuidam fœminæ grauiter languenti admouisset, duę nihil profuerät, tertia vero adhibita sanauit eā; vndeagnita fuit: Alii, vt Sulpitius seueras post tempora Ruffini eam ex mortuo resuscitato agnitam refert, quod miraculum etiam Breuiarium hisce verbis prædicat Crucis contactu consurgunt mortui, & Deimagnalia referantur.
units.tr: and recall that it was recognised by a miracle. For the Breviary, drawn from Rufinus, recounts that it was recognised through a sick woman who was healed. When Bishop Macarius had applied the individual crosses to a certain woman who was gravely ill, two did her no good, but the third, when applied, healed her; whereby it was recognised. Others, like Sulpicius Severus, after Rufinus's time, report that it was recognised by a dead man who was raised to life; this miracle the Breviary also proclaims in these words: At the touch of the cross the dead rise, and the wonders of God are told.

units.la: Videamus nunc testimonia, quæex hac inuentione crucis petit Bellarminus ad demonstrandam eius religiosam venerationem.
units.tr: Let us now look at the testimonies which Bellarmine seeks from this finding of the cross, to demonstrate its religious veneration.

units.la: Primum testimonium. Quod non promiserit Deus lignum illud demergi in mare, vel flammis absumi. Quoden im hostes Christianorum conati sint abolere crucem eiusque omnia vestigia, patet ex eo, quod altissime crucē sub terrā abscondérūt, & in loco crucis, Veneris simulachrū, in loco resurrectionis Iouis, in loco natiuitatis Adonidis posuerunt, vt refert B. Hieron. in epist. ad Paulin. de institutione Monachi, cur quæso non cremarunt crucem cum vellent & possent, nisi quia Deus illis abstulit mentem, vt ad solatium piorum lignum pretiosissimum seruaretur.
units.tr: The first testimony. That God did not promise that this wood would be sunk in the sea or consumed by flames. That the enemies of the Christians tried to abolish the cross and all its traces is clear from the fact that they buried the cross deep underground, and set up an image of Venus in the place of the cross, an image of Jupiter in the place of the resurrection, and an image of Adonis in the place of the nativity, as blessed Jerome reports in his letter to Paulinus on the training of a monk. Why, I ask, did they not burn the cross when they wished and were able to, unless because God took away their wits, so that this most precious wood might be preserved for the comfort of the pious?

units.la: Resp. I. Idoneum testimonium, quo veneratio ligni crucis Deo placere ostenditur, ex verbo Dei peti debet, vtpote q; solum certū est & indubię veritatis: hoc vero humanū est, suspectæ & dubiæ veritatis. II. Est fallacia à non causa. Nam si Deus conseruauit crucis lignum, ne in mare demergeretur, aut flamis absumeretur, non ideo conseruatum, quod venerationem crucis sibi gratam & ratam haberet, sed vt veritas crucifixionis Christi apud Ethnicos ex ipso aspectu crucis confirmaretur: atq; ita nō crucis lignea, sed ipsius Christi, cuius illa crux fuit, veneratio ex hoc testimonio inferri debet.
units.tr: Reply. I. A suitable testimony showing that the veneration of the wood of the cross pleases God must be sought from the Word of God, since that alone is certain and of indubitable truth. This testimony, however, is human, of suspect and doubtful truth. II. This is a fallacy from a non-cause. If God preserved the wood of the cross so that it would not be sunk in the sea or consumed by flames, He did not preserve it because He approved and accepted veneration of the cross. He preserved it so that the truth of Christ's crucifixion would be confirmed among the heathen by the very sight of the cross. So from this testimony what follows is veneration of Christ himself, whose cross it was, not veneration of the wooden cross.

units.la: III. Nō permisit Deus inter tot incēdia subuersiōes & ruinas, tot seculis vsq; ad p̄sens tempus, Librum sacrarum literarum demergi in mare vel flammis absumi, num hinc concludes religiosam adorationem seu venerationē libri Biblici Deo placere? honore afficiēdum esse & amandum sequitur, sed non adorādum & cultu latrias colendum. Ita si lignum crucis inuetū esset, & certo extaret, honorem suū ei deferremus, sed diuinā venerationem ei nunquam praestaremus.
units.tr: III. God did not permit the Book of the Sacred Letters to be sunk in the sea or consumed by flames amid so many fires, overthrows and ruins, through so many centuries down to the present time. Will you therefore conclude that religious adoration or veneration of the Biblical book pleases God? It follows only that the book is to be honoured and loved, not adored and worshipped with latria. So if the wood of the cross had been found and were certainly extant, we would give it its honour, but we would never render it divine veneration.

units.la: IV. Vnde cōstat Bellarmino, lignū crucis nō esse in mare demersum, vel flam-mis
units.tr: IV. How does Bellarmine know that the wood of the cross was not sunk in the sea or

units.la: mis absumptum? Nū putas in tot incē- diis & subuersionib.vrbisHierosolymæ crucem vsque ad Constantini tempora integram fuisse seruatam?In obsidioni- bus & euersionibus vrbem, ea, quæ extra vrbem sunt prædia vel ædificia siuè priuata, ligna & similia abripi vastari aut cremari solet, quo iure aut qua fortunâ crucis ligno ab hostib. Christiani nominis parcitum fuisset? At inquies, ante obsidionem, iamdudum crucem depositam & altissimè sub terram fuisse defossam & absconditam. At quomodo tunc à carie potuisset vindicari? Quod sie extra terram flammis aut aliis iniu- riis non fuit absumpta, intra terram ca- rie computruit. Verumenimuerò omnì verisimilitudine caret hæc suspicio. Corpus Christi depositū esse & sepul- tum, ex historia constat, sed crucem cum corpore depositam non legimus in scripturis. Omnia quæ contigere circa crucifixionem & sepulturam Christi diligenter annotata sunt ab Eu- angelistis, ad veritatem mortis & sepul- turæ Christi Confirmandam, sed cru- cis Christi depositæ nulla fit mentio.II. Cruces nunquam solitæ fuere deponi, cur præter consuetudinem, crucem ChriChristi depositam dixerimus, cum de eo taceat scriptura? III. Non potuissent eam deponere. Nam die crucifixionis ferum erat, sabbatumque imminebant, quo nihil operis licebat facere, ideo temporis breuitas tunc impediebat depositionem; sequentibus nouem diebus depositionem impediebat festum paschale. Cum vero in terra temporis fama de Christi resurrectione spargeretur, non est credibile, exacto festo paschali, depositam & in terra defossam esse. Spectabat enim haec depositio ad famam iam tum de resurrectione Christi sparsam confirmandam, sicut publicum eius monumentum ad mortem & resurrectionem Christi stabiliendam. Non est credibile, Iudaeos crucifixores suo facto voluisse resurrectionem Christi, cuius nomen & memoriam abolere studebant, confirmare. IV. Si deposita fuit crux Christi, vel Iosephus & Nicodemus deponendam illam curarunt, vel Iudaei & Gentiles. At non legitur a Iosepho & Nicodemo crucem depositam, sed cororis Christi tantum fuit mentio, quod Syndone pura linteisq; inuoluerunt & sepulturae tradiderunt. Soliciti fuere pij
units.tr: Do you think the cross survived intact through so many fires and overthrows of the city of Jerusalem until the time of Constantine? In sieges and overthrows of a city, the estates and buildings outside it, whether private or public, are usually carried off, laid waste, or burned, and so is timber and the like. By what right, or by what good fortune, would the enemies of the Christian name have spared the wood of the cross? But you will say that before the siege the cross had long since been laid down and buried deep underground and hidden. But how could it then have been protected from rot? If it was not consumed by flames or other injuries above ground, it would have rotted away below ground. Yet this suspicion lacks all probability. That the body of Christ was laid down and buried is established by history, but we do not read in the Scriptures that the cross was laid down with the body. Everything that happened around the crucifixion and burial of Christ was carefully recorded by the Evangelists, to confirm the truth of Christ's death and burial, yet no mention is made of the laying down of the cross of Christ. II. Crosses were never customarily taken down. Why, then, should we say, contrary to custom, that the cross of Christ was laid down, when Scripture is silent about it? III. They could not have taken it down. On the day of the crucifixion the evening was approaching and the Sabbath was at hand, on which no work was permitted, so the shortness of the time then prevented the taking down. In the nine days that followed, the Passover feast prevented it. But when the report of Christ's resurrection was spreading through the land, it is not credible that, after the Passover feast was over, the cross was laid down and buried in the earth. For this laying down would have served to confirm the report of Christ's resurrection, already spread abroad, just as his public tomb served to establish his death and resurrection. It is not credible that the Jews who crucified him wished to confirm the resurrection of Christ, whose name and memory they strove to abolish. IV. If the cross of Christ was laid down, either Joseph and Nicodemus took care to lay it down, or the Jews and the Gentiles did. But it is not read that Joseph and Nicodemus laid down the cross. Only the body of Christ is mentioned, which they wrapped in a clean linen cloth and gave to the tomb. Those pious men were anxious about the body of Christ, lest it fall into the hands of impure executioners, who were accustomed to throw the corpses of those put to death into pits.

units.la: illi viri de corpore Christi, nec illud in manus impurorum carnificum veniret qui cadauera supplicio affectorum in puteos solebant deiicere. Petitio idem confirmat; petiit Iosephus à Pilato sibi donati corpus Christi, atque illud solum ipsi permisit Pilatus, illud solum etiam dicitur sustulisse. Ioh. 19. verf 38. Quod si lignum crucis fuisset tam pretiosum ξυλον ζωης & lignum vitæ, quid in lignum cum corpore Christi petiisset, & impetratum à Pilato ad Christianorum solatium salutemq; seruasset. Neque Iudæi vel Gentiles deponere vel abscondere eam potuere; quia si sustulissent eam, fama de Christi resurrectione quæ iam tum audita fuit, confirmata fuisset, quam quia tollere potius studere, crucem procul dubio fuerunt, cuius monumento & aspectu mors Christi confirmabatur, & resurrectio negabatur.
units.tr: The request confirms the same point. Joseph asked Pilate for the body of Christ, and Pilate granted him that alone; it is said that he took away only that (John 19.38). But if the wood of the cross had been so precious, a [ξυλον ζωης] and a tree of life, why would he have asked for the wood along with the body of Christ, and, having obtained it from Pilate, kept it for the comfort and salvation of Christians? Neither the Jews nor the Gentiles could have laid it down or hidden it, for if they had removed it, the report of Christ's resurrection, which was already being heard then, would have been confirmed. Since they were eager rather to remove it, they undoubtedly took away the cross, by whose monument and sight the death of Christ was confirmed and his resurrection denied.

units.la: At, inquit Bellarminus, hostes Christianorum altissimè eam absconderunt sub terram, & in loco crucis, V eneris simulacrum in loco resurrectionis Iouis, in loco natiuitatis, Adonidis posuere, ut crucem eiusque omnia vestigia abolerent.
units.tr: But, says Bellarmine, the enemies of the Christians hid it very deep under the earth, and in the place of the cross they set up a statue of Venus, in the place of the resurrection a statue of Jupiter, and in the place of the nativity a statue of Adonis, in order to destroy the cross and all its traces.

units.la: Resp.1. Si hostes absconderunt, non
units.tr: Reply 1. If the enemies hid it, it is not

units.la: igitur Apostoli aut reliqui Christi discipuli, ac proinde eorum ingratitudo erga Deum, aut saltem religionis Christianę negligentia est culpanda, qui lignum preciossimum adeo venerabile & salutare siuerunt in hostium manus venire. II. Si hostes fuere autores depositæ & absconditæ crucis, quomodo inuentæ dicuntur tres cruces in eodem loco, ita vt quæ Christi esset, agnosci non potuerit; Neque enim hostes, latronum cruces tanti facere, vt eas voluerint abscondere & abolere. III. Falsum est, quod hostes voluerint lignum crucis eiusque vestigia abolere, nulla historia id commemorat. Christianos voluerunt opprimere, & fidem mortis atque resurrectionis Christi tollere, ideo ędem Veneris eo loci extruxe runt. Hac de re Sulpitius Seuerus audiatur.
units.tr: therefore the Apostles or the other disciples of Christ who are to be blamed, and so their ingratitude toward God, or at least the negligence of the Christian religion, who allowed the most precious, so venerable and saving wood to come into the hands of enemies. II. If the enemies were the authors of the laying down and hiding of the cross, how is it said that three crosses were found in the same place, so that the one that was Christ's could not be recognised? For the enemies would not have held the crosses of robbers in such high regard as to want to hide and destroy them. III. It is false that the enemies wished to abolish the wood of the cross and its traces; no history records this. They wished to oppress the Christians and to remove the faith in the death and resurrection of Christ, and therefore they built a temple of Venus on that spot. Let Sulpicius Severus be heard on this matter.

units.la: Ea tempestate, inquit is, Hadrianus, existimans se Christianam fidem loci iniuria perempturum, in templo ac loco dominicæ passionis, dæmonum simulacra constituit. Audin? nōne fidē Christianam conati fuere abolere? at quomodo? num altissima dessione crucis sub terram? Non, sed oci iniuria, Constituendis scilicet Dæmonum
units.tr: At that time, he says, Hadrian, thinking that he would destroy the Christian faith by an insult to the place, set up images of demons in the temple and place of the Lord's passion. Do you hear? Did they not try to abolish the Christian faith? But how? By burying the cross deep in the earth? No, but by the insult to the place, namely by setting up images of demons in those same places.

units.la: H monum simulacris in iisdem locis. Hieronymus ad Paulinum contestatur, inquiens, Ab Hadriani temporibus, usque ad Imperium Constantini per annos circiter 230. in loco resurrectionis simulachrum Iouis, in crucis rupe statua ex marmore Veneris a Gentibus posita celebratur. Existimantibus persecutionis authoribus, quo tollerent nobis fidem resurrectionis & crucis si loca sancta polluissent per Idola. Fidem ergo resurrectionis & crucis, id est mortis Christi tollere voluerunt, non defossione crucis in terram, sed ex simulachrorum constitutione, & pollutione sanctorum locorum.
units.tr: Jerome testifies to Paulinus, saying: From the times of Hadrian down to the empire of Constantine, for about 230 years, an image of Jupiter was worshipped in the place of the resurrection, and a marble statue of Venus, set up by the Gentiles, on the rock of the cross. The authors of the persecution, thinking that by polluting the holy places with idols they would take away from us the faith of the resurrection and of the cross. Therefore they wished to remove the faith of the resurrection and of the cross, that is, of Christ's death, not by burying the cross in the earth but by setting up images and polluting the holy places.

units.la: Secundò quod Deus eo tempore crucem invenire voluerit, quo tuto poterat coli, nimirum ad initium Constantini. Nam si antea relerata fuisset, regnantibus persecutoribus, magis ludibrio, quam honore accepta fuisset. Si autem diu post tempora Constantini fuisset inventa, fraudata fuisset sancta crux debito honore. Tunc igitur primum diuina prouidentia crucem manifestauit, cum primum potuit coli.
units.tr: Second, that God at that time wished to find the cross when it could safely be worshipped, namely at the beginning of Constantine. For if it had been discovered earlier, while the persecutors reigned, it would have been received more as mockery than as honour. But if it had been found long after the times of Constantine, the holy cross would have been defrauded of its due honour. Then, therefore, divine providence first revealed the cross, when it first could be worshipped.

units.la: Resp. I. Neq; hoc testimonium quicquam facit ad probandum, veneratio-nem ligni crucis Deo placere; quia non est petitum ex sacra scriptura, q sola est norma venerationis & cultus diuini. II. Negamus, Deum inueniri eo tempore voluisse crucem, vt tuto posset coli, quia simpliciter auersatur cultum creaturæ tanquam Diabolicũ: Aut fi Deus voluit eo tempore eam inueniri, non vt tuto posset coli, sed vt religio & fides Chri-ftiana confirmaretur & ppagaretur inueniri voluit. Diabolus vero cum prævideret crucem fore seminarium commodum idololatriæ & superstitionum, procul dubio inueniri voluit crucem, vt religiosè coleretur. III. Si Deus eo tempore inueniri voluit crucem, quo tuto coli potuit, cur permisit, vt mulier libera a fluxu sanguinis ante hæc tempora statuam Christi regnatibus persecutoribus apud Paneadem erigeret, teste Eusebio, qui se eā vidi sse asserit? Si hæc statua Christi, ante tempora Constanti- ni regnantibus tyrannis, tuto coli potterat, quidni & crux Christi? Narrat Eusebius statuam illam sua ætate, id est, An. 330. ꝑ foribus domus istius mulieris in editiori loco fuisse collocatam, ibiq; ad huc fuisse tempore Iuliani Apostatæ, cur non & crux Christi tunc tuto coli potuisset, non secus atque hæc statua? Quin etiam docet Bellarminus primis
units.tr: Reply I. This testimony does nothing to prove that the veneration of the wood of the cross pleases God, because it is not drawn from Holy Scripture, which alone is the rule of veneration and divine worship. II. We deny that God wished the cross to be found at that time so that it could safely be worshipped, since He utterly rejects the worship of a creature as diabolical. Or if God did wish it to be found at that time, He wished it found not so that it could safely be worshipped, but so that the Christian religion and faith might be confirmed and propagated. The devil, however, foreseeing that the cross would be a convenient seedbed of idolatry and superstitions, undoubtedly wished the cross to be found so that it might be worshipped religiously. III. If God wished the cross to be found at a time when it could safely be worshipped, why did He permit the woman freed from the flow of blood to erect a statue of Christ before these times, while tyrants reigned, at Paneas, as Eusebius testifies, who says he saw it himself? If this statue of Christ could safely be worshipped before the times of Constantine, while tyrants reigned, why not also the cross of Christ? Eusebius relates that in his own age, that is in the year 330, that statue stood before the doors of that woman's house in a more elevated place, and that it was still there in the time of Julian the Apostate. Why, then, could the cross of Christ not have been safely worshipped at that time, no less than this statue? Indeed, Bellarmine himself teaches that for the first five hundred years images were received into churches, worshipped and adored. Why, then, could the cross of Christ not have been received and honoured with due honour in those times, and therefore before the times of Constantine?

units.la: H quingentis annis imagines in templa receptas, cultas, & adoratas fuisse, cur & crux Christi temporibus istis, ac proinde ante Constantini tempora, no potuisset recipi & debito honore affici?IV Si crux Christi diu post tempora Constantini inventa, fuisset debito honore fraudata, sequitur eam ante tempora Constantini regnantibus persecutorib. quo in terra altissime defossa latebat, debito honore fraudatam fuisse. At nimis irreligiosi fuissent primi illi Christiani, si crux quae est lignum vitae per eorum cul pam debito honore spoliata fuisset. Potuissent sane in privatis locis honorem debitam illi exhibere, si publicorum locorum facultas concessa non fuisset. Ante Constantini tempora extitisse fatentur imaginem Christi Seruatoris in memoriam accepti beneficii ab haemorrhoissa apud Paneadem erectam, num ista propterea debito honore fuit fraudata? Exstiterunt imagines B. Virginis Mariae & Apostolorum, teste Eusebio & Bellarmino, neque has ludibrio sed debito honore fuisse affectas profitebuntur, cur Christi crux, si reseruata fuisset, honore debito non fuisset excepta? V. Quid cum, si ludibrio hostium fuisset exposita? Chri-
units.tr: For five hundred years images were received into churches, honoured and adored. Why, then, could the cross of Christ not have been received and given its due honour in those times, and therefore before the time of Constantine? IV. If the cross of Christ had been discovered long after Constantine's time, it would follow that before Constantine's time, under persecuting rulers, when it lay buried deep in the earth, it was deprived of its due honour. But those first Christians would have been too irreligious if the cross, which is the tree of life, had been stripped of its due honour through their fault. They could certainly have paid it that honour in private places, if permission to use public places had not been granted. They admit that before Constantine's time an image of Christ the Saviour was set up at Paneas in memory of the benefit received from the woman with the issue of blood. Was that image therefore deprived of its due honour? Images of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of the Apostles existed, according to Eusebius and Bellarmine, and they profess that these were honoured not with mockery but with due reverence. Why, then, if Christ's cross had been preserved, would it not have been received with due honour? V. What if it had been exposed to the mockery of enemies?

units.la: Lib. 7 hist. Hc. 4. a ? Christus ipse ludibrio exceptus fuit à suis, Christiani etiam regnatibus persecutoribus ignominiose habiti sunt, ita vt per ludibrium dicti fuerint religiosi crucis teste Tertulliano num de honore & dignitate crucis quicquam hostium ludificationes & iniurias derogassent? Nonne salus ipsi honos constitisset, apud pios & vere Christianos, qui debito honore eam nunquam defraudassent? Vnde constat falsum esse, quod Bellarminus contedit tum diuinam prouidentiam manifestasse crucem, cum primum potuit coli. Diuina prouidentia non manifestauit crucem ad cultum, vtpote quae omnem rei creaturae cultum auersatur. Ergo nec tum manifestari eam voluit, cum primum voluit coli, cur enim non potuisset aeque coli ante tempora Constantini, si ad cultum Deus eam voluisset manifestari? Quod si non ab hostibus persecutoribus, saltem Christianis, religiosis crucis prout tunc vocabantur, debito cultu affecta fuisset, sicut & post Constantini tempora, non nisi a Christianis potuit coli, Ethnicis, quibus adhuc erant mixti Christiani, eam ludificantibus.
units.tr: Book 7 of the Church History, ch. 4. Christ himself was treated with contempt by his own people, and Christians under persecuting rulers were held in disgrace, so that they were mockingly called religious of the cross, as Tertullian attests. Did the mockery and insults of enemies take anything away from the honour and dignity of the cross? Would not the cross have stood in honour among pious and truly Christian people, who would never have defrauded it of its due honour? Hence it is clear that what Bellarmine contends is false, that divine providence revealed the cross when it first could be worshipped. Divine providence did not reveal the cross for worship, since it rejects all worship of any created thing. Therefore it did not wish the cross to be revealed then, when it first wished it to be worshipped. For why could it not equally have been worshipped before Constantine's time, if God had wished it revealed for worship? And if it was not honoured with worship even by Christians, who were then called religious of the cross, at least not by the persecuting enemies, then, as also after Constantine's time, it could be worshipped only by Christians, while pagans, among whom Christians were still mixed, mocked it.

units.la: Denique negamus eo tempore, quo inuenta est crux, fuisse cultum. Ambrosius in oratione de obitu Theodosii Imperatoris, testatur Helenam Constantini matrem, cum crucem invenisset regem adorasse, non lignum vtique, quia hic sit gentilis error & vanitas impiorum. Et quoties priscis Christianis pagani crucis adorationem exprobrarunt, iniuriam sibi fieri dixerunt, eamque serio à se repulerunt. Sic Octauius Caecilio pagano respondit; Cruces non colimus nec optamus.
units.tr: Finally, we deny that at the time the cross was found there was any worship of it. Ambrose, in his oration on the death of the Emperor Theodosius, testifies that Helena, Constantine's mother, when she had found the cross, adored the King, not the wood, of course, because this is pagan error and the vanity of the impious. And whenever pagans reproached the early Christians for adoring the cross, they said that an injury was being done to them and earnestly repudiated the charge. So Octavius answered the pagan Caecilius: We neither worship crosses nor desire them.

units.la: Tertio, quia per euidentia miracula demonstratum sit, esse veram crucem & proinde crucis inuentionem & revelationem illam à Deo esse. Nam cum tres cruces simul inuentae fuissent, nec posset plane crux Domini à crucibus latronum internosci, admotae fuerunt omnes tres ad mulierem quandam in extremis agentem, & cum duae priores nihil egissent, tertia admota mulieri mox eam reddidit sanam, scribit hoc Ruffinus l.10.hist.cap.8. Socrates l.13. Theodoretus l.1.c.18. Sozomenus l.2 c.1. & Nicephorus l.8 c.29. nec solum mulierem aegram sanavit, sed etiam mortuum virum excitavit eodem tempore ut scribunt Paulinus epistola undecima ad Seuerum. Seuerus libro secundo historiae sacrae, & Sozomenus libro secundo, capite pitę primo, qui & viri mortui & mulieres ægrota meminit.
units.tr: Thirdly, because it has been demonstrated by evident miracles that this is the true cross, and therefore that the finding and revelation of it were from God. For when three crosses had been found together, and the cross of the Lord could not plainly be distinguished from the crosses of the thieves, all three were brought to a certain woman at the point of death. When the first two had done nothing, the third, brought to the woman, immediately restored her to health. Rufinus writes this in book 10, ch. 8 of his history; Socrates in book 13; Theodoret in book 1, ch. 18; Sozomen in book 2, ch. 1; and Nicephorus in book 8, ch. 29. It did not only heal the sick woman, but at the same time also raised a dead man, as Paulinus writes in his eleventh letter to Severus; Severus in book 2 of his sacred history; and Sozomen in book 2, ch. 1, who mentions both the dead man and the sick woman.

units.la: Respond. I. Neque hoc testimonium ex miraculis agnitæ crucis sumptum, idoneum est ad probandum crucis venerationem. Neque enim miracula sunt Canon & norma probandæ veritatis doctrinæ, sed solum Dei verbum.
units.tr: Reply. I. This testimony, taken from miracles of the recognised cross, is not suitable for proving the veneration of the cross. For miracles are not the canon and norm for proving the truth of doctrine, but God's Word alone is.

units.la: II. Vt ipsa inuentio crucis fabula est, à superstitiosis hominibus consiPta; ita & miracula sunt fictitia, vel præstigio & illusiones Diabolicæ.
units.tr: II. Just as the finding of the cross is itself a fable invented by superstitious men, so the miracles too are fictitious, or else illusions and devilish deceptions.

units.la: III. Demus vera fuisse miracula; non tamen crucis adoratio aut cultus inde probatur; quia non crucis, sed Dei virtute miracula ista edita sunt, & quidem non in eum finem, vt religiosè coleretur crux, sed tum vt doctrina Christi crucifixi confirmaretur, tum vt infideles conuincerentur.
units.tr: III. Grant that the miracles were true. The adoration or worship of the cross is still not proved thereby, because these miracles were performed not by the power of the cross but by the power of God. Nor were they performed to the end that the cross should be worshipped religiously, but both to confirm the teaching of the crucified Christ and to convince unbelievers.

units.la: Quod si ad contactum crucis dixeris esse edita miracula, non tamen propter ea adoratio crucis inde cõficitur. Nam cadauer ex contactu ossium Elisæi reuixit, vixit, non tamen offa illa templo illata & adorata fuere. IV. Testes horum miraculorum quos adducit Bellarminus non sunt idonei ad faciendam nobis eorum fidem. Quod I. ex Gelasio Papa euidenter elucescit, cuius auctoritate non potest non magnifacere Bellarminus, qui scripta, illa de inuentione crucis dominicae ita legenda esse monet à Catholicis vt Beati Pauli praecedat sententia Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete. II. Ruffinam Hieronymus setit autorem iudicii & eruditionis inopem, quod reipsa satis comprobauit, temeraria illa miraculorum quae hic & illic in vulgo mandierat confarcinatione. Atque hoc Hieronymi iudicium de Ruffino amplexus est etiam Gelasius, probans eos, quos Hieronymus probauit, reiiciens illos quos Hieronymus reiecit. Illa sententia, inquit, quae beatum Hieronymum praedictum sentire cognoscimus, & non solum de Ruffino, sed etiam de vniuersis, quos vir saepius memoratus zelo Dei & fidei religione reprehendit. Quod Gelasii iudicium probat etiam Bellarminus, Ruffinus inquit merito notatur erroris a Gelasio Papa, c. Sancta Rom. distinct. 15.
units.tr: But if you say the miracles were performed at contact with the cross, still the adoration of the cross does not follow from that. For a corpse was revived and came to life through contact with the bones of Elisha, yet those bones were not brought into the temple and adored. IV. The witnesses of these miracles whom Bellarmine adduces are not suitable to make us believe them. First, this is clear from Pope Gelasius, whose authority Bellarmine cannot but hold in high regard. Gelasius warns that the writings on the finding of the Lord's cross are to be read by Catholics in such a way that the saying of the blessed Paul goes before: Prove all things; hold fast what is good. Second, Jerome judged Rufinus to be an author lacking in judgement and learning, which he sufficiently proved in fact by that rash patching together of miracles which he had gathered here and there from the common people. Gelasius too embraced this judgement of Jerome about Rufinus, approving those whom Jerome approved and rejecting those whom Jerome rejected. That sentiment, he says, which we know the blessed Jerome held, and not only about Rufinus but about all whom that man, so often mentioned, reproves out of zeal for God and religious faith. Bellarmine too approves Gelasius's judgement: Rufinus, he says, is rightly noted for error by Pope Gelasius, c. Sancta Rom., distinct. 15.

units.la: Non igitur temere fidem derogamus
units.tr: We therefore do not rashly detract from their credibility.

units.la: lib. de script. eccles. fast. ius Ruffino, huius & similium mira-bulorum superstitioso Buccinatori. III. etiam caeteros, vt probatos & fide dig-nos testes non agnoscimus, vt qui nulla adhibita exploratione absque iudicio, vulgi superstitionib. narrationibus de-cepti mira, cultum illud in literas retu-lere, vt satis liquido Sozomenus confirmat l. 2. c. 1. Sunt haec quidem, inquit, à nobis prout accipimus commemorata, quando-quidem ea ex viris, qui ea accurate norunt, & ad quos eorum cognitio à partibus ad liberos successione quadam deriuata peruenit, audiuimus.
units.tr: (Jerome, in his book on ecclesiastical writers.) We do not regard Rufinus, that superstitious trumpeter of this and similar miracles, as a reliable witness. III. Nor do we acknowledge the others as approved and trustworthy witnesses, since without any careful examination and without judgement, deceived by the superstitious tales of the common people, they committed those wonders and that worship to writing. Sozomen clearly confirms this in book 2, ch. 1: "These things indeed, he says, we have related as we have received them, since we heard them from men who know them accurately, and to whom knowledge of them has come by a certain succession from fathers to children."

units.la: Quibus verbis diserte ostendit, haec se ex fama & relatione vulgi superstitiosi historiae suae intexuisse. Viros illos, qui ea accurate norunt, no intelligit alios, qua homines simplices, q superstitiosa credulitate decepti fabularum istarum auctoribus fidem habuere. V. Respondeat nobis Pontificii cur Eusebius qui vitam Constantini & Helenę matris. IV. libris accuratissime describit: nullam tamen horum miraculorum tam celebrium, quę isto seculo edita narrantur, mentionem faciat? Vixit isto aevo Eusebius, ita vt nemo melius nosse potuerit, & describere, quę eo tempore miracula gesta fuerint. At neq; de sanatione mulieris, neq; de refuscirefuscitatione mortui quicquam apud ipsum legitur. Ruffinus, Socrates, Theodoretus & cæteri, quos citat, sunt æui posterioris, eoque ad faciendam fidem parum idonei. VI. Etiam horum miraculorum Ambrosius & Chrysostomus, patres grauissimi & sanctissimi non meminere, cum agnitæ crucis modum describunt. Si ex his miraculis agnita fuisset, non conueniebat istorum virorum pietati, reticere aut dissimulare hunc miraculosum agnitionis modum, utpote, qui ad gloriam Christi & crucis dignitatem pertinebat: Et cur reticuissent? Reticemus ea, quorum memoriam volumus sepultam. An putas Ambrosium & Chrysostomum deletam voluisse horum miraculorum memoriam? Hæc in tantos viros non cadunt. Qualem autem agnitæ crucis modum nobis reuelat Ambrosius & Chrysostomus? Referunt illi agnitam esse crucem ex titulo nullam miraculosæ agnitionis mentionem faciunt. Quare non est dubium, quin fictitia sunt illa, quæ credula vulgi superstitio obtrusit miracula.
units.tr: By these words he plainly shows that he wove these things into his history from the report and hearsay of the superstitious common people. By "men who know them accurately" he means none other than simple folk who, deceived by superstitious credulity, gave faith to the authors of those fables. V. Let the Papists answer us why Eusebius, who describes most accurately the life of Constantine and his mother Helena in four books, nevertheless makes no mention of any of these famous miracles that are narrated as having happened in that age. Eusebius lived in that age, so no one could have known better or described what miracles were performed at that time. Yet nothing is read in him about the healing of the woman or the raising of the dead. Rufinus, Socrates, Theodoret and the others whom he cites belong to a later age, and so are of little use for establishing faith. VI. Ambrose and Chrysostom, very grave and holy fathers, also do not mention these miracles when they describe the manner of recognising the cross. If the cross had been recognised through these miracles, it would not have befitted the piety of these men to be silent about or conceal this miraculous manner of recognition, since it pertained to the glory of Christ and the dignity of the cross. And why would they have been silent? We pass over in silence those things whose memory we wish to be buried. Do you think Ambrose and Chrysostom wanted the memory of these miracles blotted out? Such a thing does not fit such great men. But what manner of recognising the cross do Ambrose and Chrysostom reveal to us? They say the cross was recognised from the title; they make no mention of any miraculous recognition. Hence there is no doubt that those miracles which credulous superstition of the common people has thrust upon us are fictitious.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus. Non obstat, inquit, quod Ambrosius orat: in Theodosium & Chrysostomus hom. 84. in Iohannem dicunt crucem rucem Domini ex titulo cognitam, quo careant alia duæ. Nam Ruffinus indicat, ex titulo quidem fuisse cognitam crucem Domini, sed omnino euidenter, quia titulus non erat affixus cruci, sed iacebat prope eam, ideo vt nulla remaneret ambiguitas, ad miraculum confugerunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine takes up the point. It is no objection, he says, that Ambrose, in his oration against Theodosius, and Chrysostom, in homily 84 on John, say that the cross of the Lord was recognised from the title, which the other two lack. For Rufinus shows that the cross of the Lord was indeed recognised from the title, but quite evidently, because the title was not fixed to the cross but lay near it; so that no ambiguity would remain, they had recourse to a miracle.

units.la: Resp. I. Ruffinus quidem scribit minus evidenter, ex titulo agnitam, sed non probat contra Chrysostomum, probat ex titulo eam agnitam esse euidenter. Cum duæ cruces, inquit, essent inuentæ, par est, quia media erat, & propter titulum Domini crucem agnitam, quia latronum cruces titulum non habeant. Ruffinus dicit titulum fuisse à cruce auulsum, sed nullo idoneo probat testimonio, eo tantum confugit ut miraculis viam sterneret, prout secum illud ferax erat miraculorum, quamvis fabulis fuere similiora, quam veris miraculis. Si minus euidenter ex titulo agnita fuisset, cur Ambros. & Chrysost. cum Ruffino ad miracula non confugere? Nunc lubitatione remaere voluerunt & incerta atque ambigua relinquere crucis agnitionem? Nunc iudicio grauior fuit Ruffinus Ambrosio & Chrysost. quam & certiore & euidentiorem nobis crucis agnitæ tenuerit? Nobis persuasum est Ruffinum eiusque sectatorum iudicii simplicitate & superstitionis temeritate deceptos, vt apparentia aut falsa pro veris & euidentib. fuerint amplexi.
units.tr: Reply I. Rufinus does indeed write that the cross was recognised from the title, though less evidently, but this does not refute Chrysostom. Rufinus proves that it was recognised from the title, and evidently so. "When two crosses," he says, "had been found, it was fitting that the middle one be taken as the Lord's, and that the cross was recognised because of the title of the Lord, since the crosses of the thieves had no title." Rufinus says the title was torn off the cross, but he proves this by no suitable testimony. He only has recourse to it in order to pave the way for miracles, since he was as fertile in miracles as he was ready to invent them, though they are more like fables than true miracles. If the cross had been recognised from the title less evidently, why did Ambrose and Chrysostom not have recourse to miracles with Rufinus? Did they now want to leave the recognition of the cross uncertain and ambiguous, out of doubt? Was Rufinus now more weighty in judgment than Ambrose and Chrysostom, that he held a surer and more evident recognition of the cross? We are persuaded that Rufinus and his followers, through the simplicity of their judgment and the rashness of their superstition, were deceived, and so embraced appearances or falsehoods as true and evident things.

units.la: Historias eorum si quis legerit, nimis temerarios miraculorum praecones & Buccinatores eos deprehendet.
units.tr: If anyone reads their histories, he will find them overly rash heralds and trumpeters of miracles.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus.
