Nec solum crux illo miraculo claruit, sed etiam clavus, quem Helena ad Constantinum misit, de eo siquidem, vt Ambrosius testatur loco citato, Iudei dicebant, ecce & clau in honore est, & quem ad mortem impressimus remedium salutis est, atq; inuisibili potestate Daemones torquet.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses on: Nor did the cross alone shine by that miracle, but also the nail which Helena sent to Constantine; for concerning it, as Ambrose testifies in the place cited, the Jews said: "Behold, the nail too is held in honour, and that which we fixed for death is a remedy of salvation, and it torments demons with invisible power."

units.la: Resp. I. Falsum est, clauum illo miraculo claruisse, imo vt crucis, ita & clavi inuentio fabulosa est & fictitia. II. Ambrosius crucis ex titulo agnitionem euidenter describit, miraculi, quo crux vel clavus eius claruerit, nullam faciens mentionem. III. Quod Iudaeos de clauo illo dixisse pronunciat Ambrosius, id more oratorio recitat, estq; metarhetoricatio ad mouendum & delectandum potius, quam ad affirmandum aut probandum accommodata. IV. Si mentem Ambrosii recte inspexeris, non tam clavum intelligit, quam Christum, cui clavus est impressus. Neq; enim adeo a ratione aberrat, vt clavum in se & sua natura túrà dicàt esse salutis remedium, & invisibili potestate torquere Dæmones, sed relate, quàteus Christum crucifixit, seu vt Ambrosius loquitur, quateus Christo ad morte impressus est, hoc est, ipse Christus clauo cruci ad morte fixus. V. Demus isthoc Bellarmino: agnoscimus clauo ὑπερβολικῶς tribui ea, quæ Christi propria sunt; quæro vero ex ipso nu Ambrosii adoratione clauu vel crucis Christi celebret? sane ne verbulo quidem eam approbat aut affirmat, imo expresse solû Deu loco citato inuocandû pronunciat, inquiens, Tu solus Domine inuocandus es, tu rogandus vt eum in filiis repræsentes, Tu Domine custodiens etiam paruulos, in hac sublimitate saluos facito sperantes in te.
units.tr: Reply I. It is false that the nail shone by that miracle; indeed, just as the finding of the cross is fabulous and fictitious, so too is the finding of the nail. II. Ambrose describes the recognition of the cross from the title in evident terms, making no mention of any miracle by which the cross or its nail shone. III. What Ambrose says the Jews said about that nail he recites in the manner of an orator, and it is a figure of speech, adapted to move and delight rather than to affirm or prove. IV. If you rightly consider Ambrose's meaning, he is thinking less of the nail than of Christ, to whom the nail was fixed. For he does not so far depart from reason as to say that the nail in itself and by its own nature is a remedy of salvation and torments demons with invisible power; rather he speaks relatively, insofar as it crucified Christ, or, as Ambrose puts it, insofar as it was fixed for the death of Christ; that is, Christ himself, fixed to the cross by the nail for death. V. Grant Bellarmine this: we acknowledge that what belongs to Christ is hyperbolically attributed to the nail. But I ask, does Ambrose in his oration celebrate the nail or the cross of Christ with any adoration? Certainly he does not approve or affirm it even in a word; indeed, in the place cited he expressly pronounces that God alone is to be invoked, saying: "You alone, Lord, are to be invoked; you are to be asked that you may present him in the sons; you, Lord, who also keep the little ones, make safe those who hope in you in this height."

units.la: Quarto, Quia Helena non ex se incitata est ad crucem Domini quærendum, sed diuinus admonita reuelationibus. Sic enim testatur Eusebius in Chronic: quod Hieronymus latinum fecit, Helena Constantini mater, inquit, diuinis monita visionibus, beatissimum crucis lignum, in quo mundi salus pependit, apud Hierosolymam reperit. Et idem dicunt Ambrosius, Ruffinus, Paulinus, Sulpitius & alij.
units.tr: Fourth, Helena was not stirred of herself to seek the cross of the Lord, but was divinely admonished by revelations. For Eusebius testifies in his Chronicle, which Jerome made into Latin: "Helena, mother of Constantine, admonished by divine visions, found at Jerusalem the most blessed wood of the cross, on which the salvation of the world hung." Ambrose, Rufinus, Paulinus, Sulpicius and others say the same.

units.la: Resp. I. Neque hoc testimonium sufficiens est ad probandam crucis adorationem. Si enim Deus incitauit Helenam
units.tr: Reply I. Neither is this testimony sufficient to prove the adoration of the cross. For even if God stirred Helena

units.la: nam, ad quærendam crucem, non ideo fecit, vt crux coleretur, sed vt passio & mors Christi, quæ à Iudæis Gentibus & quibusdam hæreticis negabatur, eo velut monumento confirmaretur. Christum igitur regem nostrum adorandum esse hinc concluditur, non lignum crucis; prout etiam fecisse Helenam Ambrosius agnoscit, Regem adoravit non lignum crucis. II. Falsum est, quod de diuino Helenæ impulsu & revelatione dicitur. Ex tota rei historia apparet eam proprio voluntatis instinctu & fœminea superstitiosaq; quadam devotione primo loca sacra adorandi causa iniisse. Nam cum tempore Constantini M. Ecclesia pace frueretur opibus ac diuitiis cumularetur, vera pietas & fidei integritas in dies cepit decrescere, & in superstitionem degenerare, adeo vt homines potius in rerum externarum cultu, quam in fide & pietate semet exercerent. Tunc igitur Helena seculi istius mores secuta, non diuino instinctu & revelatione, sed suo quodam motu proprio, qui superstitionem potius quam pietatem præsse ferebant, incitata fuit; nonvt crucem quæreret, sed vt sacra illa loca inuiseret, ibidemque Christum adoraret. Eusebius certè certè vel in historia Ecclesiastica, vel in libris de vita Constantini rem hanc admodum memorabilem tradidisset & celebrasset, si diuinis reuelationibus gesta esset. At nihil vel de inuentione crucis, vel diuina reuelatione ipsi facta traditum reperitur. Quod Bellarminus ex Chronico Eusebii affert, parum nos mouet, cum constet opus illud teste Baronio esse medosissimum, & tum ab Hieronymo, tum ab aliis varie adulteratum. Hieronymus latinum fecit Chronicū Eusebii, & fatetur ipse, se multa inter transferendum addidisse: alii deinde adulteratores varis nugis, quas vulgi superstitio prætextu religionis inuexit, opus illud contaminarunt. Ex eodem fonte Ambrosius & reliqui eam hauserunt. Vulgi enim in superstitionem plus satis inclinantis error decepti, fabulam hac speciem pietatis redolentem pro vera historia sunt amplexi. Quod si hæc nostra sordent Pontificiis, moueantur saltem Gelasii Papæ decreto, quo sancitur, narrationem hac esse apocryphaм. Apocryphi vero nomine, non id tantum, quod oppositum est Canonicæ scripturæ, intelligit. [Nam ita multa scripta essent apocrypha, quæ ibi laudantur] sed quod vt falsum & commentitium reiicitur.
units.tr: to seek the cross, he did not do so that the cross should be worshipped, but so that the passion and death of Christ, which was denied by Jews, Gentiles and certain heretics, might be confirmed by that monument as by a witness. From this it is concluded that Christ our King is to be adored, not the wood of the cross; as Ambrose also acknowledges that Helena did: She adored the King, not the wood of the cross. II. What is said about a divine impulse and revelation to Helena is false. From the whole history of the matter it appears that she set out, first for the sake of adoring the holy places, by her own impulse of will and by a certain womanly superstitious devotion. For when, in the time of Constantine the Great, the Church enjoyed peace and was heaped with resources and riches, true piety and integrity of faith began day by day to decline and to degenerate into superstition, so that men exercised themselves rather in the worship of external things than in faith and piety. Then Helena, following the manners of this age, was stirred not by divine instinct or revelation but by a certain motion of her own, which showed superstition rather than piety; not so that she might seek the cross, but so that she might visit those holy places and there adore Christ. Eusebius certainly would have handed down and celebrated this very memorable matter, either in his Ecclesiastical History or in the books on the life of Constantine, if it had been done by divine revelations. Yet nothing is found handed down either about the finding of the cross or about any divine revelation made to her. What Bellarmine brings from the Chronicle of Eusebius moves us little, since it is agreed, as Baronius bears witness, that this work is very corrupt, and it has been variously adulterated both by Jerome and by others. Jerome made a Latin version of the Chronicle of Eusebius, and he himself confesses that he added many things in translating. Then other adulterers polluted that work with various trifles which the superstition of the common people introduced under the pretext of religion. From this same source Ambrose and the rest drew it. For the common people, deceived by an error that inclines too much to superstition, embraced a fable smelling of a semblance of piety as true history. But if these things of ours are despised by the Papists, let them at least be moved by the decree of Pope Gelasius, by which it is sanctioned that this narrative is apocryphal. Yet by the name apocryphal he does not mean only what is opposed to canonical Scripture [for in that case many writings praised there would be apocryphal], but what is rejected as false and made up.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus. I Accusans impudentem blasphemiam Magdeburgensium, quod Helenam dixerint superstitiosam, quia Hierosolymam petierit ut lignum crucis quaereret, quam tamen sancti Patres, omnes mirifice laudant & Spiritu Sancto inspirante dicunt crucis lignum quaesiisse.
units.tr: Bellarmine takes up the point again: Accusing the impudent blasphemy of the Magdeburgians, who said that Helena was superstitious because she went to Jerusalem to seek the wood of the cross, which nevertheless all the holy Fathers praise wonderfully, and say that she sought the wood of the cross under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Resp. I. Recte superstitiosam vocant Helenam Magdeburgenses. Nam iidem profecta est Hierosolymam, ut crucem, quae sacrosanctum ei futura esset κειμήλιον inuenires, non video, quam ei iniuriam fecerint Magdeburgenses, qui posthabito interno Dei cultu religionem maxime in rebus externis quaerunt ac collocant, ii parum religiosi, satis vero superstitiosi nobis videntur. Quam topere vero rebus externis addicta fuerit Helena, quantum cruci & clauis tribuerit, id ex historia cuiuis obuium est. Vnam portionem crucis dicitur theca argentea inclusisse, & Hierosolymae ad memoriam illic visere cupientibus reliquisse; alteram misit ad filium, quam is postea in foro posuit, ut testatur Sozomenus lib. 1. cap. 17. Clauorum alios regiae Cassidi dicitur inseruisse, alios Camo equi indidisse, ut filio essent instar
units.tr: Reply I. The Magdeburgians rightly call Helena superstitious. For if she went to Jerusalem so that she might find the cross, which was to be a sacred treasure for her, I do not see what injury the Magdeburgians have done her. They, setting aside the inward worship of God, seek and place religion chiefly in external things; they seem to us little religious and quite superstitious. How greatly Helena was devoted to external things, and how much she attributed to the cross and the nails, is obvious to anyone from history. She is said to have enclosed one portion of the cross in a silver case and left it at Jerusalem for those wishing to visit it there in memory; she sent another to her son, which he afterwards placed in the forum, as Sozomen testifies, book 1, chapter 17. Some of the nails she is said to have inserted into the imperial helmet, and others into the bridle of the horse, so that they would serve her son as a

units.la: {y} Eadem sententia...
units.tr: {y} The same opinion...

units.la: star ἀμυνπης; Nonne superstitionem hæc omnia redolent? Religio Christiana spiritualis est, & cultum spiritualem requirit ; Helena nostra sectata fuit res externas, pietatem & religionem ab inuentione crucis & clauorum æstimauit quæ superstitionis propria sunt, vtpote, quæ ab externis dependet & externa curiose sectatur. Non quidem illud improbamus quod profecta est Hierosolymam, vt confirmaret fidem suam aspectu rerum & monumetorum passionis & mortis Christi, quæ à Iudæis, Ethnicis, & aliis quibusdam hæreticis tunc negabatur, sed illud culpamus, quod adeo rebus externis inhæserit, vt sanctitatis magnam partem in iis posuerit, & cruci, clauis ac sepulcro Christi plus fidei, quam SS. scriptis Apostolicis & Euangelicis tribuerit. II. Superstitio sa vocatur non tantum ideo, quod Hierosolymam petierit qrendæ crucis causa, sed q adorandi Christi causa eo contenderit, quasi adoratio esset alligata loco ; Sic apud Eusebium profitetur se ire Hierosolymam, vt adoraret in loco, vbi steterunt pedes Christi; Adoratio Christi religionis fuit, adoratio in locis sacris fuit superstitionis, quæ iam tum reliligioni erat adnata. III. Patres religionis zelum, amorem & studiū eius ergaChri stum laudarūt, superstitione vero cum hoc religionis zelo coniunctam non probarunt. Quod Christum quaesiuit & adorauit, laudabile fuit, quod Hierosolymis potius, quam alibi Christum quaesiuit & adorauit, culpabile, vt pote cuilo co Christus Ioh. 4. omnem eripuit prae rogatiuam. IV. Esto: laudent patres pietatem & zelum Helenae, crucis inuentionem ex Spiritu Sancto suscep-tam pdicent. Num vero quisquam eorum crucis latriam & adorationem probat ac laudat, aut Helenae eam tribuit? Reliquit vnam portionem crucis Hierosolymae, non adorauit ea, sed Christu regem ait Ambrosius; reliquit eam ad memoriam, non ad cultum & adorationem; reliquit his, qui eam videre, non qui adorare vellent. Constantino alteram partem misit, non vt adoraret, sed vt in rei memoriam conseruaret. Constantinus eam nec adorauit, neque in templo adorandam proposuit, sed in foro collocauit. V. Quid multis? Ipsam historiam de inuentione verae crucis fabulosam esse dicimus, vt supra ostendimus, aut saltem cum Magdeburgensibus dubiam & incertam esse affirmamus. Rationes Magdeburgen-sium recitat Bellarminus. I. Quia Am-brosius sit antiquissimus omnium, qui eam hi-storiam referunt, sed illis orationem in Theodo-sium, vbi hoc habetur Erasmus non recipit vt Germanam. II. Quia Eusebius l. 3. de vita Con-stant: de Helena multa narrat, & de repur-gatione montis Caluariæ, & tamen non me-minit inuentionis crucis.
units.tr: protection. Do not all these things smell of superstition? The Christian religion is spiritual and requires spiritual worship; Helena, our woman, pursued external things, and she esteemed piety and religion as residing in the discovery of the cross and the nails, which are the marks of superstition, since they depend on external things and busily pursue external things. We do not indeed disapprove that she went to Jerusalem to confirm her faith by seeing the places and monuments of the passion and death of Christ, which were then denied by Jews, pagans and certain other heretics; but we blame that she clung so closely to external things that she placed a great part of holiness in them, and attributed more faith to the cross, the nails and the sepulchre of Christ than to the holy Apostolic and Evangelical writings. II. She is called superstitious not only because she went to Jerusalem for the sake of seeking the cross, but because she hastened there for the sake of adoring Christ, as if adoration were bound to a place. So in Eusebius she professes that she goes to Jerusalem to adore in the place where the feet of Christ stood. The adoration of Christ belonged to religion; adoration in holy places belonged to superstition, which was already then attached to religion. III. The Fathers praised the zeal, love and eagerness of religion toward Christ, but they did not approve superstition joined with this zeal of religion. That she sought and adored Christ was praiseworthy; that she sought and adored Christ at Jerusalem rather than elsewhere was blameworthy, since Christ in John 4 took away all such prerogative of place. IV. Grant that the Fathers praise the piety and zeal of Helena, and proclaim that she undertook the discovery of the cross under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Yet does any of them approve or praise the latria and adoration of the cross, or attribute it to Helena? She left one portion of the cross at Jerusalem; she did not adore it, but Ambrose calls the King Christ; she left it for memory, not for worship and adoration; she left it for those who wished to see it, not for those who wished to adore. She sent the other part to Constantine, not so that he would adore it, but so that he would keep it in memory of the event. Constantine neither adored it nor set it up in a temple to be adored, but placed it in the forum. V. What more need be said? We say that the history of the finding of the true cross is itself fabulous, as we have shown above, or at least, with the Magdeburgians, we affirm that it is doubtful and uncertain. Bellarmine recites the reasons of the Magdeburgians. I. Because Ambrose is the most ancient of all who relate this history, but Erasmus does not accept as German that oration against Theodosius where this is found. II. Because Eusebius, book 3 of the Life of Constantine, narrates much about Helena, and about the purging of Mount Calvary, and yet makes no mention of the finding of the cross.

units.la: Contra I. Excipit Bellarminus. I. Non extare talem Erasmi censuram, imo ipsi Magdeburgenses centuria 4. c. 13. in vita Ambrosii, ex iudicio Erasmi hanc orationem Ambrosio tribuunt. 2. si extaret, Erasmum non esse diuinum oraculum, cui necessario credi debeat, quando nullam affert rationem.
units.tr: Against the first point, Bellarmine objects: (1) there is no such censure of Erasmus; indeed the Magdeburg Centuriators themselves, Century 4, chapter 13, in the life of Ambrose, attribute this oration to Ambrose on the judgment of Erasmus; (2) even if the censure existed, Erasmus is not a divine oracle that must necessarily be believed when he gives no reason.

units.la: Resp. Non hoc vrgent Magdeburgenses, q; Erasmus orationem in Theodosium pro spuria habeat, cui tanquam diuino oraculo credi debeat, sed quod Ambrosius sit primus omnium, qui hac de re scripserit, illud vrget. Et enim Ambrosius vir esset grauis, integer, eruditionis iudiciique laude clarus; tamen cum ea ætate non vixerit, ac proinde ipse nō viderit, quæ narrat, nec ab his, qui ea viderunt acceperit, non potuit rem istam verè nosse, atque vt gesta est describere; præsertim cum esset extraneus, quibus acciaccidit sæpè vt in rerum exoticarum de scriptione errent, quod rerum alienarum historias nō æque atq; domesticas nosse & compertas habere nequeunt. Quare vulgi potius errore tunc superstitiones plus æquo sectatis fascinatus, rem istam in literas retulit. Ex superiorū scriptorum monumentis hæc petere atque describere nō potuit, cum ante ipsum plures huius rei fide digni scriptores nō extitere, ex quibus cognoscere ac depromere ea potuerit, adeo vt non sit dubium, quin prout à vulgo acceperit & publica fama audierit, hæc literis mandarit; Omnium optimè nosse hæc potuit ac describere Eusebius, qui coæuus fuit Constantini & Helenę, eorumque veluti domesticus. Is vbi vitam Constantini & Helenæ matris describit, pietatem sanctitatem, zelum & studium Helenæ erga Christum laudat ac commendat, de crucis vero & clavorum inventione prorsus reticet; Quod filetium Eusebii res sui temporis scribentis certam exploratamq; fidem facit, de rei huius vanitate ac falsitate; præsertim cum Papa Gelasius, cuius autoritatem negare, aut in dubium vocare nequeunt, narrationem hanc reprobarit, & apocrypha habenthabendam esse sanxerit.
units.tr: Reply: The Magdeburgers do not press the point that Erasmus regards the oration against Theodosius as spurious, as though it must be believed as a divine oracle. They press the point that Ambrose is the first of all who wrote about this matter. Ambrose was indeed a grave, upright man, distinguished for learning and judgment. Yet he did not live in that age, and so he did not see what he relates, nor did he receive it from those who saw it. He could not truly know the matter or describe it as it happened, especially since he was a foreigner. It often happens that those who write of foreign affairs go astray, because they cannot know and have at hand the histories of foreign matters as well as they know domestic ones. Hence, deceived by the popular error of that time, which indulged superstitions beyond measure, he committed this story to writing. He could not have drawn these things from the records of earlier writers, since before him there were no trustworthy writers on this matter from whom he could learn and draw them. So there is no doubt that he wrote these things as he had heard them from the common people and public report. Eusebius, who was a contemporary of Constantine and Helena and almost a member of their household, could have known and described these things best of all. When he describes the life of Constantine and of his mother Helena, he praises and commends Helena's piety, holiness, zeal and devotion towards Christ, but he is completely silent about the discovery of the cross and the nails. This silence of Eusebius, who wrote of the events of his own time, gives certain and clear proof of the vanity and falsity of this matter. Especially so, since Pope Gelasius, whose authority they cannot deny or call into doubt, rejected this narrative and decreed that it be held as apocryphal.

units.la: Instat. Falsum esse, quod Ambrosius sit antiquissimus eorum, qui hanc historiam retulerunt: Nam Sulpitius, Ruffinus, Paulinus, Hieronymus, Chrysostomus, qui eadem recitant, aequa les Ambrosii dici possunt, cum eodem tempore vixerint, licet Ambrosius esset paulo fort ille senior.
units.tr: Objection: "It is false that Ambrose is the most ancient of those who related this story. For Sulpicius, Rufinus, Paulinus and Jerome, and Chrysostom, who repeat the same things, can be called as old as Ambrose, since they lived at the same time, although Ambrose was perhaps a little older."

units.la: Resp. I. Seipsum prodit hic Bellarminus. Si enim est paulo senior, fuit ergo primus tempore, ac proinde omnium illorum antiquissimus. Sed nec paulo senio rem fuisse Ambrosiū ipse Bellarminus est testis. Ambrosium scribit floruisse Anno 374. Gratiano & Theodosio Imperatoribus: Hieronymum & Ruffinū. Anno 390. Chrysostomum Anno 398. Paulinum vero & Sulpitium 420. Num hoc aequales tempore dixeris? Quod si forsan Hieronymo & Ruffino paulo senior fuerit, Chrysostomo tamen, Paulino & Sulpitio multo seniorem esse fateris necesse est. II. Hi omnes aeque atque Ambrosius, non ex aliquo fide digno Historico, sed ex vulgi, quod satis isto saeculo superstitionibus indulgebat, errore ista omnia hausere. Nemo certe illorum est, qui testetur se vel ex Eusebio aut aliis superiorum monumentis hæc obseruata, literis prodidisse. Quin nonnulli eorum ex sermonib. maiorum, se hæc deprofisse fatentur, & vt narrata tantum referunt, Alii hęc & similia sine mentione autorum, put in vulgo inaudierant superstitiosæ pietatis opinione fascinati suæ historiæ inseruere. III. Etiam hi fuerint coætanei, tamen horum omnium testimonium refutat Eusebii, qui Ambrosio & reliquis antiquior, profundum silentium. Is enim cū Constantini & Helenæ tempore vixerit, eorum res gestas omnes sibi perspectissimas habuit. Aut igitur nesciuit eam historiam Eusebius, aut sciuit, si nesciuit, fateor, eā describere nō potuit. At nesciuisse eum tā celebrem historiam, qs credat eū, eo tempore, quo hæc accidere, vixerit, & res illius temporis diligeter obseruarit, ac descripserit? Si sciuit quomodo, cum res sui temporis scriberet, hanc historiam, quæ instituto ipsius maxime conueniebat tacere & silentio præterire potuisset?
units.tr: Reply: First, Bellarmine betrays himself here. If Ambrose is a little older, he is therefore first in time, and so the most ancient of all those men. But Bellarmine himself is witness that he was not only a little older. He writes that Ambrose flourished in the year 374, under the emperors Gratian and Theodosius; Jerome and Rufinus in the year 390; Chrysostom in the year 398; and Paulinus and Sulpicius in 420. Would you call these men contemporaries? But if Ambrose was perhaps a little older than Jerome and Rufinus, you must admit he was much older than Chrysostom, Paulinus and Sulpicius. Second, all these men, like Ambrose, drew all this not from any trustworthy historian but from the error of the common people, who in that age were very much given to superstitions. None of them testifies that he published these things in writing from Eusebius or other earlier records. Indeed some of them confess that they took these things from the sermons of their elders, and they relate them only as things told. Others inserted these and similar things into their histories without mention of authorities, as they had heard them among the common people, carried away by an opinion of superstitious piety. Third, even if these men were contemporaries, the silence of Eusebius, who was older than Ambrose and the others, refutes the testimony of them all, and that silence is profound. For Eusebius lived in the time of Constantine and Helena, and he had a most thorough knowledge of all their deeds. Either Eusebius did not know that story, or he knew it. If he did not know it, I grant he could not describe it. But can anyone believe that he did not know so famous a story, when he lived at the time it is said to have happened and carefully observed and described the affairs of that time? If he knew it, how, when writing the history of his own time, could he have passed over in silence this story, which was most in keeping with his purpose?

units.la: Instat. At Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus eadem recitat Ambrosio antiquior, in epistola ad Constantium Augustum, Item Constantinus ipse, Ambrosio similiter antiquior, eiusdem meminit in epistola ad Macharium, charium, quam refert Eusebius libro tertio, de vita Constant. vbi sic habet: Tanta est Dei nostri benignitas vt nulla verborum officia praesenti miraculo digna esse queant. Hoc enim admirationem omnem stuporemq; praeterit, indicium tormenti sacratissimi tot annis humo sepultum, vsque dum interfecto communi hoste, libera familia apparuit ignorari, &c. ibidem addit nouis miraculis fidem esse declaratam.
units.tr: Objection: "But Cyril of Jerusalem relates the same things, and he is older than Ambrose, in his letter to the Emperor Constantius. Likewise Constantine himself, who is similarly older than Ambrose, mentions the same in his letter to Macarius, which Eusebius cites in the third book of the Life of Constantine, where he says: 'So great is the goodness of our God that no words of ours are fit for the present miracle. For this surpasses all admiration and wonder, the sign of the most sacred torment, buried in the earth for so many years, until, the common enemy being slain, it appeared to a free household, as if unknown...' He adds in the same place that faith was confirmed by new miracles."

units.la: Respond. I. At hic Cyrillus paulo senior fuit Ambrosio; floruit enim Anno 365. eodemque tempore vixit, quo Ambrosius. Ergo eadem, & quidem potiori iure Ambrosii aequalis dici potest, quam Sulpitius & Paulinus. 2. Epistola illa Spuria est, vt stylus indicat: Et Hieronymus etiam eius in libro de scriptt. Ecclesiasticis non meminit. Quare fides ei non adhibenda est. III. Si Cyrillus meminit crucis inuentae, cur caeteri Episcopi Hierosolymitani de ea tantopere silent? Num adeo vecordes & negligentes eos dixeris fuisse, vt tantae gratiae; tam praeciosi & sancti ligni non meminissent; praesertim cum Helena portionem crucis inuentae; Hierosolymae reliquisset ad memoriam his, qui eam videre vellent?
units.tr: Reply: First, this Cyril was a little older than Ambrose; for he flourished in the year 365 and lived at the same time as Ambrose. So he can be called a contemporary of Ambrose, and with better right than Sulpicius and Paulinus. Second, that letter is spurious, as its style shows; and Jerome does not mention it in his book on ecclesiastical writers. So it should not be given credit. Third, if Cyril mentions the discovery of the cross, why do the other bishops of Jerusalem keep such a great silence about it? Would you say they were so foolish and negligent that they did not mention such a great grace, so precious and holy a wood? Especially since Helena left a portion of the discovered cross at Jerusalem, to be kept in memory for those who wished to see it.

units.la: III. Esto meminerit inuentionis, atque adorationis crucis vbi meminit, quæ caput rei est, quam tractamus? IV. Constantinus loco citato non celebrat crucis inuentionem, sed Dominici sepulchri patefactionem. Supra cap. 28. docuerat, quomodo Ethnici ad omnem resurrectionis Christi memoriam abolendam conati fuerint sepulchrum Christi tollere ac delere, idque tum puluere & sordibus aggregatis, tu Veneris fano in loco eius extructo. Hoc capite commemorat singulari Dei beneficio factum esse vt sepulchrum Dominicum, quod tam diu ad suam vsque ætatem latuerit, nunc in lucem fuerit protractum, in quo ipse templum splendidissimum extruxerit. Depravat igitur Bellarminus epistolā Constantini, quæ nihil habet de inuentione crucis, sed sepulchri Dominici detectionem describit. Sententia epistolæ genuina est eiusmodi. Tanta Seruatoris nostri erga nos benignitas declarata est, vt nulla tam accurata dicendi ratio & Vis sit, quæ præsens miraculum pro dignitate explicare posse videatur. Nam vt insigne illud sanctissimæ illius passionis monumentum, quod terræ visceribus abditum, tot tamque multis annorum conuersionibus delituisset, tum illuceseceret seruus Dei,
units.tr: Third, granted that he mentioned the discovery, does he mention the adoration of the cross, which is the heart of the matter we are treating? Fourth, Constantine, in the passage cited, does not celebrate the discovery of the cross but the uncovering of the Lord's sepulchre. In chapter 28 above he had explained how the heathens, in an attempt to abolish all memory of Christ's resurrection, tried to remove and destroy the tomb of Christ, piling up dust and filth on it and building a temple of Venus on that spot. In this chapter he recalls that by a singular benefit of God it came about that the Lord's tomb, which had been hidden until his own time, was now brought to light, and that he built a most splendid temple on it. Therefore Bellarmine distorts the letter of Constantine, which says nothing about the discovery of the cross but describes the uncovering of the Lord's sepulchre. The genuine sense of the letter is of this kind: "So great is the goodness of our Saviour towards us that no speech, however careful and forceful, seems able to explain the present miracle as its worth requires. For that famous monument of his most holy passion, hidden in the bowels of the earth and concealed through so many and so great changes of years, when it then came to light, the servant of God..."

units.la: Dei, — no further printed text. Dei, cum illi hoste deuicto in libertatem effent vindicati, omnem profecto hominum admirationem superat. Hoc monumentum sanctissimæ passionis Christi non est crux, sed sepulchrū Christi, quod totannos latuerat idololatrico sacrario super illud extructo, & quisquiliis atque aggerib. qui in illo fano habebatur, obruto. Sed Constantinus fanū illud diruit & quisquilias & aggeres illinc quà longissime proiici iussit, & inuento tandem Christi sepulchro, templū ibidem extruxit.
units.tr: "... God, when that enemy had been overcome and they had been set free, surpasses all human admiration." This monument of Christ's most holy passion is not the cross but the sepulchre of Christ, which had lain hidden for many years, buried under an idolatrous shrine built over it and under the rubbish and heaps that were in that temple. But Constantine tore down that shrine and ordered the rubbish and heaps to be thrown out as far away as possible, and, when the sepulchre of Christ was at last found, he built a temple on the same spot.

units.la: Contra II. Bellarminus sic excipit, Eusebium in Chronico suo huius rei meminisse: in libris autem de vita Constantini non fecisse de hac re mentionem, quia res erat notissima omnibus, & satis putabat esse, quod eam attingeret in literis Constantini.
units.tr: Against the second point, Bellarmine replies as follows: "Eusebius did mention this matter in his Chronicle; but in the books on the Life of Constantine he made no mention of it, because the matter was most widely known to everyone, and he thought it enough that he touched on it in the letters of Constantine."

units.la: Resp. I. Non meminit Eusebius, sed vel Hieronymus, qui ipse fatetur, se multa inter transferendum intertexuisse, vel alius aliquis adulterator Eusebii. Est enim liber ille teste Baronio, corruptissimus, & nugis eiusmodi refertissimus. Quod si historia hæc vera fuisset, & Eusebio cognita, illius potissimum in vita Constantini fecisset mentionem, sed eius prorsus ibidem non meminit. Neque obstat, quod Bellarminus prætendit, id-
units.tr: Reply. I. Eusebius does not mention it; rather Jerome, who himself admits that he interwove many things in the course of translating, or some other corrupter of Eusebius. For that book, as Baronius testifies, is most corrupt and crammed full of trifles of this kind. And if this story were true and known to Eusebius, he would especially have mentioned it in the Life of Constantine; but he makes no mention of it there at all. Nor does it help that Bellarminus pretends that Eusebius passed over it in the Life of Constantine because it was most well known to all.

units.la: eo etiam eo eam in vita Cōstantini taceri ab Eu-sebio,q; effet omnibus notissima. Nam I.quia Eusebius id ibidem agit, vt Hele-næ matris Cōstantini pietatem descri-bat ac commendet, ea, quæ hanc maxi-me probarent, quæq; notissima essent, commeare debuit. Cum verò nihil ma-gis ad laudem pietatis facere potuisset, quam studium eius, in quæstenda & inuenienda cruce dominica certè ob eam causam quod esset notissimum pietatis τεκμήριον ac documentum,non voluisset nec potuisset tanto silentio hanc tam euidentem laudis materiam præterire.
units.tr: For, first, because Eusebius there sets out to describe and commend the piety of Helena, the mother of Constantine, he ought to have brought forward the things that most proved this and were best known. Yet since he could have made nothing more to the praise of her piety than her zeal in seeking and finding the Lord's cross, which was certainly the best known proof and evidence of piety, he would not have wished, nor been able, to pass over in such silence so evident a matter for praise.

units.la: II. Si reliqua, quæ ibidem commemo-rat de repurgatione montis Caluariæ, tanquam pietatis eius argumenta erant omnibus notissima, & tamen noluit ea seticére, cur ergo hanc historiam, si verè gesta fuisset, reticuisset.
units.tr: II. If he recorded the other things there about the clearing of the Mount of Calvary as proofs of her piety, which were well known to all, and yet did not wish to omit them, why then would he have kept silent about this story, if it had really happened?

units.la: III. Falsum & illud est, quod eam in literis Constantini attigerit. Nam li-terae illæ nihil de cruce inuentâ re-ferunt, sed sepulchri dominici in-uentionem commendant.
units.tr: III. It is also false that he touched on it in the letters of Constantine. For those letters say nothing about the cross being found, but commend the discovery of the Lord's sepulchre.

units.la: IV. Non satis fuisset, tantum mi-raculorum attingere. Loquitur ibi de miraculo, quod nulla vis rationis posset explicare, num eiusmodi miraculi di-gnitas [illegible, ~8 letters]gnitas attingenda tantum, & non plane ac pro merito exponenda fuisset? Benignitatem Seruatoris commendabat, & fidem Christi confirmabat. Quare non satis fuisset, eam attingere, sed prolixe & vbertim eam enarrare debuisset, atque etiam enarrasset.
units.tr: IV. It would not have been enough merely to touch on such a miracle. He speaks there of a miracle which no power of reason could explain. Could the dignity of such a miracle be merely touched upon, and not set out plainly and as it deserved? He was commending the goodness of the Saviour and confirming faith in Christ. Therefore it would not have been enough to touch on it; he ought to have related it at length and in full detail, and indeed he did so.

units.la: Instat ab inuentione sacrae lanceae.
units.tr: It is urged, from the finding of the holy lance.

units.la: Huic inuentioni sanctae crucis, inquit, addi potest inuentio sacrae lanceae, quae diuina reuelatione reperta est, Antiochiae, & insigni miraculo nobilitata.
units.tr: "To this finding of the holy cross," it is said, "can be added the finding of the holy lance, which was discovered by divine revelation at Antioch and made famous by a remarkable miracle."

units.la: Vide Guilielmum Tyrium libro sexto, de bello sacro. Paulum AEmilium libro quarto, de rebus gestis Francorum, & Dodechinum Mariani Scoti continuatorem in Anno MC.
units.tr: See William of Tyre, book six, On the Holy War; Paulus Aemilius, book four, On the Deeds of the Franks; and Dodechinus, the continuator of Marianus Scotus, in the year 1098.

units.la: Respond. I. Lancea illa diuina reuelatione inuenta, non propterea fuit religiose adorata, sicut nec clavi crucis. Ergo nec crux Christi, licet diuina reuelatione inuenta esset, propterea religiose adoranda est.
units.tr: Reply. I. That lance, even though it was found by divine revelation, was not for that reason religiously worshipped, any more than the nails of the cross were. Therefore neither is the cross of Christ, even if it had been found by divine revelation, for that reason to be religiously adored.

units.la: II. Aeque haec narratio inuentae lanceae, est fabula, a superstitiosis Antiochiae incolis sub religionis specie confiGta, & post ab hominibus supersuperstitiosa credulitate deceptis in literas relata. Habuit istud seculum varios miraculorum & superstitionum artifices, quibus deinde alii superstitiosa vulgi persuasione fascinati fidem habuere.
units.tr: II. This account of the finding of the lance is equally a fable, fashioned under the guise of religion by superstitious inhabitants of Antioch, and afterwards written down in books by men deceived by over-superstitious credulity. That age had various makers of miracles and superstitions, by whom others, bewitched by the superstitious persuasion of the common people, then came to believe.

units.la: III. Tyrii testimonio non agnosco; tum quia ipse hoc miraculum non vidit nec ex quoquam qui id se vidisse testatur, refert, sed post annos amplius centum ab incolis Antiochenis, hominibus superstitiosis, qui sub pietatis specie fabulam illam sunt commenti, audiuit, eorumque fidem secutus literis mandauit. Fefellit igitur Tyrium recepta illa in vulgo superstitiosa persuasio, quam deinde alia fide & integritate Christi magis ac magis degenerantes, facile amplexi fuere, itaque superstitione amplius adducti quâ certe iudicio fabulas eiusmodi pro veris historiis descripserint, & posteritati tradiderint.
units.tr: III. I do not acknowledge William of Tyre's testimony; first, because he did not see this miracle himself, nor does he report it from anyone who claims to have seen it, but heard it more than a hundred years later from the Antiochene inhabitants, superstitious men who had invented that fable under the appearance of piety, and following their word he committed it to writing. So that received superstitious opinion among the common people deceived William of Tyre; and afterwards others, degenerating more and more from the sound faith and integrity of Christ, readily embraced it, and being led on further by superstition, they described such fables as true histories, and handed them down to posterity, with a judgement that was surely unsound.

units.la: Argumentum quartum.
units.tr: Fourth argument.

units.la: ARGUMENTUM quartum à testimoniis veterum, qui passim referunt, quanto desiderio tenerentur fideles habendi, aut certè videndi particulas verâ crucis, quod ad magnum crucis honorem pertinet, nemo ignorat.
units.tr: The fourth argument, from the testimonies of the Fathers, who repeatedly report how eagerly the faithful desired to have, or at least to see, particles of the true cross. No one is unaware that this bears on the great honour due to the cross.

units.la: Resp. 1. Exempla superstitionum, religionis igionis doctrinam non probant. Supersticio est, habere aut videre velle, particulas crucis quasi peculiare κειμήλιον & γυξικον esset, cui gratia & virtus quaedam diuina infit ad promouendā & adiuuandā salutem nostram. Quod si hoc desiderio videdi & habendi crucis particulas id spectarunt, superstitiōis eos iure insimulamus. Siquidem tale desiderium pertinent quidem ad magnum honorem crucis sed superstitiosum. Quale enim hoc fuit patrum desiderium, talis & honor inde natus. Desiderium cū superstitione coniunctū fuit. Ergo & honor inde natus superstitiosus fuit, & verae religione repugnans.II.
units.tr: Reply 1. Examples of superstition do not prove doctrine. It is superstition to want to have or see particles of the cross as if they were a peculiar treasure [κειμήλιον] and something holy in themselves, in which some divine grace and power resided to advance and help our salvation. If those men sought to see and have particles of the cross with this desire, we rightly charge them with superstition. Such a desire, indeed, does pertain to a great honour of the cross, but a superstitious one. For the honour that arises from a desire is of the same kind as the desire itself. The desire of the Fathers was joined with superstition, so the honour that arose from it was also superstitious and opposed to true religion.

units.la: Negamus ex hoc fidelium desiderio erga particulas crucis consequi adorationem crucis; quia desiderabant eas videre & habere non ad adorationem, sed ad antiquitatis & rei gestae memoriam, non vt fidei & pietatis incrementa & redemptionis instrumenta, sed vt antiquitatis vestigia & monumenta. Consequitur autem adoratio si probauerit fideles particulas crucis adorasse, aut desiderio ductos esse non tantum habendi sed & adorandi eas. Id vero exempla ab ipso adducta non efficiunt.
units.tr: We deny that adoration of the cross follows from this desire of the faithful for particles of the cross, because they wished to see and have them not for adoration but for the memory of antiquity and of the event. They sought them not as increases of faith and piety, or as instruments of redemption, but as traces and monuments of antiquity. Adoration would follow only if it were shown that the faithful adored particles of the cross, or were led by a desire not only to have them but also to adore them. The examples the opponent cites do not establish this.

units.la: K III. Mul.
units.tr: K III. Mul.

units.la: III. Multos enim cepit desiderium videndi Pyramides; rudera amphitheatri, aliasque Græcas & Romanas antiquitates; hoc tamen ad peculiarem quendam ipsarum rerum honorem pertinebat, sed ad memoriam antiquitatis. Idem de hoc fidelium desiderio æstimandum est.
units.tr: III. Many were seized by a desire to see the Pyramids, the ruins of the amphitheatre, and other Greek and Roman antiquities. Yet this did not pertain to any peculiar honour of those things themselves, but to the memory of antiquity. The same judgment should be made of this desire of the faithful.

units.la: IV. Si hoc fidelium desiderium pertinet ad tantum crucis honorem, quid dicendum erit de Apostolis aliisque primæuis Christianis, qui nullo desiderio habendi aut videndi crucis particulas flagrauere? Nū ii crucé Christi suo fraudarūt honore? Non potuerūt illi ignorare crucem esse lignum vitæ, esse instrumentum redemptionis nostræ, cur adeo eam neglexerūt, vt videre vel habere eius particulas non cupiuerint?
units.tr: IV. If this desire of the faithful pertains to so great an honour of the cross, what must be said of the Apostles and the other earliest Christians, who burned with no desire to have or see particles of the cross? Did they defraud the cross of Christ of its honour? Could they have been ignorant that the cross is the tree of life and the instrument of our redemption? Why then did they so neglect it that they did not wish to see or have any of its particles?

units.la: Videamus nunc & examinemus singula Bellarmini testimonia.
units.tr: Let us now look at and examine the individual testimonies of Bellarmine.

units.la: Primum testimonium. B. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, inquit, Catech. 10. & 13. dicit, ex ligno crucis Hierosolymis inuento totū mundum repletum, plurimus inde petentibus & impetrantibus.
units.tr: The first testimony. Cyril of Jerusalem, he says, in Catechesis 10 and 13, states that the whole world has been filled with wood of the cross found at Jerusalem, many people asking for it and receiving it.

units.la: Resp. I. Catecheses illæ dubiæ sunt fidei. Earū autor putatur Iohannes Hierosolymitanus qui longe posterior fuit Cyrillo. [?]yrillo, & vixit tempore Hieronymi. Cyrillo tamen sunt attributæ, vt eò maior ipsis cōcilietur autoritas. II. Sint Cyrilli; quid tum? Nū crucis adorationi iuerint? At neq; ab ipso neq; ab aliis ad-ratam constat crucē: neq; affirmat Cy-rillus particulas eius petitas & impetra-tas in adorationem, sed in testimonium professionis fidei vel antiquitatis memo-riam. III. Notum est, hunc Cyrillum su-te hominem plus satis vanitatib. & su-perstitionibus addictum, ideoque non st mirum hoc superstitionis exemplū ab ipso fuisse celebratum, quod tamen io eo fecit animo vt crucis adorationē probaret & cōfirmaret, sed vt vrbs Hie-rosolymaā mūdo frequētaretur, eiusq; celebritas eo magis augeretur. IV. Si qd ex hoc testimonio qs velit inferre, quocunq; se vertat nō poterit religiosā crucis adorationem inde eruere, sed po-tius superstitionem Christianorū iā tūd à fide & simplicitate Christi degene-rantium inde extruet.
units.tr: Reply 1. Those catecheses are of doubtful faith. Their author is thought to be John of Jerusalem, who was much later than Cyril and lived in the time of Jerome. They were nonetheless attributed to Cyril so that they might win greater authority. 2. Suppose they are Cyril's; what follows? Did they go over to adoration of the cross? Yet it is clear that neither he nor others adored the cross. Cyril does not affirm that the particles, once sought and obtained, were used for adoration, but as a testimony of confession of faith or as a memorial of antiquity. 3. It is well known that this Cyril was a man given over to more than enough vanities and superstitions. So it is no wonder that he celebrated this example of superstition. Yet he did not do so with the aim of proving and confirming the adoration of the cross, but so that the city of Jerusalem would be made more crowded with visitors to the world, and its fame increased thereby. 4. If anyone wishes to draw any inference from this testimony, wherever he turns he will not be able to derive from it a religious adoration of the cross. He will rather construct from it the superstition of Christians already then degenerating from the faith and simplicity of Christ.

units.la: Secundum testimonium: Constantinus particulam crucis statuæ suæ inseruit, quam Co-stantinopoli collocauit, existimās per eam crucis particulam totam vrbē custodiendā, vt referūt Socrates l. 1. c. 13. & Eutropius siue Paulus Diaconus
units.tr: The second testimony: Constantine inserted a particle of the cross into his statue, which he set up at Constantinople, thinking that the whole city would be guarded by that particle of the cross, as Socrates (book 1, chapter 13) and Eutropius or Paul the Deacon report.

units.la: conus, qui multa addidit Eutropio lib. II. rerum Romanarum.
units.tr: the Deacon, who added much to Eutropius, book II of the Roman History.

units.la: Resp. I. Fictitia est historia. Ipse Socrates non obscurè id significat, cum ab auditione hæc accepisse & ex relatione illorum qui Constantinopolin incolunt, scriptis mandare commemorat. Nôn ergo ex probatæ fidei historico ista deprompta sit, sed ex imperitorum & superstitiosorum incolarum persuasione & relatione suæ inserviit historiæ. Paulus Diaconus etiam homo fuit superstitiosus, & ex fide superstitiosorum rem ista narrat, unde quid fidei huic narrationi tribuendum sit, cuius promptum est colligere. Etsi enim eius iudicii erant, ut veram à falso, fabulâ ab historia potuerint discernere: tamen superstitio tunc temporis hominum etiam doctorum oculos sic fascinarat, ut nec viderét aut agnosceret fraudes, nec videntes, auderent eas exprimere, nec ligionis videretur aduersari. II. Res ipsa falsitatis arguit historiâ. Quis superstitiosam illam opinionem Constantino tribuat? Minime Constantino ista competit, ut q ita erat in religione Christiana instituta, ut sciret, in ligno non esse vim aliquam custodiendæ ciuitatis. III. Demus eum Constantinopoli particulam [illegible, ~3 letters]rucis collocasse; quid poderis ad crucis adorationem afferr? Num Constantin° adorauit eam? Nu spe aut fiduciam ea collocauit? Proferat testem incorruptæ fidei qui testetur Constantinum crucem aut eius particulam vel adorasse vel adorari iussisse. Ipsa narratio contrarium docet. Nam statuam illam crucis condecoratam non collocauit in templo ad cultum sed in foro. Quod si vel isse eam adorare aut aliis adorandâ proponere voluisset in sacrario non in foro am reposuisset. IV. Si posuit eam in foro nō id fecit hac opinione quod per eam putaret vrbē custodiri, sed vt fidem Christum palam testaretur coram Ethnicis, eosq; hoc suo exemplo ad fidem Christi paulatim pertraheret: aut si virtutem aliquā attribuit ligno, qua posset saluam& incolumem custodire vrbem, exemplum est zeli superstitiosi & erronei, ideoq; nihil ꝑbat. Religioni statim, vbi exorta fuit, adnata est superstitio, q diligēter ꝑpterea ab illa est discernēda.
units.tr: Reply 1. The story is fictitious. Socrates himself indicates this not obscurely, when he records that he received these things by hearsay and wrote them down from the account of those who live at Constantinople. So this was not drawn from a historian of proven faith, but from the persuasion of ignorant and superstitious inhabitants, and he admitted it into his history as a matter of report. Paul the Deacon was also a superstitious man, and he relates the story on the faith of superstitious people. It is easy to see how much faith should be given to such a narrative. For although these writers were capable of distinguishing true from false, and fable from history, superstition at that time had so bewitched the eyes even of learned men that they neither saw nor recognized the frauds. And even when they saw them, they did not dare to set them down, lest they seem to oppose religion. 2. The thing itself proves the story false. Who would attribute that superstitious opinion to Constantine? That belief does not fit Constantine, who had been so instructed in the Christian religion that he knew there was no power in wood to guard a city. 3. Grant that he placed a particle of the cross at Constantinople; what does this contribute to the adoration of the cross? Did Constantine adore it? Did he place it there in hope or trust? Let the opponent produce a witness of sound faith who testifies that Constantine either adored the cross or its particle, or ordered it to be adored. The narrative itself teaches the contrary. For he did not place that statue, adorned with the cross, in a temple for worship, but in the forum. And if he had wished it to be adored, or proposed to others that it be adored, he would have put it in a sanctuary, not in a public square. 4. If he set it in the forum, he did not do so with the opinion that the city was guarded by it, but to bear open witness to Christ before the heathen, and so gradually to draw them to faith in Christ by his example. Or if he did attribute some power to the wood, by which it could keep the city safe and unharmed, that is an example of superstitious and mistaken zeal, and therefore proves nothing. Superstition arose at once, wherever religion arose, and it must therefore be carefully distinguished from religion.

units.la: Tertium testimonium Gregorius Nyssenus in vita Macrinæ sororis scribit eam gestare solitam ad collum ꝯ crucem argenteam, cui inserta erat particula vera crucis.
units.tr: The third testimony: Gregory of Nyssa, in the Life of his sister Macrina, writes that she was accustomed to wear around her neck a silver cross, into which a particle of the true cross had been inserted.

units.la: Resp. I. At non scribit eā adorare solitam litam fuisse illâ crucem, sed solùmodo gestasse eâ in signũ sc. fidei & amoris ergà Christũ. II. Exéplũ est superstitionis quæ iam tum inualuerat, in primis verò mulierculas occupauerat, quas propter ea, etiam Hieronymus merito reprehendit, vt quæ suo tempore ligno crucis abuterentur. Hoc apud nos, inquit, superstitiosæ mulierculæ facilitabant in parvis Evangelijs [id est, membranulis, quibus quædã Evangeliorum loca phylacteriorum imitatione scribebant] & in crucis ligno atque istiusmodi rebus, quæ habent quidem Zelum Dei, sed non secundum scientiam. III. Si hoc comędat pietatem Macrinæ, pietatis laudem non merebuntur sanctæ illæ mulieres, quæ Iohan. 19. v. 25. dicuntur stetisse iuxta crucem Christi, nempe Maria mater, Maria vxor Cleopæ, Maria Magdalena & discipulus Iohannes, q; nullam crucis assulam sibi excusere, quam gestarent in gratiæ diuinæ monumentum & tutissimum vitæ ἀμυντήριον. IV. Commemorat Nyssenus quid illa fecerit, quæ recte fecerit, nō docet. Zelum eius laudat, superstitionem cum zelo coniunctam in medio reliquit. Ex eius opinione seu persuasione superstitiosa loquitur. Illa enim verè crucis particulam infertam opinabatur.
units.tr: Reply 1. He does not write that she was accustomed to adore that cross, but only that she wore it as a sign of her faith and love toward Christ. 2. It is an example of the superstition which had already then taken hold, and which especially possessed foolish women. Jerome rightly rebukes them for this, since in his time they abused the wood of the cross. Among us, he says, superstitious little women make little Gospels [that is, small membranes, on which certain passages of the Gospels were written in imitation of phylacteries], and use the wood of the cross and things of this kind, which indeed have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. 3. If this commends the piety of Macrina, then those holy women who, according to John 19:25, are said to have stood beside the cross of Christ, namely Mary the mother, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene, together with the disciple John, will not merit praise for piety, for they chose for themselves no splinter of the cross to carry as a memorial of divine grace and as the safest safeguard [ἀμυντήριον] of life. 4. Nyssen relates what she did, but does not teach that she did right. He praises her zeal, but leaves superstition, joined with zeal, in the middle. He speaks according to her opinion or superstitious persuasion, for she believed that a particle of the true cross had been inserted.

units.la: In Matt. l.4.c.23.
units.tr: In Matt. l. 4. c. 23.

units.la: Quartum testimonium. Paulinus epist. 12. ad Seuerum scribit se mittere tanquam summum donum particulam crucis vera auro inclusam. Idem etiam 10. S. Felicis, scribit se restrinxisse incendium maximum offensa particula crucis, quod nulla arte extingui poterat.
units.tr: The fourth testimony. Paulinus, letter 12 to Severus, writes that he is sending, as a supreme gift, a particle of the true cross enclosed in gold. The same man, in his poem 10 on St. Felix, writes that he quenched a great fire by applying a particle of the cross, which could not be put out by any art.

units.la: Ipse, inquit, domum remeans, modicum sed grande salutis
units.tr: He himself, he says, returning home, brings out from the cross of eternity a small but great fragment of salvation, a piece of wood

units.la: De crucis aeternae sumptum mihi fragmine lignum
units.tr: Taken from the cross of eternity for me, a small but great pledge of salvation

units.la: Promo, tenensque manu aduersis procul nigero flammis, &c.
units.tr: and holding it in his hand, he shows it, the flames of black fire far off, etc.

units.la: Resp. I. Paulinum decepit recepta apud omnes superstitiosa opinio, ut crederet particulam verae crucis esse quam mittebat; reuera erat particula suppositiciae crucis. II. Nihil ad re facit hoc testimonium. Non mittit eo fine ut adoretur, sed ut tanquam donum summum acceptetur & habeatur. III. Missio illa ut & acceptio & asseruatio fuit superstitiosa. Num ossa Elisaei ad quae mortuus fuit excitatus, ut suma dona fuere missa & asseruata? Et si summum donum fuit, ad quid utile? Num ad gratiam Dei & salutem consequendam profuit? Ad quid ergo fuit nobis immaterialis illa Christi crux, passio &c. & mors Christi? Si hac agnoscis summum illud Dei patris donum, quod nobis gratiam Dei conciliat & salutem adfert, quomodo ligneæ crucis studen çomium competet? IV. Miraculum cuius meminit Paulinus ægre apud prudentes inueniet locum. Norunt illi non oportere credi illis miraculis, quæ falsæ doctrinæ fidem astruunt aut super stitionem confirmant, iuxta Dei interdictū Deut.13. Norunt etiam Paulinum simplicitate superstitiosa potius quam iudicio & exploratione inductum esse ad hoc & similia miracula commedanda. Vixit enim seculo miraculorū & superstitionum feracissimo, quo homines imperiti & superstitiosi sub specie religionis varia miracula confinxere, vt sc. Ethnicos conuerterent, & infirmorum animos confirmarent, quæ deinde scriptores simplicitate credula in fraudem inducti literis temere mandarūt. V. Demus miraclum esse verū quoad opus externum: vel ergo à Diabolo hoste Dei & salutis nostræ erit editum Deo obiustas causas permittente · vel à Christo Domino nostro & salutis nostræ autore. Si à Diabolo; crucis virtus & adoratio diabolica erit: si à Christo; Christi non crucis adoratio confirmatur; Siquidem in Christo tota virt² & gloria miraculi re-sidebat sidebat,nō in cruce. At,inquies,ad crucem tamen miraculum editum est; nihil id,inquam ego, crucis adorationem promouet. Nonne ad offa Elifæi miraculum editum est? An propterea fuerc auro & argento inclusa, templo illata, per pompam circumducta & adorata? Ad impositionem sudariorum Pauli,ad vmbram Petri curabantur ægroti, num propterea adorationis honor sudariis & vmbræ Petri exhibitus fuit ? Vt tota virtus & gloria miraculorum istorum non in sudario & vmbra, sed in Deo ventē ministerio Apostolorum existebat; Ita & hic soli Christo omnis miraculi virtus & gloria nō cruci competit. Denique si à Christo miraculum editū, extra ordinem exhibitum est,qua igitur fronte ad ordinariam crucis adorationem trahetur.
units.tr: Reply. I. The widely accepted superstition deceived Paulinus, so that he believed the piece he was sending was a fragment of the true cross; in fact it was a fragment of a supposititious cross. II. This testimony does nothing to the point. He does not send it for the purpose of being worshipped, but to be received and held as a supreme gift. III. That sending, like the receiving and keeping of it, was superstitious. Were the bones of Elisha, by which the dead man was raised, sent and kept as supreme gifts? And if it was a supreme gift, what use was it? Did it help to obtain the grace of God and salvation? What then was that immaterial cross of Christ for us, his passion, and the death of Christ? If you acknowledge that as the supreme gift of God the Father, which wins us the grace of God and brings us salvation, how does the honour of worship due to a wooden cross fit with it? IV. The miracle that Paulinus mentions will scarcely find a place among wise people. They know that one should not believe those miracles which support a false doctrine or confirm superstition, according to God's prohibition in Deut. 13. They also know that Paulinus, moved by a superstitious simplicity rather than by judgment and examination, was led to commend this and similar miracles. For he lived in an age most fruitful of miracles and superstitions, when unskilled and superstitious men, under the guise of religion, invented various miracles, namely to convert the heathen and to strengthen the minds of the weak; and these writers, led into deceit by credulous simplicity, then rashly committed to writing. V. Grant that the miracle is true as regards the external work: then it was either wrought by the Devil, the enemy of God and of our salvation, with God permitting it for hidden causes, or by Christ our Lord and the author of our salvation. If by the Devil, it will be the power of the cross and a diabolical worship. If by Christ, the worship of Christ, not of the cross, is confirmed; for in Christ resided the whole power and glory of the miracle, not in the cross. But, you will say, the miracle was wrought at the cross. That, I reply, does nothing to promote the worship of the cross. Was not a miracle wrought at the bones of Elisha? Were they therefore enclosed in gold and silver, carried into the temple, paraded about and worshipped? By the laying on of Paul's handkerchiefs, and by the shadow of Peter, the sick were healed; was therefore the honour of worship paid to the handkerchiefs and the shadow of Peter? Just as the whole power and glory of those miracles lay not in the handkerchief or the shadow, but in God working through the ministry of the apostles, so here too the whole power and glory of the miracle belongs to Christ alone and not to the cross. Finally, if the miracle was wrought by Christ and displayed outside the ordinary course, by what face is it then dragged into the ordinary worship of the cross?

units.la: Quintum testimonium.Chrysostomus homil. quod Christus sit Deus, scribit, eos qui potuerant potiri particula crucis auro inclusam seruare ac inde se valde ornari ac custodiri merito credere.
units.tr: The fifth testimony. Chrysostom, in his homily that Christ is God, writes that those who could obtain a piece of the cross, enclosed in gold, kept it and were greatly adorned and guarded by it, and rightly so, he believes.

units.la: Resp,I. Non dicit Chrysostomus merito credi debere. Vocem merito de suo assuit Bellarminus,vt ostenderet Chrysostomum superstitionem illam ap-
units.tr: Reply. I. Chrysostom does not say that it ought to be believed "rightly." Bellarmine added the word "rightly" on his own, so that he might show that Chrysostom approved that superstition, since the word "rightly" belongs to one who approves.

units.la: K s proprobasse, quia vox merito est approban- tis. Chrysostomus factum narat, nō pro- bat; ostendit in quāto pretio crucis par- ticulas habuerint & quam ei virtutem tribuerint; q; recte & pie fecerint aut se- serint, non asseric. II. Non facit mentio- nem Chrysostomus vllius adorationis aut cultus religiosi quem detulerint cru- cis particulis ; commemorat quidem e- os qui potuerunt potiri particula cru- cis, eam auro inclusisse & seruasse ad or- namentum & praesidium vitae suae, sed non adorasse, aut adorandam credidis- se, q; omnino factum oportuit si adorā- dae crucis testimonium hinc peti ido- neū debeat. III. Chrysost. ex hoc Chri- stianorum superstitio facto non voluit adorationem crucis probare, sed asserere gloriam & maiestatem Christi aduer- sum infideles, idq; tali argumento. Quem omnes gentes adeo amant & honorant, vt lig- num crucis cuius fixus est videre & habere desiderent, is pro vero Deo est agnoscendus. At omnes gentes Christum crucifixum adeo amant & honorant, vt lignum crucis cui fixus est vi- dere & habere desiderent. Ergo Christus pro vero Deo habendus. Argumentum fatemur non esse necessarium, vtpote ab autori- tate scripturae non peritum; quia scrip- turas pturas Ethnici cõtemnebat; sed probabile est, à facto superstitioso ductu; inter im ad gloriam Christi afferendam plurimum valuit, quod diuinæ benignitati non argumenti bonitati acceptum ferendum est.
units.tr: Chrysostom relates the fact; he does not approve it. He shows how highly they valued the pieces of the cross and what virtue they attributed to it; he does not assert that they did this rightly and piously or otherwise. II. Chrysostom makes no mention of any worship or religious cult which they paid to the pieces of the cross. He does recall that those who could obtain a piece of the cross had enclosed it in gold and kept it as an ornament and protection of their life; but he does not say that they worshipped it or believed it should be worshipped, which would necessarily have been stated if a testimony for the worship of the cross were to be fairly drawn from this. III. Chrysostom, from this superstitious act of Christians, did not wish to prove the worship of the cross, but to assert the glory and majesty of Christ against unbelievers, and he did so by this argument: Whom all nations so love and honour that they desire to see and possess the wood of the cross on which he was fastened, he is to be acknowledged as the true God. But all nations so love and honour the crucified Christ that they desire to see and possess the wood of the cross to which he was fastened. Therefore Christ is to be held as the true God. We grant that this argument is not necessary, since it is not drawn from the authority of Scripture; for he despised the heathen writings. But it is probable that it was prompted by a superstitious fact; meanwhile, what was very effective in asserting the glory of Christ must be credited to the goodness of the divine kindness, not to the goodness of the argument.

units.la: Sextum testimonium, Euagrius lib. 4. hist. c. 26. & Procopius l. 2. de bello Persico narrant Apameam fuisse particulam sanctæ crucis, quam sibi ostendi populus voluit, cum diu obsessa iamiam capienda videretur, ut nimirum conspecta cruce Domini, alacrius morerentur, sed cum ab Episcopo crux illa ostenderetur, semel & iterum & tertio effulsisse splendidum ignem non comburentem, sed lucentem, quo territi hostes obsidionem soluerint.
units.tr: The sixth testimony. Evagrius, book 4, history, chapter 26, and Procopius, book 2, on the Persian war, relate that at Apamea there was a piece of the holy cross, which the people wished to be shown to them when the city, long besieged, seemed about to be taken, so that, with the cross of the Lord in view, they might die more cheerfully. But when that cross was shown by the bishop, the splendid fire, not burning but shining, flashed once, twice and a third time, and the enemies, terrified by it, lifted the siege.

units.la: Resp. I Superstitiosum erat superstitio-si populi postulatum. Quæ hæc religio? Quæ fides in Christum, quod tantis periculis expositi ligni virtute mutari credebantur? Nonne fidei Christi plane repugnabat, quod in extremo vitæ discrimine Episcopum Thomam miseri homines adeunt, petentes sibi crucis lignum ostendi & exosculandum & adorandum præberi? Vera religio iubet ad Christum confugere in periculis. Invoca me in die tribulationis, & ego te eruam. II. Nō minus superstitiosa erat persuasio po-puli, puli, qua visa, illa cruce credebát se alà- crius morituros. Alacritate moriedi nó ligni crucis conspectus, sed spes & fidu- eia in Christum crucifixum excitat.III. Negamus fuisse verae crucis particulam quae ostendebatur ipsis. Supposititiciam fuisse inde licet colligere, quod Euagrius exl.2. Procopii referet, partem illa crucis ab homine Syro clam eo delatā fuisse cubitali magnitudine. Summa honoris & amoris munera ad alios clā deferri non solent. Et si ex inuento crucis ligno totus mundus est repertus, vt supra dictum, tantae magnitudinis particula Apam eam non potuit transportari, praesertim cum Helena legatur partem integrae crucis reliquisse Hierosolymis, partem ad filium misisse. IV. Miraculosa liberatio vrbis praestita non est virtute crucis, sed vel à Diabolo quod ego quidem non puto vel à Christo. Si à Diabolo, Deo permittere contigit liberatio; cultus vero crucis inde nequit probari, quia Diabolus hominibus superstitiosis illudere, superstitiosamq; crucis veneratione in animis eorum confirmare voluit. Si à Christo editu miraculum, extraordinariu fuit, non ad cultu crucis approbandum & confirmandu, sed ad Persarum gentilium in credulitatem conuincendam & damnandam pertinens.
units.tr: Reply. I. The petition of the people was superstitious. What kind of religion was this? What faith in Christ was it, that they believed the situation could be changed by the power of a piece of wood, exposed to such dangers? Did not the faith of Christ plainly oppose it, that wretched men in the extreme peril of their life should approach the bishop Thomas, asking that the wood of the cross be shown to them and offered to be kissed and worshipped? True religion bids us flee to Christ in dangers: Call upon me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. II. No less superstitious was the people's conviction that, having seen that cross, they would die more cheerfully. The cheerfulness of dying is awakened not by the sight of the wood of the cross, but by hope and trust in the crucified Christ. III. We deny that the piece of the true cross was what was shown to them. That it was supposititious may be gathered from the fact that Evagrius, in book 2 of Procopius, reports that that piece of cross had been secretly carried there by a Syrian man, and that it was a cubit in length. Great gifts of honour and love are not usually carried secretly to others. And if the whole world was found from the discovered wood of the cross, as said above, a piece of such size could not have been transported to Apamea, especially since Helena is read to have left part of the whole cross at Jerusalem and sent part to her son. IV. The miraculous deliverance of the city was granted not by the power of the cross, but either by the Devil, which I for my part do not think, or by Christ. If by the Devil, it happened that God permitted the deliverance; but the worship of the cross cannot be proved from this, because the Devil wished to deceive superstitious men and to confirm in their minds the superstitious veneration of the cross. If the miracle was wrought by Christ, it was extraordinary, and it pertains not to approving and confirming the worship of the cross, but to convicting and condemning the credulity of the heathen Persians.

units.la: Septimum testimonium Gregorius lib. Epist. 126. ad Recharedum regem Visigothorum mittit crucis particulam vt eximium munus.
units.tr: The seventh testimony. Gregory, in book 9 of his Epistles, letter 126, sends a piece of the cross to Reccared, king of the Visigoths, as a distinguished gift.

units.la: Resp. I. Est factum superstitiosum hominis superstitiosi, ex quo non crucis adoratio sed Christianae religionis corruptio probatur. II. Nō sequitur ex hac missione particulas crucis, eā esse adorandā. Misit etiam de capillis Ioh. Baptistae, quis inde colligat eos esse adorandos? Neq; enim misit vt donum adoratione colendum, sed vt argumentum afferendae gloriae Christi & religionis ac fidei Christianae commendandae.
units.tr: Reply. I. It is a superstitious act of a superstitious man, from which not the worship of the cross but the corruption of the Christian religion is proved. II. It does not follow from this sending that pieces of the cross are to be worshipped. He also sent hairs of John the Baptist; who from this would infer that they are to be worshipped? For he did not send them as a gift to be honoured with worship, but as an argument for asserting the glory of Christ and for commending the religion and faith of Christianity.

units.la: Octauum testimonium. Ambrosius in orat. in Theodosium, loquens de clauo inserto ab Helena galeae Imperatoris. Sapienter, inquit, Helena egit, quae crucem (particulam nimirum crucis, videlicet clavum vnum) in capite regnum leuauit, vt crux Christi in regibus adoretur.
units.tr: The eighth testimony. Ambrose, in his oration to Theodosius, speaking of the nail fixed by Helena in the emperor's helmet: "Helena acted wisely," he says, "who by placing a single nail of the cross, that is, a particle of the cross, in the emperor's head, raised up the cross of Christ to be adored among kings."

units.la: Resp. I. Narratio illa Ambrosii de clauis crucis Christi est suspectae fidei. Commemorat enim Helenam clauorū alios galeę, alios freno equi indidisse. Parum sane laudis & honoris inde ad Helenam redibit, si clauos sacrosanctos quotidie in os bestiæ voluit iniici. Quis hanc sacrorum clauorum in os bestiæ iniectionem vt profanam & impiam nó exhorrescat? Primus hæc prodidit Ambrosius, non quidem ex aliquo integro fidei historico, sed ex sermonibus vulgi superstitiosi, ita vt non visa & lecta sed temere ficta, audita & narrata recitet. Neque enim Eusebius, qui ætate Constantini vixit & res ab illo gestas diligenter descripsit, huius rei vllam facit mentionem. II. Ponamus fidem aliquam, historiam hanc mereri; non tamen Helenæ sapientiæ laudem inde reportabit. Neque enim sapienter, sed superstitiose egit. Quis enim sapiens in clauis sanctitatem & gratiam Dei quærat? Non sapientiæ, sed superstitionis est præsidium vitæ in clauis & similibus nugis collocare. III. Quod adorationis meminit Ambrosius non de religiosa adoratione intelligi debet, quia paulo ante profitetur Helenam religiosam crucis adorationem detestatam esse tanquam gentilem errorem & vanitatem impiorum, eamque soli regi nostro Christo detulisse: sed deciduili adoratione, vt cum populus regem suum honoraret, etiam clauum eius dia demati inditum simul honore afficeret. Nonum testimonium. Hieron. in Psq. exponit de cruce illud: Adorate scabellum pedum eius. Et in Epist. 17. ad Marcellam dicit. Ergone erit illa dies quando nobis liceat speluncam Salvatoris intrare, crucis deinde lambere lignum.
units.tr: Reply. I. That account of Ambrose about the nails of Christ's cross is of doubtful trustworthiness. For he relates that Helena set some of the nails in the helmet and others in the bridle of the horse. Very little praise or honour would redound to Helena if she wanted the holy nails put daily into the mouth of a beast. Who does not shudder at this putting of the sacred nails into a beast's mouth as profane and impious? Ambrose was the first to publish these things, not from any sound historian of the faith, but from the talk of superstitious common people, so that he recites things not seen or read but rashly invented, heard and repeated. For Eusebius, who lived in the time of Constantine and described his deeds carefully, makes no mention of this matter at all. II. Let us grant that this story deserves some belief; even so, Helena will not gain praise for wisdom from it. For she did not act wisely but superstitiously. Who that is wise seeks holiness and the grace of God in nails? To place the protection of life in nails and similar trifles belongs not to wisdom but to superstition. III. The adoration of which Ambrose speaks must not be understood as religious adoration, because a little earlier he declares that Helena detested religious adoration of the cross as a heathen error and the vanity of impious men, and that she offered it only to our king, Christ. Rather, it was a civil honour, such that when the people honour their king, they also pay honour to the nail that was placed on his diadem.

units.la: Resp. 1. Hieronymus primo locum illum interpretatur de corpore Domini; deinde allegoricam subiicit interpretationem de cruce. Allegoricæ autem interpretationes ad fidei dogmata confirmanda non debent adhiberi. II. Non intelligit Hieronymus hoc loco crucem materialem seu lignum crucis, sed immaterialem, id est, passionem Domini Iesu Christi, quod ex psal. 95. evidenter licet colligere, vbi diserte quam crucem intelligat exponit, Crux Christi, inquit, est columna generis humani. In ipsa columna ædificata est Domus eius. Quam vero intelligit crucem? Indicat id continuo dicens Ego crucem dico non lignum, sed passionem. In cruce ergo no lignum, sed ligno affixum Dominum concepit & intellectum voluit Hieronymus. Quod vero ad alterum locum attinet, continet is declamationem rhetoricam, qua Marcellæ voluit persuadere, vt relicta Roma in Bethlehem...
units.tr: Answer. 1. Jerome first interprets that passage as referring to the body of the Lord; then he adds an allegorical interpretation about the cross. Allegorical interpretations, however, ought not to be used to confirm the dogmas of faith. II. Jerome does not understand here a material cross or the wood of the cross, but an immaterial one, that is, the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ. This can be gathered clearly from Psalm 95, where he explicitly sets out what cross he means: "The cross of Christ," he says, "is the pillar of the human race. In that pillar the house of God was built." And what cross does he mean? He indicates this at once by saying: "By the cross I mean not the wood but the passion." So Jerome conceived and intended the Lord fixed to the wood, not the wood itself. As for the other passage, it contains a rhetorical declamation by which Jerome wished to persuade Marcella to leave Rome and migrate to Bethlehem.

units.la: Hieron. in Psal. 95. in Bethlehem commigraret. Eiusmodi autem declamationes non ad docendum & astruendum, sed ad commouendum & delectandum pertinent. II. Superstitiosa fuit hæc deosculatio crucis, quam Hieronymus non ex suo, sed ex Marcellæ in superstitione errantis sensu, rhetorico sermone celebrat. Nam eâ ætate superstitionum sordes Ecclesiam strenue inuaserant, inprimis mulierculæ superstitiosæ crucis ligno abutebantur, quas propterea Hieronymus in Matth. lib. 4. cap. 23. damnat, vt supra dictum.
units.tr: Jerome, on Psalm 95, [and] on migrating to Bethlehem. Declamations of this kind, however, serve to move and delight, not to teach and establish. II. This kissing of the cross was superstitious, and Jerome, speaking in rhetorical style, extols it not from his own judgment but from the perspective of Marcella, who was erring in superstition. For in that age the filth of superstitions had vigorously invaded the Church; in particular, superstitious women abused the wood of the cross, and Jerome therefore condemns them in his commentary on Matthew, book 4, chapter 23, as said above.

units.la: Decimum testimonium. Augustinus lib. 22. de ciuit. Dei, cap. 8. scribit, Ad terram sanctam ex monte Caluariæ allatam in Africam miracula viri solita, & se cum alio Episcopo eam infodisse & orationis locum super eam constituisse. Quo honore Augustinus, proseque- retur crucem, quando sic honorabat terram vbi fuerat crux.
units.tr: The tenth testimony. "Augustine, in book 22 of The City of God, chapter 8, writes that the miracles were wont to bring earth from the holy land, from Mount Calvary, into Africa, and that he himself, with another bishop, buried it and set up a place of prayer over it. With what honour would Augustine have treated the cross, when he so honoured the earth where the cross had been?"

units.la: Resp. I. Non meminit Augustinus vllius cultus religiosi, qui terræ vel crucî esset exhibitus. Multos Christianos istius temporis inprimis homines infirmos & in Christiana religione nondum recte informatos superstitiosè ligno crucis abusos esse agnoscimus, sed ab adoraidoratione crucis religiosa longe sem-per abfuere. 2. Augustinus hic factum hominis infirmi, in superstitione erran-tis, commemorat, quod Bellarminus ad ium modum producit, ac si Augustinus actum illud tanquam religiosum appro-bavit.
