Non probauit, sed tanquam infir-mitatis errorem tolerauit, non repre-hendit & correxit, sed patienter erran-tem sustinuit; ne hominem infirmum, non satis bene institutum in primo con-gressu offenderet. Eiusmodi vero su-perstitionum exempla, nihil causam Bellarmini iuuant, ac promouent. 3. Di-citur vir ille tribunitius Hesperius, pri-uatim hanc terram habuisse, & suspen-disse in cubiculo suo. Non ergo publicè in templo fuit asseruata, & ad cultum propositá, vt crux, & crucis particulae hodie in templis Pontificiis asseruan-tur, & adorandæ proponuntur. 4. Bel-larminus falso impingit Augustino, quasi ipse infoderit terram sanctam, & orationis locum super eam constitue-rit: Hesperii factum est, cui Augustinus ob hominis infirmitatem, resistere no-luit. Verba Augustini id manifeste prae se ferunt. Forte accidit, inquit, vt ego & col-lega tunc meus in proximo essemus: vt venire-
units.tr: Reply. I. Augustine makes no mention of any religious worship given either to the earth or to the cross. We acknowledge that many Christians of that time, especially weak men not yet rightly instructed in the Christian religion, abused the wood of the cross superstitiously; but they were always far from religious adoration of the cross. 2. Here Augustine recounts the deed of a weak man, who was erring in superstition, which Bellarmine produces in the way that if Augustine had approved that act as religious. He did not approve it; he tolerated it as an error of weakness; he did not rebuke and correct it, but patiently bore with the erring man, lest he offend a weak man, not well enough instructed, at the first encounter. Examples of this kind of superstition do nothing to help or advance Bellarmine's cause. 3. That tribune Hesperius is said to have held this earth privately and to have hung it in his bedroom. It was therefore not kept publicly in a church and set forth for worship, as the cross and particles of the cross are kept today in Papist churches and proposed to be adored. 4. Bellarmine falsely charges Augustine as though he himself had buried the holy earth and set a place of prayer over it. It was the deed of Hesperius, to which Augustine did not wish to object because of the man's weakness. Augustine's own words plainly show this: It happened, he says, that I and my colleague were then nearby; when he asked us to come,

units.la: L mm mus rogauit, & venimus. Cum nobis omnia retulisset, etiam hoc petiuit, ut infoderetur alicubi, atque ibi orationum locus fieret. Non restitimus; factum est.
units.tr: ...we came. When he had told us everything, he also asked that it be buried somewhere and that a place of prayer be made there. We did not resist; it was done.

units.la: Vltimum testimonium, ex carmine Sybillæ petitur, quod habetur l. 6. carminum Sybillinorum:
units.tr: The last testimony is taken from a verse of the Sibyl, which is found in book 6 of the Sibylline Oracles:

units.la: O lignum felix, in quo Deus ipse pependit.
units.tr: O happy wood, on which God himself hung.

units.la: Resp. I. Non asseritur hoc carmine crucis adoratio, sed ligni crucis felicitas hyperbolicè poetico more prædicatur. II. Si hæc poetica locutio nobis crucis adorationem commendat, etiam clauis Christi, templo, sepulchro, & præsepio Christi adoratio debetur, quia de hisce eodem modo canitur:
units.tr: Reply. I. This verse does not assert adoration of the cross, but in poetic manner extols the happiness of the wood of the cross with hyperbole. II. If this poetic expression commends to us the adoration of the cross, then adoration is also due to the nails of Christ, to the temple, the sepulchre and the manger of Christ, since of these too it is sung in the same way:

units.la: Felices clavi quibus est fixus Deus ipse.O templum felix, in quo Deus ipse resedit.Sepulcrum felix, in quo Deus ipse sepultus.Præsepium felix, in quo Deus ipse locatus.
units.tr: Happy the nails by which God himself was fixed. O happy temple, in which God himself dwelt. Happy sepulchre, in which God himself was buried. Happy manger, in which God himself was laid.

units.la: III. Intelligendum est hoc carmen de cruce immateriali, & interna, id est, passione & morte Christi, quæ metonymice felix dicitur, quia nos miseros, & infelices, beatos & felices reddit. A cruce immateriali & interna ad materialem externam & ligneam non valet consequentia.
units.tr: III. This verse must be understood of the immaterial and inward cross, that is, the passion and death of Christ, which is called happy by metonymy, because it makes us wretched and unhappy into blessed and happy. From the immaterial and inward cross to the material, outward and wooden cross, the inference does not hold.

units.la: Argumentum Quintum.
units.tr: Fifth Argument.

units.la: Argumentum V. ab exaltatione crucis. Constat enim ex Paulo Diacono, Zonara, & Cedreno in vita Heraclii, Heraclium in recuperatione crucis, quam Persæ ex Hierosolymis abstulerunt diuturnitus adiutum, ita vt etiam de cœlo Deus lapidibus grandinis pugnaret contra Persas, vt olim fecerat cum Iosue. In ipsa etiam restitutione crucis in suum locum, miracula quædam contigerunt, vt referit Sigebertus in Chronico anni 631. Vnde etiam festum institutum tenetur Otto Frisingensis l.5.c.9. Beda & Ado in Martyrologio.
units.tr: Fifth argument, from the exaltation of the cross. It is established by Paul the Deacon, Zonaras and Cedrenus, in the life of Heraclius, that Heraclius, aided by God for a long time, recovered the cross which the Persians had carried off from Jerusalem, so that God even fought against the Persians with hailstones from heaven, as he had once done with Joshua. Moreover, in the very restoration of the cross to its place, certain miracles occurred, as Sigebert reports in his Chronicle for the year 631. Hence also a feast was instituted, as Otto of Freising holds, book 5, chapter 9; Bede and Ado in the Martyrology.

units.la: Resp. I. Si verum est crucem à Persis ablatam, ab Heraclio restitutam & exaltatam, falsa erit interpretatio Bellarmini, qui laudes crucis inuentæ & exaltatę, in festo Exaltationis decantari solitas metonymicè de Christo crucifixo exponit, non de materiali ligno crucis.
units.tr: Reply I. If it is true that the cross was carried off by the Persians and restored and exalted by Heraclius, then the interpretation of Bellarmine is false. He explains the praises of the cross found and exalted, customarily sung at the feast of the Exaltation, figuratively of Christ crucified, not of the material wood of the cross.

units.la: II. Ab exaltatione crucis ad eius adorationem non valet consequentia. Nulla enim connexio est exaltationis cum adoratione, quia si exaltatio crucis facta est, non ad adorationem, sed ad asserendam gloriam Christi aduersum infideles est instituta. Atq; ita fallacia est à non causa, quia exaltata est crux non vt adoraretur, sed vt Dei gloria vindicaretur, & gentium
units.tr: II. From the exaltation of the cross to its adoration the inference does not hold. There is no connection between exaltation and adoration. If the cross was exalted, it was instituted not for adoration but to assert the glory of Christ against unbelievers. And so it is a fallacy of non-cause: the cross was exalted not so that it would be adored, but so that the glory of God would be vindicated and the incredulity of the Gentiles convicted.

units.la: L 2 increm. incredulitas conuinceretur. 3. Fabu-losa est haec narratio, de exaltatione cru-cis, vtpote idoneo & fide digno teste destituta. Testes, quos citat Bellarmin°, sine iudicio, prout ex imperitis & super-stitiosis hominibus accepere, ista literis mandarunt. Quin & veritati historiae haec narratio repugnat. Suidas in Hera-clio, teste Baronio, commemorat, recu-peratum esse lignum crucis, sine pretio, mortuo Cosroe: Bellarminus vero refert, Heraclium in praelio adiutum esse diuinitus contra Cosroen, vt recupera-ret lignum crucis. Sic n. Suidas rem re-recenset, vt dicat Syroen, filium Cosro-es, regno Persarum potitum, factaiam pace cum Romanis, captiuos, & interea-os, Zachariam Pontifice Hierosolymi-tanum dimisisse, prouincias ereptas, & lignum crucis intactum restituisse. IV. Miracula, quae dicit contigisse in crucis restitutione, non probant adorationem crucis. Nisi enim prius praeceptum habeatur de adoranda cruce, & promissio exauditionis, miracula eius adoratione nunquam probabunt. V. Miracula illa vel falsa sunt, & ab hominibus superstitiosis conficta: vel si vera sunt, aut a Diabolo, aut a Deo patrata. Si Diabol° Dei permispermissu ea patrauit, cæcitatė & super-stitionem crucis Idololatricam, in animis hominum fouere & confirmare voluit: si Deus non eo fine edidit, vt homines crucem religiose colerent, sed partim vt Persarum incredulitatė conuincerêt, ac damnaret; partim, vt doctrinâ ac fidem Christi crucifixi confirmaret.
units.tr: 3. This narrative about the exaltation of the cross is fabulous, lacking a suitable and trustworthy witness. The witnesses Bellarmine cites wrote these things down without judgment, as they had received them from unskilled and superstitious men. Indeed, this narrative even conflicts with the truth of history. Suidas, in his account of Heraclius, as Baronius records, relates that the wood of the cross was recovered without ransom when Chosroes died. Bellarmine, however, reports that Heraclius was divinely aided in battle against Chosroes so that he might recover the wood of the cross. For Suidas recounts the matter thus: Siroes, son of Chosroes, gained the kingdom of the Persians, made peace with the Romans, released the captives and the imprisoned, and sent back Zacharias, the Patriarch of Jerusalem; he restored the provinces that had been seized and the wood of the cross, untouched. IV. The miracles which he says occurred at the restoration of the cross do not prove the adoration of the cross. For unless there is first a command to adore the cross, and a promise of being heard, miracles will never prove its adoration. V. Those miracles are either false and invented by superstitious men, or, if true, were wrought either by the Devil or by God. If the Devil did them with God's permission, he wished to foster and confirm in men's minds the blindness and idolatrous superstition of the cross. If God did not produce them for this end, that men should religiously worship the cross, but partly so that he might convict and condemn the unbelief of the Persians, and partly so that he might confirm the teaching and faith of the crucified Christ.

units.la: Argumentum Sextum.
units.tr: Sixth Argument.

units.la: Argumentum VI. Si locus in quo Angelus stetit terra sanêta est Ios.c.5. Ex.3. Cur non magis crux, vbi stetit Christus? Si sudaria & semicinctia Pauli honorabantur, propter contactum; cur non magis crux Christi sanguine respersa? Si sacramenta honorantur, quia instrumenta gratiæ, cur non crux quæ instrumentum est redemptionis?
units.tr: Argument VI. If the place where the angel stood is holy ground (Josh. 5; Ex. 3), why not rather the cross, where Christ stood? If the napkins and aprons of Paul were honoured on account of contact, why not rather the cross sprinkled with Christ's blood? If sacraments are honoured because they are instruments of grace, why not the cross, which is an instrument of redemption?

units.la: Resp. I. Iesuita debuit probare crucem adorandâ esse: at de adoratione tacet. Non quæstio est, an sanêta sit crux, sed an religiose adoranda? Omne id quod sanctum est, non continuo est adorandum. Aqua Baptismi, panis & vinum sacræ cœnæ, sunt res sanêtæ, non tamen propterea religiose adorandæ. Quicquid ἀπλῶς independenter, & per se, ac sua natura sanctum est, id solû fatemur religiose adorandû esse. esse. At Deus solus ἀπλῶς, independenter, perse ac sua natura sanctus est. Ergo Deus solus est adorandus. Neque crux, nec vlla alia creatura, hoc modo sancta est: eoque nec crux, nec vlla alia creatura religiose adoranda. II. Si quæ creaturæ sanctæ sunt, non simpliciter, & natura sua sanctæ dicuntur, sed dependenter, relatè, & ob vsum sacrum ad quæ à Deo instituţ sunt, sanctæ sunt, & nuncupantur. At crux à Deo, qui solus rerum sacrarum autor est, ob vsum aliquem sacrum non est instituta. Quare sanctitas crucis nudo hominū superstitiosorum instituto est fundata, eoque vana est ac superstitiosa. III. Etsi crucis lignum esset sanctum ex Christi institutione; quod tamen nequaquam damus & agnoscimus: tamen non sequeretur religiose colendā esse. Honore debito, id est, ciuili reuerētia eam afficeremus, sed indebitum, id est, diuinū illi nequaquam exhiberemus. Est enim honor duplex, alius ciuilis seu humanus, qui pro varia rerum dignitate etiam variatur: alius religiosus, & diuinus qui vniformis est, & nulli creaturæ, sed soli creatori Deo debetur. IV. In exemplis, quæ profert Bellarminus, est ingens dissimilitudo. 1. Terra illa, in qua Angelus Iosuæ appa-
units.tr: Reply I. The Jesuit ought to prove that the cross is to be adored, but he says nothing about adoration. The question is not whether the cross is holy, but whether it is to be religiously adored. Not everything that is holy must straightway be adored. The water of baptism, and the bread and wine of the holy supper, are holy things, yet they are not on that account to be religiously adored. Whatever is holy absolutely [ἀπλῶς], independently, in itself and by its own nature, that alone we confess is to be religiously adored. But God alone is holy absolutely [ἀπλῶς], independently, in himself and by his own nature. Therefore God alone is to be adored. Neither the cross nor any other creature is holy in this way, and therefore neither the cross nor any other creature is to be religiously adored. II. If any creatures are holy, they are not called holy simply and by their nature, but dependently and relatively, on account of the sacred use for which God has instituted them; and they are called holy on that basis. But the cross was not instituted by God, who alone is the author of sacred things, for any sacred use. Therefore the holiness of the cross is founded on the bare institution of superstitious men, and is therefore vain and superstitious. III. Even if the wood of the cross were holy by Christ's institution, which we by no means grant or acknowledge, it would not follow that it is to be religiously worshipped. We would show it due honour, that is civil reverence, but we would by no means give it undue honour, that is the honour owed to God. For honour is twofold: one civil or human, which also varies according to the varying dignity of things; the other religious and divine, which is uniform and is owed to no creature, but to God the Creator alone. IV. There is great dissimilarity in the examples Bellarmine brings forward. 1. The land in which the angel appeared to Joshua

units.la: apparuit, sancta dicitur, non in se a sanctitate aliqua inhaerete, sed relate a Dei sanctissimi in terra illa apparitione & praesentia, qua cessante, cessauit etiam loci sanctitas. Relatio illa tamdiu duravit, quamdiu praesens fuit Deus, simul ac discessit Deus, terra ad pristinam, & communem rediit conditionem. At Pontificii pleriq; sanctam arbitrantur crucem inhaerente quadam sanctitate, quod salsissimum est: aut si relatione, & respectu ad Christum qui affixus illiste-tit, ac praesens fuit in ea, sancta esse nonnulli statuunt, nunc temporis non amplius sancta esse ac dici potest, quia respectus & relatio iam dudum periit, Christo non amplius in ea stante, sed in coelis gloriose regnante. Sic igitur contra Bellarminum argumentor. Crux Christi sancta dicitur, aut in se & sua natura, aut relatione ad Christum in ea stantem ac praesentem, aut deniq; institutione. Non in se ac sua natura. Nam in se ac sua natura vile est & contemptum lignum, pars scilicet, teste Nysseno, vilis & contempta arboris. Non relatione quia relatio illa desiit, quae si adhuc durarer, non tamen propterea adorationem mereretur. Relatio enim licet vera & diuinitus instituta non est causa adorationis. Non institutione vel diuina vel humana. Non diuina : quia nusquam verbum Dei hanc institutionem vel sanctificationem crucis nobis commendat, aut describit. Non humana, id est, Ecclesiae institutione: haec enim eam potestatem non habet, vt rem sacram facere, aut instituere possit. II. Terram illam Dei praesentia sanctificabat ex mandato & instituto Dei. Terra, inquit Deus, in qua stas, sancta est. De cruce vero nullum exstat mandatum, cuius vi, Christo in cruce pendente, crux sanctificata fuerit, & a nobis sancta agnosci debeat. Quare Christus sua praesentia, non sanctificauit lignum crucis; aut dicendum, omnia illa loca, in quibus Christus secundum humanitatem praesens fuit, aut stetit sancta esse, ac proinde adoranda. Torrens Cedron, inquit Belonius vir Pontificius, lapidis iactu ab urbe distat: istic lapis ostenditur, in quo impressa sunt Christi pedum vestigia, quum e ponte decideret. Num & lapis ille sanctus est, eoque adorandus? Sacellum est in summo Oliveti monte qui urbi impendet, in quo ostenditur pedis vestigium saxo impressum, & dicitur esse nota pedis Christi in Coelum ascensuri. Num & illud saxum, sanctum stumerit, & adorandum? III. Terra illa ilcet sancta esset, tamen à Mose non fuit adorata. Honorauit quidem eam, idq; ex Dei mandato; non adorauit. Ergo & crux, etiamsi sancta esset, & Dei mandato atque institutione sanctificata, non tamen propterea adoranda esset, vt faciunt Pontificii. Quod ad sudaria & semicinctia attinet; nō ea fuerūt adorata, licet miracula ad ea edita fuerint. Ergo nec crux Christi, licet ad eam edita fuerint miracula, propterea debet adorari.
units.tr: is called holy, not as having some holiness inhering in itself, but relatively, on account of the appearance and presence of the most holy God in that land. When that presence ceased, the holiness of the place ceased too. That relation lasted as long as God was present; as soon as God departed, the land returned to its former and common condition. But most Papists think the cross is holy by some inhering holiness, which is most false. Or if some hold it holy by relation and respect to Christ, who was fixed to it and was present in it, it cannot now be called holy at all, because that respect and relation perished long ago, Christ no longer standing in it but reigning gloriously in heaven. So I argue against Bellarmine thus: The cross of Christ is called holy either in itself and by its own nature, or by relation to Christ standing and present in it, or finally by institution. Not in itself and by its own nature, for in itself and by its nature the wood is vile and contemptible, being part, as Nyssen says, of a vile and contemptible tree. Not by relation, because that relation has ceased; and even if it still endured, it would not on that account deserve adoration, for relation, even if real and divinely instituted, is not the cause of adoration. Not by institution, either divine or human. Not divine, because nowhere does the Word of God commend or describe to us this institution or sanctification of the cross. Not human, that is, by institution of the Church, for the Church does not have the power to make or institute a holy thing. II. That land was sanctified by the presence of God through God's command and institution. The land, says God, on which you stand, is holy. But concerning the cross there is no command by whose force, with Christ hanging on it, the cross was sanctified and ought to be acknowledged by us as holy. Therefore Christ did not sanctify the wood of the cross by his presence; or else it must be said that all those places in which Christ was present or stood according to his humanity are holy, and therefore to be adored. The Kidron brook, says Belonius, a Papist, is a stone's throw from the city. There a stone is shown, in which the footprints of Christ are impressed, when he came down from the bridge. Is that stone too holy, and therefore to be adored? On the top of the Mount of Olives, which overhangs the city, there is a little chapel in which a footprint impressed in the rock is shown; it is said to be the mark of the foot of Christ about to ascend into heaven. Is that rock too to be held holy and adored? III. Even if that land were holy, it was nevertheless not adored by Moses. He indeed honoured it, and that by God's command, but he did not adore it. Therefore the cross too, even if it were holy and sanctified by God's command and institution, would not on that account be adored, as the Papists do. As for the napkins and aprons, they were not adored, although miracles were wrought through them. Therefore neither the cross of Christ, although miracles were wrought through it, ought on that account to be adored.

units.la: II. Sudaria & semicinctia hæc, ciuili fuerunt reuerentia cohonestata, non tamē religiose fuerunt honorata: sic & crucem Christi, si extaret; ciuiliter honoraremus & honorificè tractaremus, non vero religiosè coleremus.
units.tr: II. These handkerchiefs and aprons were honoured with civil reverence, but they were not honoured religiously. So too, if the cross of Christ were still extant, we would honour it civilly and treat it with respect, but we would not worship it religiously.

units.la: III. Honorabantur sudaria & semicinctia, non ob in fidam quandam sanctitatem, aut virtutem in hærentem, sed quod Deus ad illa, ministerio Apostolorum, fuerit dignatus miracula edere, vt doctrinam ab Apostolis annunciatam confirmaret. At Pontificii peculiarem quandam sanctitatem, & virtutem, in cruce residere opinantur, eiusq; efficatiæ miraculorum operationem ascribunt. Quod deniq, ad sacramenta attinet, honorātur eased honore debito, non indebito, qualis est honor adorationis. Agnoscimus sacramenta, vt sacra, & à Deo instituta signa, reuerenter habenda, & honorifice tractanda esse, sed negamus adoranda. Sic Baptismum honoramus, nemo vero aquâ Baptismi adorat. Sic cruce Christi, si extaret, honoremus sed ei non praestaremus cultum diuinum.
units.tr: III. The handkerchiefs and aprons were honoured not because of some inherent sanctity or virtue residing in them, but because God deigned, through the ministry of the Apostles, to work miracles through them, in order to confirm the doctrine the Apostles proclaimed. The Papists, however, think that a peculiar sanctity and virtue resides in the cross, and they ascribe the working of miracles to its efficacy. Finally, as for the sacraments, they are honoured with the honour that is due, not with undue honour such as the honour of adoration. We acknowledge that the sacraments, as sacred signs instituted by God, are to be held in reverence and treated with honour, but we deny that they are to be adored. Thus we honour Baptism, yet no one adores the water of Baptism. Likewise, if the cross of Christ existed, we would honour it, but we would not render to it divine worship.

units.la: II. Hororaturfacramenta, non per se propter insitā quandam, & inhærentem sanctitatē, & virtutem, qualem cruci tribuunt Pontifícii, sed ob vsum sacrum, & rei sacræ significationem, quam habent ex Dei institutione. Crux vero nec à Christo, nec ab Apostolis, ad vsum sacrum aut sacræ rei significationem, est instituta. Si qua tribuitur ei significatio, eam ex hominū superstitiosorum imaginatione accepit.
units.tr: II. The sacraments are honoured not in themselves, on account of an inherent and indwelling sanctity and virtue such as the Papists attribute to the cross, but on account of their sacred use and the sacred meaning of the thing, which they have from God's institution. The cross, however, was instituted neither by Christ nor by the Apostles for any sacred use or sacred signification. If any signification is attributed to it, it has received this from the superstitious imagination of men.

units.la: III. Sacramenta agnoscimus esse instrumenta gratiæ, sed non conferendæ, verum confirmandæ & obsignandæ, à Deo instituta, eoque honorā tur à nobis, non vero adorantur: crucem vero negamus esse instrumentum redemptionis nostræ. Instrumentum est supplicii quo Christus affectus ad redemptionem & salutem nobis promerendam.
units.tr: III. We acknowledge that the sacraments are instruments of grace, not to confer it but to confirm and seal it, and, instituted by God, they are honoured by us but not adored. We deny, however, that the cross is an instrument of our redemption. It was an instrument of the punishment by which Christ was afflicted, in order to merit our redemption and salvation.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: In quo 28. caput, Bellar. de Imaginecrucis examinatur & castigatur.
units.tr: In which the 28th chapter of Bellarmine, on the image of the cross, is examined and corrected.

units.la: Imaginem crucis Bellar. quinq; argumentis colendam esse contendit.
units.tr: Bellarmine contends that the image of the cross is to be worshipped on five arguments.

units.la: Primum Argumentum.
units.tr: The First Argument.

units.la: PPrimum arg: sumit ex testimonio Matth. 24. Tunc apparebit signum filii hominis in cælo, ex qua apparitione miro modo venerabile reddetur signum illud, id est, crux · Respon.I. Non sequitur: crux ante nouissimũ diem apparebit in cælo. Ergo est adoranda. Nulla consequentia ab apparitione crucis ad eius adorationē-Adoratio enim alicuius rei non ex apparitione sed ex institutione & mādato Dei æstimanda est. De crucis vero adoratione nulla institutio, nullū Dei mādatum in sacra scriptura proferri potest. Signum illud filii hominis nō est intelligendum de imagine crucis eius, in qua Christus pepędit, quasi illa imago in aere sit conspicienda: sed de ipso filio hominis qui signum erit certissimum aduentus sui ad iudicium. Interpretatio hæc probatur. I. ex similibus scripturæ locis, quib. eadē hypallag. vsurpatur, vt Rō.4. Abraham dicitur accepisse signum circumcisionis. II. Ex ipso textu, qui huius signi id est Christi ad iudicium cōparentis modum pulchre secundum partes distinguit, ac describit. Prima pars, est remotior aspectus Christi e coelo, semet ostendentis, ad significandam praesentissimam seculi consumationem.
units.tr: The first argument is taken from the testimony of Matthew 24: Then shall appear the sign of the Son of Man in heaven, by whose appearance that sign, that is, the cross, will be made venerable in a wonderful way. Reply: It does not follow that the cross will appear in heaven before the last day, and therefore that it is to be worshipped. No consequence runs from the appearance of the cross to its adoration. For the worship of anything is to be judged not by its appearance but by the institution and command of God. Yet no institution or command of God for the worship of the cross can be produced from Holy Scripture. That sign of the Son of Man is not to be understood as the image of the cross on which Christ suffered, as if that image were to be seen in the air, but of the Son of Man himself, who will be the most certain sign of his coming to judgment. This interpretation is proved: I. from similar passages of Scripture, where the same hypallage is used, as in Romans 4, Abraham is said to have received the sign of circumcision. II. from the text itself, which beautifully distinguishes and describes the manner of this sign, that is, of Christ coming to judgment, part by part. The first part is the more distant sight of Christ showing himself from heaven, to signify the very near end of the age.

units.la: T v n c, id est, omnibus aliis signis caelestibus, quae imminentis extremi iudicii prodromi erunt, exhibitis, Christus e caelo apparebit, instar signi praesentissimi mundi finem significantis II. parseft ploratus improborum, & incredulorum, per omnes tribus terrae, qui ad illum aspectum Christi e coelo ad iudicium aduentantis, expauescent, & in lachrymas effundentur, tum scelerum conscientia, tum metu instantis aeterni iudicii. III. pars, est propinquior Christi aspectus, in ipsis nubibus, in quas adueniet, ad perficiendum opus universalis consummationis & conflagrationis mundi. Hic processus vltimi Christi aduentus eodem modo in 2. Thess. 3. v. 7. exprimitur: Christum scilicet primum apparitypum e caelo, qua apparitione homines ita sint percellendi, ut amarissimum planctum sint edituri: deinde vero descensurum in hanc aeris regionem, & signum daturum vltimi iudicii.
units.tr: Then, that is, after all the other heavenly signs, which will be the forerunners of the impending final judgment, have been displayed, Christ will appear from heaven, like a most certain sign signifying the end of the world. II. The second part is the wailing of the wicked and the unbelievers, through all the tribes of the earth, who at that sight of Christ coming from heaven to judgment will be terrified and will dissolve in tears, both from the consciousness of their sins and from fear of the eternal judgment at hand. III. The third part is the nearer sight of Christ, in the very clouds in which he will come, to complete the work of the universal consummation and burning of the world. This course of Christ's final coming is expressed in the same way in 2 Thessalonians 3:7: namely, that Christ will first appear from heaven, at which appearance men will be so struck that they will utter the bitterest lament; then indeed he will descend into this region of the air and give the sign of the last judgment.

units.la: Instat. At omnes veteres ad vnum ex-ponunt de cruce. Ita Origenes, Chry-foftomus, Hieronymus, Hilarius, Theo-phylactus, Euthymius, Beda in c. 24. Matth. item Cyrillus catech. 15. & Au-guftinus sermone 130. de tempore.
units.tr: Objection: But all the ancients, without exception, explain it of the cross. So Origen, Chrysostom, Jerome, Hilary, Theophylact, Euthymius, Bede on Matthew 24; likewise Cyril, Catechesis 15, and Augustine, Sermon 130, on the season.

units.la: Refpon. I. At nulli veteres, ex hac fi-gni apparitione probarunt imaginem crucis esse adorandam. II. Veteres illam interpretationem de cruce, non vt cer-tam & necessariam, sed vt probabilem, sunt amplexi; adducti visione Conftan-tini Magni, qui, cum vellet contra ho-stes pugnare, conspexisse fertur imagi-nem, seu figuram crucis Christi, cum hac inscriptione: In hoc vinces, ita vt ve-terum de hoc loco coiectura potius fit, quam vera & solida expositio. Ex con-iecturis vero, firmae & necessariae proba-tiones extrui non debent. III. Origenes nihil habet de imagine crucis Christi, sed fignū interpretatur de virtute, qua Filius hominis ad iudicium veniens, fit declaraturus in caelo, quod scilicet ho-mines, Christi aduentu, & aspectu, adeo percellendi sint, vt, qui non crediderunt suam caecitatem, & ignorantiam, sint de-ploraturi. Chryfoftomus duplicem huius loci expositionem adfert. Prior est designo crucis, sed non simpliciter, verum de Christo ipso, cum signo crucis apparituro, ad sui iustificationem & Iudæorum incredulorum condemnationem. Veniet, inquit, ipse Christus non vulnera, sed acerbum & ignominiosum mortis suæ genus ostedes. Nō igitur simpliciter imaginem crucis intellexit, sed ipsum Christum, qui in signo crucis semet generi humano repræsentabit. Quid vero interpretatio ist hæc ad figuram crucis adorationem? Nō signi crucis, sed Christi in hoc signo semet ostendetis, adoratio hinc concludenda est, idque eo magis quod addit, exhibiturum semet Christum in signo crucis, nō ut doceret signum crucis esse adorabile: sed ut seipsum iustificaret, & Iudæorum incredulitate convinceret. Posterior expositio Chrysostomi hæc est, signum illud forte ipsum corpus Christi, quod habiturum sit testimonia passionis, vulnera manuum, pedum, ac lateris. Quidam putant, inquit, crucem Christi ostendendam esse in cælo: Verius autem est ipsum Christum in corpore suo habentem testimonia passionis, id est, vulnera lacera & clavorum, ut impleatur id quod dictum est: hi videbunt, in quem pupugerunt. Hæc sententia expresse verior priore affirmat; ergo prior nihil probat. Hieron. certa sententiam nō sequitur, sed quid probabiliter statuas possit indicat, liberum cuique permittens iudicium. Signum, ait, hic aut crucem intelligamus; aut vexillum victoriae triumphantis. Ex autoritate vero dubitantis, & nihil certi asseuerantis, dogma fidei, aut cultus diuini non debent probari. Hilarius nō meminit crucis, sed signi salutaris, quod dicit ostensum iri. Ea vero ostensio quid ad crucis imaginem? Theophylactus est recens scriptor, qui in tempus superstitionum ferax incidit, famâ & opinione recepta persuasus, de cruce interpretatur, quam statuit in cælo supra solem cum fulgore apparituram, ad coarguendos Iudæos, sed non simpliciter, verum de Christo in signo crucis semet ostensuro, plane sicut Chrisostomus: Crux, inquit, apparebit supra solem fulgens, ad arguendos Iudæos. Veniet enim Christus contra Iudæos habens crucem, ut magnam iustificandi materiam & testimonium, veluti si quis lapide percussus, ostendat lapidem contra percussorem.
units.tr: Reply: I. But none of the ancients proved from this appearance of the sign that the image of the cross is to be worshipped. II. The ancients embraced that interpretation of the cross not as certain and necessary, but as probable, being led by the vision of Constantine the Great, who, when he wanted to fight against his enemies, is said to have seen the image or figure of the cross of Christ with this inscription: In this sign you will conquer. So the ancients' conjecture about this passage is more a guess than a true and solid exposition. But firm and necessary proofs ought not to be built on conjectures. III. Origen says nothing about an image of the cross of Christ, but interprets the sign as the power by which the Son of Man, coming to judgment, will make a display in heaven, so that men will be so struck by Christ's coming and appearance that those who did not believe will lament their own blindness and ignorance. Chrysostom offers a twofold exposition of this passage. The first is about the sign of the cross, but not simply; it is about Christ himself, who will appear with the sign of the cross, for his own justification and the condemnation of the unbelieving Jews. He himself, Christ, he says, will come, showing not wounds but the bitter and shameful manner of his death. Therefore he did not understand simply the image of the cross, but Christ himself, who will show himself to the human race in the sign of the cross. But what does this interpretation have to do with the worship of the figure of the cross? It is not the sign of the cross but Christ showing himself in this sign from which worship is to be inferred. And this all the more, since he adds that Christ will display himself in the sign of the cross not to teach that the sign of the cross is to be worshipped, but to justify himself and to convict the Jews of their unbelief. Chrysostom's second exposition is this: that the sign may perhaps be the very body of Christ, which will bear the tokens of his passion, the wounds of the hands, feet and side. Some think, he says, that the cross of Christ is to be shown in heaven; but it is truer that Christ himself, having in his body the tokens of his passion, that is, the torn wounds of the nails, will come, so that what was said may be fulfilled: they will look on him whom they pierced. This opinion expressly and more truly affirms the former; therefore the former proves nothing. Jerome does not follow a certain opinion, but indicates what may be held as probable, leaving each man free judgment. Let us understand, he says, here either the cross or the banner of triumphant victory. But from the authority of one who doubts and affirms nothing certain, no doctrine of faith or form of divine worship ought to be proved. Hilary makes no mention of the cross, but of the saving sign, which he says will be shown. But what has that showing to do with the image of the cross? Theophylact is a recent writer, who fell into an age fertile in superstitions, persuaded by received fame and opinion, and he interprets it of the cross, which he holds will appear in heaven above the sun with brilliance, to convict the Jews; but not simply, rather of Christ, who will show himself in the sign of the cross, just as Chrysostom did: The cross, he says, will appear shining above the sun, to convict the Jews. For Christ will come against the Jews bearing the cross, as a great material and testimony of justification, as if someone struck with a stone should show the stone against the one who struck him.

units.la: Reliquis omissis, ad Augustinum venio, qui errorem ex viso Constantini M. conceptu & receptu secutus, crucè apparitura scribit, addita ratione, ut agnoscant consilium iniquitatis suæ, qui Dn. maiestatis crucifixerunt. Per hoc n. signum impudes Iudæorum redargultur impietas. Audimus hic Iudæorum impietatē per hoc signum redargui, sed adoratione ei approbari non audimus. Instat At Eccl. canit infesto inuetionis. Hoc signum crucis erit in cælo, cum Dn. ad indicandum venerit.
units.tr: Passing over the rest, I come to Augustine, who, following the error conceived and received from the vision of Constantine the Great, writes that the cross will appear, adding the reason that those who crucified the Lord of majesty may recognise the plan of their wickedness. For by this sign the impiety of the Jews is refuted. Here we hear that the impiety of the Jews is refuted by this sign, but we do not hear that it is approved by adoration. Objection: But the Church sings on the feast of the Invention: This sign of the cross will be in heaven, when the Lord comes to judge.

units.la: Respon. I. Ecclesiæ, in superstitione errantis, authoritatem nō agnoscimus. II. Ecclesia canit etiam in eodem festo de cruce. O crux aue spes unica: auge piis iustitiam: reisq; dona veniam. Quod Christo competit, ad crucem superstitiosè & impiè transfert, Non ergo audienda.
units.tr: Reply: I. We do not acknowledge the authority of the Church when it errs in superstition. II. The Church also sings on the same feast about the cross: O Cross, hail, our only hope: increase righteousness in the pious, and grant pardon to the guilty. What belongs to Christ, it superstitiously and impiously transfers to the cross. It is therefore not to be listened to.

units.la: Instat. Sybill al. 6. in fine canit:
units.tr: Objection: The Sibyl, in book 6 at the end, sings:

units.la: O lignum felix, in quo Deus ipse pependit!
units.tr: O happy wood, on which God himself hung!

units.la: Nec te terra capit, sed cœli tecta videbis,
units.tr: Neither the earth shall hold you, but you shall see the roofs of heaven,

units.la: Cum renouata Dei facies ignita micabit.
units.tr: When the renewed face of God shall shine out, glowing.

units.la: Respon. I. Authoritas Sybillæ tanti non est facienda, ut veritati opponi debeat. II. Sybilla nō loquitur de imagine vel signo, sed de ligno, seu lignea cruce, in quâ Christus pependit: Ecclesia verò de signo loquitur, & signi apparitionem celebrat. III. More poetico lignum alloquitur, sed ipsum Christum figuratè intelligit.
units.tr: Reply: I. The authority of the Sibyl is not to be held so highly as to be set against the truth. II. The Sibyl does not speak of an image or sign, but of the wood, or wooden cross, on which Christ hung; but the Church speaks of a sign and celebrates the appearance of the sign. III. In poetic manner she addresses the wood, but figuratively means Christ himself.

units.la: Instat. At Thomas VValdensis. To. 3. tit. 20. cap. 581. non omnino improbabiliter dicit, ipsam crucem ligneam, quæ nunc diuisa est in multas particulas, tunc reformandam & colligendam & appariturām in cœlo. Nam id videntur afferere Sybilla & Chryfostomus: in sermone de cruce & latrone: nec alij patres contradicunt.
units.tr: Objection: But Thomas Waldensis, vol. 3, title 20, chapter 581, says not altogether improbably that the wooden cross itself, which is now divided into many particles, will then be reformed and gathered together and will appear in heaven. For the Sibyl and Chrysostom seem to assert this, in the sermon on the cross and the thief; nor do the other Fathers contradict it.

units.la: Respon. Autoritatem VValdensis riici{1}eiicimus. I. quia Christi meti, adeoque {2}pfi veritatiaduerfatur. 2. nihil etiam ad {3}ropofitūfacit. Hic enim non de lignea {4}ruce, sed de eius imagine disputatur. {5}Ion lignea crucis, sed imaginis ado- {6}ratio, ex apparitione eius probanda est. {7}Ir testimonium VValdensis, est de li- {8}nea cruce. III. Absurda est eius sententia, vt quæ crucis quandam resurrectio {9}em cum corporibus statuit. IV. Neq; {10}ybilla, neque Chrysostomus, aut alii {11}tiam patres, eiusmodi fabulosam cru- {12}is collectionem asserūt, aut agnoscūt.
units.tr: Answer. We reject the authority of Waldensis: (1) because it runs against the merit of Christ and therefore against the truth itself; (2) it also has nothing to do with the point at issue. Here the discussion is not about the wooden cross but about its image. The adoration of the image, not of the wooden cross, must be proved from its appearance. (3) Waldensis's testimony concerns the wooden cross. (4) His view is absurd, since it posits a resurrection of the cross together with its bodies. (5) Neither the Sibyl, nor Chrysostom, nor any other of the Fathers asserts or acknowledges such a fabulous gathering of the cross.

units.la: {13}Quod nemo patrum contradicit, non {14}st mirum, quia figmentum illud ipsis {15}fuit ignotū, Rei incognitæ, & inauditæ {16}quis contradicat? V. Contradicit tamē {17}Ecclesia, quæ in festo Inuentionis canit: Hoc signum crucis erit in cælo. Non enim li- {18}gneæ crucis collectionem, aut reforma- tionem, sed imaginis, seu signi crucis ap- {19}paritionem, decantat.
units.tr: It is no wonder that none of the Fathers contradicts it, because that fiction was unknown to them. Who would contradict a thing unknown and unheard of? (6) The Church does contradict it, however, since on the feast of the Invention it sings: This sign of the cross will appear in heaven. For it does not sing of a gathering or restoration of the wooden cross, but of the appearance of an image, or sign, of the cross.

units.la: Instat. At etiam vera crux dici potest si- gnum crucis, id est, instrumentum, habens figu- ram crucis: sed si hoc non admittatur, saltem i- mago crucis lucida in cælo apparebit, ex aere vel igne condensato.
units.tr: Objection. But the true cross itself can be called a sign of the cross, that is, an instrument having the shape of a cross. And if this is not admitted, at least a shining image of the cross will appear in heaven, formed out of air or condensed fire.

units.la: Respon. I. Negatur veram crucem dici posse signum crucis. Signum enim cum signato non est cõfendendum. Vt signum non potest dici signatum suum: sic nec signum crucis dici potest ipsa vera crux. II. nec instrumentum habens siguram crucis, rectè dicitur esse vera illa & lignea crux, in qua Christus pendit, nisi cum V Valdensi verae crucis collectionem & resurrectionem statuas, quae absurda est & Ecclesiae ignota. Haec enim festo Inuentionis reformationem crucis non celebrat, sed eam tanquam inauditam reticet.
units.tr: Answer. (1) We deny that the true cross can be called a sign of the cross. A sign must not be confused with what it signifies. Just as a sign cannot be called its own thing signified, so the sign of the cross cannot be called the true cross itself. (2) Nor is that true and wooden cross on which Christ hung rightly described as an instrument having the figure of a cross, unless you posit with Waldensis a gathering and resurrection of the true cross, which is absurd and unknown to the Church. For on the feast of the Invention the Church does not celebrate a restoration of the cross, but passes over it in silence as something unheard of.

units.la: NVNC SEQVITVR ARGVMENTUM quod Bellarminus ex ista apparitione signi crucis deducit.
units.tr: NOW FOLLOWS THE ARGUMENT which Bellarmine deduces from this appearance of the sign of the cross.

units.la: Argumentum, inquit, multiplex est. Nam primo honorabilis est crux, quia ab ipso Christo vocatur signum eius, id est, vexillum Christi. Si enim vexillum Imperatoris adorant milites, vt patet ex Sozomeno l. 1. Inst. c. 4. cur vexillum Christi non adorabitur?
units.tr: The argument, he says, is manifold. For first, the cross is honourable, because Christ himself calls it his sign, that is, the standard of Christ. For if soldiers adore the standard of the emperor, as is clear from Sozomen, Inst. book 1, chapter 4, why should the standard of Christ not be adored?

units.la: Respon. I. Negatur imaginem verae crucis vocari ab ipso Christo signum eius. Christus semet ipsum signum appellat, quia suo aduentu & aspectu praesentissimam seculi consummationem significabit, vt supra dictū. II. Ab exemplo ethnicorum militum ad officium fidelium im Dei cultorum nô valet consequé-entia. Ethnici milites adorarunt vexilla imperatorum, quis inferat inde, oportere a fideles vexillum Christi de-sere adorare? contrarium hinc potius concludendum. Ethnici milites adora-runt vexilla suorum Imperatorum: Er-go fideles vexillum Christi non debent adorare: quia fideles, Ethnicorum super-stitionem & Idololatriam non debent imitari. Hinc Ambr. recte laudat Hele-nam, quod non crucem, sed ipsum re-gem Christum adorarit, quia adoratio lignii crucis sit error & vanitas impiorum. III. Legamus adorationem illam, quam Ethnici milites exhibuerunt vexillo Imperatoris, fuisse religiosam. Civilis tamen fuit, licet legati & tribuni, civilem illam in religiosam delabi interdum non libenter fuerint, quo militum animos quadam religione, tum ad obeúda mu-nia, tum ad ipsam pugnam eo magis obstringerent. Hinc illud Dionys. Ha-icarnassæi de signis Romanorum pro-nunciatum: Sacra censetur non secus ac deorum statuæ. Et illud Tertulliani: re-gio Romanorum tota (astrensis, signa venera-tur, signa curat signa omnibus Diis præpo-nit.
units.tr: Answer. (1) We deny that Christ himself calls the image of the true cross his sign. Christ calls himself the sign, because by his coming and appearance he will signify the most imminent consummation of the age, as has been said above. (2) The inference from the example of pagan soldiers to the duty of believing worshippers of God does not hold. Pagan soldiers adored the standards of their emperors. Who would infer from this that believers ought to adore the standard of Christ? Rather the opposite should be concluded: pagan soldiers adored the standards of their emperors; therefore believers ought not to adore the standard of Christ, because believers ought not to imitate the superstition and idolatry of the pagans. Hence Ambrose rightly praises Helena for having adored not the cross but Christ the King himself, because the adoration of the wood of the cross is the error and vanity of the impious. (3) Let us grant that the adoration which the pagan soldiers paid to the emperor's standard was religious. Yet it was civil in character. Although the legates and tribunes were not always willing for that civil honour to slide into religious worship, they wished to bind the spirits of the soldiers more firmly by a certain religious feeling, both to the performance of their duties and to the battle itself. Hence the statement of Dionysius of Halicarnassus about the standards of the Romans: They are regarded as sacred, no less than the statues of the gods. And the saying of Tertullian: The whole Roman military region reveres the standards, swears by the standards, and places the standards before all the gods.

units.la: Secundo, Horabilis est, quia in cœlo appa-rebit, rebit, loco nimirum sublimi & honorifico R I. Non crux apparebit in caelo, sed Christus semel ostendet ad opus iudicii universalis perficiendum. II. Et cum crux Christi intelligatur esse illud signum in caelo apparitururm, tamen signi crucis adoratio inde nulla consequentia potest extrui: quia multa alia signa filii hominis tunc apparebunt, in Sole, Luna, & Stellis; neque tamen propterea religiose esse colenda vllus affirmauerit.
units.tr: Second, it is honourable, because it will appear in heaven, in a lofty and honourable place, of course. (1) It is not the cross that will appear in heaven, but Christ, who will show himself once to carry out the work of the universal judgement. (2) And although the cross of Christ is understood to be that sign which will appear in heaven, no consequence can be built from this for the adoration of the sign of the cross. For many other signs of the Son of Man will then appear, in the sun, moon and stars, and yet no one has ever affirmed that these are to be honoured with religious worship.

units.la: Tertio, quia manibus Angelorum feretur, ut Augustinus docet Ser. 120. Respon. I. Gestatio illa angelorum nihil facit ad adorationem. Quia enim vel probabilis connexio gestationis illius, cum adoratione? II. Feretur manib. angelorum, non quod ineffabilis sit, aut esse debeat, sed quod dignum sit a Deo patre datum, ad oblationem generi humano vniuersalis iudicii praesentiam. III. Scriptura de hoc ministerio angelorum, cruci praestando, nihil tradit. Sunt quidem angeli ministri Dei, sed non crucis. Non ergo crucem ferunt, sed Christo inseruient, eumque velut ipsi patores sequuntur. IV. Si quis attente sermonem illum Augustini introspexerit, intelliget, hoc locum esse metam rhetoricationem, ad ornandum
units.tr: Third, because it will be carried by the hands of angels, as Augustine teaches, Sermon 120. Answer: First, that carrying by the angels has nothing to do with adoration. What probable connection is there between that carrying and adoration? Second, the cross will be carried by the hands of angels not because it is, or ought to be, unspeakable, but because it is a fitting thing, given by God the Father, for presenting to the human race the presence of the universal judgment. Third, Scripture says nothing about this ministry of the angels in rendering service to the cross. Angels are indeed ministers of God, but not of the cross. So they do not carry the cross; they serve Christ and follow him as their own pastor. Fourth, if anyone reads that sermon of Augustine closely, he will see that this passage is mere rhetorical ornament, designed to move and adorn rather than to teach. Therefore it cannot have the force of a testimony that proves anything.

units.la: mouen buendum potius, quam addocendum hibitam. Quare vim testimonii pro- ntis nequit habere.
units.tr: It was meant to move the reader rather than to teach him. Therefore it cannot have the force of a proving testimony.

units.la: Quarto, quia splendebit clarius sole. Quod ibant Augusti & Chrysostomi, quia tunc apparebit conspicietur ab omnib. quando sol & Luna, Stellae obscuratae fuerint, ut patet ex Matth. 24.
units.tr: Fourth, because it will shine more clearly than the sun. Which Augustine and Chrysostom also say: because then it will be seen by all, when the sun and moon and stars have been darkened, as is clear from Matthew 24.

units.la: Respon. I. Splendor crucis non pro- prie eius adorationem, sed Maiestatem, magnificentiam Christi iudicis, ad os sibi a Patre commissum perficien- dum comparentis. II. Non splendebit lux, sed ipse Christus, Sol iustitiae fulgentissimus. III. Augusti & Chrysostomi nulla necessaria ratione adducti, cruci hunc tribuerunt splendorem; idque persuasi visione Constantini M. qua signum crucis vidi fuisse oblatum ferunt, quae causam dedit multis superstitionibus, & receptae interpretationi de cruce, sed cum crucis adoratione, nulla specie, aut probabili ratione, cohaeret.
units.tr: Answer. (1) The splendour of the cross does not properly prove its adoration, but rather the majesty and magnificence of Christ the judge, who appears to carry out the work committed to him by the Father. (2) It is not the cross that will shine with light, but Christ himself, the most resplendent Sun of Righteousness. (3) Augustine and Chrysostom, though not led to this by any necessary reason, attributed this splendour to the cross, persuaded by the vision of Constantine the Great, in which they report that the sign of the cross was seen offered to him. This gave rise to many superstitions and to the received interpretation concerning the cross; but it coheres with the adoration of the cross by no kind of reasoning, whether apparent or probable.

units.la: Argumentum secundum.
units.tr: Second Argument.

units.la: Argumentum II. Sumi potest a testimoniis sacrorum conciliorum. Nam Synodus sexta can. 73. Synod. septima act. vlt. & Synod. 8. act. vlt. canones ediderunt de veneratione crucis.
units.tr: Argument II. It can be drawn from the testimonies of the sacred councils. For the Sixth Synod (canon 73), the Seventh Synod (final act) and the Eighth Synod (final act) issued canons on the veneration of the cross.

units.la: Respon I. Concilia etiam gene ralia, M si nobis in religione aliquid obtruserint quod nec mandatum, nec exemplum habet in scripturis, id tritum illud Hier. axioma reiici iubet: Quod de scripturis non habet authoritatem, eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur. II. Concilia, quae produxit, nō sūt orthodoxa, sed Idololatrica, eo seculo celebrata, quo Ecclesia perualerat Idololat: & superstitio, ideoq; authoritate eorū merito reiicim°atq; abillis verbū Dei, cuius regula certa, cōstans & immutabilis est, prouocamus. III. ipsi ad uerfarii canones sextę Synodi suspectos habet Bellar, in lib. de imag. sanct. affirmat, eos non esse firmae authoritatis. Alibiagnoscit, Synodum sextam & septimam, à graecis, aemulis Romanae Eccl. esse corruptā. Rursum in libro de concil. auctoritate canones huius cōcilii dicit esse errones, neque editos abvllo legitimo & probato concilio. Constat enim, inquit ex Tarasio in 7. Synodo act. 4. hos canones non esse editos à sexta Synodo, quae fuit tempore Agathonis & Iustiniani II. Imperatoris. Albertus Pighius, in Diatriba, sua has duas Synodos, sextam & septimam, ut modo extant, adulterinas, & suppositias esse, contendit. 4. Canon. 73. nihil habet de adoratione crucis, sed designo crucis humi non sculpendo, aut pedibus con-
units.tr: Response I. Even general councils, if they press upon us something in religion that has neither command nor example in Scripture, should be rejected under that well-worn axiom of Jerome: "What has no authority from the Scriptures is dismissed with the same ease with which it is asserted." II. The councils he has produced are not orthodox but idolatrous, celebrated in an age when the Church had grown full of idolatry and superstition. We therefore rightly reject their authority and appeal from them to the Word of God, whose rule is sure, constant and unchangeable. III. Bellarmine himself regards the canons of the Sixth Synod as suspect; in his book on the images of the saints he affirms that they are not of firm authority. Elsewhere he acknowledges that the Sixth and Seventh Synods were corrupted by the Greeks, rivals of the Roman Church. Again, in his book on the authority of councils, he says the canons of this council are erroneous and were not issued by any lawful and approved council. "For it is established," he says, "from Tarasius in the Seventh Synod, act 4, that these canons were not issued by the Sixth Synod, which took place in the time of Agatho and the Emperor Justinian II." Albert Pighius, in his Diatriba, contends that these two synods, the Sixth and the Seventh as they now stand, are spurious and counterfeit. 4. Canon 73 says nothing about the adoration of the cross, but only about marking the sign of the cross on the ground, not carving it, or treading on it,

units.tr: {y} Bellar. lib. 2. c. 17. de imag. sanct.

units.la: Pon. Rom. l. 11. l. 4. de concil. autor. c. 8.
units.tr: Pont. Rom. l. 11. l. 4. de concil. auctor. c. 8.

units.la: Decon. cil. autor. c. 5.
units.tr: de concil. auctor. c. 5.

units.la: ulcando, ne inde vel infirmi offendẽ- entur, vel infideles aut aduersarii ansa arriperent blasphemandi religionem Christianam. Deinde Can. 83. venerabi-
units.tr: lest thereby either the weak be offended, or the unbelievers or adversaries seize an occasion to blaspheme the Christian religion. Then Canon 83 indeed pronounces that venerable images

units.la: s quidem imagines pronunciat, sed I. on est receptus ab Ecclesia, teste Baro-io, qui sic de hoc canone disserit. Cum iter latinos acta res est, nequaquam reperies eū anone ab Eccl.Rom.esse receptū, imovsu cōtra- io improbatū. II. In illo canone etiā non gitur de adoratione crucis, sed præci- pitur I. vt impositerū loco agni Dei i- nago Christi depingatur. Deinde vt hoc fiat non in adoratione & cultū cru-cis, sed in memoriā benficiorū Christi.
units.tr: (1) is not received by the Church, as Baronius testifies, who discusses this canon as follows: "When the matter is viewed according to the Latins, you will nowhere find that canon received by the Roman Church; on the contrary, it has been rejected." (2) In that canon, moreover, there is no talk of the adoration of the cross, but it commands (1) that instead of the Lamb of God an image of Christ be painted; and (2) that this be done not for adoration and worship of the cross, but in memory of the benefits of Christ.

units.la: Verba canonis vtrumq; luculenter declarant. Prius sic declaratur. In quibusdā venerabilium imaginū pictuoris Agnus digito præcursoris monstratus depingitur, qui in lignū gratia est assumptus, verū nobis per legē Christum Dei nostrū præmoströns: deinceps Christi Dei nostri instar hominis characterē etiā in ima ginib.pro veteri agno satui iubemus. Posteriūs statim additur, estq; ratio superioris.
units.tr: The words of the canon make both points plain. The first is declared thus: "In certain venerable images the Lamb, pointed out by the finger of the Forerunner, is painted, who was taken up into grace as a wood-carved figure, but who shows us Christ our God through the law. Henceforth we command that, in place of the old lamb, the character of Christ our God in human form be set up in the images as well."

units.la: vt per ipsū verbi Dei humiliatione mete copre-hendentes, ad memoria quoq; eius in carne co-uersationis, eiusq; passionis & salutaris mortis deducamur, Aperte significatur non in adorationem, sed in memoriam institu-tam. tæesse,imòin toto canone nullafit metiò adorationis& cultus,sed tantum’. Etsi verò venerabiles dicat imagines:nō tamen adorandas esse indicat,quia non intelligit eas religiosè venerabiles, sed ciuili quadā reuerentia dignas, quā dignitatē ex eo adeptæ erāt,quod in loco sacro & religioso essēt positæ. V.Septima Synod°Nicena secunda idololatrica fuit,& à Synodo Franckfurt. cui interfuit Carolus M. damnata est vt hæretica. Testatur id Regino Abbas Prumiēl. qui floruit an.908.Pseudosynodus Græcorum,quam adorantis imaginib fecerant à Pontificib.reiecta e. Testatur idem Ado Viennensis Episcopus:Pseudosynodus,quam septimam Græci appellant,pro adorandis imaginib.penitus abdicata est. Testatur idē autor annaliū Pipini perantiquus.Synodus,inquit,quæ ante paucos annos in Constantinop. (legendum Niceæ,teste ipso Bellarm.) sub Irene & Constantino filio eius congregata, & ab illis non modo septima verum etiam universalis erat appellata, vt nec septima nec universalis haberetur, diceretur ve quasi superuacanea omnino ab omnib.est abdicata. Turpiter falluntur qui putant Francof. Synodū ideo damnasse Nicænam tum quod putarit, coactam esse sine autoritate Papæ.
units.tr: Immediately afterwards is added the reason for the foregoing: "so that, by comprehending through the humiliation of the Word of God itself, we may also be led to the memory of his life in the flesh, of his passion and of his saving death." It is clearly signified that the image was instituted for remembrance, not for adoration; indeed, in the whole canon there is not a trace of any mention of adoration and worship, but only of remembrance. And although it calls the images venerable, it does not indicate that they are to be adored, because it does not understand them as religiously venerable but as worthy of a civil kind of reverence, a dignity they had gained from being placed in a sacred and religious place. V. The Seventh Synod, the Second Nicene, was idolatrous, and it was condemned as heretical by the Synod of Frankfurt, at which Charlemagne was present. Regino, abbot of Prüm, who flourished in 908, bears witness to this: the pseudo-synod of the Greeks, which they had convened in favour of adoring images, was rejected by the Pontiffs. The same is attested by Ado, bishop of Vienne: "The pseudo-synod which the Greeks call the seventh has been utterly rejected in regard to the adoration of images." The same is attested by the author of the very ancient Annals of Pippin: "The synod which a few years ago was gathered at Constantinople (read Nicaea, as Bellarmine himself says) under Irene and her son Constantine, and which was called by them not only seventh but also universal, was so utterly abdicated by all that it is held neither seventh nor universal, but is said to be superfluous altogether." They are shamefully mistaken who think the Synod of Frankfurt condemned the Nicene because it judged that it had been convened without the authority of the Pope,

units.la: Note: the margin notes read "1.2.ad an. 794", "p 214.in Chron.ad an.794", "l.2.de Con cil c.8."; these are placed as printed. apæ: tum quod putarit, definiuisse e- imagines esse adorandas latria. Nicena enim Synodus paulo ante Francofurtensem erat congregata, sub eodem pontifice Romano Ariano, à quo fuerat confirmata. Legati eiusdem Adriatici adfuerunt concilio Francofurtensi. Quomodo potuit fieri, vt tota illa Synodus & authoritatem & doctrinam Nicenae Synodi ignoraret? Nempe à legatis Pontificis instrui potuisset, & aberrore, si quis fuit, liberari. Recte igitur Suarez in part. 3. Thomæ q.15.disp.54. Mihi, inquit, difficile creditu est, Synodum Francofurtensem potuisse ex errore facti contra Nicenam procedere. VI. Synodi octauæ acta in Tomis conciliorum non legun-tur, vt nec apud historicos. Bartholomæus vero Caranza se multifariam depravata reperisse profitetur. Et constat, omnia per vim & libidinem in ea gesta esse, ideoq; Græci eum neq; pro vniuersali octaua, neq; pro vniuersali simpliciter habuere. Adrianus II. Pontifex Romanus, & Basilius qui imperio potitus erat, per Michaelis, qui eum adoptarat, parricidium, mutuas sibi præstitere operas. Ille vt primatum; hic vt adorationem imaginum fingeret. Quod omnium niū luculentissime describit Aimoinus Monachus Gallus. In hac Synodo, inquit, quam vniuersalem synodum, octauam illud cum uenientes appellarunt, de adorandis imaginibus, aliter, quam Orthodoxi doctores antea definiuerunt, statuerunt, & quedam pro fauore Romani Pontificis, qui eorum votis de imaginibus adorandis annuit, & quedam contra antiquos canones, & contra ipsam suam synodum constituerunt, sicut qui eandem synodum legerit, patenter inueniet. Apparet simul ex hisce verbis imaginum adorationem isto seculo anno circiter 830. ab hominibus piis, & Ecclesiis non fuisse probatam.
units.tr: because it thought that the Nicene Synod had defined that images are to be adored with latria. For the Nicene Synod had been convened shortly before the Frankfurt one, under the same Roman pontiff, Hadrian, by whom it had been confirmed. Legates of the same Pontiff were present at the Frankfurt council. How could that whole synod have been ignorant of the authority and doctrine of the Nicene Synod? Surely the Pontiff's legates could have instructed them and freed them from any error, if there was one. Rightly, therefore, Suárez, in part 3 of Thomas, q. 15, disp. 54, says: "It is hard for me to believe that the Synod of Frankfurt could have proceeded against the Nicene from an error of fact." VI. The acts of the Eighth Synod are not read in the collections of councils, nor in the historians. Bartholomew Carranza, however, professes to have found them corrupted in many ways. And it is established that everything in it was done through violence and lust, so the Greeks held it neither as the universal Eighth nor as universal simply. Adrian II, the Roman Pontiff, and Basil, who had seized the throne through the parricide of Michael, who had adopted him, lent each other mutual help: the one to feign a primacy, the other to feign the adoration of images. Aimoin, the Gallic monk, describes all this most clearly: "In this synod, which the men who gathered it called the universal eighth synod, they decreed about the adoration of images otherwise than the orthodox teachers had defined before; and some things they established for the favour of the Roman Pontiff, who assented to their wishes about adoring images, and some things against the ancient canons and against their own synod, as anyone who reads that same synod will plainly find." It appears at once from these words that the adoration of images was not approved by pious men and Churches in this age, about the year 830.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Oppono deniq; omnibus illis concilis, concilium Francofurtense, quod certe fuit vere œcumenicum, vtpote Imperatoris & Pontificis in legatorum persona Theophilacti & Stephani autoritate stabilitum. Hoc concilium negat adorandam crucem, & de ea ex sensu Pauli & purioris antiquitatis loquitur, ita vt crucis nomine nō lignum intelligat, sed vniuersum redemptionis humanæ mysterium in cruce impletum: ærumnas etiam, quibus membra Christi assidue iactantur. Quo sensu Paulus se in hac cruce gloriari dicit.
units.tr: Finally, I oppose to all those councils the Council of Frankfurt, which was certainly truly ecumenical, since it was established by the authority of the Emperor and of the Pope, through their legates Theophylact and Stephen. This council denies that the cross is to be adored, and speaks of it in the sense of Paul and of purer antiquity: the cross is not understood as the wood, but as the whole mystery of human redemption accomplished on the cross, and also the afflictions by which the members of Christ are constantly harassed. It is in this sense that Paul says he glories in the cross.

units.la: Argumentum Tertium. Argumentum III. ab vsu & testimoniis veterum.
units.tr: Third Argument. Argument III, from the practice and testimonies of the ancients.

units.la: Iustinus in Apologia 2. signa, inquit, nota, quae apud nos sunt huius rei (crucis) virtute declarant. Tertull. in apolog. c. 16. obiectioni gentilium respondet de adoratione crucis igneae. Idem facit Minutius in Octavio. Ex quo apparet ab ipso Ecclesiae exordio, etiam ante crucis veram inventionem, Christianos solitos habere & venerari crucis imaginem.
units.tr: Justin, in his Second Apology, says: "The signs which are among us, marked with this sign, declare the power of the cross." Tertullian, in the Apology, chapter 16, answers the objection of the Gentiles concerning the adoration of the fiery cross. Minucius does the same in the Octavius. From this it appears that from the very beginning of the Church, even before the true discovery of the cross, Christians were accustomed to have and venerate the image of the cross.

units.la: Resp. I. Patrum autoritas non est regula veritatis, sed sola sacra scriptura, ut quae diuinitus est inspirata, eoque infalliBiliter vera, patres vero hoc testimonium non habent, & saepe errarunt & decepti sunt.
units.tr: Reply I. The authority of the Fathers is not the rule of truth; only Holy Scripture is, since it is divinely inspired and therefore infallibly true. The Fathers, however, do not have this testimony, and they often erred and were deceived.

units.la: II. Negamus veteres patres crucis adorationem probasse. Quoties de cruce magnifica praedicant, non lignum intelligunt, sed totum opus redemptionis Christi in cruce peractum.
units.tr: II. We deny that the ancient Fathers approved the adoration of the cross. Whenever they speak magnificently of the cross, they do not mean the wood, but the whole work of Christ's redemption accomplished on the cross.

units.la: Qua longe a crucis adoratione absint, id ex eorum testimoniis, quae Bellarminus producit, manifestum omnibus euadet.
units.tr: How far they are from the adoration of the cross will become plain to everyone from the testimonies that Bellarmine produces.

units.la: I. Iustinus nullam mentionem facit, vel crucis vel adorationis crucis delatae, aut deferendae. Verba haec sunt: καὶ ὑμῖν σύμβολα τὴν τοῦ σταυροῦ τὴν δύναμιν δηλοῖ. Ethnicos alloquitur, & per signa intelligit signa vexillorum, aliorumq; insignium, quæ debent figuram crucifixionis præ se ferre, & virtutem eius declarare, ita vt passionem & mortem Christi intelligat esse rem illam, cuius δυνάμει signa illa declarent. Quid vero hoc ad adorationem materialis crucis Christi? Nos non negamus virtutem passionis Christi & signa gentilium, quibus μὴ νοῦντες, id est, non intelligentes virtutem eius declararunt. II. Tertullianus etiam nullam facit mentionem crucis adorandæ, vel adoratæ, sed contra crucis adorationem reputat, id quod ex diligenti textus consideratione liquet: in quo 1. falsam Gentilium opinionem de adoratione capitis Asini refutat, ostendens Christianos non esse Asini adoratores. 2. adorationem crucis a Christianis remouet, vt initium textus indicat, quod tale est: Sed & qui crucis nos religiosos putat, id est, qui in ea est opinione, ac si adoraremus crucem, quos propter ea religiosos crucis per ludibrium vocitant, is consecraneus noster erit. III. refutat criminationem eorum, de adoratione solis, ita vt appareat, à crucis adoratione Christianos longe alienissimos fuisse. Nam alii, inquit, plane humanum, & verisimile
units.tr: I. Justin makes no mention either of the cross or of the adoration of the cross as offered or to be offered. His words are: "And the power of the cross declares to you the signs" [καὶ ὑμῖν σύμβολα τὴν τοῦ σταυροῦ τὴν δύναμιν δηλοῖ]. He is addressing the Gentiles, and by "signs" he understands the signs of standards and other insignia, which ought to bear the figure of the crucifixion and declare its power, so that he understands the passion and death of Christ to be the thing whose power those signs declare. But what has this to do with the adoration of the material cross of Christ? We do not deny the power of Christ's passion, nor the signs of the Gentiles, which, "not understanding" [μὴ νοῦντες], that is, not understanding, declared its power. II. Tertullian also makes no mention of a cross to be adored or already adored; on the contrary, he refutes the adoration of the cross, as is clear from a careful consideration of the text. In it, first, he refutes the false opinion of the Gentiles about the adoration of an ass's head, showing that Christians are not worshippers of the ass. Second, he removes the adoration of the cross from the Christians, as the beginning of the text indicates, which runs thus: "But whoever thinks us religious about the cross, that is, is of the opinion that we worship the cross, those who on that account call us religious about the cross as a mockery, he will be one of our own kind." III. He refutes their accusation about the worship of the sun, so that it appears that Christians were very far removed from the adoration of the cross. "For others," he says, "believe quite humanely and plausibly that the sun is our God."

units.la: Hmm milius solem credunt Deum nostrum. Docet igitur adorationem crucis, nec humane nec verisimiliter obiici Christianis. Deinde ostendit, quid vere adorent Christiani. Quod colimus, inquit, Deus unus est. Responditigitur Tertullianus obiectio gentilium de adoratione crucis, sed ita, vt eam neget, ac refutet, soliq; Deo asserat. Christianos quidem appellatos fuisse religiosos crucis fatetur, sed inde non sequitur, agnoscere ipsum Christianos coluisse crucem. Nam statim subiungit etiam ab Ethnicis obiectum fuisse, Christianos solem adorasse.
units.tr: Others believe, more humanely and plausibly, that the sun is our God. He therefore teaches that the adoration of the cross is not laid against Christians either humanly or plausibly. Then he shows what Christians truly worship: "What we worship," he says, "is one God." So Tertullian answers the Gentiles' objection about the adoration of the cross, but he denies it, refutes it, and asserts that worship belongs to God alone. He admits that Christians were called worshippers of the cross as a mockery, but it does not follow that he acknowledges Christians worshipped the cross. For he immediately adds that the heathen also charged Christians with worshipping the sun.

units.la: Alii, inquit, plane humanius & verisimilius credunt, solem Deum nostrum: non tamen agnoscit, Christianos solè adorasse, sed refutat crimè illud, & in Ethnicos reii- cit III. Minutio Felix in Octauio expressè remouet adorationè crucis à Christianis. Obiiciebatur Octauio à Cęcilio pagano, Christianos crucè adorare; Octauius, vt se ab ea alienū ostendat, responde t: Cruces nec colimus, nec optamus, vos plane qui ligneos Deos consecratis cruces ligneas vt Deorū vestrorū partes forsitan adoratis. Non ergo prisci Christiani fuere adoratores crucis; sed contra, si quando Christianis adorationè crucis exprobrarent Ethnici, ci, magnam sibi factam putarunt iniuriam, eamq; à se repulerunt. At, inquies, ex ipsa obiectione gentilium sequitur, crucé à Christianis fuisse honorata. Si enim nō coluissent cruces veteres Christiani, Ethnici nō fuissent illis adorationem crucis obiecturi, Resp. nō sequitur 1. quia obiectū illis est ab Ethnicis falso. 2. Si hinc concludere volūt, eos adorasse cruces, colligat similiter Christianos priscos horrenda admisisse flagitia, quia ea etiam Ethnici illis obiicere.
units.tr: "Others," he says, "believe quite humanely and plausibly that the sun is our God." Yet he does not acknowledge that Christians worshipped the sun; he refutes that charge and throws it back on the Gentiles. III. Minucius Felix, in the Octavius, expressly removes the adoration of the cross from the Christians. Caecilius the pagan objected to Octavius that Christians worship the cross. Octavius, to show that he is alien to it, answers: "We neither worship nor desire crosses; you, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps worship wooden crosses as parts of your gods." Therefore the early Christians were not worshippers of the cross; on the contrary, whenever the Gentiles reproached Christians with the adoration of the cross, they thought they were being greatly wronged and repelled the charge. But, you will say, it follows from the very objection of the Gentiles that the cross was honoured by Christians. For if the ancient Christians had not worshipped the cross, the Gentiles would not have objected the adoration of the cross to them. Reply: it does not follow, first, because the objection was made falsely by the Gentiles; second, if they want to conclude from this that they worshipped crosses, let them likewise conclude that the early Christians committed horrible crimes, since the Gentiles also objected those to them.

units.la: Ad alia testimonia veterū pergamus
units.tr: Let us go on to the other testimonies of the ancients.

units.la: 1. Origen. inquit, l. 6. in epist. ad Rom. dicit crucis figuram ante oculos positā, si attentè consideretur, valere ad depellendā omnē tentationē.
units.tr: 1. Origen, in the sixth book on the Epistle to the Romans, says that the figure of the cross, placed before the eyes and carefully considered, is effective in driving away every temptation.

units.la: Resp. I. Nō de adoratione crucis, sed de eius valore & efficacia loquitur. II. Non de cruce sed de Christo crucifixo loquitur, quē cum Apostolo Gal. 3. perpetuo nobis ante oculos descriptū habere debem°, Perperā ab illa cruce, i.e. Christo crucifixo, ad imaginem crucis deuoluuntur. Hanc Origenis sententiam ipsa inspectio verborum Origenis declarat. Sic loquitur Origen. Certum namq; est, vbi mors Christi circumfertur, non potest regnare peccatum. Est.n.tata vis crucis Christi, vt si ante oculos ponatur & fideliter retineatur in mente, ita vt in ipsam morte Christi intentis tentis
units.tr: Reply: I. He does not speak of the adoration of the cross, but of its worth and efficacy. II. He speaks not of the cross but of Christ crucified, whom, with the Apostle (Gal. 3.), we ought always to have set before our eyes; they wrongly turn from that cross, that is, Christ crucified, to the image of the cross. The very wording of Origen's text shows this opinion of Origen. Thus Origen speaks: "For it is certain that where the death of Christ is brought before the mind, sin cannot reign. For such is the power of the cross of Christ, that if it is set before the eyes and faithfully retained in the mind, so that the eyes of the mind are fixed on the death of Christ itself..."

units.la: [illegible, ~10 letters] ntis oculis mentis inspiciatur nulla cupiscentia [?]t, nulla libido, nulla superare possit invidia.
units.tr: "...are looked upon, no lust, no desire, no envy can overcome."

units.la: Hic quod prius mortem dixerat, statim per regesin vocat crucè, ita vt crux de mor[?]io Christo sit intelligèda. III. Non requirita Christianis, vt crucè adoret, sed ante oculos descripta habeant, qualè descriptione intelligat, statim declarat, [?]um eam mente fideliter retineri iubet.
units.tr: Here, what he had first called death he straightaway calls the cross by a figure of speech, so that the cross is to be understood as the death of Christ. III. He does not require Christians to adore the cross, but to have it set before their eyes; and the manner of this setting before them he immediately explains, when he bids it be faithfully retained in the mind.

units.la: V. Constantin° M. Labarum informam crucis regit, vt patet ex Eusè.l.9.c.9.Inst.& ex l.1.de vitâ Constant. Quia vero Labarum adorebatur, nunquam Constantinus crucè in labaro posuisset, si putasset, esse idololatriâ, venerari crucè. Imo Sozom.l.1.c.4.hist. ribit, ideo Constantinum vertisse Labarum in crucem vt milites assuescerent, crucem venerari.
units.tr: "V. Constantine the Great set up the Labarum in the form of a cross, as is clear from Eusebius, book 9, chapter 9, of the Institutes, and from book 1, On the Life of Constantine. But because the Labarum was adored, Constantine would never have placed the cross on the Labarum, if he had thought it idolatry to venerate the cross. Indeed Sozomen, book 1, chapter 4, of the History, writes that Constantine turned the Labarum into a cross so that the soldiers would become accustomed to venerating the cross."

units.la: Resp. I. Negatur Labarum fuisse religio- adoratum. Ciuile adorationem Labaro milites exhibuerunt, eadè postea ad Labarum crucis signo depictum translata est.
units.tr: Reply I. It is denied that the Labarum was worshipped as a religious object. The soldiers gave civil honour to the Labarum; afterwards that same honour was transferred to the Labarum painted with the sign of the cross.

units.la: II. Neque enim ciuilis honor versus fuit in adorationè religiosam, sed adoratio ciuis ab illo vexillo, ad hoc est deuoluta.
units.tr: II. For civil honour was not turned into religious adoration; rather, the worship owed to that standard was transferred to this one.

units.la: II. Negatur eum in Labaro posuisse crucem.
units.tr: II. It is denied that he placed the cross on the Labarum.

units.la: III. Non crucè sed Christi nomen quandā formā habuit crucis, labaro intexuit, partim vt ostederet se victoriā, salutèq; suam Christo crucifixo acceptam referre: partim vt milites & subditos suos sensim ab idololatria ad religionè Christi crucifixi traduceret. Vnde appa-ret pium Imperatorem non signum crucis, sed Christum crucifixum colui-se, eumq; quem ipse colebat, militibus adorandum proposuisse. III. posito, sed non concessō, crucem à Constantino inditam esse Labaro, cur propterea nō putaret idololatricum esse, crucem venerari? Vtrumq; simul probe consistit.
