Potuit in Labaro signū crucis ponere, & tamen putare, idololatriam esse crucem adorare: quia crucem in eo posuit, non vt crux, sed vt Christus crucifixus adoraretur, eoque duce & adiutore in bello vterentur, idque Sozomenus expresse significat. Non dicit Constantinum ideo vertisse Labarum in formam crucis, vt assuefierent crucem venerari, sed vt subiectos suos pedetentim à patriis ritibus defuefaceret, cumque solum Deum existimarent, quem Imperator : atq; illo duce & adiutore, in bello contra hostes gerendo, uterētur. Qui autem fuerunt isti patrii ritus? Cultus Deorum, & religiosa adoratio Labari, vt docet Tertullianus: Religio Romanorum tota castrensis, signa veneratur, signa iurat, signa omnibus Diis praeponit. IV. Negatur Constantinum Magnum primum Labarum redegisse in formā crucis. Confirmat id Baronius, inquiens: Non Labarum modo, sed & alia fuerunt in exercitu
units.tr: III. The Labarum did not bear the cross but the name of Christ, woven into the banner in a certain form of a cross, partly to show that he attributed his victory and safety to Christ crucified, and partly to lead his soldiers and subjects gradually from idolatry to the religion of Christ crucified. Hence it appears that the pious Emperor worshipped not the sign of the cross but Christ crucified, and proposed to his soldiers for adoration the one whom he himself worshipped. III. Granting, though not conceding, that the cross was placed on the Labarum by Constantine, why should he not think it idolatrous to venerate the cross? Both can well stand together. He could place the sign of the cross on the Labarum and yet think it idolatry to adore the cross, because he put the cross on it not that the cross should be adored, but that Christ crucified should be adored, and that they should use him as leader and helper in war; and Sozomen expressly signifies this. He does not say that Constantine turned the Labarum into the form of a cross so that they would become accustomed to venerate the cross, but so that he might gradually wean his subjects from their ancestral rites, and so that, thinking only of the God whom the Emperor worshipped, they might use him as leader and helper in waging war against the enemy. But what were those ancestral rites? The worship of the gods and the religious adoration of the standard, as Tertullian teaches: "The whole religion of the Romans is military; they venerate standards, they swear by standards, they place standards above all the gods." IV. It is denied that Constantine the Great first reduced the Labarum to the form of a cross. Baronius confirms this, saying: "Not only the Labarum but other standards were in the army..."

units.la: In Apolog. c. 16. citu militaria signa, longe ante Constantini tempora, signum crucis pra se ferentia. Bellarminus idem affirmat ex Tertulliano & Iustino. Sed excipit, labarum quidem ante Constantinum habuisse quandam similitudinem crucis, quia erat velum in ligno suspensum: non tamen proprie crucis figuram habuisse, nisi tempore Constantini. At quae haec est crucis distinctio? Num aliam dices propriam, aliam impropriam? Crucis figura vel propria est vel nulla. Baronius hanc Bellarminianam distinctionem crucis ignorat. Ingenue agnoscit ante tempora Constantini Labarum, & alia signa militaria eandem figuram expressisse. Minutius vero eam euidenter confutat, dicens: Signa ipsa, & cantabra, & vexilla castrorum quid aliud sunt, quam inauratae cruces & ornatae: Tropaea vestra victricia non tantum simplicis crucis faciem, sed & affixi hominis imitantur. Simplicem crucem vocat. Talis certe proprie crucis figura habuit.
units.tr: In Apolog. c. 16. Military standards carried the sign of the cross before them in battle, long before the time of Constantine. Bellarmine affirms the same, citing Tertullian and Justin. But he makes an exception: the labarum before Constantine did have a certain likeness to a cross, since it was a cloth hung on a beam, but it did not have the true figure of a cross until the time of Constantine. But what kind of distinction of the cross is this? Will you say there is one proper cross and another improper? A figure of a cross is either proper or it is not a cross at all. Baronius ignores this Bellarminian distinction of the cross. He candidly admits that before Constantine's time the labarum and other military standards displayed the same figure. Minucius, however, refutes it plainly, saying: What are the standards themselves, and the banners and flags of the camps, but crosses gilded and adorned? Your victorious trophies imitate not only the face of a simple cross but also that of a fastened man. He calls it a simple cross. Such a figure was certainly the true figure of a cross.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus. At Constantinus ut refert Eusebius l.1. de vita Constantini, Roma deiecto Maxentio, in loco celeberrimo erexit crucem, cum his verbis HOC SALVTARE SIGNVM. Et rursus in manu dextera statuae crucem apponi iussit, cum his verbis: HOC VNO VERAE FORTITVDINIS SIGNO VRBEM VESTRAM LIBERAVI. Idem iā decreto cauit, ne deinceps vlli facinorosi ci affigerentur, vt crux non amplius horrori, sed amori, & venerationi omnibus esset, vt Sozom.l.1.c.8.& Aug.ser.18. de verbis Domini. Et è contrario in pecuniis quas omnes ami, crucis figura excudi iussit, vt ibid. Sozo.refert.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses the point. But Constantine, as Eusebius reports in book 1 of the Life of Constantine, after Maxentius had been overthrown at Rome, erected a cross in a most famous place, with these words: BY THIS SALUTARY SIGN. And again he ordered a cross to be placed in the right hand of his statue, with these words: BY THIS ONE SIGN OF TRUE VALOUR I HAVE SAVED YOUR CITY. The same man also provided by decree that from then on no criminals should be fastened to it, so that the cross should no longer be an object of horror but of love and veneration to all, as Sozomen, book 1, ch. 8, and Augustine, sermon 18 on the words of the Lord. And on the contrary, he ordered the figure of the cross to be stamped on the money which all handle, as Sozomen relates in the same place.

units.la: Resp. Non video, quid hęc omnia ad probandam adorationem crucis conferāt. 1. Non erexit crucem, vt adoraretur. Neq; enim ipse eā adorauit, vt neq; ab aliis adorari iussit, sed vt esset testimonium fidei suę in Christum crucifixum, & vt subditos Ethnicos, quibus invisa & exosa fuit religio Christiana, ad Christi crucifixi fidem paulatim adduceret. II. Erexit eam in loco celeberrimo; fateor: at non in templo vel sacrario collocauit. Si Constantinus crucem iudicasset adorandam esse, aut adorari eam voluisset, in loco sacro eam erexisset, ipse coluisset eam, & aliis colendam tradidisset. III Neq; in scriptio adorationis crucis fauet. Posita enim fuit à Constantino, non vt crucem publicè adorarent, victoriam & salutem illi ascriberet, sed 1. vt Christum crucifixum colerent, ipsiq; triumphos suos acceptos ferrent 2. vt ludibria Ethnicorum crucis Christi iniinimicorum refutaret, iisq; hoc vi-ctoriæ tropæum & insigne triumphi op-teret. IV. Nec altera inscriptio stabi-liret adorationem crucis, quippe quæ nō posita eo fine, vt adoratio crucis commendaretur, sed vt veluti tropæum victoriæ hostibus crucem co-meliis afficientibus opponeretur, & eorum ludibriis vindicaretur. 2. Non significatur ista inscriptione, materialis crucis potentia, & virtute vrbem esse liberatam, sed potentia ipsius Christi crucifixi. Nicephorus enim commemorat Constantinum tribus illis crucibus, quas Constantinopoli curari fieri, hæc verba incidenda curasse: ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΝΙΚΑ, IESVS CHRISTVS vincit. Vnde constat, eum non materiali cruci, sed ipsi Christo omnem virtutem & salutem tribuisse. V. Nec decretum illud, ad adorationem crucis confirmandam, vlla specie trahi potest: quia decreto illo non voluit adorationem crucis sancire, sed dignitatem & existimationem mortis CHRISTI in cruce peractæ, ab infidelibus probro datæ CHRISTIANIS, ornare, & extollere. Cum enim infideles tam gentes, quam Iudæi,
units.tr: Reply. I do not see what all this contributes to proving the adoration of the cross. 1. He did not erect the cross so that it would be worshipped. For he did not adore it himself, nor did he order others to adore it; he set it up as a testimony of his faith in Christ crucified, and so that he might gradually bring his Gentile subjects, to whom the Christian religion was hateful and odious, to faith in Christ crucified. 2. He erected it in a most famous place, I grant; but he did not place it in a temple or sanctuary. If Constantine had judged the cross to be worthy of adoration, or had wished it to be adored, he would have erected it in a sacred place, worshipped it himself, and handed it on to others to be worshipped. 3. Nor does the inscription favour the adoration of the cross. It was set up by Constantine not so that people would publicly adore the cross and ascribe victory and salvation to it, but 1. so that they would worship Christ crucified and give him the credit for his triumphs, and 2. so that he might refute the mockery of the Gentiles against the cross of Christ, and render it a trophy of victory and an emblem of triumph. IV. Nor does the other inscription establish the adoration of the cross, since it was not set up for the purpose of commending the adoration of the cross, but so that the cross might be set against the enemies who were heaping insults upon it, as a trophy of victory, and so that it might be vindicated from their mockery. 2. That inscription does not signify that the city was freed by the power and virtue of the material cross, but by the power of Christ crucified himself. For Nicephorus records that Constantine had these words engraved on the three crosses which he had made at Constantinople: ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΝΙΚΑ, Jesus Christ conquers. From this it is clear that he attributed all power and salvation not to the material cross but to Christ himself. V. Nor can that decree be drawn into any appearance of confirming the adoration of the cross, because by that decree he did not wish to sanction the adoration of the cross, but to adorn and exalt the dignity and reputation of the death of Christ suffered on the cross, which had been held up to the Christians as a disgrace by the unbelievers. For since unbelievers, both Gentiles and Jews,

units.la: quam in cruce Christus sustinuit mortem, inhonestam & dedecoris plenam iudicarent; Constantinus, vt eius dignitatem augeret, & amplificaret, legecauit, ne deinceps illi facinorosi crucis affigerentur. Quod igitur in honorem & amorem crucis, id est, mortis Christi statum à Constantino, id perperam ad crucis signum, eiusq; adoratione transfertur. Mutum & nudum crucis signum cum ipso mortis supplicio confundi non debet. 2. Etsi in honorem & memoriam imaginis crucis, id decretum sancitum statuamus: non tamen adoratio imaginis inde conficitur. Erat enim & nomen & signum crucis ludaeis & paganis probrosum. Vtrumque vt honorificum redderet, decretum illud sanxit: adorationis decretum vero nulla fit mentio. VI. In pecuniis etiam iussit excudi figuram crucis, si-teor, sed adoratio crucis nihilominus ignota fuit. Non certe pecuniae fuere adoratae. Quis vnquam pecuniam, vel crucem in pecuniis legitur adorasse? Quis vnquam ad eas se dicitur prouol-uisse, & dixisse, Aue spes vnica? In pecu-niis fuere insculptae cruces, at cur non in templis aut locis sacris positae fuere, siadoadoratione dignas iudicauere ? 3. Causa crucium in pecuniis cusarum non fuit haec, ut adoratio earum commendaretur Christianis, sed ut signa essent professionis fidei Christianae, qui-bus palam ostenderent, se non pudere Christi crucifixi, sed eo potissimum gloriari.
units.tr: judged the death which Christ endured on the cross to be shameful and full of disgrace, Constantine, in order to increase and enlarge its dignity, decreed that criminals should no longer be fastened to the cross. Therefore what was done out of honour and love for the cross, that is, for the death of Christ, is wrongly transferred by others to the sign of the cross and to its adoration. The mute and bare sign of the cross ought not to be confused with the very instrument of execution. 2. Even if we grant that this decree was enacted in honour and memory of the image of the cross, it does not follow from it that the image is to be adored. For both the name and the sign of the cross were a reproach to Jews and pagans. The decree sanctioned this to make both honourable; but no mention is made of any decree of adoration. VI. He also ordered the figure of the cross to be struck on the money, I grant, but the adoration of the cross was nonetheless unknown. Certainly money was not worshipped. Who has ever read that money, or the cross on money, was adored? Who has ever been said to have prostrated himself before them and said, Hail, our only hope? The crosses were engraved on the coins; but why were they not placed in temples or sacred places, if they had judged them worthy of adoration? 3. The reason the crosses were stamped on the money was not that their adoration might be commended to Christians, but that they might be signs of the Christian profession of faith, by which they openly showed that they were not ashamed of Christ crucified, but gloried in him above all.

units.la: VII. Testimonium ex edicto Theodosii.
units.tr: VII. Testimony from the edict of Theodosius.

units.la: Constantini pietatem imitatus Theodosius prohibuit ne crux humi sculperetur vel pingeretur, ne sacrum signum pedibus calcaretur. Ita enim habetur l.1. codicis tit.8. L. Cum nobis. Quod testimonium ex Petro Crinito p. c 9 aduersarii corrupte citant, quasi Theodosius prohibuisset imaginem crucis sculpi vel pingi.
units.tr: Imitating the piety of Constantine, Theodosius forbade that the cross be carved or painted on the ground, lest the sacred sign be trodden underfoot. So it is found in Code 1.8, the law "Cum nobis." Our adversaries cite this testimony corruptly from Petrus Crinitus, book 9, chapter... as though Theodosius had forbidden the image of the cross to be carved or painted.

units.la: Resp. I. Lex haec (quae est Theodosii iunioris filii Arcadii) non ad adorationem & cultum diuinum crucis stabiliendum lata est, sed ad politicum & ciuilem eius honorem afferendum. Neque enim mandatur, ut religiose colatur, sed ne humi sculpatur aut pingatur; idque non religionis, sed scandali causa, quod Ethnici crucis hostes inde poterant arripere, si vidissent crucem, in qua salutem ponerent Christiani, pedibus calcari. Nihil haec lex nostrae sententiae obstat. Neque enim crucem calcariam ignominia affici volumus, sed adorare eam nolumus. II. Falsum est nos cō-ruptè hanc legem ex Petro Crinito citare. Verum edictum Theodosii quod Crinitus integrè citat his verbis: Cum sit nobis cura diligens in omnibus rebus superni numinis religione tueri, signum Salvatoris Christi nemini quidè concedimus colere, lapide, aliave materia fingere, inscalpere, aut pingere, sed quodcunque reperitur, tollatur, gravissima poena eos multâdo, qui contra nostros decretos, & imperio quicquam tentaverint, Hoc est, integrum ac incorruptum decretum Theodosii, quod Crinitus integrè & incorruptè recitat, nos ex eo. Quod si nostram citationem corruptam putat, corrupta erit Crinitii. At Crinitii esse incorruptam sic probo. Quia Crinitus testatur se illud ex libris Augustalibus recitare. Verba eius haec sunt. Sed libitum est verba ex libris Augustalibus referre, quo id tanto melius innotescat. Apparet hinc eum, dum haec scribebat, ante oculos librum habuisse, ex quo integrè edictum descripsit. Quaestio ipsa liberat Crinitum ab omni suspicione corruptionis. Quaestio erat an illa veneratione affici deberent imagines, eoque in templis haberi. Lex sancit, nemo
units.tr: Reply. I. This law (which is of Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius) was not enacted to establish the adoration and divine worship of the cross, but to secure its political and civil honour. For it does not command that the cross be worshipped religiously, but that it not be carved or painted on the ground. This was for the sake of avoiding scandal, not of religion: the heathen enemies of the cross could seize on it, if they saw that the sign in which Christians place their salvation was trodden underfoot. This law does nothing against our view. For we do not want the cross treated with contempt; we are only unwilling to adore it. II. It is false that we cite this law corruptly from Petrus Crinitus. Rather, the edict of Theodosius, which Crinitus cites in full, runs in these words: "Since it is our careful concern to protect the worship of the supreme divinity in all things, we permit no one to worship the sign of the Saviour Christ, to fashion it from stone or other material, to carve or to paint it. Whatever is found, let it be removed, punishing with the gravest penalty those who attempt anything against our decrees and commands." This is the whole and uncorrupted decree of Theodosius, which Crinitus recites entire and uncorrupted, and it is from this that we cite. If he thinks our citation corrupt, then Crinitus's own would be corrupt. But I prove that Crinitus's is uncorrupt, as follows. Crinitus states that he is reporting it from the Augustal books. His words are these: "But it has pleased me to give the words from the Augustal books, so that this may be made known all the better." It appears from this that, while writing, he had the book before his eyes, from which he copied the edict entire. The question itself frees Crinitus from every suspicion of corruption. The question was whether images ought to be honoured with that veneration and therefore kept in temples. The law sanctions that no one... [continued in the next unit]

units.la: {1} de bonis disciplina. nplis, vbi facile adorari possint, habe itur imagines. Hæc si Bellarminum n mouent, probet Crinitum esse au- rē corruptionis. Nos non dubitamus, in lex hæc in codice Iustiniano fue- à papicolis posterioribus deprauata, od & aliis constitutionibus accidisse ētissimi Iureconsulti annotarũt. Nūc uo rerum æstimatori consideranda inquo, an non Bellarminus legem nc corrupte citet ex codice, in quo à fterioribus inserta fuit mentio foli, armorum humi positorum ? Hoc igi- ir edictum Theodosii, imaginum eoq; crucis cultum refutat
units.tr: ...in public places where they can easily be adored, images are kept. If these things trouble Bellarmine, let him prove that Crinitus is corrupt. We do not doubt that this law in the Justinianic code was depraved by later Papists, as the most learned jurists have noted happened also with other constitutions. Now let the judge of such matters consider whether Bellarmine himself does not cite the law corruptly, from a code in which later hands inserted mention only of arms laid on the ground. Therefore this edict of Theodosius refutes the cult of images, and so the cult of the cross.

units.la: 7. Testimonium ex edicto Arcadii
units.tr: 7. Testimony from the edict of Arcadius.

units.la: Theodosium secutus Arcadius filius aurea mo-neta cum signo crucis cudi iussit, teste Prospero,de prædictionib. & promissionibus par. 3 c.34.
units.tr: Following Theodosius, his son Arcadius ordered gold coin to be struck with the sign of the cross, as witnessed by Prosper, On Predictions and Promises, part 3, chapter 34.

units.la: Resp. I. Neq; hoc edictum Arcadii crucis adorationem confirmat. Non enim in vel cum aurea moneta crucem adorari iubet. Quod si adorationem eius hoc edicto voluisset sancire, cur non potius in templis eam collocari, & ab hominibus adorari iussisset?
units.tr: Reply. I. Nor does this edict of Arcadius confirm the adoration of the cross. For it does not order the cross to be adored, either on or with the gold coin. If he had wished to sanction its adoration by this edict, why did he not rather order it to be placed in temples and adored by men?

units.la: II. Iussit cudi monetam auream, cum signo crucis, non vt adorandæ imagi- nis esset argumentum, sed vt esset testimonium fidei & amoris in Christum crucifixum, quod scil. crucem Christi non erubescant, sed ament, & honorét, siquidé signum seu imaginé eius, aureæ monetæ, quà omnes amant, imprimât.
units.tr: II. He ordered gold coin to be struck with the sign of the cross not as an argument for an image to be adored, but as a testimony of faith and love toward Christ crucified: namely, that people should not be ashamed of the cross of Christ but should love and honour it, since they stamp its sign or image on gold coin, which everyone loves.

units.la: VIII. Testimonii ex Tiberii edicto.
units.tr: VIII. Testimony from the edict of Tiberius.

units.la: Tiberius quoq; optimus Imperator Theodosii legé secutus, cum vidisset in palatio humi crucé in marmore incisam, mox erigi iussit dicens: Cruce Domini fronté & pectus munire debemus, & nos eam pedib. terimus: Testis Paulus Diacon. l. 18. rerum Roman. vbi & addit sub illo marmore repertum ingentem thesaurum, amplius centum millium aureorum in remuneratione videlicet pietatis tā religiosi principis.
units.tr: Tiberius also, an excellent emperor, following the law of Theodosius, when he saw a cross cut into marble on the floor of the palace, immediately ordered it raised, saying: "We ought to fortify forehead and breast with the cross of the Lord, and yet we tread it underfoot." Witness Paul the Deacon, book 18 of the Roman history, where he also adds that under that marble was found an immense treasure, more than a hundred thousand gold pieces, as the reward, to be sure, of the piety of so religious a prince.

units.la: Resp. I. Dicitur Tiberius vidisse crucem humi in marmore incisam, & quidem in palatio. Inde sequitur eam non fuisse adorata; quia alias non in palatio, sed in templo ad crucis cultum collocata fuisset. II. Erectio illa crucis, iussu Tiberii facta, non ad adorationis religiosæ sed civilis honoris causa fuit instituta. Nam cum infideles & imperiti offenderentur, quod crux quæ in tanto apud Christianos esset pretio, calcaretur pedibus, voluit Imperator eam hoc edicto ab hac dedecoris specie liberare, & honorem quendam apud istiusmodi modi homines illi conciliare. Quo magis enim Ethnici crucem Christianis exprobrarunt, eò impensius Christiani signum eius honorarunt. Quod si vero adorationem crucis hoc edicto instituere ac stabilire voluisset, non in palatio, sed in loco adorationis, vel in templo eam erigendam curasset, III. Dictū Imperatoris, quo frontem & pectus cruce muniendum pronunciauit, non pertinet ad hanc disputationem de imagine crucis, sed de signo crucis transeunte. Eo igitur lectorem remitto.
units.tr: Reply. I. Tiberius is said to have seen the cross cut into marble on the ground, and indeed in the palace. From this it follows that it was not adored; otherwise it would have been set up not in a palace but in a temple, for the worship of the cross. II. That raising of the cross, done by order of Tiberius, was instituted not for the sake of religious adoration but for civil honour. For since unbelievers and the unlearned were offended that the cross, held in such high esteem among Christians, was trodden underfoot, the emperor wished by this edict to free it from this appearance of disgrace and to win it some honour among such people. For the more the heathen reproached Christians for the cross, the more eagerly Christians honoured its sign. But if he had wished to institute and establish the adoration of the cross by this edict, he would have taken care to have it erected not in the palace but in a place of worship or a temple. III. The emperor's saying, in which he declared that forehead and breast should be fortified with the cross, does not pertain to this discussion of the image of the cross, but to the sign of the cross in passing. I therefore refer the reader to that place.

units.la: IX. Testimonium ex Lactantio.
units.tr: IX. Testimony from Lactantius.

units.la: Constantini tempore scripsit Lactantius carmen de cruce, in quo inter cetera legimus
units.tr: In the time of Constantine, Lactantius wrote a poem on the cross, in which among other things we read

units.la: Flecte genu, lignumque crucis venerabile adora.
units.tr: Bend the knee, and worship the venerable wood of the cross.

units.la: Respon. I. Carmen illud non est Lactantii. Floruit sub Diocletiano, & ad principatum Constantini Imperatoris in senectute peruenit, quo tempore nullae imagines Christi, Apostolorum aut aliorum sanctorum habuerunt, idq; ex ipsius institutionum libro conspicuum est, in quo hanc de imaginibus fert sententiam: Nō est dubium quin religio nulla sit, vbicunque simulachrum est. Nam si religio ex diuinis rebus est; diuini autem nihil est, nisi in caelecælestib.reb.caret ergo religione simulacra, quia nihil potest esse cœleste in eare, quæ sit ex ter- ra.II. Disputatur hic nō de ligno crucis, sed de crucis imagine. III. Quid si lignū crucis poeticè pro Christo cruci affixo accipiatur? Cum enim Ecclesia canit, O crux aue spes vnica, Bellarm. ait, crucè pro ipso Christo crucifixo accipi; cur non etiam, cum Lactantius canit, flecte genu lignumq; crucis, &c. lignum crucis pro Christo crucifixo accipiamus? Aut carmen eius a sententia Ecclesiæ erit alienum.
units.tr: Response 1. That poem is not by Lactantius. He flourished under Diocletian and reached the principate of the emperor Constantine in old age, at which time the Christians had no images of Christ, the Apostles, or other saints. This is clear from his own book of Institutes, in which he gives this judgment on images: There is no doubt that there is no religion wherever there is an image. For if religion comes from divine things, and there is nothing divine except what is in heaven, then images, which are made from earth, lack religion, because nothing heavenly can be in them. II. This does not concern the wood of the cross but the image of the cross. III. What if the wood of the cross is taken poetically for Christ fixed to the cross? For when the Church sings "O Cross, hail, our only hope," Bellarmine says that the cross is taken for Christ crucified himself. Why, then, when Lactantius sings "bend the knee and the wood of the cross," should we not take the wood of the cross for Christ crucified? Otherwise his poem will be foreign to the teaching of the Church.

units.la: X. Ex Athanasio, Athanasius quæst. 16. ad Antiochum reddit causam, cur Christiani faciant, & colant potius imagines crucis, quam lancea vel spongia: quia videlicet, si Ethnicis dicant, nos colere lignum, mox duobus lignis crucis disiunctis figuram crucis destruimus, nec amplius veneramur.
units.tr: X. From Athanasius. In question 16 to Antiochus, Athanasius gives the reason why Christians make and honour images of the cross rather than of the lance or the sponge: namely, that if we tell the heathens that we worship wood, at once we break up the figure of the cross by separating the two pieces of wood, and no longer venerate it.

units.la: Responsio. Testimonium hoc non est genuini Athanasii. Ipse Bellar. testatur in lib. de scriptoribus Eccles. quæstiones ad Antiochum Athanasii esse non posse, quia autor citet Athanasium magnum q. 23. Allegat etiam Theologiam mysticam Dionysii, quæ Athan. seculo ignotæ fuit, Sixtus Senen. l. 4. testatur. Quin & responsio hæc ipsa adeo futilis & inepta est, vt quiuis facile intelligat, ab ingenio veri Athanasii alienam esse, qui de imaginib. longe aliter sensit, ac locutus fuit, Imaginum in ventio, inquit, non de bono, sed de malo exstitit. Sed hæ sunt artes Iesuitarum, qui plerosque errores suos ex scriptis supposititiis confirmare solent.
units.tr: Response. This testimony is not by the genuine Athanasius. Bellarmine himself testifies in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers that the Questions to Antiochus cannot be by Athanasius, since the author cites Athanasius the Great at question 23. He also cites the Mystical Theology of Dionysius, which, as Sixtus of Siena testifies in book 4, was unknown in Athanasius's age. Indeed, this answer is itself so trifling and silly that anyone can easily see it is alien to the mind of the true Athanasius, who thought about images quite differently from what this says: "The invention of images," he says, "arose not from good but from evil." But these are the arts of the Jesuits, who are accustomed to confirm most of their errors from spurious writings.

units.la: II. Ex Christ. Chrysost. in supplicationibus argenteas cruces cum ardentibus facibus præferri iubebat, vt Socrates l. 6. c. 8. & Soz. l. 8. c. 8. testantur. Idem Chrysostomus in libro quod Christus sit Deus, dicit, suo tempore crucis figuram omnibus in locis depingi solitam, in vrbibus, in domibus, in cubiculis, in vasis, in solitudine, in montibus &c.
units.tr: II. From Chrysostom. In processions Chrysostom ordered silver crosses to be carried before the people with burning torches, as Socrates (book 6, ch. 8) and Sozomen (book 8, ch. 8) testify. The same Chrysostom, in his book that Christ is God, says that in his time the figure of the cross was customarily painted everywhere: in cities, in houses, in bedrooms, on vessels, in deserted places, on mountains, and so on.

units.la: Resp. 1. Cupimus tandem proferri testimonium crucis adoratæ. Tale præsens non est, vt quo iubentur quidem præferri cruces argenteæ, sed non adorari. II. Cruces illæ argenteæ fuerunt lychnuchi qui cruciū nomine appellatur, quod tres faces in figuram crucis, iis essent impositæ. Adhibebantur autem nocturnis conuentibus, & hymnodiis, ad significandam Trinitatem, quâ Arriani tunc oppugnabant. III. Ritus hic superstitioné potius quâ pietate redolet, ideo ineptum est ad probandam adorationem crucis, exemplum Alter locus æquè est infirmus. I. refert quidem Chryfoft. fuo tempore crucis figuram omnibus in locis depingi folitam, in vrbibus, domibus &c. non vero dicit in templis politam & adorari folitam fuiffe. Nihil igitur hic locus ad crucis adorationem confert. II. Confuetudo hæc ad teftificationem fidei Chriftianæ, non ad crucis adorationem inftituta fuit voluerunt eam effe profeffionis fidei Chriftianæ, non vero adorandæ crucis documentum.
units.tr: Response. 1. We wish at last to be shown a testimony to an adored cross. This passage is not one, since it says that silver crosses were ordered to be carried, but not that they were adored. II. Those silver crosses were lampstands which were called by the name of "cross," because three torches were placed on them in the figure of a cross. They were used at nocturnal assemblies and hymn-singings, to signify the Trinity, which the Arians were then attacking. III. This rite smells of superstition rather than piety, and so it is unsuitable as an example for proving the adoration of the cross. The other passage is equally weak. I. Chrysostom does indeed report that in his time the figure of the cross was customarily painted in all places, in cities, houses and so on, but he does not say that it was placed in temples and customarily adored. Therefore this passage contributes nothing to the adoration of the cross. II. This custom was instituted as a testimony of the Christian faith, not for the adoration of the cross. They wanted it to be a mark of the profession of the Christian faith, not a teaching to adore the cross.

units.la: XII. Teftimonium eft Auguftini. Auguftinus in Ioh. tract. 36. & in Pf. 36. Qui tantum, inquit, honorem tribuit fupplicio suo, quid feruat fidelibus suis?
units.tr: XII. Testimony of Augustine. Augustine, on John, tractate 36, and on Psalm 36: "He who pays such honour to his punishment, what does he keep for his faithful?"

units.la: Refpon. I. Abipfo fupplicio ad fupplicii inftrumentum non valet confequentia. Bellarminus de fupplicii inftrumento, id eft, cruce materiali Augufti num interpretatur; cum ipfum fupplicium, id eft, mortem Chrifti euidenter intelligat. II. Pofito fed non concefło Auguftinū de vera cruce Chrifti loqui quid hoc adrem? 5. Quæftio hic non eft de vera Chrifti cruce, fed de eius imagine. III. Negamus honorem hūc de adorationis honore intelligendum effe fatis confpicuum eft ex fequeti antithefi, dignitadignitatem, præstantiam, & efficaciam crucis id est, motis Christi commendari.
units.tr: Response. I. The consequence does not hold from the punishment itself to the instrument of punishment. Bellarmine interprets the words of the material cross, that is, the instrument of punishment, whereas Augustine clearly means the punishment itself, that is, the death of Christ. II. Even granting that Augustine speaks of the true cross of Christ, what has this to do with the matter? The question here is not about the true cross of Christ but about its image. III. We deny that this honour is to be understood as the honour of adoration. This is clear enough from the following antithesis, where the dignity, excellence and efficacy of the cross, that is, of the death of Christ, are commended.

units.la: XIII. Testimonium est Cyrilli. Cyrillus l. 6. in Iulianum respondet Iuliano reprehendenti Christianos quod lignum crucis adorarent, eiusque figuram ante domos suas (ut ait) pingerent.
units.tr: XIII. Testimony of Cyril. Cyril, in book 6 against Julian, answers Julian, who reproaches the Christians because they adored the wood of the cross and painted its image, as he says, before their houses.

units.la: Respon. Agnoscimus Cyrillum respondere Iuliano obiicienti adorationem crucis sed responsione Cyrilli debuisset adiicere. Ille crimen obiectum negat, hisce verbis. Quiistasicse habere suspicatur & impudens ac nefarium os contra eminentem Saluatoris nostri gloriam dilatat, à maligno aduersario, Dei Spiritu, à me minimè denegabitur esse arreptus. Et paulo post. Absq; labore demonstrabimus eiusmodi sermones à malis cogitationibus profectos, extremam sapere imperitiam. En quam diligenter criminationem istâ à Christianis removeat.
units.tr: Response. We acknowledge that Cyril answers Julian's objection concerning the adoration of the cross, but Cyril ought to have added his reply in full. He denies the charge, in these words: Whoever suspects that these things are in him, and opens an impudent and wicked mouth against the eminent glory of our Saviour, will by me by no means be denied to have been seized by the malign adversary. And a little after: We will demonstrate without any effort that such words proceed from evil thoughts and show extreme ignorance. See how carefully he removes this accusation from the Christians.

units.la: II. Ipsa obiectio Iuliani refutat criminationem. Obiectio fuit, quod lignum crucis adorarent, imagines illius infronte & ante domos pingentes. At templorum aut sacrariorum nullam inducit mentionem. Non ergo publicè adoratio crucis recepta fuit. Priuatam etiam in vsu nō fuisse ipse Cyrillus in responsione ad obiectionem &tionem satis indicat, vbi spirituales requirit adoratores. Vnus pro omnibus mortuus est & excitatus, vt à mortis laqueis humani redimeret genus &c. & Spirituales faceret adoratores. Ergo Christiani eius aetatis nō ligni, non signi, sed solius Christi Salvatoris ac Dn. nostri adoratores fuere. III, paulo post Cyril. expresse vsum imaginum crucis describit, ita vt recordationis & memoriae causa vsurpatas dicat à Christian: non vero adorationis. Haec omnia, inquit, recordari nos facit salutare ligni &c. Et paulo post. Vis ergo vir strenue vt ligni quod nos ad recordationem omnis virtutis in ducit, abiiciamus & relinquamus pueris & mulierculis proponamus. Huius vsus pietate non laudat; quia alienū erat à scopo, sed simpliciter describit & commemorat; adorationis vsum vero, qui obiicitur, à Christianis longissime reiicit.
units.tr: II. Julian's own objection refutes the charge. The objection was that they adored the wood of the cross, painting its image on their foreheads and before their houses. But he makes no mention of temples or sanctuaries. Therefore the adoration of the cross was not publicly received. That it was not practised privately either, Cyril himself sufficiently indicates in his answer to the objection, where he speaks of making spiritual worshippers: One died for all and was raised, to redeem the human race from the snares of death... and to make spiritual worshippers. Therefore the Christians of that age were worshippers not of wood, nor of a sign, but of Christ the Saviour and Lord alone. III. A little after, Cyril expressly describes the use of images of the cross, saying that the Christians employed them for the sake of recollection and memory, not of adoration. All these things, he says, the saving wood makes us remember... And a little after: Do you then, brave man, wish us to cast away and abandon the wood which leads us to the recollection of every virtue, and to leave it to boys and little women? He does not praise this use for its piety, since it was foreign to his purpose; he simply describes and mentions it. But the use of adoration, which is objected, he utterly rejects from the Christians.

units.la: XIV. Testimonium est Ruffini.
units.tr: XIV. The testimony of Rufinus.

units.la: Rufinus l. 2. c. 29. hist. testatur, apud AEgyptum, cum ad fidem converterentur AEgyti, vbi fuisse depictas cruces, loco thoracis Serapidis quem Ethnici venerabantur.
units.tr: Rufinus, Hist. bk. 2, ch. 29, testifies that in Egypt, when the Egyptians were converted to the faith, crosses were painted in the place of the breastplate of Serapis, which the heathens worshipped.

units.la: Resp. I. Cruces illae loco thoracis Serapidis depictae testimonia fuere Christianae religionis, non vero obiecta adorationis; quod vel ex eo apparet, quia non in templis aut sacrariis, quæ loca sunt adorationis, depictæ fuere. II. Si quæ veneratio est illis tributa, ea non fuit pontificia, id est, diuina & religiosa, qua se ad eos prouoluerunt, iisque latriam exhibuerunt, sed extrema reuerentia, qua amorem & studium erga Christi religionem declarare voluere.
units.tr: Reply. I. Those crosses painted in place of the breastplate of Serapis were tokens of the Christian religion, not objects of worship. This is clear even from the fact that they were not painted in temples or shrines, which are the places of worship. II. If any veneration was paid to them, it was not Papist veneration, that is, the divine and religious kind, by which men prostrate themselves before them and render them latria. It was the lowest reverence, by which they wished to show their love for and zeal toward the religion of Christ.

units.la: XV. Test. Beda l. 1. Hist. Angl. c. 25. scri-bit Aug. à B. Greg. missum ad Anglorum conuersione crucem argenteam & imaginem Christi in tabula depictam pro vexillo prætulisse, Ipse etiā Greg. l. 7 Ep. 5. de veneratione crucis loquitur
units.tr: XV. Testimony: Bede, Hist. Angl. bk. 1, ch. 25, writes that Augustine, sent by Blessed Gregory to convert the English, carried before them as a banner a silver cross and an image of Christ painted on a panel. Gregory himself also speaks of the veneration of the cross in Ep. 7, bk. 5.

units.la: Resp. I. Esto, Aug. prætulisse crucem argenteam, num vero eam adorauit aut Anglis adorandam proposuit? Prius scribit Beda, de posteriore nullam prosus mentionem facit. II. Vexilli loco crucem prætulit, idq; non adorationis causa, sed vt signum esset externæ professionis quo ostenderet, se non erubescere crucem Christi, id est, Christum crucifixū, sed in eo gloriari. 2. vt Ethnicos illos sensim ad fidem Christi crucifixi peer traheret. Quod vero Greg. de veneratione crucis loquitur, nō est mirū. 1. fuit magnus patronus superstitionum quibus Ecclesiam Christi & veram religionē mirum in modū onerauit & coaminauit. II. Loquitur non de veneneratione crucis religiosa, sed deshumana & ciuili; qua eam non ad adorationem, sed ad recordationé & instructionem voluit adhiberi. Nam Gregor. M. docuit imagines nullo modo adorandas, & fuit vsus hoc dicto contra adorationem imaginum; Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & illum solum coles, vt videre est libro 7. Epistola 54. & 109. & libro 9. epistola 9.
units.tr: Reply. I. Granted that Augustine carried a silver cross. But did he worship it, or did he propose that the English should worship it? Bede writes the former; he says nothing whatever about the latter. II. He carried the cross instead of a banner, and not for the sake of worship but as a sign of outward profession, by which he showed that he was not ashamed of the cross of Christ, that is, of Christ crucified, but gloried in it; and secondly, so that he might gradually draw those heathens to the faith of Christ crucified. As for Gregory speaking of the veneration of the cross, this is no surprise. First, he was a great champion of the superstitions with which he wonderfully burdened and defiled the Church of Christ and the true religion. Second, he speaks not of religious veneration of the cross but of a human and civil veneration, by which he wished it to be used not for worship but for remembrance and instruction. For Gregory the Great taught that images are in no way to be worshipped, and this saying has been used against the worship of images: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve, as may be seen in Bk. 7, Ep. 54 and 109, and Bk. 9, Ep. 9.

units.la: XVI. Testimonium. Leo Serm: 8. de passione Domini.
units.tr: XVI. Testimony: Leo, Sermon 8, on the Passion of the Lord.

units.la: Pulchra specie inquit, triumphi sui tropheum & invictissima patientiae signum salutis adorandum populis omnibus inferebat.
units.tr: In a fair form, he says, he presented to all peoples the trophy of his triumph and the most invincible sign of patience, the sign of salvation to be worshipped.

units.la: Respon. Leo loquitur de passione & morte Christi, non imagine crucis. Mors enim Christi est signum salutis adorandum omnibus populis. Quod de cruce, id est, de passione & morte Domini recte dicitur, id perperam ad crucis imaginem seu signum transfertur; atque hoc est solenne Iesuitis, vt quaecunq; Patres de vera cruce, id est passione & morte Domini praedicant, ea muto & nudo eius signo seu imagini tribuant.
units.tr: Reply. Leo is speaking of the passion and death of Christ, not of an image of the cross. For the death of Christ is the sign of salvation to be worshipped by all peoples. What is rightly said of the cross, that is, of the passion and death of the Lord, is wrongly transferred to the image or sign of the cross. And this is the usual practice of the Jesuits: whatever the Fathers preach of the true cross, that is, the passion and death of the Lord, they attribute to its mute and bare sign or image.

units.la: XVII. Et vltimum Testimonium.
units.tr: XVII. And the last testimony.

units.la: Sedulius in carmine paschali: Pax crucis ipse fuit, violentaque robora membris Illustrans propriis, poenam vestiuit honore Supplicium mq; dedit signum magis esse salutis, Ipseq; sanctificans in se tormenta beauit Neue quis ignoret speciem crucis esse colendam.
units.tr: Sedulius, in the Paschal poem: He himself was the peace of the cross; lighting up with his own limbs the violent strength of the nails, he clothed the punishment with honour, and gave the instrument of torture as the greater sign of salvation; sanctifying the torments in himself, he blessed them, lest anyone should fail to know that the form of the cross is to be worshipped.

units.la: Quæ Dominum portauit ouans.
units.tr: Who, exulting, bore the Lord.

units.la: Respon. I. Testimonium hoc est poetica Rhetoricatio, nō propheticum vel Apostolicum oraculum. Rhetoricationes poeticæ mouent tantum & delectant, nō probant. At sola oracula prophetica & Apostolica vim probādi doctrinam salutis obtinēt. II. Sedulius hic non imaginem crucis, sed crucis supplicium celebrat. Licet penultimā carmen Neue quis ignoret &c. ad ipsum signū seu imaginem crucis videatur pertinere: tamen re penitus expensa, non ipsa imago crucis, sed crucis species, id est, supplicii Christi, intelligitur, ita vt cruci fixionis & mortis Dominicæ dignitatem ac virtutem commendet.
units.tr: Reply. I. This testimony is a poetic flourish, not a prophetic or apostolic oracle. Poetic flourishes move and delight but do not prove; only the prophetic and apostolic oracles have the power to prove the doctrine of salvation. II. Sedulius here celebrates not the image of the cross but the suffering of the cross. Although the penultimate line, lest anyone should fail to know etc., seems to refer to the sign or image of the cross itself, yet on a full consideration, what is understood is not the image of the cross but the form of the cross, that is, the punishment of Christ, so that he commends the dignity and power of the Lord's crucifixion and death.

units.la: Argumentum Quartum.
units.tr: The Fourth Argument.

units.la: Argumentum quartum ab apparitione & miraculis crucis. Primo apparuit Constantino o lucidislucidissima crux in aere, cum illis verbis, ἐν τούτῳ νίκα, id est, in hoc Vince, ut referri Eusebius l. 1. de vita Constantini, ubi etiam id addit se id accepisse ab ipso Constantino iurante rem in se habere. Neq; apparuit ipsi crux in somno, ut Sozomenus lib. 1. c. 3. & Paulus Diaconus lib. 11. rerum Romanarum dicunt, sed vigilanti & iter facienti, cum toto exercitu, ut Eusebius dicit.
units.tr: The fourth argument is drawn from the appearance and miracles of the cross. First, a most bright cross appeared to Constantine in the air, with the words ἐν τούτῳ νίκα [en toutō nika], that is, In this, conquer, as Eusebius reports in Bk. 1 of the Life of Constantine, where he also adds that he had this from Constantine himself, who swore that the matter was so. Nor did the cross appear to him in a dream, as Sozomen (bk. 1, ch. 3) and Paul the Deacon (bk. 11 of the Roman History) say, but to him awake and on the march with the whole army, as Eusebius says.

units.la: Resp. I. Veritas doctrinæ saluificæ non ex apparitionibus & miraculis, sed ex verbi Dei regula dignoscitur. Quare officium Bellarmini erat prius verbi divini oracula, crucis adorationem asserentia, proferre, antequam apparitiones & miracula iactaret. II. Non video quomodo apparitiones miraculosæ crucis inferant eius adorationem, cum illæ si veræ sint, extraordinariæ censeantur, ac proinde ordinariam & perpetuam Ecclesiæ doctrinam confirmare nequeant.
units.tr: Reply. I. The truth of saving doctrine is recognised not by appearances and miracles but by the rule of the Word of God. Therefore it was Bellarmine's duty first to produce the oracles of the divine Word asserting the worship of the cross, before boasting of appearances and miracles. II. I do not see how miraculous appearances of the cross imply its worship, since, if they are true, they are regarded as extraordinary, and therefore cannot confirm the ordinary and perpetual doctrine of the Church.

units.la: 3. Nego Constantino apparuisse signum crucis. Apparuit illi signum seu character nominis Christi, qualis in multis antiquis numismatis Constantini & aliorum Imperatorum cernitur. Conflatum enim fuit ex duabus primis literis χ & ρ Christi nomen exprimentibus, littera Græcanica ρ decusata & scisa per medium
units.tr: 3. I deny that the sign of the cross appeared to Constantine. There appeared to him the sign or monogram of the name of Christ, such as is seen on many ancient coins of Constantine and other emperors. For it was formed from the first two letters, χ and ρ, which express the name of Christ, the Greek letter ρ being crossed and split through the middle by the χ. And from this he always used to wear on his helmet not the sign of the cross but those two letters by which the name of Christ was indicated. But because they presented the form of a cross, Zonaras therefore called it in Constantine τὸ τρόπαιον σημεῖον [to tropaion sēmeion], "the trophy sign", and Eusebius said it σταυροῦ σημάτι παρίστημι [staurou sēmati paristēmi], "presented the sign of the cross".

units.la: Eusebius de vita Constantini l. 1. c. 28, 29. lium χ atque hinc semper in galea sua consuevit gestare non crucis signum, sed duas illas literas, quib. nomen Christi referebatur: quia vero crucis formam præsentabant, ideo τὸ τρόπαιον σημεῖον Zo-naras in Constantino, Eusebius σταυροῦ σημάτι παρίστημι dixit, 2. Quid tum si ipsum signum crucis dicatur apparuisse? Nū proterea crux adoranda? Non sane egitur vel Constantinū aut militū quēquā crucem adorasse. Visum hoc, Constant. Maxent. aggressuro exhibitū fuit, ut de victoria confirmaretur, non ut de eius adoratione informaretur. Et cū singulare fuerit & extraordinarium visum, quomodo ordinarium Ecclesiæ dogma ex eo confici aut probari queat? Apparitiones miraculosæ & extraordinariæ non inferunt eius rei quæ apparet, adorationem, sed institutio & mandatum Dei.
units.tr: Eusebius, Life of Constantine, bk. 1, ch. 28, 29. II. What then if the sign of the cross itself is said to have appeared? Is the cross therefore to be worshipped? Certainly it is not established that either Constantine or any of his soldiers worshipped the cross. This vision was shown to Constantine as he was about to engage Maxentius, so that he might be confirmed about the victory, not so that he might be instructed about its worship. And since it was seen as singular and extraordinary, how can an ordinary dogma of the Church be made or proved from it? Miraculous and extraordinary appearances do not imply the worship of the thing that appears, but the institution and command of God.

units.la: Instat. At non frustra dictum est Constantino In hoc signo vince, ut apparet ex victoriis Constantini. Nam libro 2. de vita Constantini scribit Eusebius in præliis iussisse Constantin. semper deferri labarum cruce insignitum ad ea parte agminis quæ magis laborabat: & quoties labarum accessisset, mox etiam victoriam sequi solitam. Addit ibidem, eū qui cum metu hostium irruentium reliquisset labarum continuo necl-tum esse,qui autem illud de manu abiicientis suscepit,nunquam feriri potuisse, etsi innumer-rabilia prope tela in illum coniecta fuissent: omnia enim (mirabile dictu) in hasta cruci infigebantur.
units.tr: Objection. But the words spoken to Constantine, In this sign, conquer, were not in vain, as is clear from the victories of Constantine. For in Bk. 2 of the Life of Constantine, Eusebius writes that in battles Constantine ordered the labarum, marked with the cross, always to be carried to the part of the line that was struggling most, and that whenever the labarum came there, victory usually followed at once. He adds in the same place that whoever, through fear of the attacking enemy, left the labarum was immediately killed, but whoever took it up from the hand of the one dropping it could never be struck, even though almost countless weapons were thrown at him: for all (wonderful to tell) were fixed in the spear beneath the cross.

units.la: Respon. I. Inscriptionem corrupte recitat. Ea non facit mentionem signi; sed tali circa signū nominis Christi cō stabat scriptura ἐν τούτῳ νίκα, In hoc, scil. Christo, non signo, vince, perinde ac si Deus nomen Christi illi ostendens dixisset, Nullum aliud nomen sub cælo datum, esse, per quod oportear ipsū seruari. II. Esto. Inscriptio de signo intelligatur, prout etiam Episcopi sunt interpretati, qui inde Constantinum mysterium Christi crucifixi docuerunt. Num vero ideo dictū est,in hoc signo vince,vt religiose adoraretur? Absit. Nam cum Constantinus cum Maxentio congres surus ambigenti & anxio esset animo, Deus illum hoc extraordinario viso voluit cōfirmare,ne de victoria dubitaret, non vero adoratione eius instituere aut probare. III. Victoriæ illæ, quas memorat nō sunt partæ vi labari aut crucis labarp intextæ, sed virtute & prudentia Constantini, Christo duce & adiutore vten-
units.tr: Reply. I. He quotes the inscription corruptly. It does not mention a sign; rather, the inscription around the sign of the name of Christ read ἐν τούτῳ νίκα [en toutō nika], "In this", that is, in Christ, not in the sign, "conquer", just as if God, showing him the name of Christ, had said: There is no other name under heaven given by which we must be saved. II. Granted, let the inscription be understood of the sign, as the bishops also interpreted it, who from it taught Constantine the mystery of the crucified Christ. But was it therefore said, "In this sign, conquer", so that it might be religiously worshipped? Far from it. For when Constantine was about to meet Maxentius and was wavering and anxious in mind, God wished to confirm him by this extraordinary vision, so that he should not doubt about the victory, not to institute or prove its worship. III. Those victories which he mentions were not won by the power of the labarum or of the cross woven into it, but by the valour and prudence of Constantine, with Christ as leader and helper.

units.la: Eus. de vit. Const. c. 20. ṽrentis. Cū n. videret Constantin. parte exercitus sui nutare & laborare, statim ad signo Imperatorio seu labaro, quod fortissimis quibusve cinctu erat militib., ad eam partem aduolabat, & suppetias laborantib ferebat: Vnde postmodum victoria secuta, quae tunc non parta fuit virtute labari sed militum sub labaro Christo duce fortiter pugnantiu. Quare hinc nō virtus & adoratio labari, sed virtus & prudentia Constantini fortis & boni Imper. partes obeuntis, colligeda est. IIII. Æque inepte altera historia de occiso eo, qui labarū reliquit & confer- matione eius, qui illud suscepit, ad virtu- tē & adorationem labari, detorquetur.
units.tr: Eus. de vit. Const. c. 20. ...fighting. For when Constantine saw part of his army wavering and in difficulty, he at once flew to that part with the imperial sign, or labarum, which was surrounded by the bravest soldiers, and brought aid to those in trouble. Whence victory followed afterwards, which was then won not by the power of the labarum but by the soldiers fighting bravely under the labarum, with Christ as their leader. Therefore from this one should draw conclusions not about the power and worship of the labarum, but about the courage and prudence of Constantine, a brave and good emperor doing his duty. IIII. Equally foolish is the other story about the man who was killed after abandoning the labarum, and the strengthening of the man who took it up, which is twisted into an argument for the power and worship of the labarum.

units.la: Qui enim abiecit labarū, is cum in acie stare & hostib. irruituris resistere debuis set, acie præ metu reliquit. Fugiens igi- tur & extra acie consistens, non potuit non ab hostib. præsentibus occidi. Con- tra qui suscepit labarū, is in acie pugnā- tiū ac defendentiū militū perstitit, eoq; virtute militum quib. labarū cinctū fuit, est defensus. Quare non labari aut cru- cis virtuti conseruatio huius tribuenda est, sed militum pro labaro strenuē pu- gnantiū fortitudini. Vnde rursū a quo- uis modo sit rationis compos, intelligitur, nihil hic à cruce præstitū, quod eius sapiat adorationem, præsertim cum nó legatur àquoquam horum militum esse adoratam. Neq; occilus, neq; conscrua tus, honore adorationis eâ dignatus est.
units.tr: For he who threw down the labarum, when he ought to have stood in the battle line and resisted the enemy about to charge, left the line out of fear. Fleeing and standing outside the line, he could not help being killed by the enemy who were present. On the other hand, he who took up the labarum remained in the battle line, among soldiers fighting and defending, and so was defended by the courage of the soldiers around whom the labarum was wrapped. Therefore the preservation of this man is to be credited not to the power of the labarum or of the cross, but to the bravery of the soldiers who fought valiantly for the labarum. Hence again, to anyone who has the use of reason, it is clear that nothing here was accomplished by the cross that smacks of its adoration, especially since it is nowhere read that any of these soldiers, either the slain or the preserved, was honoured with the worship of adoration.

units.la: Secundo, apparuit crux lucidissima supra montem Oliuetum tmpore Constantini Imperatoris, de qua apparatione exstat Epistola Cyrilli Hierosolymitani ad Constantium.
units.tr: Secondly, a most bright cross appeared above the Mount of Olives in the time of the Emperor Constantine, and concerning this appearance there exists a letter of Cyril of Jerusalem to Constantius.

units.la: Resp. I. Apparitiones licet miraculosæ, non sunt idoneæ crucis adoratæ, vel adorandæ probationes. Nullæ apparitiones, sed solum mandatum seu institutio Dei nobis persuadebit crucis adorationé. Petimus vt tandé ex sacra scriptura, nobis Dei institutionē proferāt. Aequa est petitio. Quid moratur? Si nequeunt, desinant nobis obtrudere crucis adorationem. II. Historia huius apparitionis dubia est & incerta, sicut & epistola, ex qua petitur spuria est, & suppositicia, vt supra docuimus.
units.tr: Response I. Apparitions, however miraculous, are not suitable proofs of a cross that is or should be adored. No apparitions, but only the command or institution of God, will persuade us to adore the cross. We ask that at last they bring forward from holy Scripture a divine institution for us. The request is fair. Why do they delay? If they cannot, let them stop forcing the adoration of the cross upon us. II. The history of this appearance is doubtful and uncertain, and the letter from which it is drawn is spurious and fabricated, as we have shown above.

units.la: Tertio apparuit tempore Iuliani Apostatæ, qui eā persequebatur, vt narrat Greg. Nazian. orat. 1. in Iul. Nam cum Iulian. inspiceret exta pecudum, aruspicii gratia, inuenit crucem coronatam; & quidā aruspices periti, vt refert Paulus Diacon. in eius vita, dicebantq; significari, religionem Christianam, quæ crucē venerebatur fore ore perpetuam, nec posse vincià Iuliano. Adu-latores autem eius dicebant significari angusti-as & quasi carceres crucis. Sed eventus priorem sententiam veram ostendit. Eodem tempore cum udai Iuliani iussu, exstruere vellet templu Hie ofol.in dedecus crucifixi, apparuit rursus in aere irculus ingens, lucidus, crucem splendidissi-mam ambiens: & praterea fere in vestib. omni um hominum eius loci apparuerunt cruces quasi summo artificio elaborata, vt scribit Nazianz. in orat. 2. in Iulianum.
units.tr: Thirdly, it appeared in the time of Julian the Apostate, who persecuted it, as Gregory Nazianzen relates in his first oration against Julian. For when Julian was inspecting the entrails of beasts for the sake of augury, he found a crown-shaped cross; and some skilled soothsayers, as Paul the Deacon reports in his life, said that this signified that the Christian religion, which venerated the cross, would be perpetual and could not be conquered by Julian. His flatterers, however, said it signified the narrowness and, as it were, the prisons of the cross. But the outcome showed the former opinion to be true. At the same time, when the Jews, by Julian's command, wished to build a temple at Jerusalem to the dishonour of the crucified one, a great bright circle appeared in the air, surrounding a most splendid cross; and moreover crosses, as if wrought with the greatest skill, appeared on the garments of almost all the men of that place, as Nazianzen writes in his second oration against Julian.

units.la: Resp.I Si hac apparitione significata fuit perpetuitas religionis Christianæ; Ergo ad crucis adorationem significandam & stabiliendam non est facta.II.
units.tr: Response I. If the perpetuity of the Christian religion was signified by this appearance, then it was not made to signify or establish the adoration of the cross. II.

units.la: Dicimus nos hanc apparitionem crucis esse subministratam, non ut crux adoraretur; sed partim, ut religio Christiana aduersus blasphemias & tyrannidem Iuliani Apostatæ & aliorum Ethnicorum Christi hostium vindicaretur: partim, ut infirmi in fide Christi confirmaretur.
units.tr: We say that this appearance of the cross was granted, not so that the cross should be adored, but partly so that the Christian religion might be vindicated against the blasphemies and tyranny of Julian the Apostate and of other heathen enemies of Christ, and partly so that the weak in the faith of Christ might be strengthened.

units.la: 3. Extraordinaria & singularis fuit hæc apparitio crucis istis temporib. ob causas dictas concessa. Quare ordinaria, vniuersalis, & perpetua fidei doctrina ex ea exstrui & probari non potest: aut sin de aliquid elici debet, Christi crucifixi adoratio inde deducenda est; quod quidem iustis-sima fima fit ratione. Nam in cuius gratiam & honorem apparuit crux, ei exhibenda est adoratio: Apparuit crux in gratiam & honorem Christi, in cuius dedecus templum Iulianus exstrui iusserat Hierosolymis. Ergo Christo crucifixo adoratio exhibenda.
units.tr: 3. This appearance of the cross at that time, granted for the reasons stated, was extraordinary and singular. Therefore an ordinary, universal and perpetual doctrine of faith cannot be built or proved from it; or if something must be drawn from it, the adoration of the crucified Christ should be deduced from it, and that is surely the most just reasoning. For to whose favour and honour the cross appeared, to him adoration is to be offered. The cross appeared for the favour and honour of Christ, to whose dishonour Julian had ordered a temple built at Jerusalem. Therefore adoration is to be offered to the crucified Christ.

units.la: Quarto apparuit crux in aere tempore Arcadii cum Imperator bellum suscIperet pro fide contra Persas Christianorum persecutores, in quo bello diuinitus adiutus fuit. Testatur hoc Prosper in lib. de promiss. diuin. p. 3. c. 34.
units.tr: Fourthly, a cross appeared in the air in the time of Arcadius, when the emperor undertook war for the faith against the Persians, persecutors of the Christians, in which war he was divinely aided. Prosper testifies to this in the third book of On the Divine Promises, chapter 34.

units.la: Respon. I. Haec etiam apparitio extraordinaria & miraculosa fuit, ideoq; ordinariam crucis adorationem non confirmat. Verbum Dei ordinaria regula est probandi adorationē crucis. Sine hoc apparitiones eiusmodi miraculosae & extraordinariae nil proficiunt. II. Quod Deus apparitiones crucis aetate Arcadii exhibuit, non fecit in gratia crucis, sed Christianae religionis; non ut crux adoraretur, sed ut Christianorum anxii animi de victoria contra Persas, Christianorum persecutores, confirmaretur, atq; ita religio Christiana ab impietate Ethnicorum vindicaretur. Quare non crucis adoratio sed Christianae religionis veritas hic sancitur, ut quā Deus hisce apparitionibus... ritionibus tanquam diuinis documen-tis confirmare, & aduersus Ethnicos vindicare voluit.
units.tr: Response I. This appearance too was extraordinary and miraculous, and therefore does not confirm the ordinary adoration of the cross. The Word of God is the ordinary rule for proving the adoration of the cross. Without this, such miraculous and extraordinary apparitions accomplish nothing. II. That God showed the apparitions of the cross in the age of Arcadius was done not for the sake of the cross but for the sake of the Christian religion; not so that the cross should be adored, but so that the anxious minds of the Christians about victory over the Persians, persecutors of the Christians, might be strengthened, and so that the Christian religion might be vindicated from the impiety of the heathens. Therefore it is not the adoration of the cross but the truth of the Christian religion that is established here, since God wished to confirm it by these apparitions as divine proofs, and to vindicate it against the heathens.

units.la: Quinto, Apparuerunt cruces in vestibus hominum tempore Leonis Iconomachi, cum hæretici contra imagines sacras insanirent, ut testatur Paulus Diaconus in vita Leonis Iconomachi. Ad hoc genus referri potest, apparatio crucis in Anglia in arbore anno 1556. de qua vide de Alanum Copum.
units.tr: Fifthly, crosses appeared on the garments of men in the time of Leo the Iconoclast, when heretics raged against the sacred images, as Paul the Deacon testifies in the life of Leo the Iconoclast. To this kind may be referred the appearance of a cross on a tree in England in the year 1556, concerning which see Alan Copus.

units.la: Resp. I. Non fuere veræ apparitiones crucium, sed vel hominum superstitiosorum figmenta, vel portenta fallacium spirituum, quæ Diabolus ad superstitionem & Idololatriam confirmandam & propagandā exhibuit. Testimonia Pauli Diaconi & Alani Copi nullam hac quidem in causa merentur fidem. Ille fuit homo superstitiosus, temerarius miraculorum, quæ à superstitiosis & imperitis sui temporis hominibus audiuerat, præco: hic vero idololatra & Antichristi mancipium. II. licet statuamus veras fuisse apparitiones; nihil tamen hinc causæ Bellarminianæ accedet. Apparitiones crucium non sunt idonea adorandæ crucis argumenta. Vtres quæ miraculosæ apparent, adorentur; mandatum & institutio de rei apparetis adoratione, praecedat, aut coniuncta sit, necesse est. At nullum Dei mandatum vel institutio praecessit aut coniuncta fuit, cum hisce crucium apparitionibus.
units.tr: Response I. These were not true apparitions of crosses, but either the fabrications of superstitious men or the portents of deceiving spirits, which the Devil displayed to confirm and propagate superstition and idolatry. The testimonies of Paul the Deacon and of Alan Copus deserve no faith in this matter. The former was a superstitious man, a rash herald of miracles which he had heard from superstitious and ignorant men of his time; the latter was an idolater and a tool of Antichrist. II. Even if we grant that the apparitions were true, nothing will accrue from this to the Bellarminian cause. Apparitions of crosses are not suitable arguments for the adoration of the cross. Whatever miraculous things appear, if they are to be adored, a command and institution concerning the adoration of the thing appearing must either precede or accompany it. But no command or institution of God either preceded or accompanied these apparitions of crosses.

units.la: Argumentum Quintum.
units.tr: Fifth Argument.

units.la: Argumentum V. ductum est a miraculis. Praeter has apparitiones, ait, miracula sine numero per crucis figuram effecta referri possent. Infigne est illud Hilarionis quod refert B. Hieronymus factum apud Epidaurum. Nam cum mare egrederetur terminos suos, & periculum esset, ne civitatem obrueret, Hilarion in litore tres cruces pinxit; mare autem cum eo pervenisset, coepit intumescere, & in magnam altitudinem instar muri cuiusdam excreuit sursum versus, quasi fremens & indignans, quod progredi ulterius prohiberetur, tandem crucis virtuti cedens, fluctus suos in seipsum retorsit. Multa quoque miracula facta narrat Beda l. 3. c. 2. hist. Anglic. per ligneam crucem ab Oswaldo rege sancto erectam, ac illud omnium primum, quod ipse cum paucis, contra innumerabiles hostes pugnavit & vicit.
units.tr: The fifth argument is drawn from miracles. Besides these apparitions, it says, countless miracles wrought through the figure of the cross could be cited. That story of Hilarion is remarkable, which Blessed Jerome relates as having happened at Epidaurus. For when the sea was going beyond its bounds and there was danger that it would overwhelm the city, Hilarion painted three crosses on the shore. The sea, having reached that point, began to swell and rose up to a great height like a kind of wall, as if roaring and indignant that it was being forbidden to advance further; at last, yielding to the power of the cross, it turned its waves back upon itself. Bede also, in book 3, chapter 2 of the Ecclesiastical History of the English, relates many miracles wrought through a wooden cross erected by King Oswald the Saint; and the first of all, that he himself with a few men fought against innumerable enemies and conquered.

units.la: Resp. I. Miracula illa quae sine numero per crucis figuram effecta commemoranmorantur, pleraq; vel sunt falsa, & a superstitiosis Monachis, ad superstitiones suas stabiliendas, & autoritatem suam tuendam, conficta: vel sunt praestigiae & illusiones Diabolicae.
units.tr: Reply I. Those miracles which are countless and are said to have been wrought through the figure of the cross are for the most part either false, invented by superstitious monks to establish their superstitions and defend their own authority, or else are diabolical deceptions and illusions.

units.la: II. Non de veritate doctrinę ex miraculis, sed contra de miraculis ex veritate doctrinae iudicari debet. Nam Deuteron. decimotertio, vetat Moses credi miraculis, si falsae doctrinae fidem adstruant. Et Matthaei 24. praemonemur Pseudoprophetas edituros miracula cauere, & Paulus Apostolus, 2. Thessal. 2. Antichristum cum signis & miraculis venturum, praedicit. Postulamus igitur, ut primo probent adorationem crucis verbo Dei sancitam esse, & tunc miraculis ipsorum fidem adhibebimus.
units.tr: II. The truth of a doctrine must be judged not from miracles, but conversely the miracles must be judged from the truth of the doctrine. For in Deut. 13 Moses forbids us to believe miracles if they support faith in a false doctrine. And in Matt. 24 we are warned beforehand to beware of the miracles that false prophets will perform, and the Apostle Paul in 2 Thess. 2 foretells that Antichrist will come with signs and miracles. We therefore demand that they first prove that the adoration of the cross has been sanctioned by the Word of God, and then we will give credit to their miracles.

units.la: III. Etsi proba & vera sint miracula quae narrantur: non tamen crucem efficiunt adorabilem; quia non crucis, sed Dei virtute & operatione edita sunt, idque ad Christi doctrinam confirmandam, & ab hostium blasphemiis vindicandam. Ad Dei igitur, non crucis adorationem, illos excitarunt, & nos excitare debent. Docent Iesuitae, qui eo tempore eiusmodi miramiraculis adduđti fuere, vtad cruces se- se peruoluerent, easq; adorarent; Deum,non lignum vel signum adorarunt.
units.tr: III. Even if the miracles that are related are genuine and true, they do not make the cross worthy of adoration, because they were performed not by the power and operation of the cross but of God, and that to confirm the doctrine of Christ and to vindicate it against the blasphemies of its enemies. They therefore roused men to the adoration of God, not of the cross, and they ought to rouse us to the same. The Jesuits, who in that age were moved by such miracles to throw themselves down before crosses and adore them, adored God, not the wood or the sign.

units.la: IV. Per ossa Elisæi cadauer reuixit, per Petri vmbram, Pauli sudaria, curati sunt ægroti; non tamen adoratio fuit à quoquam ossibus, sudariis, vel vmbrę Petri tributa; cur si per crucem Deus aliquando extra ordinem miracula exhibuit propterea adoratione merebitur? Hinc quantum miraculum Hilarionis valeat in hac causa facile est colligere. Si verû est miraculum, non virtute crucis est effectum, sed Dei gratia & operatione. Virtus miraculi non in ossibus Elisæi, non in vmbra Petri aut sudariis Pauli, sed in Deo residebat. Ita hic non propria crucis erat vis miraculi, nec à cruce miraculum fuit subministratum, sed Dei erat, & à Deo per fidei orationem impetratum, ideoque non ad crucis sed ad Dei adorationem hinc duci impelliue debemus: idq; eo magis, quod Hieronymus, qui hoc miraculum commemorat, nullam tamen faciat mentionem crucis adoratæ, nec propterea adorandam esse doceat. Miracula Bedæ pleraq; parum obtinent veritatis: deinde crux Osualdi in loco|prælii contra CodiCoClluallum erecta fuit, sed non adorata, neq; in templo in adorationem collocata. Deniq; in prælii loco collocata fuit, non vt cruci, sed Christo crucifixo acceptam referrent victoriam, ideoq; non crucis, sed Christi adoratio hinc stabilitur.
units.tr: IV. Through the bones of Elisha a corpse came back to life; through Peter's shadow and Paul's handkerchiefs the sick were healed; yet no one paid adoration to Elisha's bones, or to Peter's shadow, or to Paul's handkerchiefs. Why then, if God has at some time worked miracles through the cross beyond the ordinary course, should it therefore deserve adoration? From this it is easy to gather how much the miracle of Hilarion counts for in this question. If it is a true miracle, it was not effected by the power of the cross but by the grace and operation of God. The power of the miracle did not reside in Elisha's bones, nor in Peter's shadow or Paul's handkerchiefs, but in God. So here the power of the miracle was not proper to the cross, nor was the miracle supplied by the cross; it belonged to God and was obtained from God by the prayer of faith. Therefore we are not to be driven or impelled from this to the adoration of the cross but of God; and this all the more because Jerome, who records this miracle, makes no mention at all of an adored cross, nor teaches that it is to be adored on that account. Most of Bede's miracles have little claim to truth. Moreover, Oswald's cross was set up at the place of battle against Cadwallon, but was not adored, nor was it placed in a temple for adoration. Lastly, it was placed at the site of the battle not so that they might ascribe the victory to the cross, but to Christ crucified; and therefore it is not the adoration of the cross but the adoration of Christ that is established by this. ## The Sixth Argument.

units.la: Argumentum Sextum.

Argumentum VI. à ratione. Signarerum sanctarum sanctia & venerabilia sunt, vt supra ostendimus. Certe quolibet crux sancta est & venerabilis, quia gerit imaginem Christi crucifixi, id est, Christi in ipso opere redemptionis occupati quo nihil sanctius cogitari potest.
units.tr: The sixth argument, from reason. The signs of holy things are holy and venerable, as we have shown above. Surely every cross is holy and venerable, because it bears the image of Christ crucified, that is, of Christ engaged in the very work of redemption, than which nothing holier can be conceived.

units.la: Resp. 1 Signa rerum sanctarum sunt venerabilia scil. veneratione humana, & ciuili, non religiosa, hoc est, honorifice tractanda, non adoranda. Sic aquam Baptismi tanquam signum sacrum veneramur & honoramus, sed non adoramus. II. Negatur minor. Signa enim rerum sacrarum ea sola sunt, quæ à Deo sanctificata sunt, & instituta ad rerum sacrarum significationem. At crux non est signum eiusmodi, quod Deus invsum sacrum ad significandum scil. Christum instituit. Quod si aliquam obtinet significationem, eam ex mera hominum imaginatione & superstitione accepit. pit. III. Negatur & illud, quamlibet crucem gerere imaginem Christi crucifixi. Crux quaelibet proprie gerit imaginem crucis, non eius qui cruci affigitur. Quod si per crucem quamlibet intelligat imaginem Christi crucifixi cruci suffixam; in promptu est responsio, cruces caruisse imaginib. Christi crucifixi per annos à Christo 400. & publice demum eiusmodi imagines inualuisse, anno 710. vt constat ex synodo Trullana. Cuius ergo ante haec tempora imaginem quaelibet crux gessit, num quaelibet crux tunc sancta fuit & venerabilis? 2. Etsi gerat imaginem Christi non tamen propterea ius adorationis accepit; quia imaginem illam, non ex Dei, qui solus res sacras dicere & facere potest, sed hominum superstitiosorum institutione, gerit.
units.tr: Reply 1. The signs of holy things are venerable, namely with a human and civil veneration, not a religious one; that is, they are to be handled with honour, not adored. Thus we venerate and honour the water of Baptism as a sacred sign, but we do not adore it. II. The minor premise is denied. For the signs of holy things are only those which have been sanctified by God and instituted to signify holy things. But the cross is not a sign of this kind, since God did not institute it as a sacred sign to signify Christ. If it has any signification at all, it has received that from mere human imagination and superstition. III. It is also denied that every cross bears the image of Christ crucified. Any cross properly bears the image of a cross, not of the one who is fastened to it. But if by "any cross" he means a cross with the image of Christ crucified fixed upon it, the answer is ready: for four hundred years after Christ crosses were without images of Christ crucified, and such images only came into public use in the year 710, as is clear from the Council in Trullo. Did any cross, then, bear such an image before those times, and was every cross then holy and venerable? 2. Even if it bears the image of Christ, it does not on that account receive a right to adoration; because it bears that image not by the institution of God, who alone can declare and make holy things, but by the institution of superstitious men.

units.la: CAPVT IV. In quo Caput 29. Bellarmini de signo crucis examinatur & castigatur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. In which chapter 29 of Bellarmine, on the sign of the cross, is examined and corrected.

units.la: Argumentum Primum.
units.tr: First Argument.

units.la: ARgumentum I, ex figuris Veteris Testamenti. Signum crucis, quod in fronte vel aere pingitur, vel supra quascunque res digito exprimitur, sacrum esse & venerabile.
units.tr: Argument I, from the figures of the Old Testament: the sign of the cross, whether it is painted on the forehead or in the air, or traced with a finger over any object, is holy and venerable.

units.la: {a} Cap. 82. Le,ostendi potest ex figuris Veteris Testamenti. Primo sanguis agni in postibus domorum, de quo Exod. 12. nihil aliud significabat nisi signū crucis in frontibus Christianorum, Augustino teste in lib. de cathechizandis rudibus cap. 20.
units.tr: {a} Cap. 82. It can be shown from the figures of the Old Testament. First, the blood of the lamb on the doorposts of the houses, spoken of in Exod. 12, signified nothing other than the sign of the cross on the foreheads of Christians, as Augustine testifies in the book On Catechizing the Uninstructed, chapter 20.

units.la: Resp. Nos negamus signum, prout eo nunc temporis papalis vtitur Ecclesia, sacrum esse & venerabile, imò idololatricum & superstitiousum esse, affirmamus. Non diffiteor, veteres Christianos solitos fuisse frontem suam cruce consignare religiosæ professionis causa, vt ostenderent, non pudere se Christi crucifixi, quem Iudæi & Gentes contumeliis proscindebant, sed sacrum ab ipsis & venerabile habitum fuisse, & haberi debere, id negamus.
units.tr: Reply: We deny that the sign, as the Roman Church now uses it, is holy and venerable; we affirm rather that it is idolatrous and superstitious. I do not deny that the early Christians were accustomed to mark their foreheads with the cross as a sign of their religious profession, to show that they were not ashamed of Christ crucified, whom the Jews and the Gentiles mocked with insults. But I deny that it was held, or ought to be held, to be holy and venerable in itself.

units.la: Quod ad argumentum attinet. 1. Ex allegoricis interpretationibus dogma fidei constitui ac probari non debet. Sunt enim ambiguæ & incertæ, quæ hominum solummodo nituntur iudicio, non verbi Diuini autoritate. Bellarminus ipse docet ex solo literali sensu peti debere efficacia argumenta, quia is sensus qui ex verbis immediatè colligitur, sensus sit Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: As to the argument. 1. Doctrine of faith ought not to be established and proved from allegorical interpretations. Such interpretations are uncertain and ambiguous, resting only on human judgement and not on the authority of the divine Word. Bellarmine himself teaches that effective arguments must be drawn from the literal sense alone, because the sense gathered immediately from the words is the sense of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Confirmat idem Thomas, inquiens: Omnes sensus fundantur super vnum, scilicet scilicet literalem, ex quo solo trahi potest argumentum, non autem ex his, quae secundum allegoriam dicuntur. III. Quae haec est consequentia: Figuris veteris Testam. adumbratū fuit signū crucis.
