Ergo est sacrum & venerabile: sacrū & venerabile illud tantū est, quod Deus instituit, & sacrū & venerabile esse voluit. Figurarum Veteris Testamenti adumbratio non est causa, vt res adumbrata sacra sit, & venerabilis, sed Dei voluntas & institutio. IV. Negatur sanguinem agni in postibus domorū significasse, signum crucis in frontibus Christianorum: Quis sanguini hūc indidit vsum significationis? Non Deus. Vana igitur & nudo hominum instituto fundata est significatio. Veram eius significationem Deus in scriptura nobis aperit, 1.Pet.1.2.1. Ioh.1.7. Ex quibus locis apparet, sanguinem illum non significasse crucis signum, sed sanguinem Iesu Christi, nos liberantem ab exitio. Nam vt agnus Paschalis significabat Christum, teste Paulo, 1.Cor.5.7. ita sanguis eiusdem agni sanguine Christi, qui pro multis effunditur in remissionem peccatorum, significabat. V. Detur significationem illam à Bellarmino notatam, esse veram, & à Deo institu-tam, tám, non tamen causa esse poterit diuinæ & religiosæ venerationis: sacrum forte & venerabile signum esse queat, sed non religiose venerabile. Potest res esse sacra & venerabilis, non tamen religiose venerabilis, id est, talis, quæ diuino cultu debeat affici, vt dies paschatis dicitur sancta & venerabilis propter significationem, & quia erat dedicata cultui diuino Exod.12. Item vestes Sacerdotales sanctæ & venerabiles fuere; scripturæ etiam sacræ sunt, & venerabiles, non tamen diuinam & religiosam venerationem, quæ solius Dei propria est, illis exhibemus. VI. Audax imo falsa affirmatio, quæ dicit Augustinum tradere, sanguinem Ægyptiorum postibus aspersum nihil aliud significare, quam signum crucis, quod omnibus palam erit, si eius verba recitauero. Sic ergo Augustinus. Apertius autem Christi passio in illo populo figurata est, cum iussi sunt omnem occidere, & manducare, & de sanguine eius, postes signare & hoc celebrare omni anno, & appellare pascha Domini. Manifestissime quippe prophetia de Domino Iesu Christo dicit; quia tanquam ouis ad immolandum ductus est. Cuius (scilicet Christi) passionis & crucis signo in fronte hodie tanquam poste signandus es, omnes Christiani signantur. Declarat his verbis aperte, sanguine agni fuisse typu sanguinis Christi, & non signi crucis: passionis vero & crucis Christi signum esse, quo Christiani in fronte signabatur. 2. Licet detur, tradere Augustinum significatione sanguinis adspersi ad postes, eamque ad signum crucis in fronte signandum accommodare: non tamen ita tradit eam, ut omnes alias significationes excludat, quasi nihil aliud velit illo sanguine significare, quam signum crucis. Coniungit enim passionem Christi cum signo crucis, ita, ut primum statuat adumbrari passionem Christi, & deinde per allusionem allegoricam ad crucis signationem in fronte transferri. Quare Bellarminus temere ea diuellit, quae Augustinus coniungit. 3. Plane tacet Augustinus de veneratione seu adoratione signi crucis: solummodo de eius signatione, quae in Baptismi administratione fiebat, disserit. Ut vero Sacramentum Baptismi non est religiose venerabile: sic nec signum crucis in Baptismo vsurpatum.
units.tr: Thomas, the same author, confirms this when he says: All senses are founded on one, namely the literal, from which alone an argument can be drawn, and not from those things which are said according to allegory. III. What is the consequence here? The sign of the cross was foreshadowed by the figures of the Old Testament; therefore it is holy and venerable. But that alone is holy and venerable which God instituted and willed to be holy and venerable. The foreshadowing by the figures of the Old Testament is not the cause of the foreshadowed thing being holy and venerable; the cause is the will and institution of God. IV. We deny that the blood of the lamb on the doorposts signified the sign of the cross on the foreheads of Christians. Who gave this blood the use of signifying? Not God. Therefore the signification is empty and rests on the bare institution of men. God opens to us its true meaning in Scripture: 1 Pet. 1.2; 1 John 1.7. From these passages it appears that that blood did not signify the sign of the cross, but the blood of Jesus Christ, which frees us from destruction. For as the Paschal lamb signified Christ, as Paul testifies, 1 Cor. 5.7, so the blood of that same lamb signified the blood of Christ, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. V. Grant that the signification noted by Bellarmine is true and instituted by God; yet it cannot be the cause of divine and religious veneration. The sign may perhaps be holy and venerable, but not religiously venerable. A thing may be holy and venerable without being religiously venerable, that is, such that it must be honoured with divine worship. Thus the day of the Passover is called holy and venerable because of its signification, and because it was dedicated to divine worship, Exod. 12. Likewise the priestly garments were holy and venerable; the sacred Scriptures too are holy and venerable; yet we do not give them that divine and religious veneration which belongs to God alone. VI. The claim that Augustine teaches that the blood of the Egyptians sprinkled on the doorposts signified nothing other than the sign of the cross is a bold and false assertion. This will be plain to all if I recite his words. Thus Augustine: More plainly, however, the passion of Christ was foreshadowed in that people, when they were commanded to kill everyone, and to eat, and to mark the doorposts with its blood, and to celebrate this every year, and to call it the Passover of the Lord. For the prophecy speaks most manifestly of the Lord Jesus Christ, since he was led like a sheep to be slaughtered. Today every Christian is marked with the sign of this passion and cross, on the forehead, as the doorpost is marked. In these words he clearly declares that the blood of the lamb was a type of the blood of Christ, and not of the sign of the cross; but that the sign of the passion and cross of Christ is what Christians were marked with on the forehead. 2. Even if it be granted that Augustine teaches the signification of the blood sprinkled on the doorposts, and applies it to the marking of the forehead with the sign of the cross, he does not so teach it as to exclude all other significations, as though he wished that blood to signify nothing but the sign of the cross. For he joins the passion of Christ to the sign of the cross, so that he first states that the passion of Christ was foreshadowed, and then that by an allegorical allusion it is transferred to the marking of the forehead with the cross. Therefore Bellarmine rashly tears apart what Augustine joins together. 3. Augustine is plainly silent about the veneration or adoration of the sign of the cross; he speaks only of its marking, which was done in the administration of Baptism. But just as the sacrament of Baptism is not religiously venerable, so neither is the sign of the cross used in Baptism.

units.la: II. Illud Thau, quod Ezechiel scap. 9. iubetur describi in frontibus gementium, apertissime signum crucis, quod in fronte potissimum pingi[illegible, ~10 letters]ingimus, indicabat, teste Cypriano in lib. adversus Demetrianum & Hieronymo in commentario Ezechielis. His adde illud Apocalyp. 4. Habentes nomen eius, & nomen Patris eius in frontibus suis, id est, signum crucis. Item illud Apocalyp. 7. Nolite nocere terræ, & mari, neque arboribus, quoad usque signemus servos Dei nostri in frontibus eorum. Hoc enim signum esse signum crucis, docent Oecumenius, Beda, Anselmus & Rupertus in hunc locum.
units.tr: II. That Thau, which Ezekiel in chapter 9 is commanded to have marked on the foreheads of those who groan, indicated most plainly the sign of the cross, which we usually paint on the forehead, as Cyprian testifies in his book against Demetrianus and Jerome in his commentary on Ezekiel. To these add Revelation 4: "Having his name and the name of his Father in their foreheads," that is, the sign of the cross. Likewise Revelation 7: "Hurt not the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, till we have sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads." For that this sign is the sign of the cross, Oecumenius, Bede, Anselm and Rupert teach on this passage.

units.la: Respond. 1. negatur illud Thau denotare signum crucis. Loquitur quidem de signo seu nota, qua signati ab exitio liberentur, sed non loquitur de signo crucis. Ex ipso textu hebraico negatio nostra confirmatur; vtpote in quo non est solitaria litera ת sed integra dictio Thau, quæ idem valet, quod signum; sicut Iobi 31. v. 35. Ecce Thau, signum meum, Omnipotens exaudiuit me; atque huic expositioni suffragantur Rabbi Abraham, Rabbi Leui, Rabbi Dauid Kinchi in libro radicum. Septuaginta etiam verterunt σημεῖον. Non valet consequentia à genere ad speciem affirmatiue. Est signum: Ergo signum crucis, aut probent oportet, dictionem Thau, notare signum crucis.
units.tr: I answer, first, that it is denied that the word Thau denotes the sign of the cross. It is true that it speaks of a sign or mark by which those who are marked are freed from destruction, but it does not speak of the sign of the cross. Our denial is confirmed from the Hebrew text itself, in which there is not the solitary letter ת but the whole word Thau, which means the same as "sign," as in Job 31:35: "Behold my Thau, the Almighty has heard me." This interpretation is supported by Rabbi Abraham, Rabbi Levi and Rabbi David Kimchi in his book of roots. The Septuagint also translated it as σημεῖον [sēmeion, a sign]. The inference from genus to species is not valid when affirmed. It is a sign; therefore it is the sign of the cross: they must prove that the word Thau denotes the sign of the cross.

units.la: II. Esto, sumatur sola hebraica litera Π quid ista commune habet cum signo crucis. Græca quidem litera τ & latina T crucis formam repræsentant, sed Ezechiel non locutus est vel græcè vel latinè, sed hebraicè. III. Signû illud quo iubentur consignari fideles in frontibus, ne cum impiis pereant, nō est de corporali & visibili aliquo signo in frontibus eorum descripto, intelligendum; sed de spirituali & inuisibili, cura scil. speciali, qua Deus suos ad salutem protegit; quia signatio illa, cuius ibi meminit Ezechiel, non est corporalis, & corporaliter perac-ta, sed spiritualis & spiritualiter in visione gesta. Non putandum est, corporaliter tunc circuiisse Christum, & signum visibile frontibus impressisse, sed spiritualis fuit descriptio signi in frontibus fidelium qua significabatur, electos esse sub Dei cura & protectione. Signum ergo, quo signantur, non indicabat signum crucis, sed Dei custodiam; neq; imprimetur illud frontibus corporum, sed cordium, id est, conscientiis, ita ut conscientia esset tabula seu frons, cui inscribebatur, id est, obsignabatur, & imprimebatur arrha salutis & electionis per Spiritum sanctum. Hoc signo qui sunt insigniti,
units.tr: II. Granted, let us take the single Hebrew letter ת alone. What does it have in common with the sign of the cross? The Greek letter tau and the Latin T do indeed represent the form of a cross, but Ezekiel did not speak in Greek or in Latin, but in Hebrew. III. That sign with which the faithful are commanded to be marked on their foreheads, so that they do not perish with the wicked, is not to be understood as some bodily and visible sign described on their foreheads, but as a spiritual and invisible one, namely the special care by which God protects his own unto salvation; for that marking which Ezekiel mentions there is not bodily, nor performed bodily, but spiritual and enacted spiritually in a vision. We should not think that Christ then went around bodily and stamped a visible sign on the foreheads, but the description of the sign on the foreheads of the faithful was spiritual, signifying that the elect are under God's care and protection. The sign with which they are marked therefore did not indicate the sign of the cross, but God's keeping; nor was it imprinted on the foreheads of bodies, but on hearts, that is, on consciences, so that the conscience was the tablet or forehead on which it was inscribed, that is, sealed, and the pledge of salvation and election was impressed through the Holy Spirit. Those who are marked with this sign

units.la: ab xab æterno exitio sunt immunes. IV. Mandatum hoc de consignandis fidelibus fuit extraordinarium & singulare, spectans ad Iudaeos fideles istius temporis. Hinc ordinaria crucis venheratio ab vniuersis Christianis praestanda nequit probari. V. Cedo. Iubentur obsignari signo crucis, num propterea sacrum fiet & venerabile signū? At non iubetur esse sacrum & venerabile. Vt res aliqua sit & habeatur sacra & venerabilis, requiritur institutio Dei. At instituit Deus signum illud, vt esset nota & tessera, qua fideles consignentur, & ab impiis discernantur, ne cum illis pereant, non vero vt sacrum esset, & venerabile. Neque enim Iudaei Hierosolymitani ad signum illud in frontibus descriptum semet prouoluerunt, talique hymno illud venerati sunt. Aue crux, spes unica, &c.
units.tr: are immune from eternal destruction. IV. This command to seal the faithful was extraordinary and singular, and it applied to the faithful Jews of that time. Hence the ordinary veneration of the cross cannot be proved to be owed by all Christians. V. Grant it. They are commanded to be marked with the sign of the cross, but does this make the sign holy and venerable? It is not commanded to be holy and venerable. For a thing to be and be regarded as holy and venerable, God's institution is required. God instituted that sign so that it would be a mark and token by which the faithful are sealed and distinguished from the impious, lest they perish with them, not so that it would be holy and venerable. Indeed, the Jews of Jerusalem did not prostrate themselves before that sign drawn on their foreheads, nor did they venerate it with such a hymn: Hail, O Cross, our only hope, etc.

units.la: Instat Iesuita ex Cypriano, sed more Iesuitico, falsum illi affingit. Non enim meminit signi crucis externi, quod corporaliter in frontibus esset descriptum, sed signum spirituale intelligit, quo Electi in frontibus cordium signantur ad salutem, nempe sanguinem Christi, quem dicit figura-tum tum esse sanguine agni paschalis, quo postes domorum, in quibus Israelitæ erant, aspersi fuerunt in Ægypto. Verbatim hæc sunt. Quid ad passionem & sanguinem Christi pertineat hoc signum, & ille salvus ac incolumis reseruetur, quisquis in hoc signo inuenitur, Dei testimonio comprobatur, dicentis. Et erit sanguis in signo voces super domos, in quibus vos eritis, & videbo sanguinem, & protegam vos, & non erit in vobis plaga diminutionis cum percutiam terram Ægypti. Quod ante occisio agno procedit in Imagine impletur in Christo, secuta postmodum veritate. Vt illic percussa Ægypto Iudaicus populus euadere non nisi sanguine & signo agni potuit; ita cum vastari cœperit mundus & percuti, quisquis in sanguine & signo Christi inuentus fuerit, solus euadet. Duo docet Cyprianus, quod nam sit illud signum seruans fideles. Non signum crucis sed sanguis Christi. II. quæ illius signi figura fuerit, videlicet occisus agnus paschalis qui in imagine præcessit, vt sequeretur veritas.
units.tr: The Jesuit presses the point from Cyprian, but in the Jesuit manner he attributes a falsehood to him. For Cyprian does not mention an external sign of the cross, physically marked on the forehead, but understands a spiritual sign by which the elect are marked on the foreheads of their hearts for salvation, namely the blood of Christ, which he says was foreshadowed by the blood of the paschal lamb, with which the doorposts of the houses in which the Israelites were had been sprinkled in Egypt. His words are these: What this sign has to do with the passion and blood of Christ, and how whoever is found under this sign is kept safe and sound, is confirmed by the testimony of God, who says: "And the blood shall be a sign upon the houses in which you are, and I will see the blood and protect you, and there shall be no plague of destruction on you when I smite the land of Egypt." What went before in the image, the slaughter of the lamb, is fulfilled in Christ, the truth following afterwards. Just as, when Egypt was smitten, the Jewish people could escape only by the blood and sign of the lamb, so when the world begins to be laid waste and struck, whoever is found in the blood and sign of Christ alone will escape. Cyprian teaches two things about what that sign is which keeps the faithful safe: first, that it is not the sign of the cross but the blood of Christ; second, what the figure of that sign was, namely the slain paschal lamb, which went before in the image so that the truth might follow.

units.la: Instat ex Hieronymo sed frustra.
units.tr: He presses it from Jerome, but in vain.

units.la: Nam nihil certi affirmat Hieronymus, sed diuersas affert sententias, ex quibus quam ipse vt veram amplectatur, diiudiiudicari nequit. II. Etiamsi Hieronymus approbaret sententiam illam de Hebraicarum literarum mutatione post captiuitatem babylonicam, num propterea vera esset? Nos autoritas Hieronymi nihil mouet, quia nullus documentis hanc sententiam probat. Verba Hieronymi haec sunt. Vt ad nostra veniamus, quibus vsque ho-die vtuntur Samaritani. Extrema Thau, litera similitudinem habet crucis, qua in Christianorum frontibus pingitur, & frequenti manus inscriptione signatur.
units.tr: For Jerome affirms nothing certain, but brings forward various opinions, and it cannot be determined from them which of these he himself embraces as true. II. Even if Jerome approved that opinion about the alteration of the Hebrew letters after the Babylonian captivity, would it therefore be true? The authority of Jerome moves us not at all, since he proves this opinion by no evidence. Jerome's words are these: To come to our own times: the Samaritans use this script even today. The final Thau has the likeness of a cross, which is painted on the foreheads of Christians and is often marked by the hand as a sign.

units.la: Non est verisimilis haec sententia. Hausit eam ex Origene, qui dixit Thau, Samaritanum simile esse cruci aut Thau latino vel graeco. Huius fidem secutus est Hieronymus; sed male. Quis enim credat Ezram, Haggaeum, Zachariam, Malachiam, & caeteros pios, qui post captiuitatem vixerunt, literas a Deo ipso acceptas abiecisse, & cum humanis imo gentilibus commutasse? Origenes ex cuius fide haec scribit Hieronymus, non ipse vidit Alphabetum Samaritanorum, sed aliena fide id commemorabat. Vt verba eius, aperte indicant. III. Si maxime verum esset,
units.tr: This opinion is not plausible. Jerome drew it from Origen, who said that the Samaritan Thau, or the Latin or Greek Thau, is like a cross. Jerome followed his belief, but wrongly. For who would believe that Ezra, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, and the other godly men who lived after the captivity, cast aside letters received from God himself and exchanged them for human, even pagan, ones? Origen, on whose belief Jerome writes this, did not himself see the alphabet of the Samaritans, but mentioned it on another's authority, as his words clearly indicate. III. Even if it were entirely true

units.la: In 9. Ezee. effet, quod scribit Hieronymus, antiquis Hebraeorum literis, quibus usque hodie vtuntur Samaritani, extremam ℶ literam habere similitudinem crucis; Quid hoc ad propositum? Num scribit etiam Hieronymus, signum crucis esse sacrum & venerabile habitum? Neque hic neque alibi vsquam vel sanctitatem vel venerationem crucis describit aut commendat. IV. Ipsum Hieronymum Bellarmino oppono. Is enim sub finem capitis scribit, Virum illum sacerdotalibus vestibus indutum, signaculo literæ, frontes signasse lugentium. Vir autem ille erat Christus. Atqui hic non est quæstio, de illo signo, quo signamur à Christo, sed de tali, quod fideles suis frontibus infigunt.
units.tr: that which Jerome writes in his commentary on Ezekiel chapter 9, that the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans still use today, have the final letter Thau with the likeness of a cross, what does this have to do with our point? Does Jerome also write that the sign of the cross is a holy and venerable thing? Neither here nor anywhere else does he describe or commend any holiness or veneration of the cross. IV. I set Jerome himself against Bellarmine. For at the end of the chapter he writes that the man clothed in priestly garments marked the foreheads of those who mourned with the sign of the letter. That man was Christ. But the question here is not about that sign by which we are marked by Christ, but about the kind that the faithful imprint on their foreheads.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus ex cap. 14. Apocalyp. Sed locus hic non fauet sententiæ Bellarminianæ. Nam nomen patris Christi non significat signum crucis, sed fidem, & fidei constantem confessionem. Non enim loquitur de aliqua externa nota aut signo transeunte, frontibus impresso, sed de interna nota cordibus fidelium impressa, presta, fide in Deum patrem, & fidei pro missione, quæ ore & opere constat, estq; signum omnium Dei filiorū, ita vt nomen patris Christi in frontibus scriptū habere, duo significet. 1. profiteri fidē in Deum patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi. 2. nomen patris cælestis sanctificare sermone & vita. Hæc interpretatio est Anselmi. Habentes nomen eius, quia Christiani dicuntur: & nomen patris eius quia Dei dicentur, vel quia Deum esse non tacebunt: scriptum in frontibus suis aperta confessione oris & operis.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses the point from Revelation chapter 14. But this passage does not favour Bellarmine's view. For the name of Christ's Father does not signify the sign of the cross, but faith and the constant confession of faith. For John is not speaking of some external mark or passing sign impressed on the forehead, but of an internal mark impressed on the hearts of the faithful, consisting in faith in God the Father and in the profession of faith, which is shown in word and deed, and which is the sign of all the sons of God. So to have the name of Christ's Father written on the forehead signifies two things: first, to profess faith in God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ; second, to sanctify the name of the heavenly Father by speech and life. This is the interpretation of Anselm: Having his name, because they are called Christians, and the name of his Father, because they will be called sons of God, or because they will not be silent that God is God, written on their foreheads by the open confession of mouth and deed.

units.la: Instat ex 7 cap. Apocalyp. Sed non loquitur Iohannes de extrema quadam ceremonia seu nota, qua serui Dei signātur, verum de interna quadam obsignatione, qua Electi discernuntur à reprobis, vt custodiantur, ne angeli perditores noceant. Quod vero obsignatio facta est in frontibus seruorum Dei, eo significatur, angelis grassaturis in orbe notos fuisse, à quorum læsione sibi tepe-rare debeant. Nihil de figura crucis hic auditur, quod eius honorem vel venerationem possit edocere. II. Explicatur versu 14. quodnam signum hic notetur.
units.tr: He presses it from chapter 7 of Revelation. But John is not speaking of some outward ceremony or mark by which the servants of God are sealed, but of an inner sealing by which the elect are distinguished from the reprobate, so that they may be kept safe from the destroying angels who would harm them. That the sealing was made on the foreheads of the servants of God signifies that the angels who were to ravage the world were given the marks, and that they should refrain from harming those so marked. Nothing is heard here about the figure of the cross that could teach its honour or veneration. II. What sign is meant here is explained in verse 14.

units.la: Sic ibi dicitur: dealbarunt stolas in sanguine agni. Sanguis igitur Christi est, quo lauamur ac iustificamur, ac iustifi-cati ab impiis discernimur; quod signû, cum sit electorum proprium, ad crucis signum non debet imperite detorque-ri, cum signum crucis sit electis cum impiis & hypocritis commune III. sumtus est hic locus ex 9 c. Ezech. vbi pii ciues Hierosolymitani dicuntur signandi in fronte, ne cū impiis pereât. At ibi non intelligitur extremum & materiale signum crucis, sed internum, videlicet fides in Christi sanguine recumbens, & ingenua eius confessio. Non ergo huic loco explicatio de signo crucis potest conuenire. Quod Oecumenius, Beda, Anselmus, & Rupertus crucis signû opinantur intelligi, falluntur, nec mirum est eos falli, cum recentiores sint, & vixerint illis temporibus, quibus omnis generis superstitiones Ecclesiam contaminauerant. Debuisset Bellarminus ostendere, veteres Christianos, qui tempore Apostolorum vixerunt, se crucis signo signasse. At tempore Apostolorum non fuit in vsu, vt signo crucis se Christiani signarent, imò nec Christus nec Apostoli hoc vel facto vel verbo docuerunt.
units.tr: There it is said: "They have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb." The blood of Christ is therefore that by which we are washed and justified, and having been justified we are distinguished from the impious. This sign, since it belongs to the elect, should not be carelessly twisted into the sign of the cross, since the sign of the cross is common to the elect along with the impious and hypocrites. III. This passage is taken from Ezekiel chapter 9, where the godly citizens of Jerusalem are said to be marked on the forehead, lest they perish with the impious. But there it is understood not as an external and material sign of the cross, but as an internal one, namely faith resting on the blood of Christ and its sincere confession. Therefore an explanation about the sign of the cross cannot fit this passage. That Oecumenius, Bede, Anselm, and Rupert think the sign of the cross is meant is an error, and it is no wonder they erred, since they are later writers and lived in those times when every kind of superstition had defiled the Church. Bellarmine ought to have shown that the ancient Christians who lived in the time of the Apostles marked themselves with the sign of the cross. But in the time of the Apostles it was not the custom for Christians to mark themselves with the sign of the cross; indeed neither Christ nor the Apostles taught this either by deed or by word.

units.la: III. Iacob cum cancellatis manibus benedixit
units.tr: III. Jacob blessed with crossed hands

units.la: dixit filiis Iosephi Genes. 48. significauit fore aliquando tempus, quo benedictiones signo crucis fierent.
units.tr: He said to the sons of Joseph (Gen. 48.) that a time would come at some point when blessings would be given with the sign of the cross.

units.la: Respond. commentitia est significatio quam Bellarminus affert: nullibi in scriptura vel verbo notata est. Vera significatio fuit translatio honoris primogenituræ à Manasse in Ephraimum, vnde etiam Manassitæ postea subiecti fuere tribui Epraimitarum. Decussauit manus, non in hunc finem, vt significaret, fore aliquando tempus, quo benedictiones signo crucis fierent, sed vt à Manasse, qui ad dextram stabat, ad Ephraimum, qui ad sinistram erat collocatus, honorem primogenituræ transferret, ita vt decussatio illa manuum collocationem & situm nepotum benedicendorum, non verò benedictiones crucis in Nouo Testamento à Christianis vsurpandas, significarit.
units.tr: Reply: The meaning Bellarmine offers is invented; it is nowhere noted in Scripture or in the Word. The true meaning was the transfer of the honour of the firstborn from Manasseh to Ephraim, whence the Manassites were afterwards made subject to the tribe of the Ephraimites. Jacob crossed his hands, not for the purpose of signifying that a time would come when blessings would be given with the sign of the cross, but so as to transfer the honour of the firstborn from Manasseh, who stood at his right hand, to Ephraim, who was placed at his left. Thus that crossing of the hands signified the arrangement and position of the grandsons being blessed, and not blessings with the cross to be used by Christians in the New Testament.

units.la: Argumentum Secundum.
units.tr: Second Argument.

units.la: Argumentum Secundum à testimoniis veterum qui primis quingentis annis floruerunt.
units.tr: The second argument, from the testimonies of the ancients who flourished in the first five hundred years.

units.la: Respon. I. Qui patres primis duobus seculis vixerunt,Ignatius, Iuft. Irenæus, Clemens Alexandr. ne mentionem quidem aliquam fecere signi crucis:tantum abest, vt venerationem aut efficaciam aliquam illi tribuerint Tertullianus qui circa annum Christi 200.floruit,primus est,qui meminit signi crucis,in librodecoronamilitis.c.3. sed nec ipse,necalii adorationem crucis probant, nec à Criftianis veteribus probatam &vsurpatam docent:imo Ethnicos, qui Christianis adorationem crucis criminosè obiiciebant, grauiter refutarút,vt videre licet Arnobium contra Gentiles,& Cyrillum contra Iulianum.Hoc quidem ex illis veterum testimoniis constat, veteres Christianos signaculo crucis frontem terere solitos, sed venerationis honore ab ipsis culta fuisse crucem,nemo est qui commemorat.Consignatione frontis vsi fuere, tanquam folenni quadam ceremonia,qua suam fiduciam in crucem,id est, morte Christi voluerunt testari,atque eo quasi pignore significare fe esse Christian. nec pudereChristi crucifixi,qui vsus eo vfq; pius & sanctus fuit. Causam huic ceremoniæ præbuerútEthnicorũ,quibus admixti viuebant Christiani, ludibria
units.tr: Answer I. The Fathers who lived in the first two centuries (Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria) make no mention at all of the sign of the cross, so far are they from ascribing to it any veneration or efficacy. Tertullian, who flourished around the year of Christ 200, is the first to mention the sign of the cross, in his book On the Crown of the Soldier, chapter 3. But neither he nor others prove the adoration of the cross, or teach that it was approved and practised by the ancient Christians. On the contrary, they vigorously refuted the pagans who charged Christians with adoring the cross, as one may see in Arnobius against the Gentiles and Cyril against Julian. From those testimonies of the ancients it is clear that the ancient Christians were accustomed to sign their foreheads with the cross, but no one records that the cross was honoured by them with the reverence of worship. They used the signing of the forehead as a solemn ceremony, by which they wished to testify their trust in the cross, that is, in the death of Christ, and by that pledge, as it were, to show that they were Christians, not ashamed of the crucified Christ; and this use was pious and holy up to that point. The cause of this ceremony was provided by the pagans among whom the Christians lived, and by their mockeries.

units.la: l.8 / l.6 marginal references (line markers), printed in the left margin. bria.Insultabant enim Ethnici Chriftia nis,eosque fatuos dicebat, quod Chri- ftum crucifixum pro Deo haberet,& vt Deum adorarent; Christiani hisce ludibriis & contumeliis Ethnicorum opposuerunt crucis signaculum,in testi- monium fidis suæ,in Christum crucifixum, ita vt signi illius vsurpatio fuerit ingenua & intrepida fidei confessio de Christo crucifixo: Hæc ceremoniaa veteribus fine culpa fuit vsurpata, sed tem poris successu in abusum transiit,& mutata fuit in Idololatriā, de quo abusu ne fomniarunt quidem patres,vt ex illis testimoniis, quæ à Bellarmino hic citantur,manifestum euadet: atque hæc causa est,cur Ecclesiæ reformatæ hunc v- sum crucis abrogarint,statuerintque vt veri adoratores Deum adorarent in spi ritu & veritate : idque exemplo regis Ezech. Cùenim Deus serpentem æneum fieri iussisset, ne serpentino morsu populus interiret, & populus colere atq; venerari ipsum cepisset,rex eum de struxit,quem Deo iubente fecerat Moses. Quidni & Ecclesiæ nostræ signū cru cis à prædecessoribus vi & maiorib. no- stris sine culpa illo tempore vsurpatum, & postea in errorem & superstitionem versum, sine tarditate aliqua & cum magna authoritate abrogauere? II. Patres synecdohicè de hoc signo locuti sunt,ita vt sub eius mentione adiuncta Christi crucifixi inuocatione intellexerint. Nam quia veteres precibus suis adiungere solebant signum crucis ad professionem fidei suæ testandam hinc factum,vt patres sæpe sub mentione signi ipsam orationem signo coniunctam intellexerint, ipsiq; signo quod orationis fidelis virtute impetratum fuit,adscripserint.
units.tr: For the pagans insulted the Christians and called them foolish, because they held the crucified Christ to be God and worshipped him as God. The Christians opposed to these mockeries and insults the sign of the cross, as a testimony of their faith in the crucified Christ, so that the use of that sign was a frank and fearless confession of faith concerning the crucified Christ. This ceremony was used by the ancients without fault, but with the passing of time it turned into abuse and was changed into idolatry. Of this abuse the Fathers did not even dream, as will become clear from those testimonies which Bellarmine cites here. And this is the reason why the reformed Churches have abrogated this use of the cross, and have decreed that true worshippers should worship God in spirit and truth, following the example of King Hezekiah. When God had commanded that the bronze serpent be made, so that the people might not perish from serpent bites, and the people had begun to worship and venerate it, the king broke it in pieces, although Moses had made it at God's command. Why then should not our Church, which has abrogated the sign of the cross that was used without fault by our predecessors and forefathers at that time, and afterwards turned into error and superstition, abrogate it without delay and with great authority? II. The Fathers spoke of this sign by synecdoche, so that under the mention of it they understood the invocation of Christ crucified joined to it. For because the ancients were accustomed to join the sign of the cross to their prayers, to attest their profession of faith, it came about that the Fathers often, under the mention of the sign, understood the prayer joined to the sign, and ascribed to the sign itself what was obtained by the power of the faithful prayer.

units.la: NVNC VETERVM TESIMONIA dispiciamus.
units.tr: Now let us examine the testimonies of the ancients.

units.la: Dionysius ca.4.5.6. Ecclesiast.hierarch. dicit, In omnibus Sacramentis haberi signum crucis.
units.tr: Dionysius, Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapters 4, 5 and 6, says that the sign of the cross is found in all the Sacraments.

units.la: Resp.I,Dionys.ille,qui opus illud de Eccl.hierarchia edit,non est ille apostolicus Dionys: Areopagita à Paulo Act. 17.conuersus sed supposititius,qui illius veri nomen sibi asciuit. Neq; enim Eusebius vel Hieronymus in catalogo suo vllam huius vel aliorum scriptorum Dionysii mentionem faciunt, qui cum aliasdiligentissimè libros veteres conquisiuerint & collegerint, operum tamen Dionysii non meminere. Citat etiam in libro de diuinis nominibus epistolam Ignatii, quae tamen post mortem Dionysii scriptafuit. Scripsit enim illam epistolam Ignatius cum ad martyrium obeundum esset profecturus Traiano Imperatore, vt testatur Eusebius. At Dionysius Areopagita obiit temporibus Domitiani, qui Traianum praecessit. Quod vero Bellarminus notat in lib. de sacris scriptis superuixisse Dionysium vsq; ad Imperiu Hadriani, id cofutatur a Methodio in martyr. Dionys. Areopagitae. Suffragantur Laurentius Valla Erasmus, Caietanus Cardinalis & alii II.
units.tr: Reply I. That Dionysius who published that work on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy is not the apostolic Dionysius the Areopagite, converted by Paul (Acts 17), but a spurious writer who took to himself the true name. Neither Eusebius nor Jerome, in their catalogues, make any mention of this work or of any other writings of Dionysius, although they diligently sought out and collected the ancient books, yet they do not remember the works of Dionysius. He also cites in his book On the Divine Names an epistle of Ignatius, which, however, was written after the death of Dionysius. For Ignatius wrote that epistle when he was about to set out to undergo martyrdom under the Emperor Trajan, as Eusebius testifies. But Dionysius the Areopagite died in the time of Domitian, who preceded Trajan. As for what Bellarmine notes in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, that Dionysius survived until the reign of Hadrian, this is refuted by Methodius in his work On the Martyrdom of Dionysius the Areopagite. Laurentius Valla, Erasmus, Cardinal Cajetan and others agree with this.

units.la: Sententia ex adulterino Dionysio allegata de veneratione crucis nihil continet, sed ceremoniam signi crucis in Sacramentis vsurpatam fuisse commemorat. Nos vero testimonium signi crucis veneratione & adoratione a veteribus affecti petimus. Ab vsu huius ceremoniae in Sacramentis ad vsum adorationis non valet consequentia. Multa in hoc lib. de Eccl. hierarch scribit autor de templis, altaribus & choro, nullam tamen vel hic vel alibi adorationis sanctorum, crucis aut aliarum creaturarum mentio fieri audies. III, agnosco ritu hunc in Sacra-
units.tr: The passage from the spurious Dionysius that is cited about the veneration of the cross contains nothing of the kind, but records that the ceremony of the sign of the cross was used in the Sacraments. We, however, seek testimony to the sign of the cross being regarded with veneration and adoration by the ancients. The inference from the use of this ceremony in the Sacraments to the use of adoration does not hold. In this book on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy the author writes much about temples, altars and the choir, yet you will hear no mention, either here or elsewhere, of the adoration of saints, of the cross, or of other creatures. III. I acknowledge that this rite

units.la: Hist. Eccl. l. c. 36. & Chron. Sacramentis vsurpari cepisse circa annum 400. quod vero temporibus Apostolorum & Areopagitæ in administratione Sacramentorum adhibitus fuerit, id negamus. Meminit hic supposititius Dionysius templorum, altariū & chori à templis distinctis, quorum tamen illis temporibus nihil extitisse constat. In domib. n. & abditis atque occultis locis convenire soliti fuerunt. Meminit etiam Monachorum, cum tamen constet Paulum atque Antonium, primos Monachorum parentes post Areopagitam aliquot seculis floruisse. Non igitur mirū est huius ceremoniæ in Sacramentis vsurpatæ etiam mentionem fieri, cuius tamen vsus, vel Apostolorum aut Areopagitæ temporibus in Ecclesia aut Sacramentis, plane fuit ignotus. Annis à Christi tempore trecentis, postquam Ethnici Christianis crucé Christi probro darent, inualuit hæc ceremonia, & nihil aliud fuit quam signum professionis fidei, in vita communi adhibitum.
units.tr: (Ecclesiastical History, book 1, ch. 36; and Chronicle) began to be used in the Sacraments about the year 400; but that it was employed in the administration of the Sacraments in the times of the Apostles and of the Areopagite, that we deny. This spurious Dionysius mentions temples, altars and a choir distinct from the temples, though it is clear that nothing of this sort existed in those times. For they were accustomed to meet in houses and in hidden and secret places. He also mentions monks, though it is certain that Paul and Anthony, the first fathers of the monks, flourished several centuries after the Areopagite. It is therefore no wonder that mention is made of this ceremony being used in the Sacraments, though its use in the Church or in the Sacraments in the times of the Apostles or of the Areopagite was entirely unknown. About three hundred years after the time of Christ, when the pagans were reproaching the Christians with the cross of Christ, this ceremony prevailed, and it was nothing other than a sign of profession of faith, used in common life.

units.la: Postea circa annum 400. cepta est adhiberi in administratione Sacramentorum, idque nō venerationis & operationis, sed significationis causa, non vt veneratiōnis honore afficeretur & ab eius eiús virute gratia diuina impetraretur, sed vt crucis Christi efficacia ac benefi-cia quæ fidelibus virtute crucis seu mor-tis suæ communicat, significaret. Iustinus q. 118. respondet Gentibus quæren-tibus, cur Christiani ad orientem orarent: & di-it causam esse, quia Deo dada sint meliora. Sicut tiam, inquit, dextera potius quam sinistra si-gnū crucis exprimimus, cū alicui benedicimus.
units.tr: Afterwards, about the year 400, it began to be employed in the administration of the Sacraments, and that not for the sake of veneration and operation, but of signification: not so that it might be honoured with veneration and that divine grace might be obtained through its power, but so that it might signify the efficacy and benefits of Christ's cross, which he communicates to the faithful by virtue of his cross or death. Justin, Questions 118, answers the Gentiles who asked why Christians prayed toward the east, and says the reason is that better things are given to God. "Just as," he says, "we form the sign of the cross with the right hand rather than the left when we bless anyone."

units.la: Resp. I. Libellus ille quæstionum & responsionum non est Iustini, etiam teste Bellarmino. Nam q. 82. & 86. facit mentionem Origenis. & quæst. 115. citatur Irenæus & martyr appellatur, cum tamen vtroq; Iustinus antiquior fuerit: quin & ipse Irenæus lib. 5. Iustinum tanquam se antiquiorem adducit. In hoc eode libro sæpe fit mentio Manicheorum, quos tamen post mortem Iustini exortos esse constat. Deniq; nec Eusebius in historia, nec Photius in bibliotheca huius libri meminerē. II. Quod hoc in loco dicitur, non pertinet ad crucis venerationem, sed vsum eius in bene dictionibus seu orationibus adhibitum fuisse ostendit, quiuisus ea ætate non fuit idololatricus & superstitiosus, sed pius & Christianus. Solebant enim veteres Christiani cora Ethnicis quib. admixti erant,
units.tr: Reply I. That little book of questions and answers is not Justin's, even by the testimony of Bellarmine. For in questions 82 and 86 it makes mention of Origen, and in question 115 Irenaeus is cited and called a martyr, although Justin was older than both; indeed Irenaeus himself, in book 5, cites Justin as an earlier writer than himself. In this same book the Manichaeans are often mentioned, who, however, are known to have arisen after Justin's death. Finally, neither Eusebius in his History nor Photius in his Bibliotheca mentions this book. II. What is said in this place does not pertain to the veneration of the cross, but shows that its use was employed in blessings or prayers; and this use in that age was not idolatrous or superstitious, but pious and Christian. For the ancient Christians, among the pagans with whom they lived mixed,

units.la: Scribit Eccles. p. 72. erantreligionem&fidem suam in Chri-ftum crucifixũ profiteri,tum verbis, tũ gestu. Verbis,nempe oratione seu preci bus. Gestu,videlicet signo crucis, quod orationi adiungebant ad testandam fiduciam suam in mortem Christi. Quod si aliquando verbis, id est, orationem confirmari suam in Christum fiduciam non potuere,solo gestu, id est,signo crucis eam demonstrarunt,& tunc signum crucis nō manifestam,sed tamen tacitā inuocationem Christi habuit sibi adiu-ctam. Non vim aut efficaciam aliquam huic signo , sed inuocationi nominis Christi siue manifestæ siue tacitæ, quæ cū hoc signo fuit coiuncta, tribuerunt, non signum crucis sed Christum crucifixum venerationediuinaprosecuti fuere.
units.tr: He writes (Eccles. p. 72) that they professed their religion and faith in Christ crucified both by words and by gesture. By words, namely by prayer or supplication. By gesture, namely by the sign of the cross, which they added to their prayer to attest their trust in the death of Christ. But if at times they could not confirm their trust in Christ by words, that is by prayer, they showed it by gesture alone, that is by the sign of the cross. In that case the sign of the cross had joined with it an invocation of Christ, not spoken aloud but tacit. They did not attribute any power or efficacy to this sign, but to the invocation of the name of Christ, whether spoken or tacit, which was joined with the sign. They did not pay divine worship to the sign of the cross but to Christ crucified.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Nullibi Iustinus tradit, signum crucis sacrum esse & venerabile ; cur hunc locum, qui nullam venerationis cruci exhibitæ, sed tantum benedictionis Deo præstitæ mentionem facit, eo trahunt? Signum, inquit, exprimimus, cum alicui benedicimus, id est, precibus eum Deo commendamus. Ergo preces signo coniunctæ intelliguntur, non veneratio signo præstita significatur.
units.tr: Justin nowhere teaches that the sign of the cross is holy and venerable. Why do they drag in this passage, which makes no mention of any veneration shown to the cross but only of a blessing offered to God? We make the sign, he says, when we bless someone, that is, when we commend them to God in prayers. So it is prayers joined with the sign that are meant, and the passage does not signify any veneration paid to the sign.

units.la: Hippolytus quidam scriptor vetustissi-mus mus & Apostolis familiaris cuius librum citat Palladius in hist. Laufiaca cap. 14. scribit virgi-nem quandam signo crucis munitam ex pro-stibulo illæsam euasisse.
units.tr: A certain Hippolytus, a very ancient writer and familiar with the Apostles, whose book Palladius cites in the Lausiac History, chapter 14, writes that a certain virgin, protected by the sign of the cross, came out unharmed from a brothel.

units.la: Respond. I. Nullus unquam extitit Hippolytus qui familiaris fuerit Apostolis, quicquid fabuletur Palladius. Agnoscimus illum Hippolytū martyrem, Episcopum Antiochenum, qui floruit an. 220. cuius scripta enumerantur ab Eusebio & ab Hieronymo in lib. de script. Eccles. qui sub Alexandro Seuero martyriū consummauit; quod cum ipse Bellarminus expresse nobiscum fateatur, in libro de script. Eccl. quomodo tam medaciter audet affirmare, eum familiaritate Apostolorum vsum esse?
units.tr: Response. I. There never was a Hippolytus who was familiar with the Apostles, whatever Palladius may invent. We know him as the martyr Hippolytus, bishop of Antioch, who flourished around the year 220, whose writings are listed by Eusebius and by Jerome in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers, and who completed his martyrdom under Alexander Severus. Since Bellarmine himself expressly agrees with us on this in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, how can he dare to assert so falsely that Hippolytus enjoyed familiarity with the Apostles?

units.la: II. Virginis illius miraculosa euasio non est tribuenda virtuti crucis, sed orationi fideli cū signo crucis coniunctæ. Quãdo n. Christum crucifixū inuocabant, gestu illo eundem etiā profitebantur coram Ethnicis, pœnas licet minantibus. Hic signi vsus pie quidem ea ætate observatus fuit, sed cum in idololatriam lit mutatus pie et abrogatus. III. Miraculosa hæc euasio virginis extra ordine a Christo ad orationem signo crucis expressa, iam præstita fuit, non quod sacrum & venerabile effet signum crucis & prosa cro atq; venerabili vellet coli & haberi, sed vt nomen Christi crucifixi propaga retur, & Ethnicorum infidelitas con- uinceretur.
units.tr: II. That virgin's miraculous escape is not to be attributed to the power of the cross but to faithful prayer joined with the sign of the cross. For when they invoked Christ crucified, by that gesture they also professed the same before the Gentiles, even though they were threatened with punishment. This use of the sign was indeed observed piously in that age, but when it was turned into idolatry it was piously abrogated. III. This miraculous escape of the virgin, brought about by Christ outside the ordinary course in answer to prayer expressed by the sign of the cross, had already taken place, not because the sign of the cross was holy and venerable and wished to be worshipped and regarded as such, but so that the name of Christ crucified might be spread abroad and the unbelief of the Gentiles be refuted.

units.la: Tertul.ita loquitur lib. de corona militis Adomne progressum & promotum, ad omne a- ditum & exitum, ad vestitum, ad calceatum, ad lauacra, mensas, ad lumina, ad cubicula, ad fedi- lia, quandocunq; nos conuersatio exercet, fronte crucis signaculo terimus. Idem habet lib. 2. ad uxorem & in principio Scorpiaci.
units.tr: Tertullian speaks thus in his book On the Crown of the Soldier: at every going forth and coming in, at putting on clothes and shoes, at baths, tables, lamps, beds, and seats, whenever our daily life occupies us, we wear out the forehead with the sign of the cross. He says the same in the second book To His Wife and at the beginning of Scorpiacus.

units.la: Refp.I. Tertul facit mentionem no- uarum prophetiarum in hoc libro, quarum autor fuit Montanus: unde liquet Montaniftam fuisse, cum hunc librum scripsit. Montanus autem multas super- ftitiones in Ecclesiam inuexit; inter quas illa fuit; quod signo crucis nos ad- uersus dæmonas putauit munitos; qua li. de refur. carnis ex sententia Monta- ni recitat inquiens: Caro signatur, vt & a- nima muniatur. II. Si Tertul. hæc vt catho licus scripsit, synecdohice more Catho licorum istius temporis locut° est, intelli- gens per signum crucis preces, quibus Christo crucifixo sese, adhibito signo crucis commendabat. Cum enim Ter- tulliani seculo & aliquot sequentibus, Criftiani Christiani cum Ethnicis, quibus & nomine & signū crucis Christi erat pro bro- dium, permixti viuerent, in precibus suis signo crucis frontem terere consueuerunt, vt eo veluti monitorio suam fidem excitarent, seque Christi crucifixi minimè pudere testarentur, ita vt hæc ceremonia tunc fuerit Christianismi symbolum, quæ quia cum precibus siue dictis siue manifestis coniungebatur, ideo signo hoc nominato, preces, quæ anima huius signi fuerunt, intellexerunt signo illo vestitas & expressas.
units.tr: Response. I. Tertullian mentions the new prophecies in this book, whose author was Montanus. It is therefore clear that he was a Montanist when he wrote it. Montanus introduced many superstitions into the Church, and among them was the notion that we are fortified against demons by the sign of the cross. Tertullian recites this in his book On the Resurrection of the Flesh, in line with Montanus' view, saying: The flesh is signed, that the soul may be protected. II. If Tertullian wrote these things as a Catholic, he spoke in the synecdochic manner of the Catholics of that time, understanding by the sign of the cross the prayers by which he commended himself to Christ crucified with the sign applied. For in Tertullian's age and some centuries after, Christians lived mixed with Gentiles, to whom the name and sign of Christ's cross were a reproach. They were accustomed in their prayers to make the sign of the cross on the forehead, so that by this sign, as a kind of reminder, they might stir up their faith and testify that they were not at all ashamed of Christ crucified. Thus this ceremony was then the symbol of Christianity. Since it was joined with prayers, whether spoken or manifest, they named the sign and understood by it the prayers, which were the soul of that sign, clothed and expressed in it.

units.la: III. Non legitur, nec probare possunt Pontificii, signo crucis à Tertul: aut Christianis sui seculi sanctitatem, aut venerationem religiosam fuisse tributam; soli Christo crucifixo eam animo fideli exhibuerunt, quam quia Ethnici vt stultam & probrosam traducebant, ideo signo crucis adhibito fidem suam testati fuere, ostendentes se cum Paulo in cruce gloriari: nunc vero cum Ethnicis nō simus permixti, & multiplici idololatria fœdata sit hæc ceremonia, merito ex Ecclesis exturbata est.
units.tr: III. The Papists cannot show that Tertullian or the Christians of his age ascribed holiness or religious veneration to the sign of the cross. They paid that veneration with a faithful heart to Christ crucified alone. Since the Gentiles mocked the sign as foolish and shameful, they attested their faith by applying it, showing that they gloried in the cross with Paul. But now that we are not mixed with the Gentiles, and this ceremony has been defiled by manifold idolatry, it has rightly been cast out of the Churches.

units.la: Cyprianus lib. 4. Epist. 6. in fine. Muniatur frons, vt signum Dei incolume seruetur. Et libro de vnitate Ecclesiæ, vltra medium dicit cit, Oziam lepra in fronte percussum, offenso Domino, in qua parte corporis signantur, qui Dominum promerentur. Et libro de lapsis in principio. Frons cum signo Dei pura, Diaboli coronam ferre non potuit, coronae se Domini reseruauit.
units.tr: Cyprian, book 4, Epistle 6, near the end: Let the forehead be fortified, that the sign of God may be kept safe. And in the book On the Unity of the Church, a little past the middle, he says that Uzziah, struck with leprosy in the forehead, was struck because the Lord was offended, since that is the part of the body where those who deserve the Lord are signed. And in the book On the Lapsed, at the beginning: The forehead, pure with the sign of God, could not bear the Devil's crown; it reserved itself for the crown of the Lord.

units.la: Respond. Primus locus de signo crucis non loquitur: quia signum crucis est id, quo homines frontem signabant. Loquitur autem hic de signo, quod scilicet Deus imprimit hominibus per Spiritum Sanctum, estque fides & confessio Christi, sicut id sequentia verba aperte confirmant. Muniatur frons, inquit, ut signum Dei incolume seruetur: muniatur os; ut Dominum suum Christum victrix lingua fateatur. Per exegesin ostendit, quid per signum Dei intelligat, ut scilicet Dominum suum Christum victrix lingua fateatur.
units.tr: Response. The first passage does not speak of the sign of the cross, because the sign of the cross is that with which men signed their foreheads. Cyprian is speaking here of the sign which God impresses on men through the Holy Spirit, and which is the faith and confession of Christ, as the words that follow clearly confirm: Let the forehead be fortified, that the sign of God may be kept safe; let the mouth be fortified, that a victorious tongue may confess its Lord Christ. By way of explanation he shows what he means by the sign of God: that a victorious tongue confess its Lord Christ.

units.la: II. Pammelius Pontificius Doctor agnoscit hoc in loco alludi ad signum crucis, quod frontibus in Baptismo infigitur. Cum vero ex allusione neque at fidei dogma probari, cur huius loci authoritate crucis venerationem probare contendit Bellarminus? Nihil aliud ex hoc testimonio elicitur, quam signū hoc isto seculo fuisse in vsu; non in vsu adorationis, sed professionis Christi. Alias enim dixisset: Muniatur os, vt signum Dei victrix lingua confiteatur. At Dominum suum Christum iubet linguam confiteri, quam confessionem signum crucis excitabat, & magis illustrabat.
units.tr: II. The Papist doctor Pamelius acknowledges that this passage alludes to the sign of the cross which is impressed on the foreheads in Baptism. But since no article of faith can be proved from an allusion, why does Bellarmine labour to prove the veneration of the cross by the authority of this passage? Nothing else can be drawn from this testimony than that this sign was in use in that age, not in use for adoration but for the profession of Christ. Otherwise he would have said: Let the mouth be fortified, that a victorious tongue may confess the sign of God. But he bids the tongue confess its Lord Christ, and the sign of the cross stirred up and made more illustrious that confession.

units.la: Secundus locus itidem non loquitur simpliciter de signo crucis, sed de Baptismo, quo olim Christiani dicebantur cōsignari adhibito signo crucis. Qui enim Dominum promerebantur, hoc est per Baptismum, illum eiusq; beneficia impetrabant, consignabantur in administratione Baptismi. Primum itaque signum crucis erat externum professionis Christi testimonium; sed mox in Baptismo & aliis rebus etiam fuit vsurpatum, in quo vsu plus superstitionis fuit quam religionis.
units.tr: The second passage likewise does not speak simply of the sign of the cross but of Baptism, at which Christians were formerly said to be signed with the sign of the cross. For those who deserve the Lord, that is, who obtain Him through Baptism, obtain Him and His benefits, and are signed in the administration of Baptism. The first use of the sign of the cross was therefore an external testimony to the profession of Christ. Soon, however, it was also used in Baptism and other matters, and in that use there was more superstition than religion.

units.la: Tertius deniq; locus omnium minimè ad crucis venerationem confert. Loquitur itidem de consignatione crucis in Baptismo. Baptismo autem signaculum crucis adiungebant, non vt illius virtute Diabolus fugaretur, & praeterea tanquā propupropugnaculum cōtrà diabolū sit ado-randū, sed vt eo tanquā solenni ceremo-nia se Christianos profiterentur. Neq; hic in signo crucis, sed in sanguine Chri-sti omnis vis collocatur. Frons cū signo Dei pura, id est, purgata sanguine Chri-sti per Baptismum, & cruce in testimo-nium fidei consignata, Diabolum ferre nequit.
units.tr: Finally, the third passage contributes least of all to the veneration of the cross. It too speaks of the signing with the cross in Baptism. But they added the seal of the cross to Baptism not so that the Devil might be put to flight by its power, nor so that it might be adored as a bulwark against the devil, but so that by this solemn ceremony they might profess themselves Christians. Nor is all the power placed here in the sign of the cross but in the blood of Christ. The forehead, pure with the sign of God, that is, cleansed by the blood of Christ through Baptism and sealed with the cross in testimony of faith, cannot bear the Devil.

units.la: Cornelius Papa in Epist. ad Fabianum quae est apud Eusebium lib. 6. histor. ca. 33. dicit Novatianum à daemonio arreptum, quod non ac-cepisset in fronte signaculum Christi.
units.tr: Pope Cornelius, in his Epistle to Fabian, which is found in Eusebius, Church History, book 6, chapter 33, says that Novatian was seized by a demon because he had not received the seal of Christ in his forehead.

units.la: Resp. 1. depravat mentem Cornelii. Non vult Novatianum ideo arreptum fuisse, quod signo crucis non esset con-signatus, sed quod Ecclesiam Christi contemnisset, & haeresin docuisset. Nā signaculum Christi, quod dicitur no-luisse accipere, synecdochicè significat Baptismum, cum quo signaculum cru-cis erat in solenni administratione con-iunctum. Hunc ergo solennem Bapti-smum in Ecclesia contemnisse Novatia-num & propterea à Deo punitum esse testatur Corn. Accepérat quidem Ba-ptismum Clinicus, cum iam de vita eius desperaretur, sed publicè extra morbum norbum in Ecclesia eo debuisse initia-i, & solennem consignationem ab Episcopo fieri solitam, accipere, quod cum excusaret, Ecclesia, & cum ea Baptismum contemsit, & propter hunc contemptum punitus dicitur. II. Consignatio illa crucis, de qua Cornelius Papa loquitur, longe diuersa est ab illa pro qua pugnat Bellarminus. Nam illa in Baptismo debebat ab Episcopo administrari insigne Christianae testimonium, ita vt publicus & solennis esset ritus, Baptismo quasi symbolum Christianismi adiunctus. At consignatio quae hodie vigat in papatu a vulgo superstitioso, pmi cuiè extra vsum baptismi exoperato exercetur, ita vt multiplex superstitio & idololatria concurrat, quae paulatim huic ceremoniae adnata est, ac prorsus de ex Ecclesia eliminanda.
units.tr: Reply: first, the author distorts the mind of Cornelius. Cornelius does not mean that Novatian was seized because he had not been marked with the sign of the cross, but because he had despised the Church of Christ and taught heresy. The "seal of Christ" that he says Novatian refused to receive stands by synecdoche for baptism, with which the sign of the cross was joined in the solemn administration. Cornelius therefore testifies that Novatian despised this solemn baptism in the Church and was for that reason punished by God. Novatian had indeed received baptism when he was bedridden and his life was despaired of, but he ought to have received the beginnings of the faith publicly in the Church, outside sickness, together with the solemn consignation customarily performed by the bishop. When he made excuses for not doing so, he despised the Church and, with it, baptism, and he is said to have been punished for this contempt. II. The consignation of the cross of which Cornelius speaks is very different from the one Bellarmine defends. In baptism that mark was to be administered by the bishop as a distinguishing testimony of the Christian, so that the rite was public and solemn, joined to baptism as a kind of symbol of Christianity. But the consignation that now flourishes in the Papacy is practised by a superstitious crowd on anyone at all, outside the use of baptism, so that a manifold superstition and idolatry gather around it, which have gradually grown onto this ceremony and must be utterly removed from the Church.

units.la: Origenes in Exod. c. 15. hom. 6. sica t: Timor & tremor cadunt super eos (daemones) cum signum in vobis viderint crucis fideliter fixum.
units.tr: Origen, on Exodus, chapter 15, homily 6, says: Fear and trembling fall upon them (the demons) when they see the sign of the cross faithfully fixed in you.

units.la: Resp. I. Origenes plenus fuit erroum, ita vt Epiphanius in libro de haeretibus, eum in numero haereticorum ponat; & in quinta synodo generali collatione 8. can. 11. dicatur anathema Origenes. rigeni & scriptis eius teste Bellarmino. II. Synecdochicè loquitur Origenes, & quod proprium est invocationis, tribuit signo invocationi coniuncto. Implorabant veteres praesentiam & virtutem Christi crucifixi adiuncta externa professione Christi in signo crucis positâ. Haec preces non poterant non esse timori & tremori daemonibus. Nullaitaq; vis signo per se competit, sed tota est invocationis Christi. Si quae signo attribuitur, eam totam ab invocatione, cui est coniuncta, habet.
units.tr: Reply: I. Origen was full of errors, so much so that Epiphanius, in his book on heresies, counts him among the heretics; and in the fifth general council, collation 8, canon 11, Origen is declared anathema, as Bellarmine himself admits concerning Origen and his writings. II. Origen speaks by synecdoche and attributes to the sign what belongs properly to the invocation joined with it. The ancients called upon the presence and power of the crucified Christ, with an outward profession of Christ placed in the sign of the cross. Such prayers could not but cause fear and trembling in the demons. Therefore the sign has no power of its own; all its power lies in the invocation of Christ. Whatever power is ascribed to the sign, it has entirely from the invocation with which it is joined.

units.la: Gregorium Neocaesariensem saepe usum signo crucis contra daemones testatur Gregorius Nyssenus in eius vita.
units.tr: Gregory Thaumaturgus of Neocaesarea is said to have often used the sign of the cross against demons, as Gregory of Nyssa testifies in his life.

units.la: Resp. I. Gregorius Neocaesar. nonvsus est signo superstitiosè ex animo merendi de Christo, ut pontificii, sed religiosè, ex animo testificandi fidem Christi crucifixi, eamque propagandi apud infideles, eoque non ad venerationem, sed ad aedificationem Ecclesiae, & Christi glorificationem. II. vsus est signo crucis contra daemones, non virtuti aut operationi crucis fugationem daemonum tribuens, sed invocationi Christi, cui adiungebat externum crucis signum, ad fidei suae testificationem, & aedificationem aliorum. LactanLactantius l. 4. c. 26. Dicit Christum eis omnibus prodesse, qui signum crucis in fronte conscripserint.
units.tr: Reply: I. Gregory of Neocaesarea did not use the sign superstitiously, as the Papists do, with the intention of earning merit from Christ, but religiously, with the intention of testifying to the faith in the crucified Christ and spreading it among unbelievers, and so not for veneration but for the edification of the Church and the glorifying of Christ. II. He used the sign of the cross against demons, ascribing the driving out of demons not to the power or working of the cross but to the invocation of Christ, to which he added the outward sign of the cross, as a testimony of his faith and for the edification of others. Lactantius, book 4, chapter 26, says that Christ profits all those who have inscribed the sign of the cross on their foreheads.

units.la: Resp. I. At ipse Bellarminus testatur Lactantii opera omnia, erroribus variis sic deformata esse, ut non sine causa Gelasius Papa in concilio Romano apocrypha censeri voluerit. II. Dictum Lactantii synecdochice intelligendum, non de virtute & operatione ipsius signi, sed Christi, quem invocabant & signo crucis externo profitebantur. Non huius signi veneratio, sed fidelis invocationis Christi efficacia probatur. Signi vero meminit tantum, tum quia orationem suam externo illo professionis signo excitabant, & confirmabant, tum quia hac ceremonia ostendebant, unde vis illa orationis proficisceretur videlicet a Christo crucifixo.
units.tr: Reply: I. But Bellarmine himself testifies that all the works of Lactantius are so deformed by various errors that Pope Gelasius, in the Roman council, rightly wished them to be counted apocryphal. II. The saying of Lactantius must be understood by synecdoche, not of the power and working of the sign itself but of Christ, whom they called upon and professed with the outward sign of the cross. What is proved is not veneration of this sign but the efficacy of faithful invocation of Christ. He mentions the sign only because they stirred up and strengthened their prayer by that outward sign of profession, and because by this ceremony they showed whence that power of prayer came, namely from the crucified Christ.

units.la: Cyrillus Catechesi 4. Non pudeat, inquit, nos crucis Christi, quod si aliquis id occultit, tu manifeste te signa cruce in fronte. Et infra. Fac autem hoc signum & manducans & bibens, & sedens & stans, & loquens & ambulans, & in summa, in omni negotio. Idem repetit Catechesi 13.
units.tr: Cyril, Catechesis 4: Let us not be ashamed, he says, of the cross of Christ; but if anyone hides it, you openly sign yourself on the forehead with the cross. And below: Make this sign both when eating and drinking, sitting and standing, speaking and walking, and in short in every business. He repeats the same in Catechesis 13.

units.la: Respond. I. Licet Cyrillus iste plus satis superstitionibus deditus fuerit: non tamen crucis venerationem probauit. Signationem crucis tantum vt symbolum Christianismi & professionis Christi, apud infideles, quibus tunc admixti erant Christiani commendauit. Non pudeat, inquit, nos crucis Christi, id est, Christum crucifixum cô fiteri: signa te fronte, id est, ostende ista ceremonia te non erubescere Christi crucem, sed ea potius gloriari. Nunc non amplius gentilibus commixti sumus, ideo hic signi vsus in Ecclesia cessare debet, præsertim cum tot erroribus & superstitionibus sit contaminatum.
units.tr: Reply: I. Although this Cyril was quite addicted to superstitions, he did not approve the veneration of the cross. He commended the signing of the cross only as a symbol of Christianity and of the profession of Christ before unbelievers, among whom Christians then lived mixed in. "Let us not be ashamed," he says, "of the cross of Christ," that is, to confess Christ crucified; "sign yourself on the forehead," that is, show by this ceremony that you are not ashamed of the cross of Christ but rather glory in it. Now we are no longer mixed with the Gentiles, so the use of this sign ought to cease in the Church, especially since it has been contaminated with so many errors and superstitions.

units.la: In altero loco Synecdochice loquitur Cyrillus, Fac signum, id est, precibus te Deo commenda, adhibito signo. Solebant enim eo tempore precibus suis ordinarie adiungere signaculum crucis, vt non tantum ore, sed & gestu Christum confiterentur. Gestus & ritus illius observatio, vt superstitiosa, & idololatrica, nunc recte est sublata.
units.tr: In the other passage Cyril speaks by synecdoche: "Make the sign," that is, commend yourself to God in prayer with the sign added. For at that time they were accustomed to join the sign of the cross ordinarily to their prayers, so that they confessed Christ not only with the mouth but also with a gesture. The observance of that gesture and rite, since it has become superstitious and idolatrous, has now rightly been abolished.

units.la: Athanasius lib. de incarnatione verbi Signo crucis omnia magica, inquit, compescuntur.
units.tr: Athanasius, in his book on the incarnation of the Word: By the sign of the cross, he says, all magic is restrained.

units.la: Resp. Figurate loquitur, & virtutem Christi quem precibus implorabant, externaq; signi ceremonia profitebantur, tur, Synecdochicè signo tribuit: signi vero nominatim facit mentionem, non quod virtutem aliquam compescendi magica illi putauerit inesse, sed partim vt ceremonia illa significarent à Christo crucifixo quem inuocabant virtute illam proficisci, partim vt quem oratione, eundem & gestu, signoq; ordinario profiterentur.
units.tr: Reply: He speaks figuratively, and attributes by synecdoche to the sign the power of Christ, whom they implored in prayer and professed by the outward ceremony of the sign. He names the sign itself not because he thought that any power of restraining magic dwelt in it, but partly so that this ceremony signified that that power proceeded from Christ crucified, whom they invoked, and partly so that they professed by gesture the one whom they professed in prayer.

units.la: Basilius lib. de Spiritu S. cap. 27. inter primas traditiones Apostolicas ponit signare se signo crucis.
units.tr: Basil, in his book on the Holy Spirit, chapter 27: He counts among the first apostolic traditions the signing of oneself with the sign of the cross.

units.la: Resp. I. Constat Basilium nimium interdum fuisse traditionibus addictū. Praeter signationem crucis, etiā inter Apostolicas traditiones numerauit conuersione precantium ad Orientē πρὸς ἀνατολὰς τῆς ἡλίου ... II. Nos agnoscimus signationem crucis veterem esse ceremoniam, quae ab ipsis pene religionis Ecclesiaeq; Christianę incunabulis fuit vsurpata, sed non superstitioso modo, quo à Pontificiis, qui effectus supernaturales signo huic tribuunt, eoq; diuina veneratione crucem prosequuntur: sed vt Christiani, qui tum inter Ethnicos à Christi religione alienissimos viuebant, se Christi crucifixi cultores & adoratores esse testarentur publicè.
units.tr: Reply: I. It is clear that Basil was at times too much given to traditions. Besides the signing of the cross, he also numbered among apostolic traditions the turning of those who pray toward the East, πρὸς ἀνατολὰς τῆς ἡλίου [toward the rising of the sun] ... II. We acknowledge that the signing of the cross is an ancient ceremony, which was adopted almost from the very cradle of the religion and the Christian Church, but not in the superstitious manner in which the Papists use it, ascribing supernatural effects to this sign and thereby paying divine veneration to the cross. It was used as a public testimony by Christians who then lived among the heathens, who were very much alienated from the religion of Christ, that they were worshippers and adorers of the crucified Christ.

units.la: III. Etiamsi detur signaculum crucis traditionem esse Apostolicam: non tamen sequitur, eius venerationem, aliasque superstitiones, ceremoniae huic statim adnatas, esse traditiones apostolicas. Vsus huius ceremoniae primis illis temporibus per se non fuit malus, sed post in abusum transiit venerationis idololatricae, ideoque tollendus.
units.tr: III. Even if the sign of the cross were granted to be an apostolic tradition, it would not follow that its veneration and the other superstitions immediately attached to this ceremony are apostolic traditions. The use of this ceremony in those first times was not evil in itself, but afterwards it passed into the abuse of idolatrous veneration, and therefore must be removed.

units.la: Gregorius Nazianzenus Orat. in Iulianum dicit Etiam milites in mensa signum crucis adhibere solitos.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration against Julian, says: Even soldiers were accustomed to make the sign of the cross at table.

units.la: Resp. Sic est, ut fuere milites crucis signo in mensa, sed ita ut suis precibus illud adiunxerint, idque non studio merendi de Christo, sed fiduciam suam in Christum testificandi & confirmandi.
units.tr: Reply: It is so, as soldiers used the sign of the cross at table, but they added it with their own prayers, and not with the eagerness of earning merit from Christ, but to testify and confirm their trust in Christ.

units.la: II. Non putarunt a signo cibos sanctificari, sed a Christo crucifixo, quae precibus invocabant, & signo crucis tanquam vexillo professionis suae confitebantur, sanctificationem ciborum implorabat.
units.tr: II. They did not think that the food was sanctified by the sign, but by Christ crucified; they implored the sanctifying of the food by their prayers, and confessed it with the sign of the cross as with the banner of their profession.

units.la: Chrysostomus hom. 55 in Matth. c. 12. Signo crucis omnia sacramenta perfici docet. Et homil. quod Christus sit Deus, plurima de gloria huius signi & eloquentissime persequitur.
units.tr: Chrysostom, homily 55 on Matthew, chapter 12: He teaches that all sacraments are perfected by the sign of the cross. And in the homily that Christ is God: he pursues very many things about the glory of this sign, most eloquently.

units.la: Respond. I. Prius dictum si proprie accipiatur inconsideratum & tanto pa-tre tre indignū censetur, sed constat Chry-sostomum metoynimicè loquutū esse, ita vt ipsam Christi crucem, seu mortem signo crucis repraesentatam intel-lexerit, vtpote in qua omnia sacramenta & fidei mysteria veluti radicantur, & sine qua omnis doctrina vana & inutilis est. Sic & homi. 55. in Matth. cum dicit, Crucem non simpliciter digito in corpore, sed magna profecto fide in mente confirmare oportere. non ipsum signum crucis, sed metonymicè passionem & mortem Christi crucifixi designat. II. Si Metonymica haec interpretatio displicet, synecdochicam quae Patribus valde familiaris, amplectatur, ita vt per signum crucis invocationem Christi, quae hanc ceremoniam annexam habebat, intelligat, perfectionem vero de benedictione, seu consecratione accipiat; non quod per ceremoniā signi crucis sacramenti benedictionem seu consecrationem puta fieri, sed per invocationem Christi, quae hanc ceremoniam habebat adiunctam.
units.tr: Reply: I. If the former saying is taken properly, it is thoughtless and judged unworthy of so great a father; but it is clear that Chrysostom spoke by metonymy, so that he understood the very cross of Christ, or his death represented by the sign of the cross, in which all sacraments and mysteries of faith are as it were rooted, and without which all doctrine is vain and useless. So also in homily 55 on Matthew, when he says, the cross must be confirmed not simply by the finger on the body, but certainly by great faith in the mind, he designates not the sign of the cross itself but, by metonymy, the passion and death of the crucified Christ. II. If this metonymical interpretation displeases, let them embrace the synecdochical one, which is very familiar to the Fathers, so that by the sign of the cross one understands the invocation of Christ, which had this ceremony attached to it, and takes the "perfecting" to mean the blessing or consecration; not that the blessing or consecration of the sacrament is effected through the ceremony of the sign of the cross, but through the invocation of Christ, which had this ceremony joined to it.

units.la: III. laudes illae quib. gloriam crucis persequitur Chrysostomus, sunt merę Rhetoricationes, quae non probant, sed tantum movent & delectant. Deinde non commendat abusum signi idololatricū, errores & superstitiones huic ceremoniæ adhærentes, sed vsum à veteribus Christianis pie obseruatu; qui hic fuit. 1. vt hac solenni ceremonia fiduciam suam in crucem seu mortem Christi testarentur, 2. vt esset veluti monitorium quoddam, quo fidem suam excitarent, qua omnia mala depellebant. Nullibi vero meminit eius superstitionis, qua hodie externo signo vim & efficaciam ad supernaturales effectus attribuunt; nullibi sacrum illud & venerabile celebrat & agnoscit. Hic abusus Chrysostomo aliisque superioribus Patribus plane ignotus fuit.
units.tr: III. The praises with which Chrysostom extols the glory of the cross are mere rhetorical flourishes, which do not prove anything but only stir and delight. Further, he does not commend the idolatrous abuse of the sign, or the errors and superstitions attached to this ceremony, but the practice observed piously by the ancient Christians, which was this: (1) that by this solemn ceremony they bore witness to their trust in the cross or death of Christ; (2) that it served as a kind of reminder by which they stirred up their faith, through which they drove off all evils. But nowhere does he mention that superstition by which people today attribute power and efficacy for supernatural effects to an external sign; nowhere does he celebrate and acknowledge that sacred and venerable thing. This abuse was entirely unknown to Chrysostom and the other earlier Fathers.

units.la: Ephraem lib. 2. de Pœnit. c. 3. Pingimus, inquit, in fronte, in ianuis atque in frontibus nostris & in ore nostro, & in pectore, & in membris omnibus vivificum signum: armemur in super rabili hac armatura Christianorum. Item, libro de armatura spirit. cap. 2. Scuti vice crucis signo teipsum muni. Validissima enim armatura est.
units.tr: Ephraem, book 2 on Repentance, chapter 3: We paint, he says, on the forehead, on the doors and foreheads of our houses, on our mouths, on our breasts, and on all our limbs, the life-giving sign. Let us be armed with this unconquerable armour of the Christians. Likewise, in the book on the spiritual armour, chapter 2: Protect yourself with the sign of the cross in place of a shield, for it is a most powerful armour.

units.la: Resp. I. Vere de scriptis Ephraemi Syri iudicavit Bellarminus in libro de script. Ecclesia. Opera Ephraemi magis pia, quam docta esse: pietatem spirat, quod huius signi picturam vt symbolum Christianismi & publicam fidei professionem vrget & commendat; à doctrina alienum est, quod signum illud vocat viuificum, ficum, signo effectu Christi proprium tri-buens; quauis si re bene consideres syn-ecdochice locut° videatur, ita vt per signum intellexerit inuocatione Christi cum signo coniuncta, qua gratia Christi viuifica implorabant. Quare facile respondebitur Iesuitae sic ratiocinanti: Signum viuificu est venerabile; At veteres statuerunt signu viuificum. Ergo statuerunt esse venerabile. Signum in se & sua natura viuificu est venerabile. At veteres no asseruerunt signu, ex se & sua natura, viuifica vi pditum esse, sed ex inuocatione fideli, quę cum gratiam viuifica à Christo impetrauit, signu cum inuocatione illa coniunctu ab effectu isto denominatione accepit, & viuificum dicitur est. II. Signum crucis erat extremu symbolum, quod in vita communi, tum ad fidei propriae testificationem, & aliorum aedificationem, tum ad Ethnicorum ludibria elidenda adhiberi solebat.
