Merito igitur vir pius hortatus est Christianos, vt in ianuis, frontibus, ore, ac pectore signum illud pingerent, quia picturam illam absque superstitione & meriti opinione exercebant, efficaciam viuificandi & sanctificandi externae ceremoniae non affingebant, sed fidei, quam tum precibus declarabant, & magis ac magis excitabant, tum ceremonia illa testabantur, omnem virtutem & operationem esse propriam significabant. Hæc enim est quæ vincit mundum, ideoque insuperabilis illa armatura, qua qui præditi sunt, adversus omnes spirituales malitias muniti sunt & consistere possunt. Superstitiones & errores quibus in papatu hoc signum est conflatum, hic neverbo quidem attinguntur.
units.tr: Answer. I. Bellarmine rightly judged the writings of Ephraem the Syrian in his book on ecclesiastical writers: the works of Ephraem are more pious than learned; they breathe piety in that he urges and commends the painting of this sign as the symbol of Christianity and a public profession of faith; but it is foreign to sound doctrine that he calls that sign life-giving, attributing to the sign the effect that belongs to Christ. Yet if you consider the matter carefully, the language seems to be synecdochical, so that by the sign he understood the invocation of Christ joined with the sign, by which they implored the life-giving grace of Christ. Therefore one can easily answer the Jesuit who reasons thus: The life-giving sign is venerable; but the ancients affirmed a life-giving sign; therefore they affirmed it to be venerable. A sign in itself and by its own nature is venerable. But the ancients did not assert that the sign, of itself and by its own nature, was endowed with life-giving power, but that it came from faithful invocation, which, having obtained life-giving grace from Christ, received from that effect the name of life-giving when joined with that invocation. II. The sign of the cross was the outward symbol that was commonly used in ordinary life, both to witness one's own faith and to edify others, and to repel the mockery of the heathen. Rightly, therefore, this godly man urged Christians to paint that sign on their doors, foreheads, mouths and breasts, because they practised that painting without superstition or the opinion of merit; they did not ascribe to the external ceremony the power to give life and sanctify, but by it they declared their faith, which they expressed in prayers and increasingly stirred up, and by that ceremony they bore witness, signifying that all virtue and operation is proper to God alone. For this is the faith that overcomes the world, and therefore that unconquerable armour, with which those who are equipped are fortified against all spiritual wickedness and are able to stand firm. The superstitions and errors by which this sign has been encrusted in Papistry are not touched on here even in a single word.

units.la: B. Antonius, vt refert Athanasius in vita eiusdem Antonii Contra omnes terrores imbebat solo crucis signaculo tutos esse Monachos.
units.tr: Blessed Antony, as Athanasius relates in the life of the same Antony: Against all terrors he used to teach that monks are safe by the sign of the cross alone.

units.la: Resp. I. Scriptum illud de vita Antonii est dubiæ fidei, & nuper operibus Athanasii additum fuit. Testatur quidem Hieronymus & Augustinus, Athanasium scripsisse vitam Antonii Abbatis, sed quod ea quæ nunc exstat, sicut illa ipsa cuius meminit Hieronymus & Augustinus non est verisimile, cum in multis sit nugatoria. II. Non simpliciter & per se cremoniam signi crucis intelligit, quasi eius virtute tuti fuerint Monachi contra omnes terrores, sed
units.tr: Answer. I. That writing about the life of Antony is of doubtful faith, and was added recently to the works of Athanasius. Jerome and Augustine do indeed testify that Athanasius wrote a life of the abbot Antony, but that the one now extant is not likely to be the very one Jerome and Augustine mention, since it is in many places trifling. II. He does not understand the ceremony of the sign of the cross simply and in itself, as though the monks were safe against all terrors by its power, but

units.la: In lib. de Script. Eccles. lib. 8. confess. c. 6 ed synecdochicè fidem Christi eiusque professionem externam quam signo crucis testabatur. Hæc enim tantæ virtutis, ut nos adversus omnes terrores tutos reddat, sed quid ista ad superstitiosam crucis veneratiónem?
units.tr: in the book on ecclesiastical writers, and in the eighth book of the Confessions, chapter 6, he understands synecdochically the faith in Christ and its external profession, which he witnessed by the sign of the cross. For this has such power that it makes us safe against all terrors; but what has this to do with superstitious veneration of the cross?

units.la: Palladius in historia Lausiaca capite scribit. Sanctum senem quendam, cum vidisset in puteo aspidem, signo crucis munitum illum puteum, ac deinde sine timore hausisse aquam & bibisse.
units.tr: Palladius, in the Lausiac History, chapter , writes that a certain holy old man, when he saw an asp in a well, fortified that well with the sign of the cross, and then drew water from it without fear and drank.

units.la: Respond. Palladius hic fuit Galatà Ruffini æqualis & amicus, tum ab Hieronymo in Epistola ad Ctesiphontem, tum ab Epiphanio in Epistola ad Iohannem Hierosolymitanum, quæ extat in secundo tomo, reprehenditur, teste Bellarmino. Molanus etiam præfatione in Martyr c. 20. excuso Louanii anno 1568. Palladium inter scriptores non satis probatæ autoritatis numerat: Sanè cuiuis legenti manifestum est, historiam eius Lausiacam farragínem esse anilium fabularum, quæ nullam prebet legentibus utilitatem. Quare eius autoritatem non agnoscimus.
units.tr: Answer. This Palladius was a contemporary and friend of Rufinus of Galatia, and is rebuked both by Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon and by Epiphanius in his letter to John of Jerusalem, which is found in the second volume, as Bellarmine testifies. Molanus too, in his preface to the Martyrology, chapter 20, printed at Louvain in 1568, counts Palladius among writers of insufficiently proven authority. Indeed it is plain to anyone who reads it that his Lausiac History is a farrago of old wives' tales, which offers readers no benefit. Therefore we do not acknowledge his authority.

units.la: II. Si vera est historia, negamus virtute crucis curatum esse puteum. Totum hoc opus fuit Christi, invocationem fidelem externo crucis signo expres-sam acceptantis,& exaudientis. Nimis familiaris error hic est Bellarmini, vt opus Christi proprium, invocatione, professioneq; eius impetratum, externae ceremoniae,ab hominibus institutę, tribuat.
units.tr: II. If the story is true, we deny that the well was cleansed by the power of the cross. The whole work was Christ's, who accepts and hears the faithful invocation expressed by the external sign of the cross. This is a very familiar error of Bellarmine's, to attribute to human-instituted external ceremony a work proper to Christ, obtained by invocation and profession of him.

units.la: Theodoretus in historia religiosa passim meminit crucis & virtutis eius.
units.tr: Theodoret, in his Religious History, makes frequent mention of the cross and its power.

units.la: Respond. Virtus illa, cuius meminit Theodoretus fuit ex invocatione nominis Christi, quae signum professionis additum habebat. Signi per se nulla est virtus, si quam habet, ea vel est a natura, vel ex pacto cum Daemone, vel ex divina institutione. Non ex natura, nec expacto cum Daemone, vt ipse Bellarminus cap.seq.fatetur; nec denique ex divina institutione. Nusquam enim eius institutio sancita est praecepto Dei, promissione vel exemplo. Ergo nullam habet.
units.tr: Answer. That power which Theodoret mentions came from the invocation of the name of Christ, which had the sign of profession added to it. The sign in itself has no power; if it has any, that comes either from nature, or from a pact with the Devil, or from divine institution. Not from nature, nor from a pact with the Devil, as Bellarmine himself confesses in the following chapter; nor finally from divine institution. For its institution is nowhere sanctioned by a command of God, a promise, or an example. Therefore it has no power.

units.la: Ambrosius sermone 43. Hortatur vt omnia opera a signo crucis incipiamus. Et serm. 90. recitantur verba S. Agnetis dicentis. Posuit signum in faciem meam, & nullum praeter eum amatorem admittam, id enim est signum crucis quo dedicamur Dei.
units.tr: Ambrose, sermon 43: He urges that we begin all our works with the sign of the cross. And in sermon 90 the words of Saint Agnes are quoted, saying: She placed the sign on my face, and I will admit no lover besides him, for that is the sign of the cross by which we are dedicated to God.

units.la: Resp. Primus locus synecdochice intelitelligendus: hortatur vt opera nostra incipiamus à signo crucis, id est, ab invocatione nominis Christi, coniuncta cum hoc professionis signo. Nam debemus inquit, surgentes gratias agere & diei opus in signo facere saluatoris. Requirit ergo gratiarum actionem, id est, invocationem coniunctā cum signo professionis Christi. Erat enim tunc signum crucis ordinaria ceremonia quam inter orandum adhibebant ad fidem suam testificandam, & excitandam. Quod ad alterum attinet, I. Sermo iste S. Agnetis est dubiæ fidei teste ipso Bellarmino.
units.tr: Answer. The first passage must be understood synecdochically: he urges that we begin our works with the sign of the cross, that is, with the invocation of the name of Christ joined with this sign of profession. For, he says, we ought, rising, to give thanks and to do the work of the day under the sign of the Saviour. He therefore requires the giving of thanks, that is, invocation joined with the sign of the profession of Christ. For the sign of the cross was then the ordinary ceremony that they used in praying, to bear witness to and stir up their faith. As for the second, I. this sermon of Saint Agnes is of doubtful faith, as Bellarmine himself testifies.

units.la: I. Locus est de Baptismo intelligen-dus, quo tunc signari vel consignari vulgo dicebantur, idque à signo crucis, quod tunc in administratione baptismi adhibebatur, ita vt signum, non crucis, sed Baptismi, quo Deo consecramur, intelligat. Signum crucis enim non poterit sibi ipsis. Loquitur autem de tali signo, quo ab alio fuit in nomine Christi consignata. Ergo non de signo crucis.
units.tr: I. The passage is to be understood of Baptism, by which people were then commonly said to be signed or sealed, and that from the sign of the cross, which was then used in the administration of baptism; so that the sign meant is not the sign of the cross but of Baptism, by which we are consecrated to God. For a person cannot sign himself. But the passage speaks of such a sign as was impressed by another in the name of Christ. Therefore it is not about the sign of the cross.

units.la: Hieronymus in epist. ad Demetriadem: Claudas cubiculum pectoris, crebro signaculo crucis munias frontem tuam. Item ad Eustochium. Ad omnem incessum manus ingat Domini Crucem.
units.tr: Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias: Shut the chamber of your breast, and often fortify your forehead with the seal of the cross. Likewise, to Eustochium: At every step let him take the cross of the Lord.

units.la: R
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Resp. I. Non diffiteor temporibus Hieronymi fuisse in more positum, ut crucis signaculo frontem signarent, verum non fecere animo demerendi sibi Deum, sed ut se Christianos & professores Christi crucifixi ostenderent, quae Iudei & gentes contumeliis afficiebant, propter mortem illam, quam in cruce sustinuit. Haec Christianorum istius temporis consuetudo pia fuit, sed nunc idololatrica, ideoque non ferenda. II. Non iubet Hieronymus animam muniri, sed frontem, quae sedes est pudoris, animi sciuit fide muniri. Frontem vero tanquam pudoris sedem muniri vult, tum ut testaretur, se non erubescere crucem Christi, quam Ethnici pro fatuitate habebant, tum ut in fiducia mortis Christi semet magis confirmarent. Eodem modo ad omnem incessum iubet pingi crucem, non superstitiose ad gratiam Dei demerendam, & diabolos virtute crucis fugandos, sed religiose ad fiduciam passionis & mortis Christi excitandam & testificandam.
units.tr: Answer. I. I do not deny that in Jerome's time it was the custom to mark the forehead with the seal of the cross; but they did not do so with the intention of earning God's favour, but to show that they were Christians and professors of Christ crucified, whom Jews and Gentiles insulted on account of that death which he suffered on the cross. That custom of the Christians of that time was pious, but now it is idolatrous and therefore not to be tolerated. II. Jerome does not bid us fortify the soul but the forehead, which is the seat of shame; he wishes the forehead, as the seat of shame, to be fortified with the sign of faith, both so that one may testify that one is not ashamed of the cross of Christ, which the heathen regarded as folly, and so that one may be more firmly confirmed in trust in the death of Christ. In the same way he bids the cross be painted at every step, not superstitiously to earn God's grace, and to put the devils to flight by the power of the cross, but religiously to stir up and testify to trust in the passion and death of Christ.

units.la: Augustinus tract. 118. in Ioannem ad finem. Quid est quod omnes noverunt signum Christi, nisi crux Christi? quod signum nisi adhibeatur sive frontibus credentium, sive ipsi aquae qua
units.tr: Augustine, tractate 118 on John, at the end: "What is it that everyone knows as the sign of Christ, except the cross of Christ? What sign, unless it is applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to the water by which they are regenerated, or to the oil with which they are anointed with chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are fed, is rightly completed in any of these?"

units.la: qua [illegible, ~10 letters] regenerantur, sive oleo, quo chrismate inunguntur, sive sacrificio, quo alluntur, nihil eorum rite perficitur. Item l. 1. Confess. c. 11. signari iam signo crucis & condiebar sale Christi.
units.tr: Likewise, Confessions book 1, chapter 11: "I was already signed with the sign of the cross and seasoned with the salt of Christ." [qua [illegible, ~10 letters] regenerantur]

units.la: Resp. Non diffiteor Christianos temporibus Augustini, & ante illa tempora signum crucis in communi vita vsurpasse, tum ad fidei suae testificationem, tum ad aliorum aedificationem. Agnosco etiam ritum hunc in sacramenta inductum esse, verum non fuit tanquam obsoleta quaedam ceremonia vsurpatus, sed ad fine, vt efficaciam & operationem crucis Christi, in qua fundata sunt sacramenta, implorarent. Quid hoc ad superstitiones Pontificias? Eas sane nec Augustinus, nec quisquam Patrum alius probauit vnquam. Si signum definiueris ex Augustini & aliorum Patrum sententia, nihil aliud est, quam invocatio quaedam nominis Christi, externo protestionis signo expressa & declarata. Absque tali signo quid recte queat perfici? in publicis & sacris actionibus cum signi visu praesentiam & efficaciam Christi implorabant. In communi vita cum frontes consignabant, Christo sese precibus suis commendabant. Haec spectauit Augustinus, cum dixit, omnia re-
units.tr: Response: I do not deny that Christians in Augustine's time, and before that time, used the sign of the cross in ordinary life, both to testify to their faith and to edify others. I also acknowledge that this rite was introduced into the sacraments, but it was not used as some obsolete ceremony; rather, they sought by it the efficacy and operation of the cross of Christ, on which the sacraments are founded. What has this to do with Papist superstitions? Augustine certainly did not approve of them, nor did any other of the Fathers ever approve them. If you define the sign according to the opinion of Augustine and the other Fathers, it is nothing other than a certain invocation of the name of Christ, expressed and declared by an external sign of profession. Without such a sign, what could be rightly accomplished? In public and sacred actions they implored the presence and efficacy of Christ while looking at the sign; in ordinary life, when they signed their foreheads, they commended themselves to Christ by their prayers. This is what Augustine had in view when he said that all things...

units.la: R 4 ... hoc (s)le hoc signo persici. Ne putes Augustinũ ad eò stultũ, & superstitiosum fuisse, vt crediderit omnia virtute & operatione signi huius recte persici. Fidei in Christũ tribuit hanc laudem, quem signo adhibito inuocabant, & profitebantur.
units.tr: ... that all things are accomplished by this sign. Do not think that Augustine was so foolish and superstitious as to believe that everything is rightly accomplished by the virtue and operation of this sign. He attributed this praise to faith in Christ, whom they invoked and professed with the sign applied.

units.la: B. Martinus apud Sulpitium. Ego, inquit, signo crucis, non clypeo protectus aut galea, cuneos penetrabo securus.
units.tr: St Martin, according to Sulpicius: "I," he says, "protected by the sign of the cross, not by shield or helmet, will penetrate the wedges of the enemy securely."

units.la: Resp. Intelligit se penetraturum hostium cuneos, non signi virtute, & adoratione crucis, sed virtute & adoratione Christi; non cruce, sed Christum precibus suis implorabant, & signo crucis externo profitebantur. Cum signo crucis intelligenda & coniungenda est res significata, inuocatio sc. nominis Christi, quæ duo iniquè disiungit Bellarmin.
units.tr: Response: He understands that he will penetrate the wedges of the enemy not by the virtue and adoration of the sign of the cross, but by the virtue and adoration of Christ. They implored Christ by their prayers, and professed him by the external sign of the cross. The thing signified must be understood together with the sign of the cross: namely, the invocation of the name of Christ. Bellarmine wrongly separates these two things, which ought to be joined.

units.la: Prudentius in hymno ante somnum: Fac cum vocante somno Castum pedis cubile, Frontem locum cordis Crucis figura signes. Crux pellet omne crimen Fugiunt crucem tenebræ. Tali dicata signo Mens fluctuare nescit.
units.tr: Prudentius, in the hymn before sleep: Grant that, when sleep calls, I may have a chaste bed for my feet; sign my forehead, the place of the heart, with the figure of the cross. The cross drives out every crime; shadows flee from the cross. Dedicated by such a sign, the mind knows not how to waver.

units.la: Ref. Fronte iubet signare signo crucis, i.e. inuocatione fideli signo crucis ex-pressâ ressa & confirmata semet Christo co-nendare. Rursum hic à Bellarmino se-tarantur, quæ coniungi debebant: sub igno crucis synecdochicè debet intel-ligi inuocatio nominis Christi, cū qua coniungebant signum, ad fidei suæ testi-ficationem & confirmationem. Non crux pellebat omne crimen, non fuga-bat crux tenebras, sua quadam virtute & efficacia, aut ex opere operato, sed vir-tus Christi fidelem inuocationem & professionem sui nominis acceptantis & exaudientis. Effectus Christi proprius, malè tribuitur externæ ceremoniæ humanitus institutæ.
units.tr: Reply: He bids them sign the forehead with the sign of the cross, that is, to commend themselves to Christ by a faithful invocation, expressed by the sign of the cross, and confirmed and strengthened. Here again Bellarmine separates what ought to be joined. In the phrase "sign of the cross" the invocation of the name of Christ must be understood by synecdoche, which was joined with the sign, for the testifying and confirming of one's faith. It was not the cross that drove out every crime, nor did the cross put shadows to flight by some virtue and efficacy of its own, or by the work performed; rather, it was the virtue of Christ, who accepts and hears the faithful invocation and profession of his name. The proper effect of Christ is wrongly ascribed to an external ceremony instituted by human beings.

units.la: Paulinus natali 8. S. Felicis. Nos crucis invicta signum & confessio munit Armatique Deo mentem non quærimus arma Corporis, & quanquam membris videamur inermes Arma tamen gerimus quibus & sub pace serena Contra incorporeos animis decernimus hostes.
units.tr: Paulinus, on the birthday of St Felix 8: The invincible sign and confession of the cross fortifies us; and we do not seek the weapons of the body for a mind armed by God. Although we seem unarmed in our limbs, yet we bear arms by which, under a calm peace, we resolve against the incorporeal enemies of souls.

units.la: Respon. expresse hic cum signo crucis coniungit fidelem Christi crucifixi confessionem, absque qua signum cru-cis cis otiosa & inutilis est ceremonia. Confessionem hanc significabat & testabatur signum crucis. Ideoque omnes illi effectus, qui confessionis sunt, signo ipsi metonymice tribuuntur. Neque enim externo signo, sed confessioni Christi crucifixi effectus hi accepti feredi sunt; ita ut haec vere illos munierit adversus hostes incorporeos. No aliter egia crux inuicta dicitur ac censetur, quasi ratione fidei & fidelis confessionis. Fide enim fidelique confessione mundum vincimus, omniaque mala depellimus.
units.tr: Response: Here he expressly joins the sign of the cross with the faithful confession of Christ crucified, without which the sign of the cross is an idle and useless ceremony. The sign of the cross signified and testified this confession. Therefore all those effects which belong to the confession are attributed to the sign itself by metonymy. For these effects are to be ascribed not to the external sign but to the confession of Christ crucified; so it is this that truly fortified them against incorporeal enemies. In the same way the cross is called and reckoned "invincible", as by reason of faith and faithful confession. For by faith and faithful confession we conquer the world and drive away all evils.

units.la: Tertium Argumentum.
units.tr: Third Argument.

units.la: Tertio probatur ex miraculis signo crucis factis, quae deinceps Bellarminus prolixe recitat.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is proved from miracles wrought by the sign of the cross, which Bellarmine then recites at length.

units.la: Resp. I. Miracula quae ad crucis signum edita narrantur, pleraque fabulosa sunt & ficta, atque aliena a Christiana religione, qualia reperire licet apud Gregorium Magnum in dialogis & plurimorum Monachorum historiis atque libris. Fuere enim teste Ludovico Viue qui magnae pietatis loco ducerent, mendaciola pro religione confingere. Cuius pietatis? Canus idem concludit. Ait enim: Eos qui fictè & fallaciter historiam Ecclesiasticam scribunt, totam narra-
units.tr: Response I. Most of the miracles narrated as performed by the sign of the cross are fabulous and made up, and foreign to the Christian religion. Such are to be found in Gregory the Great's Dialogues and in the histories and books of many monks. For, according to Ludovicus Vives, they regarded it as a mark of great piety to fabricate little lies for the sake of religion. Of what piety? Canus draws the same conclusion. For he says: Those who write church history falsely and deceitfully direct their whole narrative

units.la: Locorum Theol. II. cap. 6. narrationem suam dirigere ad quaestum aut ad errorem. Id genus honorum intellexit Paulus, 1. Tim. 6. qui quaestu habent pietatem, Multis eiusmodi impostoribus abundavit olim Ecclesia, qui zelo huius pietatis accensi, miracula non scripserunt modo, sed etiam fabricarunt. Nicolaus Lyranus in Comment. supra historiam Apocryphaм, seu fabulam Belis & Draconis, idem confirmat. Quemadmodum, inquit, sacerdotes Babylonis abusi sunt populo in cultu Draconis; Similiter aliquando in Ecclesia fieri maximam deceptionem populi in miraculis fictis a sacerdotibus, vel iis adhaerescentibus propter lucrum temporale.
units.tr: ...to gain or to error. (Loci Theol. II, chapter 6.) Paul understood men of this kind in 1 Timothy 6, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain. The Church of old abounded in many such impostors, who, fired with zeal for this piety, not only wrote down miracles but also fabricated them. Nicholas of Lyra, in his commentary on the apocryphal history, or fable, of Bel and the Dragon, confirms the same: As the priests of Babylon abused the people in the worship of the Dragon, so it sometimes happens in the Church that the greatest deception of the people occurs through fictitious miracles, produced by priests or those who adhere to them, for temporal gain.

units.la: II. Demus aliqua, quae narrantur, vera fuisse: ea tamen non virtutem quandam spiritualem ipsius signi demonstrant, nec eius adorationem probant. Quia non signi, sed Christi adorationem fidelem, signo crucis externo expressam, acceptantis & exaudientis virtute edita sunt, idque non ad signi crucis venerationem probandam, aliisque commendandam, sed ad fideles in fide Christi confirmandos, & infidelium ludibria retundenda. Quoties igitur miracula commemorantur ad signum crucis edita fyncdochicè intelligito, ea non signo solitario, sed fideli inuocatione & professione Christi, signo externo declarata, à Christo impetrata esse III. Miracula eiusmodi Deus extra ordinem, quoties ipsi visum fuit, ad gloriam suam & Ecclesiæ ædificationem exhibuit; ex iis igitur ordinariam signi huius naturam, virtutem, & venerationem, qui metiatur, impius est.
units.tr: II. Grant that some of the things narrated were true. Even so, they do not demonstrate any spiritual virtue of the sign itself, nor do they prove its adoration. For they were performed not by the adoration of the sign alone, but by the faithful adoration of Christ, expressed by the external sign of the cross, accepted and heard by his virtue; and this not to prove the veneration of the sign of the cross or to commend it to others, but to confirm the faithful in faith in Christ and to repel the mockery of unbelievers. Therefore, whenever miracles are recorded as performed by the sign of the cross, they are to be understood by synecdoche: they were obtained from Christ, not by the sign alone, but by a faithful invocation and profession of Christ, declared by the external sign. III. God has displayed miracles of this kind beyond the ordinary course, whenever it pleased him, for his glory and the edification of the Church. Therefore whoever measures the ordinary nature, virtue, and veneration of this sign by them is impious.

units.la: AVDIAMVS NVNC PATRVM testimonia, de miraculis signo crucis editis.
units.tr: Let us now consider the testimonies of the Fathers concerning miracles performed by the sign of the cross.

units.la: Tertullianus initio Scorpiaci dicit, Christianos signando vel adiurando, non solum Christianis, sed etiam Ethnicis saepè prodesse.
units.tr: Tertullian, at the beginning of the Scorpiace, says: by signing or adjuring, we Christians often help not only Christians but also heathens.

units.la: Respons. I. Non loquitur Tertullianus de signatione crucis, sed de signatione id est compressione seu iuclusione bestiæ (Scorpii) ne lese dimoueat. Idloci ipsius recitatio manifestum faciet. Nobis fides est, inquit, Tertullianus præsidium, si non & ipsa percutitur diffidentia, signandi statim & adiurandi & ungendi bestiæ calcem. Hoc denique modo etiam Etiam Ethnicis saepe subuenimus, donati à Deo potestate, quam Apostolus dedicauit, cum morsum viperae spreuit. Aperte signatione explicat de adiuratione ad expressionem puris seu saniei, quae dein ad calce à bestia ad morsam adhibebatur. Hanc interpretatione Franciscus Iunius nobis aperuit, qui sententiam loci sic expressit. Nobis, inquit, fides praesidium est, qua confidimus nos bestiam signaturos nefe dimoueat, & adiuraturos ut succum & pus ipsius expressum adhibeamus, & unctuos calce qua admorderit, bestia id est pure & sanie bestiae: hocaute impedit diffidentia signandi, adiurandi, & vngendi, id est, si is quae petit scorpius, diffidat se habere eu, & coercere posse. Signare hic est sub sigillo includere & clausum tenere. Adiurare est χυλαν η χυλιζει in ius & sucu cogere eu que exprimere, aiure quod est χυμος. II. Etsi locus de signatione crucis esset intelligendus: non tamen virtus quaedam & efficacia nudae ac solitariae signationi tribuitur, sed fidei miraculorum, quam inuocatione nominis Christi, cum crucis signo coniuncta, testaban tur: Hunc sensum textus ipse ostendit.
units.tr: Reply 1. Tertullian is not speaking of the sign of the cross but of the signing, that is, the pressing down or confining, of the scorpion, so that it does not harm. The passage itself will make this plain. Faith, says Tertullian, is our protection, if distrust does not also strike us down, of signing at once, and adjuring, and anointing the scorpion's sting. In this way we often help even heathens, having been given by God the power which the Apostle shook off when he shrugged off the viper's bite. He clearly explains the signing as the adjuration by which the poison or matter was drawn out, which was then applied to the bite. Francis Junius has made this interpretation clear to us, and he expressed the sense of the passage thus: Faith, he says, is our protection, by which we trust that we shall seal up the beast so that it does not harm, and adjure it, so that we may apply its juice and pus, drawn out, and anoint the place the beast has bitten with the beast's own pus and matter. Distrust prevents this signing, adjuring and anointing, that is, if the scorpion that attacks us, we distrust that we have it in our power and can restrain it. To sign here means to enclose under a seal and keep shut up. To adjure is to force out the juice [χυλᾶν ἢ χυλίζειν] and squeeze out the sap, the juice [χυμός] being what is pressed out. II. Even if the passage were to be understood of the sign of the cross, a power and efficacy is not attributed to the bare and solitary signing, but to the faith which the miracles attested, joined with the invocation of Christ's name. The passage itself shows this sense.

units.la: Nam hoc modo, inquit, Ethnicis saepe subuenimus donati a Deo ea potestate, qua Apostolus dedicauit &c. Ergo non a simplici signatione crune crucis, sed tali, quæ potestatem faciendi miracula & nominis Christi invocationem coniunctam habuit, hoc auxilium Ethnicorum profectum dicitur.
units.tr: For in this way, he says, we often help heathens, having been given by God that power which the Apostle shook off, etc. Therefore this help to heathens is said to have come not from a simple signing with the sign of the cross, but from such a sign as had the power of working miracles joined with the invocation of Christ's name.

units.la: Lactantius lib. 4. cap. 27. dicit præsente Christiano, qui crucem fronte signauerat, Diabolus no ausu Imperatori poscenti respondere.
units.tr: Lactantius, book 4, chapter 27, says that when a Christian who had marked his forehead with the cross was present, the devil did not dare to answer the emperor who questioned him.

units.la: Resp. I. Nemo est qui ignorat Dæmonem callidum esse, & fallacem ac mendacem spiritum, qui fingat se timere signum crucis, vt faciat nos externo signo crucis magis confidere quam ipsi Christo.
units.tr: Reply 1. Everyone knows that the Devil is a cunning, deceitful and lying spirit, who pretends to fear the sign of the cross so that we may put more trust in the external sign of the cross than in Christ himself.

units.la: II. Series contextus indicat vim crucis hic non commendari, sed piæ invocationis & professionis nominis Christi efficaciam describi. Sic enim primo disserit. Quanto terrore sit dæmonibus hoc signum sciet, qui viderit, quatenus adiurati per Christum de corporibus, quæ obsederunt, fugiunt. Apparet hinc non signo, sed inuocationi nominis Christi, quæ signum habebat adiunctum, omne vim acceptam ferri. Paulo post. Christi sectatores, inquit, eosdem spiritus inquinatos de hominibus & nomine Magistri sui & signo passionis excludunt. Quilibet æquus rerum æstimator intelligit, non modo signo vim depellendi dæmones adscribi, sed piæ orationi, quæ fit in nomine Magistri, id est,
units.tr: II. The sequence of the context shows that the power of the cross is not commended here, but the efficacy of pious invocation and of the profession of Christ's name is described. For he first argues thus: How great a terror the sign is to demons, he will know who has seen them flee from bodies they have possessed when they are exorcised through Christ. It appears from this that all the power is ascribed not to the sign but to the invocation of Christ's name, to which the sign was attached. A little later: The followers of Christ, he says, drive out the same unclean spirits from people by the name of their Master and by the sign of the passion. Any fair judge of things understands that the power of driving out demons is ascribed not only to the sign, but to the pious prayer offered in the name of the Master, that is,

units.la: Christi crucifixi, cui signum passionis ad fidem in mortem Christi testandam adiungebatur. Signum ergo ab ipsa re significata non est diuellendum, vt pote quae hic expresse coniunguntur.
units.tr: of Christ crucified, to whom the sign of the passion was added to bear witness to faith in Christ's death. The sign therefore must not be separated from the thing signified, since here they are expressly joined together.

units.la: Epiphanius haeres: 30. scribit. Quendam Iosephum nondum Christianum signo crucis Daemones expulisse, & deinde Christiani effectu, eodem signo incantationes Iudaeorum destruxisse.
units.tr: Epiphanius, Heresy 30, writes: A certain Joseph, not yet a Christian, drove out demons with the sign of the cross, and afterwards, having become a Christian, with the same sign destroyed the incantations of the Jews.

units.la: Resp. I. Nego virtute signi daemones expulsos & fugatos esse, sed ad crucis signationem sponte cesserunt, vt superstitiosa & idololatrica crucis veneratione in hominum animis confirmaret.
units.tr: Reply 1. I deny that demons were expelled and put to flight by the power of the sign; they gave way at the signing of the cross of their own accord, so that by the superstitious and idolatrous veneration of the cross it might be confirmed in men's minds.

units.la: II. Nego et incantationes Iudaeorum signo crucis fuisse destructas. Fluxit hic effectus ab invocatione Christi & virtute fidei, quam illi signo crucis testabantur, & Christus ita acceptabat, probabatque vt destructione, incantationum eahonoraret.
units.tr: II. I also deny that the incantations of the Jews were destroyed by the sign of the cross. This effect flowed from the invocation of Christ and from the power of the faith which they attested by the sign of the cross, and Christ so accepted and approved it that he honoured it by the destruction of the incantations.

units.la: Atq; hoc est q Iacob. de Orat. dicit, Oratio iusti multum valet. Vbi de signo a quoqua Apostolorum tale quid pronunciatur?
units.tr: And this is what James says in his chapter on prayer: The prayer of a righteous man avails much. Where is anything of this kind pronounced by any of the Apostles about the sign?

units.la: Nihil aliud est signum crucis quam externa ceremonia, neq; a Christo sed ab hominibus instituta. Vnde tanta illi vis inesset ad destruendas incantationes?
units.tr: The sign of the cross is nothing other than an external ceremony, instituted not by Christ but by men. How could it have such great power to destroy incantations?

units.la: Nazianzenus Orat. I. Iulian. scribit ipsum Iulianum licet Ethnicum cum spectra speƈtra quæda viderët, dum necromantici sua mysteria operarentur, signo crucis se ipsum munisse, & mox speƈtra omnia euanuisse.
units.tr: Gregory Nazianzen, in his first Oration against Julian, writes that Julian himself, although a heathen, when he saw certain phantoms while the necromancers were performing their rites, fortified himself with the sign of the cross, and at once all the phantoms vanished.

units.la: Resp. I. Refert Nazianzenus Iulia num cū nesanda quædam sacra celebra- ret, & multi dæmones in eo loco, quo illa peragebantur, conuenirent, nonni- hil territum & suim toblitu, se cruce si- gnasse, vti solebat, cum esset Christia- nus, & tunc omnes cacodæmonas dissu gisse. Sed dic quæso, num virtute signa- tionis, fugatos opinaris? Non opinor equidem. Diabolus, prout est mendax & impostor, fugam tantum simulauit: reuera non est fugatus. II. separat Bellar minus quæ Nazianzenus coniungit; co memorat is, signo crucis Iulianum se confignasse adversus terrores, eumq; quæ persequebatur, in auxilium asciuisse. Indicat hæc narratio non signi, sed Christi au- xilio profligatos fuisse cacodæmonas. Deus enim nonnunquam incredulos & persecutores miraculosis beneficiis ornat & afficit, vt incredulitatis eos da- mnet ac conuincat reddatque inexcu- sabiles.
units.tr: Reply 1. Gregory Nazianzen relates that when Julian was celebrating certain unspeakable rites, and many demons gathered in the place where they were performed, he was somewhat terrified and out of his wits, and signed himself with the cross, as he was accustomed to do when he was a Christian, and then all the evil demons fled. But tell me, I ask you, do you think they were put to flight by the power of the signing? I do not think so. The Devil, being a liar and an impostor, merely pretended to flee; he was not really put to flight. II. Bellarmine separates what Gregory joins together. He mentions that Julian signed himself with the cross against the terrors, and called on the one he was pursuing to help him. This narrative indicates that the cacodemons were routed not by the sign but by the help of Christ. For God sometimes adorns and favours unbelievers and persecutors with miraculous benefits, so that he may condemn and convict them of unbelief and render them inexcusable.

units.la: Nyssenus in vita Gregorii Tauma- turgi scribit, diaconum eius signo crucis munitum exiuisse noctu incolumem ex balneis inter iter innumerabilia spectra. Ex quibus balneis nemo unquam vivus exiuerat eorum, qui no- tu intrauerant.
units.tr: Gregory of Nyssa, in the life of Gregory the Wonder-worker, writes that his deacon, fortified with the sign of the cross, came out safely by night from the baths, through countless phantoms. Of those who had gone into those baths unaware, none ever came out alive.

units.la: Resp. Hæc Diaconi fortuna fuit vel impostura Dæmonis, vel fidei & inuocationis Christi signo crucis expressæ, effectu. Vera enim profligatio Dæmonum, quæ sine fictione peragitur, ita ut Sathanas cedere cogatur, nolit velit, idque cum suo & Christi gloria, soli Christi virtute administratur, & fide ac preces requirit: Ad fictam vero dæmonis profligationem, fide & precib, opus non est, eoque superstitionem tantum pa-rit & confirmat. Quare hæc ficta fuit diaboli cessio; sin vera, fide & seria invocatione Christi, quam Diaconus crucis signaculo testatus est, impetrata fuit.
units.tr: Reply. This was the deacon's good fortune, either the trickery of the Devil or the effect of faith and of the invocation of Christ expressed by the sign of the cross. For a true putting to flight of demons, which is carried out without pretence, so that Satan is compelled to give way whether he likes it or not, and this to his own loss and to Christ's glory, is accomplished by the power of Christ alone, and requires faith and prayers. But for a feigned putting to flight of the demon, there is no need of faith and prayer, and so it only produces and confirms superstition. Hence this was a feigned yielding of the Devil; but if it was a true one, it was obtained by faith and earnest invocation of Christ, which the deacon attested by the seal of the cross.

units.la: Athanasius in vita Antonii. Hieronymus in vita Pauli primi Eremitæ. Theodoretus lib. 5. historiarum cap. 21. & Gregorius lib. 3. dialog. cap. 7. multa scribunt miracula, quæ ad solum crucis signum Deus fecit, ac potissimum in dæmonum expulsione.
units.tr: Athanasius in the life of Antony. Jerome in the life of Paul the first hermit. Theodoret, Histories, book 5, chapter 21, and Gregory, Dialogues, book 3, chapter 7, write of many miracles which God performed by the sign of the cross alone, and especially in the expulsion of demons.

units.la: Respon. I. Non negamus aliquando ad signum crucis diabolum revera expulsum fuisse, sed vis expellendi dæmones tunc non resedit in cruce, sed in Christo, à quo per fidem & invocationem signo crucis declaratam beneficium expulsionis Christiani impetrarūt, adeo vt falsa sit Bellar. assertio, ad solum crucis signū multa miracula fecisse Deum. Non ea fecit ad solum signum crucis, sed ad fidem, & fidelem orationē signo crucis testatam, iuxta illud Marci credenti omnia sunt possibilia, id est, nihil est quod credens à Deo nō possit impetrare, modo ad Dei gloriam & salutem nostram faciat II. Ipse Bellar. agnoscit, ipsū Deū fecisse ista miracula. Deo igitur adoratio competit, non signo. Quod si signo dicas impetrata miracula, falleris. Neq; enim diuinitus signum est institutum, vt per illud beneficia à Deo impetrarem. Fide & oratione opus est ad veram dæmonū expulsionē, id est eam, qua Diabolus cedere cogitur, nolit velit, idque cum damno suo & gloria Christi. Alias scio multos olim expulisse dæmones, sed cū dæmonum cōmodo, & detrimento gloriæ Christi. Hæc expulsio vera non est, nec vere agitur, neq; fide & precatione opus habet. Palladius in historia Lausiaca c. 34. scribit quenda signo crucis munitū in mediis flamis lógo tepore illæsū permansisse.
units.tr: Reply 1. We do not deny that sometimes the devil was really expelled at the sign of the cross, but the power of expelling demons then did not reside in the cross but in Christ, from whom Christians obtained the benefit of expulsion through faith and the invocation declared by the sign of the cross. So Bellarmine's assertion that God worked many miracles by the sign of the cross alone is false. He did not work them by the sign of the cross alone, but by faith and by prayer attested by the sign of the cross, in accordance with the saying of Mark: all things are possible to him who believes, that is, there is nothing that a believer cannot obtain from God, provided he asks for the glory of God and our salvation. II. Bellarmine himself acknowledges that God himself performed these miracles. Adoration is therefore due to God, not to the sign. But if you say the miracles were obtained by the sign, you are mistaken. For God did not institute the sign so that benefits might be obtained from him through it. Faith and prayer are needed for a true expulsion of demons, that is, the kind by which the Devil is compelled to give way whether he likes it or not, and this to his own loss and to Christ's glory. Otherwise I know that many have once driven out demons, but to the advantage of the demons and to the detriment of Christ's glory. Such an expulsion is not true, nor is it truly carried out, nor does it need faith and prayer. Palladius, in the Lausiac History, chapter 34, writes that a certain man, fortified with the sign of the cross, remained unharmed in the midst of flames for a long time.

units.la: Resp. I. Miraculum est dubiæ veritatis, quia cōstat historiā Laufiacā fabulis de sanctorum vitis referta esse II. Detur erumesse miraculum, non tamen in si- no virtus miraculi residebat, sed in Christo; non signi efficacia factu est mi- raculum, sed Christi, quem fide & ordi- aria ceremonia, intrepide fuit profes- sis, coniuncta fideli precatione, quæ ad bona temporalia atq; æterna impetran- da est efficax.
units.tr: Reply. First, it is a miracle of doubtful truth, since it is established that the Lausiac History is full of fables about the lives of the saints. Second, grant that it was a miracle. Yet the power of the miracle did not lie in the sign. It lay in Christ, whom he fearlessly professed with the sign, an ordinary ceremony, joined to faithful prayer, which is effective for obtaining both temporal and eternal good things. The miracle was wrought not by the efficacy of the sign but by Christ's.

units.la: Theodoretus in vita S. Iuliani & S. Marciani scribit, ab utroq; suo tempore signo crucis ingentes dracones occisos Item in vita Aphraatis, & S. Macedonii & S. Petri aliorum scribit, eos signo crucis varios orbos curasse. Quod idem Sulpitius in vita B. Martini, & Hieronymus in vita Hilarionis August. lib. 22. de ciuitate Dei cap. 8. similiter ibunt. Resp. I. Nego virtute signi per draconesoccisos, aut morbos esse pro- igatos. Ad hosce enim effectus produ- endos non est institutū, nec natura & substantia sua idoneū. Fidei, sese per ora- one exeretis, opera & effecta sunt. Nā- ide prosternimus ipsū diabolū, multo agis dracones 1. Pet. 5. fide vincimus undum, 1. Iohan. 5. quid ni & draco- es eius virtute superem? Theod. vero alii scriptores signo hosce effectus ad- ripsere, nō q p per se efficaciā aliquam ontineat, aut exerat, sed quod ex fide S.
units.tr: Theodoret, in the lives of S. Julian and S. Marcian, writes that in their own time huge dragons were killed by the sign of the cross. Likewise, in the lives of Aphraates, S. Macedonius and S. Peter, and of others, he writes that by the sign of the cross they cured various sick people. The same things are related by Sulpicius in the life of St. Martin, by Jerome in the life of Hilarion, and by Augustine, City of God, book 22, chapter 8. Reply. First, I deny that dragons were killed or diseases driven off by the power of the sign. The sign was not instituted to produce these effects, nor is it by its nature and substance fit for them. These are the works and effects of faith exercised through prayer. For by faith we cast down the devil himself, and much more we overcome dragons. (1 Pet. 5; 1 John 5: "by faith we overcome the world"). Why should we not also overcome its dragons by his power? Theodoret and the other writers ascribed these effects to the sign, not because it contains or exerts any efficacy of its own, but because it is administered out of faith S.

units.la: & precibus administretur, quae nisi adsint, signum prorsus res est inanis. Omnis efficacia est fidei, & seriae precationis, ita ut separatim nihil efficiat signum. Fides & precatio sunt illa media, quibus quiduis a Deo, modo ad eius gloriam & salutem nostram faciat, impetratur. In epistola ad Hebraeos recenset Apostolus prolixum catalogum operum mirandorum, quae per fidem designarunt olim sancti viri; precatio vero est veluti ala fidei, qua fides in altum ad Deum sublevat, bonaque tum temporalia, tum aeterna impetrat. Valeat ergo signum, cuius nulla operatio & efficacia est.
units.tr: and prayers, without which the sign is altogether an empty thing. All efficacy belongs to faith and earnest prayer, so that the sign by itself accomplishes nothing. Faith and prayer are the means by which anything at all is obtained from God, provided it is for his glory and our salvation. In the Epistle to the Hebrews the Apostle recounts a long catalogue of wonderful works which holy men once performed through faith. Prayer, moreover, is like the wing of faith, by which faith is lifted up to God and obtains both temporal and eternal good things. So let the sign go hang, since it has no operation or efficacy at all.

units.la: Victor Vticensis lib. 2. de persequut. Vandal. scribit, ab Eugenio Episcopo Catholico cum illuminatum solo crucis signo. Quod si addant vellemus miracula edita post primos quingentos annos, quae referuntur a probatis autoribus, de S. Benedicto, Bernhardo, Francisco, & aliis, nunquam finiremus.
units.tr: Victor of Vita, book 2, On the Vandal Persecution, writes that a blind man was illuminated by Eugenius, the Catholic bishop, by the sign of the cross alone. And if we were willing to add the miracles performed after the first five hundred years, which are reported by approved authors concerning S. Benedict, Bernard, Francis and others, we would never finish.

units.la: Resp. Ex praecedentibus facile colligere licet, quid de hoc insolenti miraculorum praeconio sit iudicandum. I. Miraculorum argumentum nequaquam probat venerationem crucis. Nam cum ad deorum gentilium adorationem multa miracula sint effecta, idololatria et gentilium miraculorum argumentis defendi poterit. No [illegible, ~8 letters]ie plurimorum ægrotorum curationes [illegible, ~3 letters]d deorum implorationè gentiles im- [illegible, ~3 letters]etrarunt? nonne ad idola gëtium mul- [illegible, ~3 letters]a millia ægrotorû sanitati sunt restitu- [illegible, ~3 letters]a? Num sacros & venerabiles Deos gë- [illegible, ~3 letters]ilium? num sacra & venerabilia idola [illegible, ~3 letters]pforum dixeris? II.Illuminatio cæci & [illegible, ~3 letters]ætera miracula, vel fuere impostura dia- [illegible, ~3 letters]oli, quib. hominû mentib. à vero Dei [illegible, ~3 letters]ultu auersis Staurolatriâ fouit & cõfir- [illegible, ~3 letters]nauit: vel si vera fuere miracula, Chrifti [illegible, ~3 letters]irtute facta funt, & fide atq; precatio- [illegible, ~3 letters]ie, non signo crucis impetrata. Apofto- [illegible, ~3 letters]i certè signi virtute & efficacia non eic- [illegible, ~3 letters]ere immundos spiritus, & miracula tâ- [illegible, ~3 letters]a edidere, sed fide & precatione. Et Vti- [illegible, ~3 letters]en fis ille folo signo crucis cæcum illu- [illegible, ~3 letters]ninaffet? Sanctior f. & potetior fuit A- [illegible, ~3 letters]oftolis. Quin si solo signo illuminauit [illegible, ~3 letters]æcû, quid Dei effecit virtus? potetius [illegible, ~3 letters]t Deo signû dixeris? Ogganies, factum [illegible, ~3 letters]ffe miraculum ex Dei virtute, adhibito [illegible, ~3 letters]olo signo. Ergo, inquâ ego, in Deo vis & [illegible, ~3 letters]loria miraculi residebat, nô in signo, ae [illegible, ~3 letters]pinde Deo soli, non signo laus & honor [illegible, ~3 letters]ebetur. Deniq; ex virtute Dei aliquid [illegible, ~3 letters]acere, requirit fidé diuinæ virtutis. Fi- [illegible, ~3 letters]des autè per seriâ precatione exerit suâ [illegible, ~3 letters]fficacia. Aut igitur fide & precibus, nô solo signo miraculum hoc patratum est aut, si solo signo, virtute Dei non effigestu.
units.tr: Reply. From what has been said, it is easy to gather what should be judged about this immoderate boasting of miracles. First, the argument from miracles by no means proves the veneration of the cross. For since many miracles were also wrought for the worship of the gods of the Gentiles, idolatry could be defended by the same arguments from the miracles of the Gentiles. Did not the Gentiles obtain the cure of many sick people by invoking their gods? Were not many thousands of sick people restored to health at the idols of the Gentiles? Would you call the gods of the Gentiles holy and venerable? Would you call the idols of the Gentiles sacred and venerable? Second, the illumination of the blind man and the other miracles were either deceptions of the devil, who by them fostered and confirmed Staurolatry in the minds of men turned away from the true worship of God; or, if they were true miracles, they were done by the power of Christ, and obtained by faith and prayer, not by the sign of the cross. Certainly the Apostles did not cast out unclean spirits and work such great miracles by the power and efficacy of a sign, but by faith and prayer. And would that he had illumined the blind man by the sign of the cross alone! Was he holier and more powerful than the Apostles? Indeed, if he illumined the blind man by the sign alone, what did the power of God accomplish? Would you call the sign more powerful than God? You will concede that the miracle was wrought by the power of God, with the sign alone employed. Therefore, I say, the power and glory of the miracle resided in God, not in the sign, and so praise and honour are owed to God alone, not to the sign. Finally, to do anything by God's power requires faith in divine power, and faith puts forth its efficacy through earnest prayer. Either, then, this miracle was wrought by faith and prayers, not by the sign alone; or, if by the sign alone, it was not effected by the power of God.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: IN QVO NOSTRA ARGVMENTA proponuntur ac defenduntur, itaut simul c. 30. Bellarmini examinetur & castigetur.
units.tr: IN WHICH OUR ARGUMENTS are set out and defended, and at the same time chapter 30 of Bellarmine is examined and corrected.

units.la: Scopus Bellarmini est, argumenta nostra quae peculiariter ad crucis adorationem euertendam a nostris opponuntur, refutare. Refutationem illam, quam solida & nervosa sit, nunc ut dispiciamus, restat.
units.tr: Bellarmine's aim is to refute the arguments which our side brings against the adoration of the cross, especially those aimed at overturning it. It remains to see how solid and sinewy that refutation is.

units.la: Primum Argumentum.
units.tr: The First Argument.

units.la: Primum nostrum argumentum sic a Bellarmino proponitur. Crux dolore & ignominia Christo attulit. Ergo non adoranda, sed potius detestanda iis, qui Christum diligunt. Nos vero tali argumentatione non utimur. Longe validioribus argumentis Pontificiorum profligamus. Quod si tamen paulo aliter ratio haec formetur, fortiter contra staurolatriam militabit. Tale igitur primum nostrum esto argumentum. Instrumentum doloris & supplicii, quo Christus ab hostibus sui fuit excarnificatus, & e medio sublatus, non est adorandum: quia qui hostium instrumenta ad dolores & supplicium Christo inferendum usurpata adorant, ipsam illorum crudelitatem approbant. At lignum crucis fuit
units.tr: Bellarmine sets out our first argument as follows: The cross brought pain and disgrace to Christ. Therefore it is not to be adored, but rather abhorred by those who love Christ. We, however, do not use such an argument. We overthrow the Papists with far stronger arguments. Yet if this reasoning is framed somewhat differently, it will fight vigorously against staurolatry. Let our first argument therefore be this: The instrument of pain and punishment by which Christ was tortured to death by his enemies, and removed from the world, is not to be adored. For those who adore the instruments which his enemies used to inflict pain and punishment on Christ approve the very cruelty of those enemies. But the wood of the cross was

units.la: {c} 101. fuit instrumentū doloris & supplicii, quo Christus ab hostibus suis excarnificatus fuit, è medio sublatus. Ergo lignum crucis nullo modo à quoquaq; qui Christū diligit, adorādū est. Hoc argumento sic formato, exceptio Bellarmini per se concidit. Sed tamen responsionem non dedignabimur.
units.tr: {c} 101. the instrument of pain and punishment by which Christ was tortured to death by his enemies and removed from the world. Therefore the wood of the cross is in no way to be adored by anyone who loves Christ. With the argument framed in this way, Bellarmine's exception falls of its own accord. Nevertheless we will not disdain to answer it.

units.la: Exceptio Bellarmini contra primum argumentum talis est. Si solum crux attulit Christo dolorem & ignominiam, merito est exe cranda. Atqui attulit etiam laetitiam & gloriā propter diabolum deiectum, & genus humanum redemptum; quae laetitia tanta fuit, ut dolorē & ignominiā priorem plane absorbuerit, ut patet.
units.tr: Bellarmine's exception against the first argument runs thus: If the cross alone brought pain and disgrace to Christ, it would rightly be detested. But it also brought joy and glory, because the devil was cast down and the human race redeemed; and this joy was so great that it completely swallowed up the earlier pain and disgrace, as is plain.

units.la: Resp. I. Licet crux Christo attulerit dolorē & ignominiā; tamen si extaret, non propterea eā detestaremur, violare mus, aut abiiceremus, sed magnificaremus, & in rei gestae memoriā coseruaremus; nequaquā vero veneratione aut λα τρεια cultū illi exhiberemus. II. Lignū crucis in se neque dolorem & ignominiam, neque laetitiam & gloriam attulit Christo, sed supplicium crucis, id est, mors, quā Christus in cruce subiit; atq; haec quidē per se dolorē & ignominiā attulit ipsi, sed per accidēs, voluntate & dispēsatione Dei, laetitiā & gloriā. Hic vero nō de morte crucis, sed de ligno crucis non de cruce materiali, sed immateriali, controuersia elt. III. etiā lanceæ, claui, virgæ quib. Christus confossus, fixus ac vulneratus, spinæ, quibus coronatus fuit, Christo nō tantum dolorem & ignominiam attulerunt, sed simul lætitiam & gloriam. Eadem ratione hisce omnibus cultus veneratiònis erit deserè dus. Sed cum hæc etiam impiè adorent quid de Iuda & Iudæis dicent? Iudas atqi Iudæi suo modo fuere instrumenta lætitiæ & gloriæ Christi, quare & ipsi vigore Bellarminianæ exceptionis erunt adorabiles. 4. Si Crux attulit Christo lætitiam & gloriam, non crux, sed Christus lætitia & gloria condecoratus, est adorandus. Si enim in crucem competeret veneratio, eo quod Christo attulit lætitiā & gloriā et lætitiā illa & gloria ad crucē ita pertineret, vt sicut veneratio-nis, ita & lætitiæ & gloriæ Christi capax esset. At lætitia illa & gloria ad solum Christum spectat, ei soli conuenit. Quare Christum crucifixum, cuius hæc est lætitia & gloria, adoramus, non crucem.
units.tr: Answer. (1) Although the cross brought pain and disgrace to Christ, yet if it were still standing, we would not on that account detest it, violate it, or throw it away; we would rather honour it and keep it in memory of the deed done. But we would never offer it veneration or latreia worship. (2) The wood of the cross did not in itself bring pain and disgrace to Christ, nor joy and glory; it was the punishment of the cross, that is, the death which Christ underwent on the cross, that brought pain and disgrace to him directly, and joy and glory indirectly, by the will and disposition of God. But the question here is not about the death of the cross, but about the wood of the cross: not the material cross, but the immaterial one. (3) Even the spear, the nails, the rod by which Christ was pierced, fixed and wounded, and the thorns with which he was crowned, brought Christ not only pain and disgrace but at the same time joy and glory. By the same reasoning, veneration would have to be paid to all of these. But since the Papists impiously adore these things too, what will they say about Judas and the Jews? Judas and the Jews, in their own way, were instruments of Christ's joy and glory, so by the force of Bellarmine's exception they too would be adorable. (4) If the cross brought Christ joy and glory, it is not the cross but Christ, adorned with joy and glory, who is to be adored. For if veneration were due to the cross because it brought Christ joy and glory, and if that joy and glory so belonged to the cross that it was capable of veneration just as it was capable of Christ's joy and glory, then... But that joy and glory look only to Christ and belong to him alone. Therefore we adore Christ crucified, whose joy and glory these are, not the cross.

units.la: Secundum Argumentum.
units.tr: The Second Argument.

units.la: Secundū Argumentum sumitur à similitudine eorū, quorū parētes in patibulis pepēderunt, runt, qui impii viderentur, si eiusmodi patibula honorarent. Argumentum hoc est.
units.tr: The second argument is drawn from the likeness of those whose parents hanged on gibbets, who would seem impious if they honoured such gibbets. The argument is this.

units.la: Filius amans & honorans patibulum, in quo parens eius est suspensus, stultus & impius filius omnium confessione iudicatur. At qui amat, & honorat crucem, cui affixus est Christus, similis est filio qui amat, & honorat patibulum patris. Ergo amans, & honorans crucem, cui Christus affixus est, stultus & impius iudicatur.
units.tr: A son who loves and honours the gibbet on which his parent hangs is, by everyone's admission, judged a foolish and impious son. But whoever loves and honours the cross on which Christ was fastened is like the son who loves and honours his father's gibbet. Therefore whoever loves and honours the cross on which Christ was fastened is judged foolish and impious.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus, non esse similia. Nam qui nunc in patibulis suspenduntur, ex sententia iudicis, culpa sua suspenduntur; aut vera, aut certe in iudicio legitime probata: praeterea inuiti suspenduntur; deniq; ex ipsa morte nihil lucrantur, nisi poenam & infamiam. At Christus non propter culpam veram aut probatam crucifixus fuit. Adhaec sponte sua se tradidit crucifixoribus. Deniq; ex ipsa morte plurima retulit bona, & sibi, & nobis. Neq; id solum in morte Christi videmus, sed etiam in mortibus aliorum, qui propter Deum aut patriam occiduntur. Amici enim libentissime instrumenta passionum eorum, tanquam monumenta virtutis conseruant.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects that the two are not alike. For those who are now hanged on gibbets are suspended by the sentence of a judge, for their own guilt, either true or at least legitimately proved in court; moreover they are hanged against their will; and finally, from death itself they gain nothing but punishment and infamy. But Christ was not crucified for any true or proved guilt. Besides, he gave himself up voluntarily to his crucifiers. Finally, from his death he brought many blessings, both to himself and to us. Nor do we see this only in the death of Christ, but also in the deaths of others who are killed for God or for their country. For friends most willingly keep the instruments of their sufferings as memorials of their virtue.

units.la: Resp. Dissimilitudines hae vim argumenti non euertunt. I. quia non externae & materialis, sed spiritualis, & immaterialis, id est, mortis & passionis Christi dignitatem virtutem & operationem tionem commendant; atq; hanc cru-cem, non lignum dico, sed passionem & morte Christi veneramur, fide ample-ctimur, & tanquam vnicam salutis no-strae causam exosculamur. II. quia amor & veneratio non ex Christi innocen-tia, ex spontanea traditione eius, ex bo-nis deniq; & fructibus, qui inde redun-dant, sed ex institutione & promissione Dei aestimada est. At nulla extat institu-tio de eius veneratione, multo minus promissio veneration.i est annexa. Exé-plum in fine additū aeque infirmum est. Agnosco instrumenta passionis eorum, qui propter Deum aut patriā occidun-tur, tanquam virtutis & doctrinae monu-menta saepe conseruari, sed stultè & im-piè facit, qui adorat ea. Nos etiā instru-meta passionis Christi, si extarent, & ad manus nostras peruenissent, non conte-neremus, aut ignominia afficeremus, i-mò coseruaremus, & in pretio ac hono-re haberemus, sed minimè colerem ea, aut diuino amore & veneratione prose-queremur. In summa. Nullus pius & bo-nus filius iustrumentū illud, quo pater propter Deum & patriā supplicio asse-ctus, adorat; quia scit cultum adoratio-nis nulli creaturae, sed soli Deo conue-nire. nire. At lignum crucis est instrumentum, quo Christus pater noster supplicio est affectus. Ergo nullus pius & bonus Christi filius lignum crucis adorat.
units.tr: Answer. These dissimilarities do not overturn the force of the argument. (1) Because we commend not the external and material, but the spiritual and immaterial dignity, virtue and working of the death and passion of Christ; and it is this cross, I say, not the wood, that is the passion and death of Christ, which we venerate, embrace by faith, and kiss as the one cause of our salvation. (2) Because love and veneration are to be judged not by the innocence of Christ, nor by his voluntary surrender, nor finally by the good things and fruits which flow from it, but by the institution and promise of God. But there is no institution about the veneration of the cross, and still less is a promise of veneration attached to it. The example added at the end is equally weak. I grant that the instruments of the sufferings of those who are killed for God or for their country are often kept as monuments of virtue and doctrine; but he acts foolishly and impiously who adores them. We too, if the instruments of Christ's passion were still standing and had come into our hands, would not despise them or treat them with disgrace; rather we would keep them and hold them in esteem and honour. Yet we would by no means worship them, or pursue them with divine love and veneration. In sum: no pious and good son adores the instrument by which his father was put to death for God and country, because he knows that the worship of adoration belongs to no creature, but to God alone. But the wood of the cross is the instrument by which Christ, our father, was put to death. Therefore no pious and good son of Christ adores the wood of the cross.

units.la: Argumentum Tertium.
units.tr: The Third Argument.

units.la: Tertium argumentum sic a Bellarmino proponitur, quod honorare crucem, sit quasi laetari de passione & morte Christi, quemadmodum faciebant inimici Christi: ita ut qui crucem Christi amant & honorant, illi tentur hostes Christi qui gaudebant de passione Domini, & de resurrectione dolebant. Nos vere non sic praecise argumentamur. Fortius nectimus rationes nostras Oppugnabit tamen staurolatriam hoc modo formatum argumentum.
units.tr: Bellarmine sets out the third argument thus: to honour the cross is almost to rejoice in the passion and death of Christ, just as Christ's enemies did; so that those who love and honour the cross of Christ are held to be enemies of Christ, since those who rejoiced at the Lord's passion grieved over his resurrection. We do not argue in exactly this way; we bind our reasons more firmly. Nevertheless, he will attack Staurolatry with an argument framed as follows.

units.la: Qui crudelitatem adversum Christum adhibitam approbant, deque ea gaudent, ii sunt hostes Christi. At qui instrumenta a crucifixoribus adversus Christum usurpata, honorant, & adorant, illi crudelitatem crucifixorum approbant, deque ea gaudent & laetantur. Ergo qui instrumenta crudelitatis, atque adeo lignum crucis honorant, & adorant, sunt hostes Christi.
units.tr: Those who approve of the cruelty used against Christ and rejoice in it are enemies of Christ. But those who honour and adore the instruments that the crucifiers used against Christ approve of the crucifiers' cruelty and rejoice and delight in it. Therefore those who honour and adore the instruments of cruelty, and so the wood of the cross, are enemies of Christ.

units.la: Excipit Bellarm. Dico nos nihil cum hostibus Christi habere commune. Nam cum gaudemus de Christi passione non gaudemus de eo, de quo quo hostes eius gaudebant, sed de eo, de quo ipse gaudebat. id est, de triumpho eius, non de ignominia. Alioqui enim etiam nouimus, Christum patienti esse compatiendum, & dolores eius piis lacrymis decorandos.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects: I say that we have nothing in common with the enemies of Christ. For when we rejoice in the passion of Christ, we do not rejoice in that thing in which his enemies rejoiced, but in that in which he himself rejoiced, that is, in his triumph, not in his shame. For otherwise we also know that Christ, while suffering, is to be pitied, and his sufferings are to be honoured with pious tears.

units.la: Respond. I. quæstio non est de ipsa passione & morte Christi, sed de instrumento crudelitatis in passione & morte Christi adhibito, id est, de ligno crucis. Qui instrumentum illud amat & adorat, is certè crudelitatem crucifixorum Christi approbat, & gaudet, ac lætatur de ea, non secus atq; hostes Christi. Neque obstat elusio qua dicunt se crudelitate ea lætari, tanquam de eius triumpho. Nam hostium crudelitas non est triumphus Christi, neq; vt triumphus Christi considerari potest, licet eius triumphus tanquam euentus ex ea consecutus fuit. De passione quidem & morte Christi, vt triumpho lætari possumus atq; debemus, sed si hoc modo de passione Christi gaudeant, tunc sequetur, eos crucis instrumentum seu lignum amare, & adorare, non vt instrumentum est passionis Christi, sed tantum, vt instrumentum est triumphi eius. Atque tusquisq; est staurolatrarum, qui de passione & morte Christi gaudet, vt de eius triumriumpho? Quis staurolatrarum, sepo-ita carnali ratione crucis materialis, ad Christum eiusq; triumphum mentem stollit? Ligno externo capiuntur homines superstitiosi, illudque tanquam ιερώλιον quoddam sanctissimum & efficacissimum ad Dei promerendam gratiam adorant, & ampleƈtuntur. II. Etsi gaudent de Christi passione tanquam triumpho eius: tamen, cum ita gaudent de passione Christi, vt instrumentum passionis, id est, crucem adorent, staurolatriam committunt. Gaudium de passione Christi cum adoratione crucis coniunƈtum carnale est, & idololatricum. Tale est gaudium Pontificiorum. Ecce lignum, inquiunt, in quo solus pependit, venite, adoremus. III. Non simpliciter dicimus, quod honorare crucem sit lætari de morte Christi, sed honorare honore illicito & indebito. Nā si extaret vera crux, & in nostra esset potestate, honoraremus eam, vt rei gestæ monumentum, non vero vt salutem mundi, vt medicinam Christianam adoraremus.
units.tr: Reply I. The question is not about the passion and death of Christ itself, but about the instrument of cruelty used in the passion and death of Christ, that is, the wood of the cross. Whoever loves and adores that instrument certainly approves the cruelty of the crucifiers, and rejoices and delights in it, no differently from the enemies of Christ. Nor does their evasion help them, by which they say they rejoice in that cruelty as in its triumph. For the cruelty of enemies is not the triumph of Christ, nor can it be regarded as his triumph, although his triumph followed from it as an outcome. We can and ought to rejoice in the passion and death of Christ as his triumph; but if they rejoice in Christ's passion in this way, then it follows that they love and adore the wood or instrument of the cross not as the instrument of Christ's passion but only as the instrument of his triumph. And which of the staurolaters rejoices in the passion and death of Christ as in his triumph? Which of the staurolaters, setting aside the material cross by carnal reasoning, raises his mind to Christ and his triumph? Superstitious men are caught by the external wood, and they adore and embrace it as a certain most holy and most efficacious [ἱερώλιον] thing for obtaining God's grace. II. Even if they rejoice in Christ's passion as his triumph, yet, when they rejoice in Christ's passion in such a way that they adore the cross, the instrument of the passion, they commit staurolatry. Joy at Christ's passion joined with adoration of the cross is carnal and idolatrous. Such is the joy of the Papists: Behold the wood, they say, on which he alone hung; come, let us adore it. III. We do not simply say that to honour the cross is to rejoice in the death of Christ, but that it is to honour it with an unlawful and undue honour. For if a true cross existed and were in our power, we would honour it as a monument of the deed done, but we would not adore it as the salvation of the world or as the Christian remedy.
