units.la: Argumentum Quartum.
units.tr: The Fourth Argument.

units.la: Quartum argumentum.Si omnes cru-ces adoranda sunt, quia Christus in cruce pendit, oportebit etiam adorare omnia sepulchra, quia in sepulchro dominus quievit, & omnia praesepia, quia in praesepi reclinatus fuit, omnes columnas, lanceas, spongias, flagella, &c. imo & oës asinos, quia Christus asinovecto fuit.
units.tr: The fourth argument: If all crosses are to be adored because Christ hung on a cross, it will be necessary also to adore all sepulchres, because the Lord rested in a sepulchre, and all mangers, because he was laid in a manger; all pillars, lances, sponges, scourges, etc.; indeed even all asses, because Christ was carried on an ass.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus, non sequi, si omnes cruces honoramus, oportere etiam nos honorare omnia praesepia, omnes spinas, omnes lanceas, omnes virgas, &c. Nam omnes cruces adoramus, quia omnes sunt imagines verae crucis in qua Dominus pependit, & praeterea etiam ipsius Christi crucifixi: at praesepia, spineta, lancea, & similia, non sunt imagines Christi, nec & iam praesepii, spinarum, lanceae, & similium, quae Christum tetigerunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects: it does not follow that, if we honour all crosses, we must also honour all mangers, all thorns, all spears, all rods, etc. For we adore all crosses, because they are all images of the true cross on which the Lord hung, and besides of Christ himself crucified. But mangers, thorn bushes, spears and the like are not images of Christ, nor are the manger, the thorns, the spear and the like that touched Christ.

units.la: Resp. I. Est petitio principii. Negamus, & veram crucem, & imagines verae crucis adorandas esse. Nulla imago est adoranda. Ergo ne cruces, tanquam imagines verae crucis adorandae sunt. Nulli creaturae competit honor adorationis. Omnis imago est creatura (excipio imaginem Dei subsistentialem, quae est Dei Filius) Quare nec crucis Christi imagines adorandae sunt, sicut nec ipsa etiam [illegible, ~6 letters]tiam crux vera, quae aeque creatura est, atque eius imago.
units.tr: Answer I. This is begging the question. We deny that either the true cross or images of the true cross are to be adored. No image is to be adored. Therefore crosses, as images of the true cross, are not to be adored either. Honour of adoration belongs to no creature. Every image is a creature (I except the substantial image of God, which is the Son of God). Therefore images of Christ's cross are not to be adored, any more than the true cross itself, which is equally a creature, and so is its image. [illegible, ~6 letters]

units.la: II. Ponamus paulisper, veram crucem adorandam esse, quod tamen idolatricum est; cur propterea imagines huius crucis adorationem merebuntur? Imago enim propter suum archetypum non debet adorari. Honor exemplaris in exemplum non transit. Imago propter repraesentationem archetypi suam naturam non mutat. Ita enim repraesentat, ut nihilominus creatura maneat. Nulli vero creaturae deferri debet adoratio, ut quae soli debetur creatori. Et quodcunque adoratur, non propter obiecti adorabilis repraesentationem adoratur, sed propter Dei institutionem & mandatum. At nullibi in Dei verbo instituta est, & mandata imaginum verae crucis adoratio.
units.tr: II. Let us suppose for a moment that the true cross is to be adored, which is in any case idolatrous. Why then should images of this cross deserve adoration? For an image is not to be adored on account of its archetype. The honour of the original does not pass over to the copy. An image does not change its nature by representing its archetype; it represents in such a way that it nevertheless remains a creature. But adoration must not be paid to any creature, since it is owed to the Creator alone. And whatever is adored is adored not because of the representation of an adorable object, but because of God's institution and command. Yet nowhere in God's Word is the adoration of images of the true cross instituted or commanded.

units.la: III. Negamus etiam cruces esse imagines Christi crucifixi. Non enim Christum crucifixum repraesentat, sed veram crucem, in qua Christus pependit, quomodo & cunae non ipsum Christum in cunis iacentem, sed cunas in quib. Christus olim iacuit; lanceas, baculi, virgae non ipsum Christi virgis caesum, sed ipsas lanceas, baculos, virgas, quib. corp° Christi afflictum
units.tr: III. We also deny that crosses are images of Christ crucified. For they do not represent Christ crucified, but the true cross on which Christ hung, just as a cradle does not represent Christ himself lying in the cradle, but the cradles in which Christ once lay; or spears, staves and rods do not represent Christ himself scourged with rods, but the very spears, staves and rods with which the body of Christ was afflicted

units.la: {y} Lanceas, baculos, virgas. afflictum fuit, repræsentant. Id enim est imago alicuius rei, quod fit ad rem illam exprimendam, ait Bellarminus. At cruces non fiunt ad exprimendum Christum, sed ad exprimendam veram crucem, in qua Christus pependit: Hoc manifestissimum est in iis crucibus, quæ pinguntur sine imagine crucifixi. Quod si cruces intelligant cum imagine crucifixi, sciant, cruces in Ecclesia imagine crucifixi caruisse per annos à Christo 400. Ergò saltem eo tempore cruces non fuere imagines Christi crucifixi. Et cū hodie etiam nonnullas pingant, sine ila imagine, eæ saltem non repræsentat Christum crucifixum, ac proinde non sunt imagines Christi crucifixi. Tantū igitur cruces illæ, quæ cum crucifixi imagine pinguntur & sculpuntur, erunt veræ crucis Christi imagines. Sed cum præsepia, columnæ, & cunæ non minus pingantur & adorentur cum imagine crucifixi, ad repræsentandam eius nativitatem & flagellationem, ut agnoscit Bellarminus, cur non eadem ratione illa essent Christi crucifixi imagines? IV. Nunquam diximus præsæpia, spineta, lanceas, & similia esse imagines Christi crucifixi, sed præsepii, spinarum, lanceæ & similium, quæ Christum tetige-unt, imagines esse diximus, ac proinde eodem iure adoranda, quo cruces, quæ sunt veræ crucis Christi imagines. Quod etiam similitudine sua aliud repræsentat, recte eius imago dicitur. At præsepia, spinæ, lanceæ, & similia, repræsentat sua similitudine præsepium, spinas, & lanceas, & similia, quæ Christum tetigerunt. Ergo & horum imagines recte dicuntur.
units.tr: (Margin: Spears, staves, rods.) was afflicted. For that is the image of a thing which is made to express that thing, says Bellarmine. But crosses are not made to express Christ, but to express the true cross on which Christ hung. This is most evident in those crosses which are painted without an image of the crucified. But if they mean crosses with an image of the crucified, let them know that for 400 years after Christ the Church had crosses without an image of the crucified. Therefore at least in that time crosses were not images of Christ crucified. And although today some people paint crosses without such an image, these at least do not represent Christ crucified, and so they are not images of Christ crucified. Only those crosses which are painted and carved with the image of the crucified will therefore be images of the true cross of Christ. But since mangers, columns and cradles are painted and adored no less with the image of the crucified, to represent his birth and scourging, as Bellarmine admits, why would they not on the same reasoning be images of Christ crucified? IV. We never said that mangers, thorn bushes, spears and the like are images of Christ crucified; we said that images of the manger, of the thorns, of the spear and of the like, which touched Christ, are images, and therefore are to be adored by the same right as crosses, which are images of the true cross of Christ. What by its likeness represents something else is rightly called its image. But mangers, thorns, spears and the like represent by their likeness the mangers, thorns, spears and the like that touched Christ. Therefore images of these too are rightly so called.

units.la: Instat contra Bellarminus. Ad imaginem non sufficit similitudo, sed requiritur, ut unum exprimatur ex alio. Quare frater non dicitur imago fratris, licet similes sint; quia unus non est ab alio. Filius autem, quia non solum est similis patri, sed etiam ab eo prodiit, idcirco vere dicitur, & est imago patris. Iam cruces omnes fiunt ad exprimendam illam primam, & sic imagines illius sunt. At præsepia, lanceæ & similia non fiunt ad illa exprimenda, sed ad alios usus, ideo nec imagines sunt. Quando autem pingitur, vel sculpitur præsepe, ad repræsentandam Christi nativitatem; vel columna ad repræsentandam flagellationem, quia tunc præsepe & columna sunt imagines, non carent sua aliqua veneratior.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses the objection again: Likeness is not enough for an image; it is required that one thing be expressed from another. Hence a brother is not called the image of a brother, although they are alike, because one is not from the other. But a son, because he is not only like his father but has also come forth from him, is rightly called and is truly the image of his father. Now all crosses are made to express that first cross, and so they are its images. But mangers, spears and the like are not made to express those things, but for other uses; therefore they are not images either. Yet when a manger is painted or carved to represent Christ's birth, or a column to represent the scourging, then the manger and the column are images, and they lack nothing of their own veneration.

units.la: Respond. I. Secundum hanc Bellarmini larmini sententiam non tantum præpia, lanceæ, & similia non erunt imagines præsepii, lanceæ, & similium, quæ Christum tetigerunt, sed nec cruces siue solæ, siue cum imagine crucifixi, primæ illius & veræ Christi crucis imagines erunt. Nam ad imaginem requiritur primũ similitudo, ait Bellarminus.
units.tr: Answer 1. On Bellarmine's view, not only the manger, the lance and similar things that touched Christ would fail to be images of the manger, the lance and the like, but neither would crosses, whether alone or with an image of the crucified Christ, be images of that first and true cross of Christ. For Bellarmine says that an image requires first of all a likeness.

units.la: At nulla est similitudo inter primam Christi crucem, & cruces illas, quæ sine Christo crucifixo pinguntur & sculpütur. Deinde ad imaginem requiritur, vt vnum ex alio fit expressum. At cruces, quæ cum imagine crucifixi pinguntur & sculpuntur, licet ad illam exprimendam factæ sint, non tamen ex illa expressæ sunt; aliud est exprimere rem ad rei exemplar, aliud ex re ipsa exprimere.
units.tr: But there is no likeness between the first cross of Christ and those crosses which are painted or carved without the crucified Christ. Next, an image requires that one thing be expressed from another. But crosses which are painted or carved with the image of the crucified Christ, although they are made to express that cross, are not expressed from it. It is one thing to express a thing according to the pattern of a thing, and another to express it from the thing itself.

units.la: II. Etsi non omnia præsepia, lanceæ, & similia fiunt ad exprimendum primum præsepium, lanceam, & similia: tamen illa, quæ in eum finem fiunt, eorum imagines erunt, ac proinde adoranda, vt, cum præsepe fingitur, aut sculpitur, ad repræsentandum Christi præsepe, eiusque natiuitatem: Columna ad repræsentandam Christi columnam eiusq; flagellationem. Hoc pacto ergo columnæ & præsepia illa imagines ines erunt, ac proinde adoranda. At unc, inquies, non carebūt sua ALIQVA ve- neratione.
units.tr: II. Although not all mangers, lances and similar things are made to express the first manger, lance and the like, yet those made for that purpose will be images of them, and therefore to be worshipped. So when a manger is painted or carved to represent Christ's manger and his birth, or a column to represent Christ's column and his scourging, the column and the manger will in this way be images, and therefore to be worshipped. But, you will say, they will not lack SOME veneration.

units.la: Quæ verò est illa aliqua veneratio? vel est humana, vel diuina. Si est humana, de ea est quæstio; Si diuina, negamus illis rebus deberi. Quod enim Deo soli in solidum debetur, id non est aliqua ratione tribuendum imagini, aut creaturæ. At veneratio diuina in solidum debetur Deo. Ergo non imaginibus. Superuacaneū certè est disputare de ALIQVA imaginis veneratione, cui omnino nulla veneratio debetur.
units.tr: But what is that SOME veneration? It is either human or divine. If it is human, that is a question to be debated. If it is divine, we deny that it is owed to such things. For what is owed wholly and solely to God may by no means be given to an image or a creature. But divine veneration is owed wholly to God. Therefore it is not owed to images. It is certainly pointless to dispute about SOME veneration of an image to which no veneration at all is due.

units.la: Deinde aut verę imagines sunt, aut falsę. Falsas esse non dicent. Si verę, ērō vera adoratione non debent carere. Cur ergo ALIQVA saltem Adoratione ignas esse dicit? Si sunt imagines, quæ non aliqua ratione, sed plenè & solidè exprimunt sua exemplaria plena & solida, non ALIQVA tantum veneratione carere debent. Tales autem esse necesse est, cum similitudo eorum, vt intuit, non sufficiat ad id, vt imaginum licem sustineant. Quod si verò ALIQVA saltem dignæ sunt veneratione, similitudo sufficiet, vtpote qua fit, vt a qua tantum ratione repræsentent, & imagines sint.
units.tr: Again, images are either true or false. They will not say they are false. If they are true, they should not lack true worship. Why then do they say they lack even SOME worship? If they are images which express their originals not in some respect but fully and solidly, they should not lack merely SOME veneration. Yet such images must be of this kind, since their likeness, as they claim, does not suffice for them to be images. But if they are worthy of at least SOME veneration, then likeness suffices, since by it they represent in some respect and are images.

units.la: Instas
units.tr: Objection

units.la: Instat Bellarminus. At crux sola refert Christum crucifixum. præsepia, columnæ & similia hoc non faciunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses further: But the cross alone refers to the crucified Christ. Mangers, columns and the like do not do this.

units.la: Respond. negatur solam crucem referre Christum crucifixum. Nam I. nulla similitudo est inter crucem & Christum crucifixum: vt vero crux tanquam imago Christum crucifixum referat, similitudo requiritur. II. Crux non exprimitur ex Christo crucifixo. Ergo vt imago ad Christum crucifixum non potest referri. Ad imaginem enim requiritur, vt vnum exprimatur ab alio, ait Bellarminus. III. vt cruces, quæ fiunt ad exprimendam primam illam crucem, eo ipso crucifixum referunt Christum, quia prima illa crux fuit in Christo crucifixo: ita etiam præsepia, columnæ & similia, quæ fiunt ad exprimendum primum illud præsepe, primam columnam & similia, quæ ab iis Christo non fuerunt, eodem iure Christum referre dicimus, si non crucifixum, saltem natum & flagellatum.
units.tr: Answer: we deny that the cross alone refers to the crucified Christ. For first, there is no likeness between the cross and the crucified Christ; yet for the cross to refer to the crucified Christ as an image, a likeness is required. Second, the cross is not expressed from the crucified Christ. Therefore it cannot be referred to the crucified Christ as an image. For an image requires that one thing be expressed from another, says Bellarmine. Third, just as crosses made to express that first cross refer to the crucified Christ by that very fact, because that first cross was on the crucified Christ, so too mangers, columns and the like, made to express that first manger and first column and the like, which were not Christ's, we say by the same right refer to Christ, if not as crucified, at least as born and scourged.

units.la: Instat. At crux non habet alium vsum, quam repræsentandi, præsertim post edictum Constantini, de non crucifigendis hominibus. At illa alia habent alios vsus: & ideo, qui videret vnam columnam depictam, non facile poterit scire, quid illa significaret, an columnæ Christi, Christi, an Traiani, vel Hadriani, vel Herculis, vel aliorum.
units.tr: He presses: But the cross has no use other than representing, especially since the edict of Constantine against crucifying men. But those other things have other uses; and so someone who saw a single painted column could not easily know what it signified, whether the column of Christ, or of Trajan, or of Hadrian, or of Hercules, or of others.

units.la: Respond. I. negamus crucem habere vsum repræsentandi. Vnde enim hûc habet? an ex diuina institutione? At nec Christus, nec Apostoli, facto vel verbo vsum hunc crucis instituerunt. Si ex humana institutione, vel edicto Constantini nititur, vel hominum superstitiorum traditione. Edictum Constantini primum fuit de labaro primario castrorum vexillo, cui non crucem, sed nominis Christi characterem inscripsit, cuius hac inscriptione: ἐν τούτῳ νίκα, i.e. In Isto (non in signo) Sed Christo Vince. Hoc edictum non fuit de vsu crucis sed de vsu signi imperatorii Christi nomine depicti, qui non aliud fuit, quam vt victorias & triumphos suos Christo crucifixo acceptos referret. Alterum edictum fuit de non crucifigendis hominibus. Neque hoc ad vsum crucis pertinet, sed ad honorem nominis Christi crucifixi, quod cum esset probrosum Iudæis & paganis, voluit Constantinus hoc edicto honorificum reddere. Alia deinde edicta, quibus vel Constantinus, vel alii post ipsum Imperatores & Principes, cruces ces insignibus, vexillis, scutis nummis, postibus,parietibus imprimi atq; inscul piiusserunt,aut curarunt, nō eo tende- bant, vt vsum repræsentandi sancirent ac crucibus tribuerent, sed ad testifica- dum & profitendum Christi nomen & Christianam religionem spectabant.
units.tr: Answer: first, we deny that the cross has the use of representing. For where does it get this use? From divine institution? But neither Christ nor the apostles instituted this use of the cross by deed or word. If it rests on human institution, it rests either on the edict of Constantine or on the superstitious tradition of men. The first edict of Constantine concerned the labarum, the chief standard of the army, on which he inscribed not a cross but the character of Christ's name, with this inscription: ἐν τούτῳ νίκα [en touto nika], that is, In this (not in the sign) but in Christ, conquer. This edict did not concern the use of the cross but the use of the imperial standard marked with the name of Christ, whose only purpose was to refer his victories and triumphs to the crucified Christ as their source. The other edict was about not crucifying men. This too does not pertain to the use of the cross but to the honour of the name of the crucified Christ, which, since it was shameful to the Jews and pagans, Constantine wished to make honourable by this edict. Then the other edicts, by which Constantine or other emperors and princes after him ordered or arranged that crosses be stamped on insignia, standards, shields, coins, posts and walls, did not aim to establish and assign to crosses a use of representing, but looked to bearing witness to and professing the name of Christ and the Christian religion.

units.la: II. dicit, crucem non habuisse alium v- sum,quam repræsentandi post edictum Constantini. Cōstat ergo eam ante hoc edictum alios habuisse vsus. Fuerunt etiam in paganorum vexillis, teste Minu- tio, quæ tamen repræsentandi vsum nō habuere, nec imagines Christi fuere. Hoc non obstitit, quo minus factæ sint imagines Christi & adoratæ. Quidigi- tur obstabit, quo minus præsepia, co- lūnæ,& similia nunc sint imagines Chri sti, & adorentur, licet præter vsum re- præsentandi, etiam alios habeant v- sus. Tunc adoratæ fuere cruces, quia e- rant imagines veræ crucis, in qua pe- pendit Christus, licet præter vsum re- præsentādi etiam alios habuerint vsus, cur & nunc præsepia & columnæ, quia imagines sunt præsepii,in quo Christus infans iacuit, & columna, in qua sacrū eius corpus cæsum fuit, sua adoratione carerent, licet alios vsus præter repræ- sensentandi vsum habeant: III. Etsi plurima præsepia, columnæ, & simi-lia alios vsus habeant, tamen, quæ ad exprimendum & repræsentandum primum præsepe, primam columnam & similia adhibentur, nullum alium vsum habent, quam repræsentandi, non secus atq; cruces, quæ primam illam crucem, in qua Christus pependit, repræsentat. Quare qui videt columnam factam, & erectam ad exprimendam columnam Christi, is certo nouit, illam non significare columnam Traiani vel Hadriani, quia vsum repræsentandi columnam Christi tantum nacta est. IV. Etiamsi præsepia, & columnæ non ad præsentandum sed ad alios vsus extructa sint; tamen quatenus sanctulis vestris præsepe & columnam Christi repræsentant, cur non æque atque cruces adorentur? Qui columnam Hadriani vel Herculis videt, si eam pro columna Christi habeat, afferatq; hanc intentionem in ea adoranda, quod Christi columnam repræsentet, nonne pari iure eam, quo cruces Christi, adorationis honore afficeret. En quo Saurolatræ isti vanitate suorum sophismatum delabantur? Ex staurolatris etiam stylolatræ, & φαρvολατραι euadunt.
units.tr: II. He says the cross had no use other than representing after the edict of Constantine. It is clear, then, that before this edict it had other uses. There were also crosses on the standards of the pagans, as Minucius testifies, which nevertheless did not have the use of representing and were not images of Christ. This did not prevent them from being made into images of Christ and worshipped. What then will prevent mangers, columns and the like from now being images of Christ and being worshipped, even though, besides the use of representing, they have other uses as well? The crosses were worshipped then because they were images of the true cross on which Christ hung, although they also had other uses besides representing. Why should mangers and columns now lack their worship, since they are images of the manger in which the infant Christ lay and of the column to which his sacred body was scourged, even though they have other uses besides the use of representing? III. Although very many mangers, columns and similar things have other uses, yet those used to express and represent the first manger, the first column and the like have no other use than representing, just as the cross represents that first cross on which Christ hung. Therefore whoever sees a column made and erected to express the column of Christ knows for certain that it does not signify the column of Trajan or Hadrian, since it has acquired the use of representing the column of Christ alone. IV. Even if mangers and columns were built not to represent but for other uses, yet insofar as they represent Christ's manger and column for your pious purposes, why should they not be worshipped just as crosses are? If someone sees the column of Hadrian or Hercules, and if he takes it for the column of Christ and brings this intention to its worship, that it represents the column of Christ, would he not by the same right honour it with worship as he would the crosses of Christ? See into what vanity these worshippers of the cross slide by the sophistries of their own making! From cross-worshippers they become pillar-worshippers too, and idolaters [εἰδωλολάτραι].

units.la: Instat ex Athanasio, qui quaestione decima sexta, ad Antiochum inquit: cum accusamur, quod adoremus lignum, possumus statim ofcendere, nos colere figuram, non materiam, separando duo illa ligna ab invicem, quod in columna, lancea, spongia & similibus non tam facile fieri potest.
units.tr: He presses from Athanasius, who in question sixteen, to Antiochus, says: when we are accused of worshipping wood, we can at once show that we worship the figure, not the material, by separating those two pieces of wood from each other, which cannot so easily be done with a column, a lance, a sponge and similar things.

units.la: Respond. Hanc Athanasii auctoritatem iure non amplectimur; quia non magnus ille Athanasius, sed recens scriptor, vt ipse Bellarminus in libro de scriptor. Ecclesiast. agnoscit. Quaestiones ad Antiochum, inquit, Athanasii esse non possunt. Nam quaestion. 23. citat autor magnum Athanasium, & ab eo dissentit. Quaestione 108. dicit, Romanos esse Francorum genus, ex quo apparet, esse autorem recentem. II.
units.tr: Answer. We do not rightly accept this authority of Athanasius, because it is not the work of the great Athanasius but of a recent writer, as Bellarmine himself acknowledges in his book on ecclesiastical writers. He says that the Questions to Antiochus cannot be Athanasius'. For in question 23 the author cites the great Athanasius and dissents from him. In question 108 he says the Romans are a branch of the Franks, from which it is clear that the author is recent. II.

units.la: Quid tum, si non tam facile id fieri possit in columna, spongia, lancea, quod fit in cruce, modo repraesentent & exprimant columnam, & lanceam Christi. Fieri potest, ut una imago facilius & expressius, alia difficilius & obscurius suum antitypum exprimat ac repraesentet, nihilominus tamen imaginis usum, nomen & honorem retinet.
units.tr: What of it, if it cannot be done as easily with a column, a sponge or a spear as it is done with the cross? Provided they represent and express the column and the spear of Christ, that is enough. One image may express and represent its antitype more easily and clearly, another more difficultly and obscurely, and yet both still keep the use, the name and the honour of an image.

units.la: III. Haec excusatio Pontificios non iuvat, vt qui de ligni adoratione gloriantur: Ecce lignum crucis, in quo [illegible, ~3 letters] {a}Galu pepen lit: Venite, adoremus. Item O crux lignum triumphale, mundi vera salus, quale inter ligna nullum tale flore, fronde, germine. Medicina Christiana, sanos salva, ægros sana. Quod nō valet vis humana, fit in tuo nomine.
units.tr: III. This excuse does not help the Papists, who boast of adoring wood: Behold the wood of the cross, on which [illegible, about three letters] the salvation of the world hung: Come, let us adore. Likewise: O cross, triumphal wood, true salvation of the world, than which no tree bears such flower, leaf or bud. Christian medicine, save the healthy and heal the sick. What human strength cannot do, is done in your name.

units.la: Quintum Argumentum.
units.tr: The Fifth Argument.

units.la: Quintum argumentum sic proponit Bellarminus. Si ratione contactus, vel quia instrumentum passionis fuit adoranda est crux, oportebit etiam adorare labia Iudæ, quæ contigerunt os Domini osculando, & manum illius servi, qui Dominum tetigit, cum alapam infligit illi; nam hæc omnia tetigerunt Dominum & instrumenta passionis fuerunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine sets out the fifth argument thus: If by reason of contact, or because it was the instrument of the passion, the cross is to be adored, then it will also be necessary to adore the lips of Judas, which touched the Lord's face in kissing him, and the hand of that servant who struck the Lord when he gave him a blow; for all these touched the Lord and were instruments of the passion.

units.la: Argumentum hoc nostrum esse agnoscimus, cuius categorica forma hæc est.
units.tr: We acknowledge this to be our argument, whose categorical form is this:

units.la: Qui adorant crucem ob contactum corporis Christi, & quod instrumentum est passionis Christi, eos oportet etiam labia Iudæ & manus crucifixorum eadem ratione adorare. At Pontifici adorant crucem ob contactum corporis, & quia instrumentum est passionis Christi. Ergo eadem ratione oportebit eos labia Iudæ & manus crucifixorum adorare.
units.tr: Those who adore the cross because of the contact with the body of Christ, and because it is an instrument of the passion of Christ, ought by the same reasoning to adore also the lips of Judas and the hands of the crucifiers. But the Papists adore the cross because of the contact with the body, and because it is an instrument of the passion. Therefore by the same reasoning they will be bound to adore the lips of Judas and the hands of the crucifiers.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus. Inter crucem, & labia Iudæ ac manus crucifixorum Christi magnam esse differentiam: quia crucem Dominus elegit, & amanter amplexus est ut rem innoxiam deservientem redemtioni. At labia Iudi, & manus impiorum Christus non elegit, nec amavit, sed execrabatur, ut res impias & sceleratas. Nos autem illa solum amare & honorare debemus, quae Dominus amavit & honoravit.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects: There is a great difference between the cross, and the lips of Judas and the hands of Christ's crucifiers: because the Lord chose the cross and embraced it lovingly, as an innocent thing serving redemption. But the lips of Judas and the hands of the impious Christ did not choose or love, but abhorred them, as impious and wicked things. We ought, however, to love and honour only those things which the Lord loved and honoured.

units.la: Respon. Differentia haec non soluit argumentum. Nam I. licet ratione electionis & amoris Christi sit discrimen: tamen rationes contactus, in quo argumenti vis posita est, nullum est discrimen. II. tam Iudam, & labia Iudae, atque Iudaeos, quam crucem elegit Dominus, ut redemptioni nostrae deseruirent. Act. 4. coacti sunt vere adversus sanctum filium tuum Iesum, quem unxisti, Herodes Pontius Pilatus cum gentibus & populis Israel, ut facere quacunque manus tua, & consilium tuum prius definiuerant facienda. III. agnoscimus nos illa amare & honorare debere, quae Christus amavit & honorauit. At quomodo Christus amauit & honorauit crucem, num ut obiectum adorationis? Absit. sed ut instrumentum passionis, subeundo mortem in ea, & patri obedientiam praestando usque ad mortem crucis. Sic ergo & nos amamus, & honoramus crucem, non ut obiectum adorationis, sed ut instrumentum passionis & supplicii cii,quod Chriftus pro nobis fubiit. IV. ipfe Bellarminus refponlionem nobis fuppeditat ; paria fcilicet funt ludæ labia& crux. Nam vt labia ludæ fue- runt inftrumentum fceleris ludæ, quæ al oqu non erant capacia culpæ: ita & crux tuit inftrumentum fceleris ludæo- rum. Et ficut Dominus elegit crucem non vt inftrumentum fceleris,fed vt in- ftrumentum pafsionis, ita quoq; elegit labia ludæ &manusinterfectorum,non vt inftrumenta fceleris, fed vt inftru- menta pafsionis.
units.tr: Answer. This difference does not dissolve the argument. For, first, although there is a distinction by reason of Christ's choice and love, yet in respect of contact, on which the force of the argument rests, there is no distinction. Second, the Lord chose Judas and the lips of Judas, and the Jews as well as the cross, to serve our redemption. Acts 4: Truly there were gathered together against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had decided beforehand should be done. Third, we acknowledge that we ought to love and honour those things which Christ loved and honoured. But how did Christ love and honour the cross? Was it as an object of adoration? Far from it. He loved it as the instrument of his passion, by undergoing death on it and by rendering obedience to the Father even to the death of the cross. So too we love and honour the cross, not as an object of adoration, but as the instrument of the passion and of the punishment that Christ underwent for us. Fourth, Bellarmine himself supplies us with the answer: the lips of Judas and the cross are alike. For just as the lips of Judas were the instrument of Judas' crime, though in themselves they were not capable of guilt, so the cross too was the instrument of the crime of the Jews. And just as the Lord chose the cross not as an instrument of crime but as an instrument of passion, so too he chose the lips of Judas and the hands of the slayers, not as instruments of crime but as instruments of passion.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus contra.Differentiam effe in duobus.Prima differentia: quia labia ludæ & manus interfectorum Christi,non folum inftrumentum pafsionis erant,fed etiam partes illorû hominum impiorum, & ideo non poterant honorari, vt inftrumenta paffionis, quin fimul ipfi impii homines honorari videntur: at crux,fpina,columna, & fimilia, non sunt partes illorum hominum,fed sunt res per se exi stentes,& sua natura innoxia. &c.
units.tr: Bellarmine objects again: There is a difference in two respects. The first difference: because the lips of Judas and the hands of the slayers of Christ were not only instruments of the passion, but also parts of those impious men, and therefore they could not be honoured as instruments of the passion without the impious men themselves seeming to be honoured at the same time. But the cross, the thorn, the column and similar things are not parts of those men, but are things existing in their own right and innocent by nature. etc.

units.la: Refp.I. Confimili modo de cruce ect excipere. Crux non tantum eft instrumentum pafsionis,fed etiã res creata,res muta & & bruta,ideo non poteft honorari vt inftrumetû pafsionis, quin fimul creatura & res bruta ac muta honoretur noretur. II. nihil hoc ad robur argu- menti eneruādum facit, quod labia di- cuntur fuisse partes illorum impiorum hominum;manet nihilominus paritas in eo, in quo vis argumenti consistit, quod scilicet sint instrumenta passionis talia,quæ sacrum Christi corpus tetige- rint æque atq; crux.Si lignea crux ideo adoratur,quod est instrumetum passio- nis,àcontactuChristi ita sanctificatum, vt sancta sit & venerabilis, quid ni & labia Iudæ proditoris non sint sancta & venerabilia?cum & illa sint instrumenta passionis,& corpus dominicum contigerint. Si crux res bruta & inanima à Christo ad hoc select a, vt esset instrumentum passionis & redemptionis, ita fuit contactu corporis sanctificata, vt sancta & venerabilis euaserit:cedò quid repugnat quo minus partes impiorum, à Christo ad hoc selectæ, vt sint instrumenta passionis, contactu corporis sic fuerint sanctificatæ, vt parem cum cruce sanctitatem & venerationem sibi acquisiuerint; præsertim cum partes illorum impiorum hominum æquè innoxiæ sint atque crux, spinæ, columna & similia. Neque enim partes illæ per se sceleris illius fuere conscīæ, sed anima impioimpiorum istorum. ALTERA DIF-FERENTIA est: quia in passione Domini ossumus considerare actionem & passionem, quarum prior scelerata: posterior sanctissima fuit. Porro labia Iudæ & manus impiorum fuerunt instrumenta propinqua ipsius actionis scelestæ: remota autem & mediata passionis salutaris: e contrario crux & clavi, & similia fuerunt instrumenta propinqua, & immediata passionis sanctæ, & remota ac mediata actionis scelestæ ut patet; & ideo labia Iudæ magis participant actione, quam passione. & crux e contrario magis passione quam actione. Propterea crux simpliciter est venerabilis, labia Iudæ simpliciter detestanda.
units.tr: Answer. In a similar way one may object about the cross, etc. The cross is not only an instrument of the passion, but also a created thing, a dumb and brute thing; therefore it cannot be honoured as an instrument of the passion without the creature, a dumb and brute thing, being honoured at the same time. Second, this does nothing to weaken the force of the argument, that the lips are said to have been parts of those impious men. The parallel remains in that in which the force of the argument consists, namely that they are instruments of the passion, and such as touched the sacred body of Christ just as the cross did. If the wooden cross is therefore adored because it is an instrument of the passion, sanctified by contact with Christ so that it is holy and venerable, why should the lips of Judas the traitor not also be holy and venerable, since they too were instruments of the passion and touched the Lord's body? If the cross, a brute and lifeless thing, was chosen by Christ for this purpose, that it might be an instrument of passion and redemption, and was so sanctified by contact with the body that it became holy and venerable: then tell me, what prevents the parts of impious men, chosen by Christ for this purpose, that they might be instruments of the passion, from being so sanctified by contact with the body that they acquire for themselves holiness and veneration equal to the cross? Especially since those parts of impious men are just as innocent as the cross, the thorns, the column and similar things. For those parts were not conscious of that crime by themselves, but the impious souls of those impious men. SECOND DIFFERENCE: because in the passion of the Lord we can consider the action and the passion, of which the former was wicked, the latter most holy. Moreover, the lips of Judas and the hands of the impious were instruments near to the wicked action itself, but remote and mediate to the saving passion; on the contrary, the cross and the nails and similar things were instruments near and immediate to the holy passion, and remote and mediate to the wicked action, as is plain. Therefore the lips of Judas share more in the action than in the passion, and the cross, on the contrary, more in the passion than in the action. Therefore the cross is simply venerable, the lips of Judas simply to be detested.

units.la: Respon. neque hæc differentia euer-tit paritatem hypothesios, ex qua procedit nostra argumentatio. Etsi labia Iudæ & manus interfectorum fuerunt instrumenta propinqua actionis scelestæ, remota vero & mediata passionis salutaris; tamen cum corporis Domini contactu sanctificentur, eodem iure, quo crux, adorationis honore digna sunt; aut saltem hoc manebit discrimen, ut labia & manus interfectorum, tanquam remota & mediata passionis salutaris in instrumenta, propinqua & immediata actionis scelestæ, crux vero & clavi ut instrumenta propinqua & immediata actionis passionis sanctæ, remota vero & immediata actionis scelestæ adoranda sint. II. Si labia Iudæ & manus interfectorum ideo non sunt adoranda, quia remota sunt & mediata instrumenta sanctæ Christi passionis, crux etiam & clavi non erunt adorandi, quia sunt remota & mediata instrumenta actionis scelestæ. Quotusquisque vero hanc novit & observat distinctionem, in crucis & clavorum adoratione. III. Sequitur contactum corporis Christi vim & efficaciam suam tantum in propinqua & immediata passionis instrumenta exercere. At cur non æque in propinqua & immediata actionis scelestæ exerceret? Et si labia Iudæ magis participent actionem, & crux passionem; tamen cum æq; contactu corporis domini ut partem venerationem sanctificentur? IIII. Etiam si crux, clavi & similia sint propinqua & immediata passionis instrumenta, sunt tamen & manent creaturæ, & quidem mutæ atq; inanimæ, quo iure igitur instrumenta eiusmodi licet propinqua & immediata passionis dominicæ, adorationis honore afficiantur? Creatura creatori non debet exæquari.
units.tr: Answer. Nor does this difference overturn the parity of the hypothesis from which our argument proceeds. Even if the lips of Judas and the hands of the slayers were instruments near to the wicked action, but remote and mediate to the saving passion, yet since they are sanctified by contact with the Lord's body, they are worthy of the honour of adoration by the same right as the cross. Or at least this distinction will remain: that the lips and hands of the slayers, as instruments remote and mediate to the saving passion but near and immediate to the wicked action, are to be adored, while the cross and nails, as instruments near and immediate to the holy passion but remote and mediate to the wicked action, are to be adored. Second, if the lips of Judas and the hands of the slayers are not to be adored because they are remote and mediate instruments of Christ's holy passion, then neither will the cross and the nails be adored, because they are remote and mediate instruments of the wicked action. But how few know and observe this distinction in the adoration of the cross and nails! Third, it follows that the contact with Christ's body exercises its power and efficacy only on the instruments near and immediate to the passion. But why would it not equally exercise it on the instruments near and immediate to the wicked action? And if the lips of Judas share more in the action, and the cross in the passion, yet are they not equally sanctified by contact with the Lord's body as a part of the venerating? Fourth, even if the cross, the nails and similar things are instruments near and immediate to the passion, they are nonetheless and remain creatures, and indeed dumb and lifeless ones. By what right, then, are such instruments, though near and immediate to the Lord's passion, honoured with the honour of adoration? A creature ought not to be made equal to the Creator.

units.la: Sextum Argumentum:
units.tr: The Sixth Argument:

units.la: Sextum argumentum Superstitio & Magia est tribuere figuris virtutem aliquam. At papistæ tribuunt signo crucis virtutem pellendi dæmones, & omnia mala. Ergo superstitionis & Magiæ sunt rei.
units.tr: The sixth argument: superstition and magic is to attribute some power to figures. But the Papists attribute to the sign of the cross the power of driving away demons and all evils. Therefore they are guilty of superstition and magic.

units.la: Excipit Bellarminus, tantū abesse à Maria signū crucis, vt potius eo signo omnis Magia debeatur, teste Athanasio lib. de incarnat. Domini. Signo crucis, inquit, omnia magica cōpescūntur, veneficia ineffıcacia sunt. Et infra. Venit qui istorum dictorum experimentū capere vellet, & in ipsis præstigiis dæmonū, & imposturis vaticinorum, & in miraculis magiæ, vtatur signo crucis ab ipsis deriso, nomem Christi inuocet; & videbit quomodo eius rei motu dæmones fugiant, vaticinia conquiescant, & veneficia iaceant. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies: so far is the sign of the cross from being ascribed to Mary, that rather all magic is owed to that sign, as Athanasius testifies in his book on the Incarnation of the Lord. By the sign of the cross, he says, all magical arts are restrained, poisonings are rendered ineffective. And below: Let anyone who wishes to test the truth of these sayings come, and in the very tricks of demons, the impostures of prophecies, and the miracles of magic, let him use the sign of the cross, which they mock, and invoke the name of Christ; and he will see how, at the motion of this thing, demons flee, prophecies fall silent, and poisonings lie dead. Thus he.

units.la: Resp. I. Negamus crucis signo omnem Magiā soluī. Aut naturaliter hāc vim soluendi magiā obtinet, aut supernaturaliter, vt ipse Bell: paulo post fatetur. Neq; n. quisquā ex peritissimis naturæ contemplatoribus huc vsq; obseruauit, signo crucis naturaliter indită esse vim soluēdi omnē magiā: Et quomodo esse supernaturalis à virtute naturali pducē retur? Neq; supernaturaliter. Eorum enim quæ supernaturaliter operantur, & effectus supernaturales producunt testis est spiritus Dei. At is nullibi in sacris literis de supernaturali crucis virtute & operatione restatur. II. Signum crucis ad eiusmodi effectum diuinitus non est institutum. Qui igitur signo crucis vtuntur ad effectus eiusmodi, ad quos diuinitus non est institutum, iure superstitionis accusantur. Atqui ad Magiam insoluendā diuinitus non est institutū: Superstitionis igitur iure Pōtificios accusamus: atq; huius accusationis æquitatem etiā autoritas Augustini Hunæ comprobat. Is in secunda secundæ generatim asserit, uti rebus ad eos effectus asequendos & producendos, quorum illa res neque causæ sunt, neque legitima secundum diuinam vel humanam institutionem signa, superstitiosum est & à religione Christiana alienum. Signum crucis non est causa soluendi omnem magiam. Causa est cuius vi existit effectus. At nulla vis in signo vel naturalis, vel supernaturalis, ad effectum hunc supernaturalem producendum. Neque signaculum crucis signum est legitimum producendi illius effectus; cum neque ex diuina neque ex humana institutione hunc vsum acceperit. Diuina institutio in verbo Dei extat nusquam: Humana quidem institutione non caret hoc signum, sed ad solvendam omnem magiam institutum esse, nullus nisi superstitiosus, affirmauerit, vt merito Ferrus in hanc eruperit querelam dicens: Quam multa instituerunt sancti bona intentione, quamtamen nunc videmus, partim in abusum, partim in superstitionem verti. Quapropter crucis ceremonia vtuntur, ea plerique quasi illegitimo signo sancti cum daemone utuntur. Athanasii auctoritas non liberat ipsos a crimine superstitionis. Neque enim signo crucis vim aliquam tribuit, qua hos effectus producat, sed omnem vim in invocatione nominis Christi acceptam refert. Nam sic docet utendum signo crucis, ut invocetur nomen Christi. Christum igitur invocatum a piis, & signo crucis professum, daemones fugare significat, non externam crucis ceremoniam, quae separatim nihil prodest & proficit.
units.tr: Reply. First, we deny that all magic is dissolved by the sign of the cross. Either it has this power of dissolving magic by nature, or by supernatural means, as Bellarmine himself admits shortly afterwards. For none of the most skilled contemplators of nature has so far observed that a natural power of dissolving all magic is inborn in the sign of the cross; and how could what is supernatural be produced by a natural power? Nor is it supernatural: for of those things that work supernaturally and produce supernatural effects, the Spirit of God is the witness, and he nowhere in Holy Scripture bears witness to any supernatural power or operation of the cross. Second, the sign of the cross was not divinely instituted for such an effect. Therefore those who use the sign of the cross for effects of this kind, for which it was not divinely instituted, are rightly accused of superstition. But it was not divinely instituted for dissolving magic; therefore we accuse the Papists of superstition with good right, and the authority of Augustine (Hunnius) confirms the fairness of this accusation. He asserts in general, in the Secunda Secundae, that to use things to attain and produce those effects of which that thing is neither the cause nor a lawful sign according to divine or human institution is superstitious and foreign to the Christian religion. The sign of the cross is not the cause of dissolving all magic: a cause is that by whose power an effect exists; but there is no power in the sign, either natural or supernatural, to produce this supernatural effect. Nor is the sign of the cross a lawful sign for producing that effect, since it has received this use neither from divine nor from human institution. Divine institution is found nowhere in the Word of God; human institution indeed does not lack this sign, but no one except a superstitious man will affirm that it was instituted for dissolving all magic. Thus Ferrus rightly broke out into this complaint: How many things holy men have instituted with good intention, which we now see turned partly into abuse, partly into superstition. Therefore many who use the ceremony of the cross use it as an illegitimate sign, as the saints did with the demon. The authority of Athanasius does not free them from the crime of superstition. For he does not ascribe to the sign of the cross any power by which it produces these effects, but refers all power to the invocation of the name of Christ. For he teaches that the sign of the cross is to be used so that the name of Christ is invoked. Therefore, when Christ is invoked by the pious and professed with the sign of the cross, it signifies that demons are put to flight, not the external ceremony of the cross, which by itself helps and profits nothing.

units.la: Instat ex Iacobo Springero, qui in malleo maleficorum part. 2. q. 2. scribit, magos & sagas, quando initiantur sacris daemonis, palam polliceri diabolo pro tribunali sedenti, & coram testibus, se crucem Domini conculcaturos, quia videlicet, ubi crux honoratur, nulla magica artes sint efficaces;
units.tr: It is urged from Jacob Sprenger, who in the Hammer of Witches, part 2, question 2, writes that magicians and witches, when they are initiated into the rites of the demon, openly promise the devil, who sits on the tribunal and in the presence of witnesses, that they will trample underfoot the cross of the Lord, because, namely, where the cross is honoured, no magical arts are effective;

units.la: V
units.tr: V

units.la: Respon. I. non quid ille scribat, sed quid veritas, & Dei verbum praescribat nos amplecti conuenit. II. Magorum & Sagarum nefaria pollicitatio non est idoneum documentum, ex quo de virtute signi crucis iudicari debet, sed potius diaboli malitiam & astum, homines a vero Dei cultu ad Staurolatriam traducentis, inde aestimare debemus. III. Falsum est, vbi crux honoratur, ibi magicas artes non esse efficaces: contrarium verum est, vt docet scriptura. Non est divinatio contra Israelem, nec incantatio contra Iacobum. Crux non honorabatur ab Israelitis, & tamen magicas incantationes nihil quicquam posse significat, aduersum Israelitas, quos Deus sua praesentia protegebat. Eadem gratia fideles Christianos Deus complectitur. Quin & experientia id abunde testificatur, vbi crux honoratur, ibi artes magicas maxime efficaces esse. Unde videmus tot effectus magicos ad signum crucis & alias ceremonias produci, quia crux ab illis honoratur; non quod vi crucis honoratae hi effectus sequantur, sed daemonis ope & astu, qui praescripsit cruces, crucium adorationes, & alias ceremonias, quas vbi adhibent, pent, talia ope dæmonis efficiunt, quæ almiranda & obstupescenda viden-tur. Initat. Ideo superstitiosum esse & prohibitum, citcharactēribus & figuris ad effectus aliquos producendos, vt magis faciunt, quia effectus illi non possunt esse naturales, quia characteres & figuræ non sunt operativa naturaliter: nec proveniunt illi effectus à Deo, cum nulla talis Dei promissio reperitur, nec Deus ab illis invocatur; sed fiunt illa omnia à Dæmone, & characteres solum deserviunt pro signo fœderis inter diabolum & magos. At signum crucis operatur mirabilia nō ex virtute sua naturali, quam habeat, nec ut signum pacti cum Dæmone, sed ut signum divinitus institutum.
units.tr: Reply. First, it is fitting that we embrace not what he writes, but what truth and the Word of God prescribe. Second, the wicked promise of magicians and witches is not a fit proof from which the power of the sign of the cross ought to be judged; rather, we should judge from it the malice and cunning of the devil, who draws men away from the true worship of God to crucifix-worship. Third, it is false that where the cross is honoured, there magical arts are not effective; the contrary is true, as Scripture teaches: There is no divination against Israel, nor enchantment against Jacob. The cross was not honoured by the Israelites, and yet it signifies that magical enchantments could do nothing against the Israelites, whom God protected by his presence. God embraces the faithful Christians with the same grace. Indeed experience abundantly testifies that where the cross is honoured, there magical arts are most effective. Hence we see so many magical effects produced by the sign of the cross and other ceremonies, because the cross is honoured by them; not that these effects follow from the power of the cross honoured, but by the help and cunning of the demon, who prescribed crosses, adorations of crosses, and other ceremonies, which, wherever they are used, they accomplish by the help of the demon, things that seem wonderful and astonishing. The objection: It is therefore superstitious and forbidden to use characters and figures to produce some effects, as magicians do, because those effects cannot be natural, since characters and figures are not naturally operative; nor do those effects come from God, since no such promise of God is found, nor is God invoked by them; but all those things are done by the Devil, and the characters serve only as a sign of the covenant between the devil and the magicians. But the sign of the cross works wonders not by any natural power it has, nor as a sign of a pact with the Devil, but as a sign divinely instituted.

units.la: Respondetur negamus signum crucis diuinitus esse institutum Scriptura, quæ diuinarum institutionum est instrumentum, de cruce diuinitus instituta nihil commemorat, quin ipse Bellarminus agnoscit, signum crucis esse ab hominibus verbo non scripto institutum.
units.tr: The answer: we deny that the sign of the cross was divinely instituted. Scripture, which is the instrument of divine institutions, makes no mention of a cross divinely instituted; indeed Bellarmine himself acknowledges that the sign of the cross was instituted by men through unwritten word.

units.la: Nam Tom. 2. libro 2. controuers. e Missa cap. 15. ait, in Missa varias ceremonias: primam notat esse euationem manuum, eamque probat exapostolo: volentes orare omni loco, levantes puras manus, alteram dicit esse signi crucis, eamq; probat esse antiquissimam: priorem fatetur à Deo in scripturis institutam: alteram ab hominibus verbo Dei non scripto. Alibi dicit, quaedam, etsi ex se non sint necessaria, tamen postquam praecepta sunt, ita esse necessaria, ut si de industria omittantur, graviter peccetur, ut signum crucis in consecratione aquae, Eucharistiae, chrismatis. At quod divinitus institutum est, ex se est necessarium. Quod si ergo ut signum divinitus institutum mirabilia operatur, institutio & promissio divina reperietur eius, quod mirabiles & supernaturales eiusmodi effectus producat. At nullibi vel institutio, vel promissio Dei reperitur. Aut ergo a Deo proveniunt eiusmodi effectus, aut a daemone: non a Deo; alias Dei institutio & promissio horum effectuum reperiretur. Ergo a Daemone.
units.tr: For in volume 2, book 2 of the Controversies, on the Mass, chapter 15, he says that in the Mass there are various ceremonies: he notes the first as the lifting of hands, and proves it from the Apostle: I will that men pray everywhere, lifting up holy hands; the other, he says, is the sign of the cross, and he proves that it is most ancient; he confesses that the former was instituted by God in the Scriptures, the latter by men through the unwritten word of God. Elsewhere he says that certain things, though in themselves they are not necessary, yet once they have been commanded, become so necessary that if they are omitted deliberately, a grave sin is committed, as the sign of the cross in the consecration of water, of the Eucharist, and of chrism. But what has been divinely instituted is in itself necessary. If, then, the sign of the cross works wonders as a divinely instituted sign, a divine institution and promise of that effect, that it produces such wonderful and supernatural effects, would be found. But neither an institution nor a promise of God is found anywhere. Therefore such effects come either from God or from the demon: not from God, otherwise a divine institution and promise of these effects would be found. Therefore from the demon.

units.la: Instat. At tres sunt, inquit Bellarminus, effectus crucis mirabiles. 1. terret & fugat daemones. 2. pellit morbos & omnia mala. 3. Sanctificat ea, quibus imprimitur.
units.tr: It is urged: There are three wonderful effects of the cross, says Bellarmine: 1. it terrifies and puts to flight demons; 2. it drives away diseases and all evils; 3. it sanctifies those on whom it is impressed.

units.la: Respond. Negamus. Neque enim a natura vim habet producendi eiusmodi modi effectus, ut testatur ipse Bellarmius. Neque a Deo, utpote qui nullibi d eiusmodi effectus crucis signum instituit, nec promissionem eius rei tradiit. Fidei, per orationem semet exentis, proprii effectus sunt, non crus. Fides in crucifixum, & oratio seduimpetrat a Christo eiusmodi effeus, ita ut efficacia, & vis, non in signo, d in fide & precibus, quae sola sunt meia a Christo ad tales effectus conseuedos instituta, & horum effectuum promissiones habent. Sic Matth. 17. Christus fidem & orationem ardentem requirit ad daemones expellendos, nulum facienς mentionem signi crucis.
units.tr: Reply: we deny it. For it does not have by nature the power of producing effects of this kind, as Bellarmine himself testifies; nor does it have them from God, who nowhere instituted the sign of the cross for such effects, nor handed down a promise of such a thing. The effects proper to faith, which goes forth in prayer, are not the cross's. Faith in the crucified and prayer obtain such effects from Christ, so that the efficacy and power lie not in the sign but in faith and prayers, which alone have been instituted by Christ for attaining such effects and have the promises of these effects. Thus in Matthew 17 Christ requires faith and fervent prayer for casting out demons, making no mention of the sign of the cross.

units.la: Hinc Petrus, ubi significat Satanam circumire tanquam leonem, fide dicit resistendum, non signo crucis. Quod interdum daemones leguntur conspeto signo crucis eiecti, non est vera eiectio, sed ficta. Impostor fugam tanum simulavit. Vera daemonum eietio est, qua inviti expelluntur, idque cum detrimento ipsius Satanae. Fictaiectio est, qua sponte cedunt, & conspecto signo fingunt se fugere, idque cum suo commodo, & detrimento gloriae riæ Christi ad fouendam & confirman- dam staurolatriam. Sic Iacobus 5. cap. Orate, inquit, alii pro aliis, vt sanentur. Multum enim valet deprecatio iusti efficax. Ene efficaciam non signi, sed orationis Signum est nuda & inanis ceremonia quæ non valet ad sanitatem præstan- dam. Omnis efficacia sanitatis impe- trandæ est orationis, de qua Iacobus ait, multum valere deprecationem iusti efficacem.
units.tr: Hence Peter, when he says that Satan goes about like a roaring lion, bids us resist him by faith, not by the sign of the cross. As for the places where demons are said to have been cast out at the sight of the sign of the cross, that is not a true expulsion but a feigned one. The impostor only pretended to flee. A true expulsion of demons is one in which they are driven out against their will, and that to Satan's own loss. A feigned expulsion is one in which they yield of their own accord and, at the sight of the sign, pretend to flee, and this to their own advantage and to the loss of the glory of Christ, in order to foster and confirm the worship of the cross. So James says in chapter 5: Pray for one another, that you may be healed. For the effective prayer of a righteous man avails much. The sign is not what is effective here but prayer. The sign is a bare and empty ceremony, which does not avail to bring about healing. All the power to obtain health comes from prayer, of which James says that the effective prayer of a righteous man avails much.

units.la: Quod si signo adhibito interdum mor- bi curantur, non vis aliqua est in ligno, sed in Dæmone, cuius ope sæpe morbi curantur.
units.tr: But if, when the sign is applied, diseases are sometimes cured, the power is not in the wood but in the demon, by whose help diseases are often cured.

units.la: Nam vult dæmon, quæcunque po- test, beneficia in homines conferre, vt illud impetret, quod commemoratur Matth. 4. vt procidens adoret eum. Sic 1. ad Timoth. 4. omnis creatura Dei dicitur sanctifi- cari per verbum Dei, & preces. Signi cru- cis non meminit. Quin & ipse Bellar- minus in leuatione manuum nulla col- locat sanctificandi vim, quam tamen ce- remoniam diuinitus institutam fate- tur, multo minus vis sanctificandi est ponenda in ligno crucis quæ est ceremonia humanitus instituta. Leuandæ quidem sunt manus in precibus, sed effi- cacia & impetratio est in oratione iusti [illegible, ~6 letters]iusti Iacob. f. non in ceremonia, Nam expandentibus Iudaeis manus suas, Deus non exaudiebat. Esa. 1. Et nonne stulta atque superstitiosa ratio est sanctificandi creaturas, quae ea, quibus imprimitur signum crucis, ad alios usus, quam diu initus institutos sanctificari volunt? Exempli gratia, candelas agnoscimus concessas esse ad pellendas tenebras, sed dicunt pontifices, se candelas benedicere non solum ad usus naturales, verum ad effectum supernaturalem fugandos daemonas. Formam huius sanctificationis Missale describit in festo purificationis.
units.tr: For the demon wishes to confer whatever benefits he can on men, so that he may obtain what is recorded in Matthew 4: that they should fall down and worship him. Likewise, 1 Timothy 4 says that every creature of God is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. It makes no mention of the sign of the cross. Indeed, even Bellarmine places no power of sanctifying in the lifting up of hands, though he admits that this ceremony was instituted by God; much less, then, should the power of sanctifying be placed in the wood of the cross, which is a ceremony instituted by men. Hands indeed are to be lifted up in prayer, but the efficacy and the obtaining of the request lie in the prayer of the righteous man, as James says, and not in the ceremony. For when the Jews spread out their hands, God would not hear them. Isaiah 1. And is it not a foolish and superstitious reasoning to sanctify creatures, marking them with the sign of the cross, and then to want them used for other purposes than those for which they were first instituted? For example, we acknowledge that candles were given to dispel darkness, but the pontiffs say that they bless candles not only for their natural uses but also to drive away demons by a supernatural effect. The Missal describes the form of this sanctification in the feast of the Purification:

units.la: Benedic. Domine Iesu, hanc Creaturam cerae, ut, qui eam ad repellendas tenebras humano usui tribuisti, talem signaculo crucis tuae fortitudinem benedictionemque accipiat, ut quibuscunque locis accessa fuerit, diabolus discedat.
units.tr: Bless, O Lord Jesus, this creature of wax, so that, as you have appointed it for the dispelling of darkness for human use, it may receive such strength and blessing by the sign of your cross that, in whatever places it is lit, the devil may depart.

units.la: At Petrus non candelas, sed fidem Satanae circumeunti & insidianti nobis, iubet opponere.
units.tr: But Peter bids us oppose to Satan, who goes about and lies in wait for us, not candles but faith.

units.la: Et Paulus ad Ephes. 6. instiuens militem Christianum omni ex parte, nullam facit mentionem candelarum. Valeant huiusmodi impiae ineptiae Christianis indignae.
units.tr: And Paul, in Ephesians 6, instructing the Christian soldier in every respect, makes no mention of candles at all. Let such impious absurdities, unworthy of Christians, be gone.

units.la: Instat Bellarminus, ut probet signo crucis hosce effectus competere. Primum effectum, dicit, ex tribus causis existere, ex apprehensione daemonis, ex devotione hominis, & ex institutione Dei. Prima causa est ex apprehensione daemonis, Nam dum ubi crucem videt, mox recordatur crucifixi Christi victum, spoliatum, ligatum, & enervatum fuisse. Inde crucem timet & fugit, quemadmodum fugit lapidem & baculum quo percussus est.
units.tr: Bellarmine presses the point, in order to prove that these effects belong to the sign of the cross. He says that the first effect arises from three causes: from the demon's apprehension, from the devotion of the man, and from the institution of God. The first cause is the demon's apprehension: For when he sees the cross, he at once remembers that Christ crucified was conquered, despoiled, bound and enfeebled. Hence he fears the cross and flees from it, just as he flees the stone and the stick with which he was struck.

units.la: Respon. I. Bellarmino probandum erat crucis signum habere hanc vim fugandi daemones, antequam ostenderet, unde eam haberet. Nos dicimus signum illud nihil esse aliud, quam externam ceremoniam, cuius nulla vis est & efficacia, ad eiusmodi supernaturalem effectum producendum. II. Si ex apprehensione illa daemonis, qua se cruce Christi victum, & spoliatum ac ligatum fuisse recordatur, effectus ille exstitit, non ia a crucis signo sed a victoria, spoliatione & ligatione, eius per crucem facta, id est, a passione ne & morte Christi provenit. Sed effectus fugae in cane, non est a baculo & lapide, sed a percussione baculi & lapidis a cane ap-prehensa [illegible, ~8 letters]rehensa. III. qua cruce se victum & eneruatum recordatur dæmon, eandem timet: at non ligno vel signo inani se victum & ligatum recordatur, sed morte & passione Christi. Ergo non lignum vt signum inanimum timet, sed passionem & mortem Christi. Fingit quidem interdum callidus impostor, se crucem timere & fugere, sed vere non timet; timorem & fugam simulat, vt superstitionem crucis confirmet, & homines ad eius venerationem eo magis excitet. Neque diffiteor, ipsum vere interdum timuisse signum crucis, ac per illud fugatum esse; sed id non est factum vi signo indita, sed virtute fidei in Christum crucifixum, qua prædicti erant fideles, in fugam conuersus est diabolus. IV. Similitudo canis aduersatur Bellarmino. Vt enim canis lapidem & baculum timet, sed non imaginem eius & signum: Ita etiam diabolus imaginem aut signum crucis non timet, sed veram crucem, id est, passionem & mortem Christi, seu ipsum Christum crucifixum.
units.tr: Answer. I. Bellarmine had to prove that the sign of the cross has this power of driving out demons before he showed where it got it. We say that the sign is nothing other than an external ceremony, which has no power or efficacy to produce such a supernatural effect. II. If that effect arises from the demon's apprehension, by which he remembers that he was conquered, despoiled and bound by the cross of Christ, then it does not come from the sign of the cross but from the victory, despoiling and binding that were accomplished by the cross, that is, it comes from the passion and death of Christ. But the dog's flight is not caused by the stick or the stone, but by the blow of the stick or the stone as the dog has apprehended it. III. The demon fears the cross by which he remembers that he was conquered and enfeebled; but he does not remember that he was conquered and bound by a lifeless wood or an empty sign, but by the death and passion of Christ. Therefore it is not the wood as an inanimate sign that he fears, but the passion and death of Christ. Indeed, the crafty impostor sometimes pretends to fear and flee the cross, but he does not truly fear it; he feigns fear and flight so as to confirm the superstition of the cross and to stir men the more to its veneration. Nor do I deny that he has sometimes truly feared the sign of the cross and been driven off by it; but this was not done by a power put into the sign, but by the power of faith in Christ crucified, which the faithful possessed, and by which the devil was turned to flight. IV. The comparison with the dog works against Bellarmine. For just as the dog fears the stone and the stick, but not their image or sign, so the devil does not fear the image or sign of the cross, but the true cross, that is, the passion and death of Christ, or Christ himself crucified.

units.la: Secundam causam effecti primi dicit esse ex deuotione hominis, eamque sic proponit. Crux habet vim ex opere operantis eo modo, quo vim habet oratio. Nam signum crucis Crucis est invocatio quaedam meritorum Christi crucifixi, signo expressa. Loquimur enim corde, voce & nutibus. Itaque opponere contra diabolum signum crucis, est opponere meritum passionis Christi, id est, invocare Deum per merita Christi, contra diabolum. Unde effectus tunc magis procedit ex fide & fiducia ac devotione interiore, quam ex ipso charactere crucis; sicut quando oramus voce & impetramus, effectus tribuitur potius fidei & fiduciae interna, quam sono vocis. Et de his duobus modis nullum est dubium.
units.tr: For the second cause of the first effect he says is the devotion of the man, and he sets it out thus: The cross has power from the work of the one working, in the same way that prayer has power. For the sign of the cross is a kind of invocation of the merits of Christ crucified, expressed by a sign. For we speak with the heart, the voice and the nods. Therefore to oppose the sign of the cross to the devil is to oppose the merit of Christ's passion, that is, to call on God through the merits of Christ against the devil. Hence the effect then proceeds more from faith, trust and inner devotion than from the very mark of the cross; just as when we pray with the voice and obtain our request, the effect is ascribed rather to inward faith and trust than to the sound of the voice. And there is no doubt about these two ways.

units.la: Resp. I. Negamus crucē habere vim ex opere operantis, eo modo, quo oratio. Oratio enim est actio a Deo praecepta, habens promissionem additam, ut ex 5. c. Iacobi liquido constat, ubi praeceptum & promissio extat. Orate alii pro aliis, ut sanemini. Multum enim valet oratio iusti efficax. Quare omnis vis & efficacia orationis est ex mandato & promissione Dei. At signum crucis est ceremonia humanitus instituta, cuius nullum in verbo Dei mandatum, nulla promissio extat. Nulla igitur ei vis inesse potest ex opere operantis. Siquidem talis vis, quae ex opere operantis dependet, mandato Dei & promissione eius niti debet.
units.tr: Answer. I. We deny that the cross has power from the work of the one working, in the same way that prayer does. For prayer is an action commanded by God, with a promise added, as is clear from the fifth chapter of James, where both the command and the promise stand: Pray for one another, that you may be healed. For the effective prayer of a righteous man avails much. Therefore all the power and efficacy of prayer comes from the command and promise of God. But the sign of the cross is a ceremony instituted by men, for which there is no command and no promise in the Word of God. Therefore no power can belong to it from the work of the one working, since such power as depends on the work of the one working must rest on the command of God and his promise.

units.la: II. Negamus etiā signum crucis esse invocationem tionem quandam meritorū Christi cru-cifixi. Quid ergo? Est ceremonia exter-na ad professionē religionis Christianę olim inter orandū obseruata. Etsi enim signū synecdochicè sæpè pro oratione, signo crucis declarata, apud veteres ac-cipitur: tamen cū inuocatione Christi, tanquā re significata, non est confundē-dum. Inuocatio est diuinitus instituta, habēs promissionē exauditionis & ope-rationis Christi. Signum verò & institu-tione & promissione diuina caret. A diun-ctum quidem est inuocationis voluntā-riū, sed non ipsa inuocatio. Alias inter signū & inuocationē nexus esset necef-sarius, & insep arabilis: at potest esse in-uocatio absq; signo, & contra signū absq; inuocatione, ac tunc quidē, cum sepa-ratim absq; inuocatione vsurpatur, ritus plane inanis & inutilis est.
units.tr: II. We also deny that the sign of the cross is an invocation of the merits of Christ crucified. What then is it? It is an external ceremony, used of old in praying, as a profession of the Christian religion. For although the sign, by synecdoche, is often taken among the ancients for the prayer declared by the sign of the cross, yet it must not be confused with the invocation of Christ as the thing signified. The invocation is divinely instituted and has the promise of Christ's hearing and working. The sign, however, lacks both divine institution and divine promise. It is indeed joined to the invocation by the will, but it is not the invocation itself. Otherwise there would be a necessary and inseparable bond between the sign and the invocation; but there can be invocation without the sign, and the sign without invocation, and when it is used apart from invocation, the rite is plainly empty and useless.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Negamus nos nutib. loqui. Ore & corde loquimur: sed nutibus vtraq; loquela significamus. Quare inuocatio alia est manifesta, alia tacita. Illa fit ore, hæc fit corde. Vtraq; nutu significatur. Nō verò datur inuocatio proprie, quæ fit nutu, sed inuocatio siue oris, siue cordis, nutu seu gestu, qualis est signum crucis, significatur.
units.tr: We deny that we speak by nods. We speak with mouth and heart, but both kinds of speech may be signified by a nod. So invocation is of two kinds, manifest and tacit. The first is made by mouth, the second by heart, and both are signified by a nod. But invocation itself is not properly what is made by a nod. Rather, invocation, whether of mouth or of heart, is signified by a nod or gesture, such as the sign of the cross.

units.la: Talem inuocationem Christi crucifixi nutu, seu ceremonia exprestam opponebant olim contra diabolum, eius que virtute diabolum profligabant. Atq; hinc manifestum est, quid sit opponere signum crucis contra diabolu. Non est formaliter opponere meritum passionis Christi, vt opinatur Bellarminus, vel inuocare Deū per merita Christi aduersus diabolum, sed externo signo fidem in Christum profiteri, adiunctâ inuocatione nominis crucifixi, qua Christi præsentia & operatio cōtra diabolum impetrabatur. Sed num in hoc vsu hodie pōtificii signum crucis cōtra diabolum opponūt? Nudo & soli signo vim spiritualem tribuunt eiiciendi & fugandi dæmones, idq; ex opere operato, qualem vim nec habet, nec exercuit vnquam.
units.tr: Such an invocation of the crucified Christ, expressed by a nod or ceremony, was once set against the devil, and by its power the devil was put to flight. From this it is clear what it means to oppose the sign of the cross to the devil. It is not formally to oppose the merit of Christ's passion, as Bellarmine supposes, nor to invoke God through the merits of Christ against the devil. Rather, it is to profess faith in Christ by an outward sign, with the invocation of the name of the crucified One added, by which the presence and working of Christ against the devil was obtained. But do the Papists today, in this practice, oppose the sign of the cross against the devil? They attribute to the bare sign alone a spiritual power of casting out and driving away demons, and this by the work wrought (ex opere operato), a power which it neither has nor ever exercised.

units.la: IV. Et illud diligenter est notandum, quod dicit, effectum magis ex fide, & fiducia ac deuotione interiori, quā ex charactere crucis procedere. Si ita est, cur tanta contētione eum virtuti signi tribuunt? cur tot miracula soli signo, omissis fide, fiducia ac deuotione interiore, accepta referunt? Vnde effectus magis & potius procedit, ei etiā potius & magis tribuendus est. At ex fide, fiducia, & interiore deuotione magis procedit effectus, quam ex crucis charactere, vt ait Bellar-
units.tr: IV. It must also be carefully noted that he says the effect proceeds from faith, and confidence, and inner devotion more than from the character of the cross. If that is so, why do they contend so stubbornly that it belongs to the power of the sign? Why do they ascribe so many miracles to the sign alone, leaving out faith, confidence and inner devotion? Whatever a cause produces more and more truly, that is the cause to which the effect should rather and more be ascribed. But the effect proceeds more from faith, confidence and inner devotion than from the character of the cross, as Bellar-

units.la: Bellarminus. Ergo fidei potius, fiduciæ, & deuotioni interiori tribuendus est.
units.tr: Bellarmine says. Therefore it is to be ascribed rather to faith, confidence and inner devotion.

units.la: Cur ergo tantopere pugnant pro solius crucis virtute, & operatione, nulla facta mentione potioris causæ? Cur adorant potius mutu crucis characterem? Christus, cuius fide & fiducia effectus impetratur, adorandus erat, non crucis character. V. Fateor, verum esse, quod dicit Bellarminus, cum oramus voce, & impetramus, effectum tunc fidei potius, quam vocis sono tribui. At cum nemo adeo vesanus fuerit, vt sono vocis tribuat effectum, fide & invocatione Christi impetratum, cur ergo characteri crucis effectum tribuunt, qui fidei proprius est, eiusq; virtute acquisitus?
units.tr: Why, then, do they fight so hard for the power and operation of the cross alone, making no mention of the stronger cause? Why do they rather adore the mere character of the cross? Christ, by whose faith and confidence the effect is obtained, was the one to be adored, not the character of the cross. V. I grant that what Bellarmine says is true: when we pray aloud and obtain our request, the effect is to be ascribed to faith rather than to the sound of the voice. But since no one is so mad as to ascribe to the sound of a voice an effect obtained by faith and the invocation of Christ, why then do they ascribe to the character of the cross an effect which belongs to faith and was won by its power?

units.la: Tertiam causam sic proponit Bellarminus. Excitimo etiam tertio modo, id est, ex instituto Dei, & ex opere operato, valere signū crucis contra Diabolum. Nā videmus Iudæos, & paganos sine vlla fide in Christum, solum intendentes facere, quod Christiani faciunt, fugasse daemones signo crucis, vt patet ex Nazianzeno orat. 1. in Iulian. Epiphanio haeresi 30, & Gregorio lib. 3. dialog. c. 7. Ex quo apparet, non deuotione aut fide operantis, sed ipso signo crucis fugatum daemonem.
units.tr: Bellarmine sets out a third cause in this way: We say also, in a third way, that is, by the institution of God and by the work wrought (ex opere operato), the sign of the cross avails against the devil. For we see Jews and pagans, without any faith in Christ, merely intending to do what Christians do, to have put demons to flight by the sign of the cross, as is clear from Nazianzen, Oration 1 against Julian, Epiphanius, heresy 30, and Gregory, Dialogues book 3, chapter 7. From this it appears that the demon was driven off not by the devotion or faith of the one acting, but by the sign of the cross itself.

units.la: Respond. Negatur vtrumq;. Nam I, Si ex instituto Dei valet, tum Christus, vel Apostoli verbo, aut facto illud declá- rassent. At nec verbo vel facto illud de- clararunt. Ergo non valet ex instituto Dei. II. Si ex opere operato valet, iam effectus ex ipso charactere crucis, non ex fide & devotione operantis, vtloqui tur Bellarminus, procedet: quia esse- ctus ex opere operato productus, non procedit ex vi fidei; & opere operantis. At supra posuit contrarium, ex fide & deuotione operantis effectum procedere. Deinde si ex opere operato valet; Ergo ex vi & efficientia signi effectus procedet. Hæc autem vis erit vel natu- ralis, vel supernaturalis. Nō est natura- lis, teste ipso Bellarmino. Si supernatu- ralis, non ex ipsa signi virtute & efficacia, sed à causa superiori & supernaturali proueniet. Et cum effectus sit super- naturalis, etiam causa talis sit, necesse est. III. Probatio ab exemplis Iudæorū & paganorū, quos solo signo crucis fugasse dæmones iactat, nulla est. Vel enim Deus extra ordinem ad probra & ludibria eorum aduersus Christum crucifixum, eiusq; cultores cōtundenda, & Christianę religionis veritatem confirmandam, dæmones fugare dignatus est: vel ficta fuit fugatio, qua dæmones sin[illegible, ~3 letters]unt se fugere, vt homines facerent externo signo crucis magis confidere, quā ipso Christo crucifixo. IV. Exemplū ex Nazianzen. de Iuliano, nō confirmat Bellarmini propositū. Nam & illa Satanæ ꝑ pfligatio, non à signi, sed Dei virtute profluxit. Cum n.
