Apostata Iulianus hostis esset Christianorum, & Christum Christiq; crucē, in qua Christiani gloriabantur, contumeliis & probris afficeret, ita vt Christū contumeliosè vocitaret crucifixum & suspensum; Deus extra ordinē Apostatæ perfidia contundere & frägere voluit, Christumq; crucifixum, & Christiana religione à probris & contumeliis vindicare, quam palam præstabat, dum Christus, qui nō viuere, sed crucifixus ac mortuus putabatur, in signū vitæ & potentiæ suæ ad signū crucis vitam eius singulari beneficio cōtra dæmones defēdebat. Verum quid si fuga illa dæmonū fuerit figmentū, & simulatio. Cū multi dæmones in eum conuenirēt locū, vbi Iulian⁹ sacra nefanda celebrabat, is dæmonū conuentu territ⁹, & sui oblitus cruce semet signauit, ꝑ ut solebat, cū esset Christianus. Ecce diffugiunt repetè oēs illi cacodæmones. Nū ea vis fuit operis operati, vt tā repetè fugerint cacodæmones? Apostoli hanc figni vim ignorarunt; alias vt effent si-gno crucis ad dæmones ex opere ope-rato eiiciendos & fugandos. Fugamen-go simulatunt, vt Christianorum fidem à Christo abduceret, & ad cultum signi externi traduceret, vbi tantam vim cru-cis inesse viderent signo crucis, vt etiā hostes Christi ex opere operato tam mirabilia perficerent. Exemplum ex-piphanio adductū, est deformina Chri-stiana, ideoq; impertinens. Exemplum illius Iudæi, quod recitat Gregorius, et fabulosum. Nam 1. commemorat Iudæum noctu ingressum esse templum ido-li. At Iudæi non solent ingredi templa idolorum, vtpote à quibus abhorrent. Deinde commemorat principem dæmo-niorum diabolo cuidam iussisse, vt il-lum Iudæum accederet & exploraret, quis nam esset; hunc deinde, postquam cum esset contemplatus, rediisse & di-xisse, vas inueni vacuum, sed signa-tum. Unde vero Iudæus ille potuit co-gnoscere, quid diabolus ille princeps Dæmoniorum renunciarit? Num ale aut dæmone quodam habuit? Multæ-ciusmodi Gregorius Magnus in primis in librum 3. dialogorum congessit, quæ & fabulosa, & à Christiana etiam reli-gione.
units.tr: I answer: both are denied. For, first, if it avails by the institution of God, then Christ or the Apostles would have declared it by word or deed. But they declared it neither by word nor by deed. Therefore it does not avail by the institution of God. Second, if it avails by the work wrought, then the effect will proceed from the character of the cross itself, not from the faith and devotion of the one acting, as Bellarmine puts it. For an effect produced by the work wrought does not proceed from the power of faith and of the work of the one working. Yet above he laid down the contrary, that the effect proceeds from the faith and devotion of the one acting. Further, if it avails by the work wrought, then the effect will proceed from the power and efficacy of the sign. This power will be either natural or supernatural. It is not natural, as Bellarmine himself testifies. If it is supernatural, it will not come from the virtue and efficacy of the sign itself, but from a superior and supernatural cause. And since the effect is supernatural, its cause must of necessity also be such. III. The proof from the examples of Jews and pagans, whom he boasts of having put demons to flight by the sign of the cross alone, is worthless. For either God, beyond the ordinary course, deigned to put demons to flight, to crush the mockeries and insults of these men against the crucified Christ and his worshippers, and to confirm the truth of the Christian religion; or the flight was feigned, the demons pretending to flee so that men would trust more in the outward sign of the cross than in Christ crucified himself. IV. The example from Nazianzen about Julian does not confirm Bellarmine's proposition. For that putting of Satan to flight also flowed not from the power of the sign but from the power of God. For when the apostate Julian was an enemy of the Christians, and heaped insults and reproaches on Christ and on the cross in which Christians gloried, calling Christ contemptuously "the crucified and hanged one," God beyond the ordinary course willed to crush and break the apostate's treachery, and to vindicate the crucified Christ and the Christian religion from reproaches and insults. This he openly showed, while Christ, who was thought not to live but to be crucified and dead, as a sign of his life and power, by a singular kindness defended that life of the sign of the cross against demons. But what if that flight of the demons was a fiction and a pretence? When many demons had gathered in the place where Julian was performing his unholy rites, he, terrified by the gathering of the demons and forgetting himself, made the sign of the cross on himself, as he was accustomed to do, since he was a Christian. Behold, all those evil demons fled again at once. Was there such power of the work wrought that the evil demons fled so repeatedly? The Apostles were ignorant of this power of the sign; otherwise they would have used the sign of the cross to cast out and drive off demons by the work wrought. Rather, the demons pretended to flee, so that they might lead the faith of the Christians away from Christ and turn it to the worship of an outward sign, where they would see such great power in the sign of the cross that even enemies of Christ could perform such marvels by the work wrought. The example adduced from Epiphanius is from a heretical sect and therefore irrelevant. The example of that Jew which Gregory recites is also fabulous. For, first, he relates that a Jew entered at night the temple of an idol. But Jews do not usually enter temples of idols, from which they shrink. Next, he relates that the prince of the demons ordered a certain demon to approach that Jew and find out who he was; then, after the demon had looked him over, he returned and said, "I found a vessel empty but sealed." But whence could that Jew have known what that demon, prince of the demons, had reported? Did he have an angel or some demon? Gregory the Great, above all in book 3 of the Dialogues, has gathered many such things, which are both fabulous and foreign even to the Christian religion.

units.la: . [illegible, ~20 letters]rione aliena sunt. II. detur verum esse exemplum, num propterea signi virtus am efficax fuit, ut ex opere operato diabolum profligarit? Finxit daemon esse fugere conspecto signo crucis, ut sig-ni venerationem simplicium animis instillaret. III. detur etiam veram, non mutatam fuisse Diaboli fugationem, tamen cum effectus is sit particularis, & extraordinarius, vim operis operati no-robat, nempe quae necessaria est & ordinaria, ut & effectus, ex opere operato procedens, necessarius & ordinarius.
units.tr: ...religion. Grant that the example is true: does it follow that the virtue of the sign was so efficacious as to drive the devil off by the work wrought? The demon feigned fleeing at the sight of the sign of the cross, so as to instill reverence for the sign into the minds of simple people. III. Grant also that the flight of the devil was true and not altered; yet since that effect is particular and extraordinary, it does not prove the power of the work wrought, which is necessary and ordinary, just as an effect proceeding from the work wrought is necessary and ordinary.

units.la: Instat. Augustinus libro 83. quaestionum quaestione 179. dicit, indictum a Deo daemonibus, ut cedant cruci, tanquam sceptro summi regis, quomodo populi militibus cedunt, cum bis illis profertur signum Imperatoris: Nec mirum est, inquit, quod haec signa valent, cum bonis Christianis adhibentur, quando etiam usurpantur ab extraneis, qui omnino summam nomen ad istam militiam non dederunt, propter honorem tamen excellentissimi Imperatoris valent. Cum autem non cedunt hus signis huiusmodi potestates, Deus ipse prohibet occultus modis, cum id iustum atque utile iudicat. Nam nullo modo ulli spiritus audent haec signa contemnere. Contremiscunt haec vbicunque illa perspexerint.
units.tr: Objection. Augustine, in book 83 of Questions, question 179, says that it was decreed by God that the demons should yield to the cross, as to the sceptre of the highest king, just as the people yield to soldiers when the sign of the Emperor is brought forward to them. Nor is it strange, he says, that these signs avail, since they are used by good Christians, and also are used by outsiders, who have not at all given their name to that warfare, yet by honour of the most excellent Emperor they avail. But when these powers do not yield to such signs, God himself forbids them by hidden means, when he judges it just and useful. For in no way do any spirits dare to despise these signs. They tremble whenever they have seen them.

units.la: X
units.tr: X

units.la: Resp.I. Si à Deo indictum est dæmo-nibus, vt cedant cruci. Non ergo operis operati, sed Dei virtute cedunt. II. Au-gustinus hoc in loco nullâ signo crucis vim tribuit, quâ ex opere operato exe-rat, sed signorum à Deo institutorum & in legitimo vsu vsurpatorum propriam comendat efficaciam. Nullam .n. facit mentionem signi crucis. Signa quidem nominat generatim, sed signa à Deo in-stituta intelligit, qualia sunt verbū Dei, oratio fidei, impositio manuum & similia, non verò speciatim signum crucis, vtpote cuius neq; in præcedentib. neq; sequentib. vllâ fecerat mentionem. III. dicit valere signa illa propter honorem excellentissimi Imperat. Non ergo valet propter opus operatum, q; ipsum erat probandum. IV. dicit, cum nō cedunt his signis potestates, Deum ipsum id prohi-bere occultis modis. Non ergo signū va-let ex opere operato, sed ex Dei mandā-tis arbitrio & gloria. V. Si valet signum ex opere operato contra potestates dæ-monū, sequetur plura esse Sacramenta quâ 7. Docent.n. sacramenta ad gratiâ Dei ex opere operato cōferendâ esse in-stituta. Si igitur signū crucis valet ad gra-tiâ cōtra dæmones cōferendâ ex opere operato, erit sacramentum, ac proinde pluribus erunt quam septem sacramenta. Excipit Bellarminus. Signum crucis non est proprie dictum sacramentum, tum quia non confert gratiam iustificantem, tum quia non habet effectum infallibilem, ut Augustinus dicit, & experientia etiam testatur.
units.tr: Reply. I. If it was decreed by God that demons should yield to the cross, then they yield not by the work done but by the power of God. II. Augustine in this place attributes no power to the sign of the cross as acting by the work done. He commends the proper efficacy of the signs instituted by God and used in their lawful use. He makes no mention of the sign of the cross at all. He names signs in general, but he means the signs instituted by God, such as the word of God, the prayer of faith, the laying on of hands, and the like, and not specifically the sign of the cross, which he had not mentioned in the preceding or following text. III. He says that those signs are valid because of the honour of the most excellent Emperor. Therefore they are not valid because of the work done, which was the very point to be proved. IV. He says that when the powers do not yield to these signs, God himself prohibits it by hidden means. Therefore the sign is valid not by the work done but by the judgement and glory of God's commands. V. If the sign is valid by the work done against the powers of demons, it will follow that there are more sacraments than seven. For the sacraments are taught to have been instituted for conferring the grace of God by the work done. If therefore the sign of the cross is valid to confer grace against demons by the work done, it will be a sacrament, and so there will be more than seven sacraments. Bellarmine excepts: the sign of the cross is not properly called a sacrament, both because it does not confer justifying grace and because it does not have an infallible effect, as Augustine says and experience also testifies.

units.la: Resp. 1. Hæc non sunt idoneæ & veræ causæ constituentes sacramentum. Ad verum sacramentum requiritur. 1. Autor sacramentorum Deus, cuius solius est, signa voluntatis suæ dare. At Deus non instituit signum crucis, ut esset nouæ Ecclesiæ sacramentum. Deinde requritur verbum, i.e. mandatum & promissio gratiæ. At hoc signum non constat mandato nec promissione gratiæ. 11. neque hic est vsus & finis sacramentorum, ut gratia iustificandi cōferat. Nullum sacramentum cōfert gratiam iustificantē. Sequeretur n. vim iustificantem impressam vel alligatam esse symbolis, & sic in vtentes ex opere operato transfire, qui de sacramentis statuunt, naturā illorum ignorat. Neq; hæc sacramenta vim iustificandi sibi insitam habent, sicut pharmaca vim medendi, sed Christum eiusq; beneficia legitimè vtentibus significant & obsignant. Opus S. sancti proprium non est adscribendum sacramentis. Conferre gratiam iustiiustificantem est opus Spiritus sancti proprium. III. Si effectus qui dependet ex opere operato non est infallibilis, efficacia operis operati fallax erit ac dubia. At illa ex Bellarmini hypothesi, certa est & indubia. Nam paulo post do cet, effectu de fugandis morbis ideo nō sequi infallibiter, quia nō ex opere operato, sed operantis procedit. Vult ergo effectum, ex opere operato productum, necessarium esse & indubium. Deinde si ex Dei institutione vim habet effectum ex opere operato producendi, infallibilem habeat effectum necesse est. Nam quia institutio infallibilis est, ideo vim, ad effectum infallibilem producendum, largitur. At testatur ipse Bellarminus, signum crucis habere, ex Dei institutione, vim producendi effectum ex opere operato. Ergo infallibilem effectum vt habeat, necesse est. En quomodo semet iugulent suis gladiis veritatis hostes.
units.tr: Reply 1. These are not suitable and true causes constituting a sacrament. A true sacrament requires: 1. An author of sacraments, who is God, whose alone it is to give signs of his will. But God did not institute the sign of the cross to be a sacrament of the new Church. Next, the word is required, that is, a command and a promise of grace. But this sign rests on neither a command nor a promise of grace. 11. Nor is this the use and end of the sacraments, that they confer justifying grace. No sacrament confers justifying grace. For it would follow that justifying power is impressed upon or bound to the symbols, and so passes over by the work done into those who use them. Those who lay down doctrine about the sacraments are ignorant of their nature. Nor do these sacraments have a power of justifying implanted in them, as medicines have a power of healing; rather they signify and seal Christ and his benefits to those who use them lawfully. The proper work of the Holy Spirit is not to be ascribed to the sacraments. To confer justifying grace is the proper work of the Holy Spirit. III. If the effect which depends on the work done is not infallible, the efficacy of the work done will be deceptive and doubtful. But by Bellarmine's hypothesis that efficacy is certain and indubitable. For a little later he teaches that the effect of driving off diseases does not follow infallibly, because it proceeds not from the work done but from the worker. He therefore wants the effect produced by the work done to be necessary and undoubted. Furthermore, if by God's institution it has the power of producing an effect by the work done, it must of necessity have an infallible effect. For since the institution is infallible, it grants the power to produce the effect infallibly. But Bellarmine himself testifies that the sign of the cross, by God's institution, has the power of producing an effect by the work done. Therefore it must have an infallible effect. See how the enemies of the truth cut their own throats with their own swords.

units.la: Secundus effectus crucis. Quod ad morbos, inquit, & catera mala, quae non possunt percipere vim signorum, dicimus ea fugari per crucem, tanquam per signum fidei & fiducia, vel potius tanquam per invocationem signo expressam. Christus enim promisit fidelibus se daturum, quicquid peterent cum fide, & nominatim Marci vltim. de morbis dixerat: Serpentes tollent, super aegros manus imponent, & bene habebunt, & si mortiferum quid biberint, non eis nocebit. Fideles igitur contra morbos & reliqua mala implorant Dei auxilium per Christi meritum, idq; faciunt ore, corde, & mutibus: Et quia tunc effectus producitur, non ex opere operato more Sacramentorum, sed ex opere operantis, ideo non infallibiliter sequitur effectus.
units.tr: As to diseases and other evils which cannot perceive the power of signs, we say that they are put to flight by the cross, as by a sign of faith and trust, or rather as by an invocation expressed in the sign. For Christ promised the faithful that he would give whatever they asked with faith, and in the last chapter of Mark, speaking of diseases, he said: They shall take up serpents, they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover, and if they drink any deadly thing it shall not hurt them. The faithful therefore implore the help of God against diseases and other evils through the merit of Christ, and they do so with mouth, heart and nods. And because the effect is then produced not by the work done, after the manner of the sacraments, but by the work of the worker, the effect therefore does not follow infallibly.

units.la: Respon. I. Haec cum supra dictis non consueniunt. Si morbi, & alia mala fugantur per crucem tanquam per signum fidei & fiducie, cur supra Dixit ab Eugenio Episcopo solo crucis signo caecum illuminatum esse? Quomodo ex Athanasio, Gregorio, & aliis tot miracula ad Solum crucis signum a Deo edita Dicit? Quod si pagani & Judei, sine ulla fide in Christum, fugarunt daemones per signum crucis idq; ex opere operato, quare nunc per crucem, ut per signum fidei, fugari morbos Dicit. Si ad fugandos diabolos valet signum crucis absq; fide, etiam ad fugandos morbos, aliaq; mala absq; fide valebit, aut maior crucis efficacia erit adversus daemonas, quam adversus morbos & cetera mala. Sed cum
units.tr: Reply. I. These things do not agree with what was said above. If diseases and other evils are put to flight by the cross as by a sign of faith and trust, why did you say above that a blind man was given sight by Bishop Eugenius by the sign of the cross alone? How, according to Athanasius, Gregory and others, do you say that so many miracles were wrought by God by the sign of the cross alone? But if pagans and Jews, without any faith in Christ, put demons to flight by the sign of the cross, and that by the work done, why do you now say that diseases are put to flight through the cross as through a sign of faith? If the sign of the cross is valid for driving out devils without faith, it will also be valid for driving out diseases and other evils without faith; or else the efficacy of the cross will be greater against demons than against diseases and other evils. But since

units.la: Notes in the left margin are largely illegible and are not transcribed. cuiu Dæmon hostis atrocior sit & potentior morbis & cæteris malis, nonne remedium validius opponendum erit dæmoni, quam morbis? Quare si fides aut invocatio fidelis, signo expressa valet ad pellendos morbos, aliaq; mala, multo magis valebit ad pellendos dæmones. Valeat igitur signū crucis absq; fide. Inanis & plane superstitiosa est ceremonia. II. Si per crucem vt signū fidei ac fiduciæ morbi pelluntur, effectus ille magis pendebit ex fide & fiducia, quā ex charactere crucis, atq; ita signū crucis non erit causa curati morbi, vt contendit Bellarminus, sed tantū (si libet) σωτήρως quodda; vera causa erit fides & fidelis invocatio. Vnde autē effectus primo & potiori ratione dependet ac procedit, illi etiam iure adscribi debet. At ex fide (seu fiducia invocatis tanquā vera causa primò & potiori ratione depēdet. Ergo fidei, non signo crucis adscribi debet. III. docet Bellarminus, signū crucis, mirabilē hunc effectum operari, vt pellat morbos aliaq; mala. Erit igitur causa pellēdi morbos. At si per eam tanquā per signū pelluntur morbi, nō poterit esse causa pellendorū morborum. Signum si præter vim significandi etiā vim habet causandi, natura signi amittit, ita vt desinat esse signû & causæ suscipiat vsum & officium. IV. Signa nihil iuntaliud quam characteres & figuræ. Characteres autem & figuræ non operantur naturaliter, teste Bellarmino: neq; etiā supernaturaliter, cum huius operationis nulla habeant institutione & promissionem. Vnde ergo signû seu character crucis hoc sortitur priuilegiû, vt morbos pelleret? At Christus promisit, se daturum fidelibus quicquid peterēt cū fide, &c. Resp. Sed non promisit, se fugaturū morbos & alia mala per crucem. Preces fidelium efficaces sunt ex Dei promissione: si- gnum crucis vero nulla habet promis- sionem, eoq; caret efficacia. II. Pugnat secum Bellarminus. Si ex promissione Dei effectus ille ad signû fidei sequitur, qua fronte dicit, effectum nō infallibi- liter sequi? Quod Deus promisit, id se- quitur infallibiliter. At promisit, se per signû fidei fugaturum morbos. Ergo ef- sectus ille infallibiliter sequetur. Deni- que nec illud causam iuuat aduersarii; q/p dicit, fideles auxilium Dei implorare, idq; ore, corde & nutibus. Quid inde? num propterea sacrum erit & venera- bile signum crucis, & virtutem fugan- di morbos habebit? pari iure, & ora, corda & quilibet alii nutus sacri erunt & venerabiles, virtutemque obtinent pellendi morbos. Si enim nutus, id est, signo crucis, quo fideles auxilium Dei contra morbos implorant, vis ad pellendos morbos inerit, etiam ora, corda sibi facultatem hanc potioni iure arrogabunt, vtpote quibus auxilium Dei verius & expressius contra morbos imploratur. Nobis persuasum est, fide, & fidelem invocationem, quam Christus acceptat, haec omnia sibi in solidum vendicare.
units.tr: Notes in the left margin are largely illegible and are not transcribed. whose demon is a fiercer enemy and more powerful than diseases and other evils, shall not a stronger remedy have to be set against the demon than against diseases? Therefore, if faith, or the faithful invocation expressed in the sign, is valid for driving out diseases and other evils, much more will it be valid for driving out demons. Let the sign of the cross then be valid without faith; it is an empty and plainly superstitious ceremony. II. If diseases are driven out through the cross as a sign of faith and trust, that effect will depend more on faith and trust than on the character of the cross. So the sign of the cross will not be the cause of the cured disease, as Bellarmine contends, but only (if you like) a kind of instrument, and the true cause will be faith and the faithful invocation. But whatever an effect depends upon and proceeds from in the first and chief degree, to that it ought rightly to be ascribed. But the effect depends and proceeds first and chiefly from faith, or from the trust invoked, as the true cause. Therefore it ought to be ascribed to faith, not to the sign of the cross. III. Bellarmine teaches that the sign of the cross works this wonderful effect of driving out diseases and other evils. It will therefore be the cause of driving out diseases. But if diseases are driven out by it as through a sign, it cannot be the cause of driving out diseases. If a sign, besides the power of signifying, also has the power of causing, it loses the nature of a sign, so that it ceases to be a sign and takes on the use and office of a cause. IV. Signs are nothing other than characters and figures. Characters and figures do not work naturally, as Bellarmine witnesses, nor supernaturally either, since they have no institution or promise for this operation. Whence then does the sign or character of the cross obtain this privilege of driving out diseases? But Christ promised that he would give the faithful whatever they asked with faith, etc. Reply: But he did not promise that he would drive out diseases and other evils through the cross. The prayers of the faithful are efficacious by God's promise; but the sign of the cross has no promise, and so lacks efficacy. II. Bellarmine contradicts himself. If that effect follows through the sign of faith from God's promise, how can he say that the effect does not follow infallibly? What God has promised follows infallibly. But he promised that he would drive out diseases through the sign of faith. Therefore that effect will follow infallibly. Finally, that does not help the adversary's cause, that he says the faithful implore God's help, and do so with mouth, heart and nods. What follows from that? Will the sign of the cross therefore be holy and venerable, and have the power of driving out diseases? By the same right, mouths, hearts and any other nods will be holy and venerable, and will obtain the power of driving out diseases. For if power to drive out diseases resides in the nods, that is, in the sign of the cross by which the faithful implore God's help against diseases, then mouths and hearts will with equal right claim this faculty for themselves, since God's help is implored against diseases more truly and more expressly by them. We are persuaded that faith and the faithful invocation, which Christ accepts, claim all these things wholly for themselves.

units.la: Tertius effectus. Quantum ad benedictiones attinet, idem fere dicendum. Nam cum benedicimus homines, domos, agros, & similia, illo signo commendamus Deo per Christi merita res illas, quas benedicimus: & similiter cum benedicimus aquam, oleum, candelas, &c. commendamus res eas Deo, & precamur, ut velit illas nobis esse salutares, utque per eas tanquam instrumenta nos adiuvet.
units.tr: The third effect. As far as blessings are concerned, the same can be said almost word for word. For when we bless men, houses, fields, and similar things, with that sign we commend to God, through the merits of Christ, the things we bless. And likewise when we bless water, oil, candles, etc., we commend those things to God and pray that he will be willing to make them salutary for us, and that he will help us through them as instruments.

units.la: Respond. Benedictionum pontificiarum forma, modus, & finis esta Christiana religione alienus. Nam I. Non tantum Deo res & personas commendant, sed coelestem etiam virtutem iis infundi volunt, ad effectus supernaturales producendos, id quod expresse significant in benedictione candelarum. Rogant enim Deū, vt benedicat creaturæ ceræ supplicantibus ipsis: deinde adiungunt, vt benedictionem cælestem infundat ei per sanctam crucem: tertio loco postulant, vt cera talem signaculo crucis sanctæ fortitudinem & benedictionem accipiat, vt quibuscunq; locis acensa fuerit & apposita, discedat diabolus. Formam igitur benedictionis non ponunt in precibus, quibus personæ & res Deo commendantur, sed in cælestis & super naturalis virtutis infusione.
units.tr: Answer. The form, method, and purpose of the Papists' blessings are foreign to the Christian religion. For, first, they not only commend persons and things to God, but also want heavenly power to be poured into them to produce supernatural effects. They express this clearly in the blessing of candles. For they ask God to bless the wax creature at their request; then they add that he would pour heavenly blessing into it through the holy cross; third, they ask that the wax may receive such strength and blessing through the sign of the holy cross that, wherever it is lit and placed, the devil may depart. Therefore they do not place the form of the blessing in prayers by which persons and things are commended to God, but in the infusion of a heavenly and supernatural power.

units.la: II. Modus benedictionum scripturæ ignotus est.
units.tr: II. The method of blessings is unknown to Scripture.

units.la: Tradit enim scriptura, verbo Dei, & oratione, creaturas sanctifica ri. Pontificii autem signo crucis sancti-ficādi officiū, præter & contrascriptura assignant, ita vt interdū illud cū oratione coniūgat, interdū illud solū sine oratione adhibeant, prout faciunt imprimis illi, qui orare nescinut.
units.tr: For Scripture teaches that creatures are sanctified by the word of God and by prayer. But the Papists assign to the sign of the cross the office of sanctifying, apart from and contrary to Scripture, so that sometimes they join it with prayer, and sometimes they use it alone without prayer, as especially those do who do not know how to pray.

units.la: III. Finis benedictionum impius est.
units.tr: III. The purpose of the blessings is impious.

units.la: Cum enim in benedictionib. suis precatur, vt Deus velit res illas esse salutares, & per res illas tanquam per instrumenta nos iuuet, hoc significant, vt ad super naturales effectus producendos valeant. Impium vero est creaturas ad alios vsus sanctificare, quâ diuinitus institu-tos. Panem, aquâ, vinum aliaq; sanctifi-camus ad eum vsum, quem Deus sibi dinauit, panem ad corroborandum, vi-num ad exhilarandum cornostrum, a-quam ad purgandum immunda. Aquâ strè, panem & vinum sacramento Ba-ptismi & Cœnæ sanctificamus exprè-cepto Christi ad vsum mysticum, ad re-missionem & ablutionem peccatorum. Sic & reliqua ad eos vsus consecra-mus ad quos Dominus ea instituit. Si quis vero res illas ad alios vsus ab homi-nibus excogitatos, nec diuinitus insti-tutos consecrauerit, næ is manifesto tenetur impietatis crimine. Huncauté finem & vsum seu potius abusum esse benedictionum pontificiarum supra do-cui ex Missali in festo purificationis, in quo candelæ, quæ datæ sunt ad pellen-das tenebras, benedictione consecran-tur ad effectum supernaturalé, ad fugā-dos dæmonas. Doceo idé ex ipso Bellar. Recte inquit, ad effectus supernaturales efficiendos & significandos, vtimur aquâ, oleo, aliisq; rebus benedictione consacra-tis. Effectus supernaturales commemorat trium generum, deletionem venialium peccatorum, fugationé dæmonum & mor-borum curatione. Hinc igitur sic concludo. Qui creaturas ad effectus supernaturales ad quos a Deo non sunt instituta, per benedictionem consecrant, impii sunt in De. At Pontifex hoc faciunt, ut patet. Ergo Impii sunt in Deo. Instat. At quod explicite petimus precibus, idem implicite petimus per signum crucis.
units.tr: For when in their blessings they pray that God would be willing for those things to be salutary and would help us through them as through instruments, they signify by this that they may be able to produce supernatural effects. Indeed it is impious to sanctify creatures for other uses than those divinely instituted. We sanctify bread, water, wine, and other things for the use that God has appointed for them: bread to strengthen, wine to gladden our hearts, water to cleanse what is unclean. Certainly by the express command of Christ we sanctify water, bread, and wine for the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, for the mystical use, for the forgiveness and washing away of sins. So too we consecrate the rest for those uses for which the Lord instituted them. But if anyone consecrates those things to other uses devised by men, and not divinely instituted, he is manifestly held guilty of the crime of impiety. I have shown above from the Missal, in the feast of the Purification, that this is the purpose and use, or rather the abuse, of Papist blessings: the candles, which were given to dispel darkness, are consecrated by a blessing to produce a supernatural effect, namely to drive away demons. I show the same from Bellarmine himself. He rightly says: "We use water, oil, and other things consecrated by blessing to produce and signify supernatural effects." He lists three kinds of supernatural effects: the removal of venial sins, the driving away of demons, and the healing of diseases. Hence I conclude thus: Those who consecrate creatures by blessing to supernatural effects for which they were not instituted by God are impious towards God. But the Papists do this, as is plain. Therefore they are impious towards God. Objection: But what we ask explicitly in prayers, we ask implicitly through the sign of the cross.

units.la: Resp. I. non dantur preces implicitae, quae fiunt per signum crucis. Implicitae preces eae solae sunt, quae concipiuntur corde, sicut explicite dicuntur quae ore & lingua fiunt. Signum crucis nihil aliud fuit quam ceremonia precibus adjuncta, ad fidem Christi crucifixi testificandam usurpata. Verae preces nituntur mandato & promissione Dei. At preces illae implicitae per signum crucis, ut vocat Bellarminus, nullo nituntur Dei mandato ac promissione. Quare non sunt verae preces. Coniunctae fuere verae preces cum signo crucis, sed non per signum crucis conceptae aut, sicut cum elevatione manuum preces coniunguntur, sed per elevationem manuum non fiunt aut concipiuntur preces, quae tamen ceremonia divinitus est instituta, cum signum crucis ceremonia sit mere humana.
units.tr: Answer, first: there are no implicit prayers made by the sign of the cross. Implicit prayers are only those conceived in the heart, just as explicit prayers are those made with the mouth and tongue. The sign of the cross was nothing other than a ceremony added to prayers, used to bear witness to faith in Christ crucified. True prayers rest on the command and promise of God. But those implicit prayers "through the sign of the cross," as Bellarmine calls them, rest on no command or promise of God. Therefore they are not true prayers. True prayers were joined with the sign of the cross, but they were not conceived through the sign of the cross; and just as prayers are joined with the lifting of hands, yet prayers are not made or conceived by the lifting of hands, so the sign of the cross is a merely human ceremony, whereas the lifting of hands was divinely instituted.

units.la: Instat.Nō potest nec debet negari, quin etiā aliqua accedat sanctitas rebus, cū significantur cru ce, non quidē sanctitas quæ sit aliqua qualitas physica, sed sanctitas in relatione consistens, qualis est crucis, clavorum, vestium, aliarū rerum, quæ tetigerūt Christum aut sanctos: & qualis est eorū, qui tangunt reliquias sanctorū.
units.tr: Objection. It cannot and must not be denied that some holiness also attaches to things when they are marked with the cross: not indeed a holiness which is some physical quality, but a holiness consisting in relation, such as belongs to the cross, the nails, garments, and other things which touched Christ or the saints, and such as belongs to those who touch the relics of the saints.

units.la: Resp. Falsa sunt omnia. Nā 1. Si ex cru cis signo sanctitas aliqua rebus accedit, quibus imprimitur, ipsi signo sanctitas quædam supernaturalis inerit ex institutione & promissione Dei, at nulla huius rei institutio aut promissio reperitur. II. nulla signa à Deo instituta sūt organa conferendæ sanctitatis. Ergo multo minus signū crucis, q; est ceremonia humanitus instituta. III. scriptura docet, sanctificationē rerū fieri per verbū & orationē. Signū crucis, neq; verbū est, neq; oratio, neq; pars verbi vel orationis. IV. Fictitia est illa sanctitas in relatione cōsistens. Relatiua illa sanctitas in Dei institutione & promissione cōstare debet. At hæc iis caret est q; hominū superstitiosorū imaginatione introducta. V. detur esse veram & à Deo institutam relationem, quid inde lucrabitur Bellarmin? Cū.n. per relationē res non mutetur, aut noua qualitate imbuantur, neq; per relatiua sancti[illegible, ~12 letters]inctitatem res ad supernaturales esse-ctus efficiendos idoneæ reddi poterunt I. Falsum est, crucem, vestes, claues, & quamlibet miles res contactu Christi esse sanctifi-catas. Sic enim & labia Iudæ & manus veneficum contactu corporis Christi sanctificatæ essent. Cōtactus rei sanctæ non sanctificat, sed verbū Dei, & fidelis ratio. Si contactus corporis & sancto-rum sanctificaret, hunc vsum & hoc habere t, vel naturaliter vel supernaturaliter. Non habet naturaliter: quia effectus sanctificationis est su-pernaturalis, ideoque à causa naturali nequit prouenire. Si supernaturali-ter, à causa supernaturali nempe à Dei institutione accepit. At nulla eius institutio in verbo Dei reperitur. Quod si alicuius Ecclesiæ institutio reperiatur, Ecclesia non habet potestatem efficiendi vt res aliqua aut rei contactus supernaturale effectu sanctificandi pro-ducat. Deniq; & illud falsum est, quod de reliquiis subiicit. Vnde probat reliquias contactu suo homines sanctificare? Ieq; Christus neq; patres reliquiarum contactum ita vllibi commendant vt dicant, eos qui reliquias tangunt, vel simpliciter vel aliquo modo sanctificari.
units.tr: Answer: all these claims are false. For, first, if some holiness accrues to things from the sign of the cross with which they are stamped, then some supernatural holiness would be in the sign itself by the institution and promise of God; but no institution or promise of this thing is found. Second, no signs instituted by God are instruments for conferring holiness; therefore much less the sign of the cross, which is a ceremony instituted by human authority. Third, Scripture teaches that the sanctification of things takes place through the word and prayer. The sign of the cross is neither word, nor prayer, nor part of the word or prayer. Fourth, that holiness consisting in relation is fictitious. Relational holiness must rest on the institution and promise of God; but this lacks these, and was introduced by the imagination of superstitious men. Fifth, even if there were a true relation instituted by God, what would Bellarmine gain from it? For since a thing is not changed by a relation, nor imbued with a new quality, things cannot be made fit to produce supernatural effects by a relational holiness. First, it is false that the cross, garments, nails, and any other things are sanctified by contact with Christ. For thus the lips of Judas and the hands of poisoners would also have been sanctified by contact with the body of Christ. Contact with a holy thing does not sanctify; the word of God and a faithful mind do. If contact with the body and the saints sanctified, one would have this use and this property either naturally or supernaturally. He does not have it naturally, because the effect of sanctification is supernatural and therefore cannot come from a natural cause. If supernaturally, he received it from a supernatural cause, namely from God's institution. But no such institution is found in the word of God. And if an institution of some Church is found, the Church does not have the power of making any thing or contact with a thing produce a supernatural sanctifying effect. Finally, what he adds about relics is also false. From where does he prove that relics sanctify men by their contact? Neither Christ nor the Fathers anywhere commend the contact of relics in such a way as to say that those who touch relics are sanctified, either simply or in any way.

units.la: Instat
units.tr: Objection

units.la: Instat. At Basilius in ps. 115. Gregorius Nyssenus in vita S. Theodori, S. Chrysostomus in homine de Sanctis Iuvetio & Maximo, & alii cent aliquo modo sanctificari eos, qui reliquias tangunt. Si autem contactus reliquiarum sanctificat, cur non & contactus vexilli salutaris? Certe Augustinus libro 2. de pecc. merit. & remiss. c. 26. id affirmit. Catechumenos, inquit, quendam modum sui per signum Christi & orationem manus impositionis puto sanctificari: & quod accipiunt, quamvis non sit corpus Christi, sanctum est tamen.
units.tr: Objection: But Basil, in Psalm 115; Gregory of Nyssa, in the Life of St Theodore; and St Chrysostom, in his homily on the saints Juventius and Maximus, and many others, say that those who touch relics are in some way sanctified. If the touch of relics sanctifies, why not the touch of the saving banner (the cross)? Certainly Augustine, in book 2 of On Sins, Merits and Forgiveness, chapter 26, affirms this. "I think," he says, "that catechumens are sanctified in a certain manner by the sign of Christ and by prayer and the laying on of hands; and what they receive, although it is not the body of Christ, is nevertheless holy."

units.la: Resp. I. Expectaveram locum, quo Christus reliquias ad visum sanctificandi instituerit, aut virtute eiusmodi illis conserit, sed frustra. II. Si aliquo modo sanctificantur ii qui tangunt reliquias, debuisset modum illum & gradum exprimere. Est ergo modus ille fictitius. Si aliquo modo tantum sanctificantur reliquiae, ergo & reliquiae aliquo modo tantum sanctae erunt, & aliquo modo erunt ad randas. Quis vero hunc modum determinavit? non Deus. Ergo Diabolus. III. Basilius in ps. hac de re nihil habet. Nyssenus non ex sua sententia loquitur, sed superstitiosorum opinione recitat, q. sanctorum reliquias tangebant. Chrysostomus nodo cet, & probat, sed rhetoricatur. Ex rhetorica ationibus patrū, de eorū assertionibus on est concludendū. II. Non suā sentē iam sed vulgi errore, qui tunc inualue- at, recitat, non approbat. III. Nullā mē one facit sanctificationis, quam impri- nant reliquiæ tangentibus illas. Verba ius sic sonat. Idcirco sæpe eos inuisamus, tu- ules adornemus, magnaq; fide reliquias eorū tingamus, vt inde benedictionē consequamur.
units.tr: Reply. I. I expected some passage where Christ instituted relics for the purpose of sanctifying by sight, or bestowed such a power on them, but in vain. II. If those who touch relics are sanctified in some way, the objector ought to have stated that way and its degree. That way, then, is a fiction. If relics are holy only in some way, then they will also be holy only in some way, and they will be to be venerated in some way. But who determined this way? Not God. Therefore the devil. III. Basil says nothing on this matter in the psalm. Gregory of Nyssa does not speak from his own opinion but recounts the opinion of superstitious people, who touched the relics of the saints. Chrysostom wanders off, and argues, but in rhetorical fashion. Nothing should be concluded about the assertions of the Fathers from their rhetorical arguments. II. He recounts not his own opinion but the error of the crowd, which then prevailed; he does not approve it. III. He makes no mention of the sanctification which relics impart to those who touch them. His words sound like this: "Therefore we often visit them, adorn their tombs, and with great faith touch their relics, so that we may thereby obtain a blessing."

units.la: Loquitur igitur de quadā benedictione qua ex pietatis studio accipiant: neq; si- gnificat, contactu reliquiarū, per se, & ua vi, conferre benedictionē, sed Deū studio & amori ergo sanctos etiā demor- tuos benedicere. Augustin. deniq; nō solī signo sanctificationis vim & effectū ad- scribit, sed fidele innocatione, atq; im- positione manuū coniungit. Oratio ita que quæ temporibus istis hac ceremonia excitabatur, à Christo impetrauit bene- ficiū sanctificationis. Et ne quid signo videretur tribuere quod signi non est, ideo addit incundū quēdā modū ē signi- ficare volēs, nōipsum ritum seu signum per se solum, sed quatenus invocatio- nem nominis Christi adiunctam habe- at, sanctificationem impetrare.
units.tr: He therefore speaks of a certain blessing which people receive from zeal for piety; nor does he mean that the touch of relics confers a blessing by itself and by its own power, but that God, for the sake of our zeal and love, blesses even the saints who have died. Augustine, finally, does not ascribe power and effect only to the sign of sanctification, but joins to it faithful invocation and the laying on of hands. Therefore the prayer which was offered with this ceremony in those times obtained from Christ the benefit of sanctification. And lest it seem that he attributed to the sign something that is not a sign, he adds "a certain manner," meaning that the rite or sign by itself alone does not obtain sanctification, but only insofar as it has the invocation of Christ's name joined to it.

units.la: Sic quidem argumenta illa, quæ à no- stris contra crucis adoratione vsurpata putat Bell:ab eius sophisticis elusionib: vindicari:aliis praeterea argumentis vt mur quæ longè potetius Stauro1atriâ Antichrist:elidút; sed illa ne attingit quidè Bell.quia nulla ex parte captiolis elusionib.sentiebat esse obnoxia. Nō igitur operæ prætium duxi,vt iis propo nendis & confirmandis immorater : saltem duos argumentorum veluti arietes ex superiori tractatione conclusionis loco Staurolatris oppono. PRIMVM, omnis Staurolatria est detestanda idololatria. At adoratio crucis religiosa est Staurolatria: quia adoratio religiosa est actus proprius latriæ. Ergo adoratio crucis religiosa est detestanda idololatria. SECVNDVM. Nullum idolū est religiosè adorandum, sed potius fugiendum. At crux cui Christus affixus, & effigies eius, cruces lignea & lapideæ apud Papistas, sūt idola. Ergo non sunt religiosè adorandæ. Minor probatur. Quicquid præter Deum honore soli Deo debito colitur, idolum est: At crux cui Christus est affixus, & effigies eius honore soli, Deo debito à Papistis coluntur, vt supra ostendimus. Ergo sunt idola. Hi validissimi sunt arietes, quorum robore Staurolatria penitus concussa & prostrata iacet.
units.tr: Thus indeed Bellarmine thinks that those arguments which our people have used against the adoration of the cross are rescued by his sophistical evasions; but he does not even touch upon other arguments, of which there are many, which far more powerfully overthrow the Antichristian Staurolatry. He does not touch them because he thought that they were in no way open to captious evasions. I have therefore not thought it worth the effort to dwell on setting out and confirming these; at least, from the earlier treatment, I set against the Staurolatrists, in place of a conclusion, two arguments like battering rams. FIRST: every Staurolatry is detestable idolatry. But the religious adoration of the cross is Staurolatry, because religious adoration is the proper act of latria. Therefore the religious adoration of the cross is detestable idolatry. SECOND: no idol is to be religiously adored, but rather to be shunned. But the cross to which Christ was fixed, and his image, and wooden and stone crosses among the Papists, are idols. Therefore they are not to be religiously adored. The minor premise is proved thus: whatever is worshipped, apart from God, with the honour due to God alone, is an idol. But the cross to which Christ was fixed, and his image, are worshipped by the Papists with the honour due to God alone, as we showed above. Therefore they are idols. These are the most powerful battering rams, by whose strength Staurolatry lies utterly shaken and prostrate.
